    Blood Vessels

    16 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Hypertensive Vascular Disease

    B1

    What is hypertension? Important causes and complications of hypertension.

    Hypertension is a sustained elevation of systemic arterial pressure, defined in Robbins as a diastolic pressure of 90 mm Hg or more or a systolic pressure of 130 mm Hg or more. In about 90–95% of patients the cause is unknown (essential hypertension), and in the remaining 5–10% it is secondary to renal, adrenal or other identifiable disease. Its major complications are ischaemic heart disease and heart failure, stroke, aortic dissection and renal failure.

    Blood pressure is a continuously distributed variable, and the harmful effects of pressure rise progressively with no sharp threshold. Both systolic and diastolic levels carry risk. Individuals with systolic pressures below 120 mm Hg and diastolic pressures below 80 mm Hg are normotensive, and the range of 120–130 mm Hg systolic is borderline. Lower thresholds apply when other risk factors such as diabetes coexist.

    Between one-third and one-half of adults in the general population are hypertensive by these criteria, and prevalence and vulnerability to complications rise with age. Because blood pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by peripheral vascular resistance, sustained hypertension reflects an increase in blood volume (mostly through renal sodium retention), an increase in arteriolar resistance, or both.

    Causes

    • Essential (primary) hypertension (90–95%). This is a multifactorial disorder arising from the cumulative effects of many genetic polymorphisms interacting with environmental factors. Family history, twin studies and genome-wide studies (more than 500 variants) support a genetic contribution. Heavy salt intake, obesity, smoking, physical inactivity and stress are the main environmental contributors. A common final pathway is inadequate renal sodium excretion, which expands volume, raises cardiac output and causes peripheral vasoconstriction, so that pressure is "reset" at a higher level to restore sodium balance (resetting of pressure natriuresis). Vasoconstrictive stimuli and structural thickening of the arteriolar wall add to the rise in resistance.
    • Secondary hypertension (5–10%).
    • Renal: renal artery stenosis (renovascular hypertension, in which reduced afferent arteriolar pressure activates renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone), glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, polycystic kidney disease and other parenchymal renal disease.
    • Endocrine: primary aldosteronism (frequently an aldosterone-secreting adenoma), Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, acromegaly, thyroid disorders, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia or licorice ingestion.
    • Cardiovascular: coarctation of the aorta and polyarteritis nodosa.
    • Neurologic: raised intracranial pressure.
    • Pregnancy-induced: preeclampsia.
    • Drugs and hormones: oral contraceptives, glucocorticoids, sympathomimetics, tyramine-containing foods with MAO inhibitors.
    • Monogenic disorders: Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC mutations) and defects of aldosterone metabolism (e.g., aldosterone synthase, 11β-hydroxylase and 17α-hydroxylase defects).

    Special clinical form. In up to 5% of hypertensive patients the pressure rises rapidly (systolic above 180 mm Hg and diastolic above 120 mm Hg), producing malignant hypertension with renal failure, retinal haemorrhages and exudates, with or without papilloedema. Untreated, it is fatal within 1–2 years. It is often superimposed on pre-existing "benign" hypertension.

    Complications

    1. Vascular: Hypertension accelerates atherosclerosis and damages the walls of large and medium arteries. This leads to aortic dissection and to cerebrovascular haemorrhage. In small vessels it produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis (homogeneous pink thickening from plasma protein leakage and increased smooth muscle matrix synthesis, narrowing the lumen) and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ("onion-skin" laminated thickening in severe disease, with fibrinoid deposits and necrosis in malignant hypertension), as well as necrotising arteriolitis, particularly in the kidney.
    2. Heart: Pressure overload causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (hypertensive heart disease), which can lead to diastolic dysfunction, left atrial dilation with atrial fibrillation, demand ischaemia, congestive heart failure and sudden death. Hypertension also increases the risk of ischaemic heart disease by about 60%.
    3. Brain: Cerebral infarcts and intracerebral haemorrhage (stroke), and multi-infarct dementia.
    4. Kidney: Arteriolar nephrosclerosis with glomerular scarring, progressing to renal failure.
    5. Eye: Hypertensive retinopathy.

    Hypertension is usually asymptomatic until late in its course. Left untreated, roughly half of patients die of ischaemic heart disease or heart failure and about one-third of stroke, and effective antihypertensive treatment dramatically lowers these outcomes.

    Arteriosclerosis

    Arteriosclerosis: definition and types

    Define arteriosclerosis.

    DU07Ja

    Arteriosclerosis, literally "hardening of the arteries," is a generic term for thickening of the arterial wall with loss of elasticity. It comprises several distinct patterns of arterial disease that differ in the size of the vessel affected and in the pathologic process. The most important of these is atherosclerosis, an intimal lesion of large and medium-sized arteries characterised by plaque formation, so that the two terms are not synonymous. Arteriosclerosis is the broader category, and atherosclerosis is one variety within it.

    What are the types of arteriosclerosis?

    DU07Ja

    Robbins recognises four general patterns of arteriosclerosis, each with different clinical and pathologic consequences.

    TypeVessels affectedEssential features
    ArteriolosclerosisSmall arteries and arteriolesTwo anatomic variants associated with hypertension and diabetes. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis shows homogeneous pink thickening from plasma protein leakage and increased matrix synthesis, with luminal narrowing. Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis shows concentric, laminated "onion-skin" smooth muscle and reduplicated basement membrane thickening, and in malignant hypertension fibrinoid necrosis. It causes ischaemic injury, most prominently in the kidney.
    Mönckeberg medial sclerosisMedium-sized muscular arteriesCalcification of the media, beginning along the internal elastic lamina, usually in people over 50 and often with renal insufficiency and secondary hypercalcaemia. The calcification does not encroach on the lumen and is usually clinically insignificant.
    Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasiaMuscular arteries larger than arteriolesA healing response to inflammation (healed arteritis, transplant arteriopathy) or to mechanical injury (stents, angioplasty). It can produce marked stenosis and underlies in-stent restenosis and graft loss in transplanted organs.
    AtherosclerosisElastic and large to medium muscular arteriesIntimal atheromatous plaques composed of a lipid core and fibrous cap. It is the most frequent and clinically important form.

    Define atherosclerosis (short note).

    5DU26MDU25MDU22MDU18MDU06Ja

    Definition. Atherosclerosis (Greek athere, "gruel," and sclerosis, "hardening") is a chronic, progressive intimal disease of elastic arteries and large and medium-sized muscular arteries, characterised by the formation of atheromatous plaques. An atheroma is a raised intimal lesion with a soft, grumous core of lipid (mainly cholesterol and cholesterol esters) covered by a fibrous cap. It is the underlying cause of coronary, cerebral and peripheral vascular disease and accounts for roughly half of all deaths in Western countries. Myocardial infarction alone causes almost a quarter of deaths in the United States.

    Risk factors. Constitutional risk factors are family history (the most important independent factor), age and male sex. Modifiable major factors are hyperlipidaemia (particularly raised LDL cholesterol), hypertension, cigarette smoking and diabetes mellitus. Additional factors include inflammation (raised C-reactive protein), hyperhomocysteinaemia, metabolic syndrome, raised lipoprotein(a), and haemostatic factors such as raised PAI-1. These factors act multiplicatively rather than additively.

    Pathogenesis. The accepted "response to injury" hypothesis views atherosclerosis as a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury. Endothelial dysfunction, caused above all by disturbed (nonlaminar) flow, hypercholesterolaemia and inflammation, increases permeability and leukocyte adhesion. LDL accumulates in the intima and is oxidised, monocytes adhere and enter the intima and become foam cells after engulfing modified lipid through scavenger receptors, and platelets adhere.

    Macrophages, platelets and endothelial cells release growth factors and cytokines that recruit smooth muscle cells (SMCs) from the media. These proliferate and synthesise extracellular matrix, forming the fibrous cap, while T lymphocytes add to the inflammation. Cholesterol crystals activate the inflammasome, which generates IL-1 and perpetuates inflammation.

    Morphology. The lesion begins as the fatty streak (flat yellow macules of foamy macrophages) and progresses to the atheromatous plaque, which has a fibrous cap overlying a necrotic lipid core with cholesterol clefts, foam cells and calcification, with neovascularisation at the periphery. Plaques are eccentric and patchy.

    Complications. The main complications are plaque rupture or erosion with thrombosis, intraplaque haemorrhage, atheroembolism, and aneurysm formation. Slow luminal stenosis causes chronic ischaemia. The clinical consequences are myocardial infarction, stroke, aortic aneurysm and gangrene of the legs.

    Arteriosclerosis vs atherosclerosis
    Complications

    B1

    Difference between arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis. Complications of atherosclerosis.

    Arteriosclerosis is the general term for hardening and thickening of arterial walls with loss of elasticity, and it includes arteriolosclerosis, Mönckeberg medial sclerosis, fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is one specific type, an intimal plaque disease of large and medium arteries made of a lipid core and fibrous cap. Its main complications are plaque rupture with thrombosis and infarction, aneurysm formation, atheroembolism, intraplaque haemorrhage and chronic ischaemia from stenosis.

    FeatureArteriosclerosisAtherosclerosis
    ScopeGeneric term for arterial thickening and stiffeningA specific form of arteriosclerosis
    VesselsArterioles, small arteries, muscular and elastic arteriesElastic arteries and large and medium muscular arteries (aorta, coronary, carotid, iliac, popliteal)
    Layer involvedVariable: intima (fibromuscular hyperplasia), media (Mönckeberg), arteriolar wall (hyaline, hyperplastic)Intima, with secondary damage to the media
    LesionHyaline or onion-skin thickening, medial calcification, or neointimal thickeningAtheroma: fibrous cap, lipid-rich necrotic core, foam cells, calcification
    Lipids and inflammationNot centralCentral to pathogenesis
    AssociationsHypertension, diabetes, age, renal failure, vascular injuryHyperlipidaemia, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, family history, age
    Clinical importanceMostly arteriolar ischaemia (especially renal)
    Mönckeberg is usually silent    		Myocardial infarction, stroke, aneurysm, peripheral gangrene

    Complications of atherosclerosis

    1. Stenosis with chronic ischaemia. Slow luminal narrowing (critical stenosis at about 70–75% loss of cross-sectional area in the coronaries) causes stable angina, chronic ischaemic heart disease, intermittent claudication, mesenteric ischaemia and ischaemic encephalopathy. Collateral flow can compensate when stenosis develops slowly.
    2. Acute plaque change. Rupture or fissuring, erosion or ulceration, and haemorrhage into the plaque expose thrombogenic material. The resulting thrombosis, often completely occlusive, causes acute myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction or sudden cardiac death. Thin-capped, inflamed, lipid-rich "vulnerable" plaques are most prone to rupture, often when stenosis was previously only mild to moderate.
    3. Intraplaque haemorrhage, which expands the plaque and may precipitate rupture.
    4. Atheroembolism of cholesterol-rich debris, which causes microinfarcts distally (for example in the kidneys and legs).
    5. Aneurysm formation (especially abdominal aortic aneurysm) from pressure and ischaemic atrophy of the media with loss of elastic tissue, with the risk of rupture.

    Atherosclerosis: pathogenesis

    B1

    Define atherosclerosis. Tell me the pathogenesis of the development of an atherosclerotic plaque.

    Atherosclerosis is a chronic intimal disease of large and medium-sized arteries in which atheromatous plaques, each with a lipid core and fibrous cap, narrow the lumen and predispose to thrombosis. According to the response-to-injury hypothesis, it begins with endothelial dysfunction, followed by lipid accumulation and oxidation in the intima, monocyte recruitment and foam cell formation, platelet adhesion, smooth muscle cell migration and proliferation, and matrix synthesis, all driven by chronic inflammation.

    Pathogenesis. The contemporary view holds that atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury, driven by modified lipoproteins, macrophages and T lymphocytes interacting with endothelial cells and SMCs. The sequence is as follows.

    1. Endothelial injury and dysfunction. Early lesions begin at sites of morphologically intact endothelium that show increased permeability, leukocyte adhesion and altered gene expression. The three most important causes are haemodynamic disturbances, hypercholesterolaemia and inflammation (toxins from cigarette smoke and hypertriglyceridaemia also contribute). Plaques localise at vessel ostia, branch points and the posterior abdominal aorta because nonlaminar flow turns off atheroprotective genes such as KLF2, whereas laminar flow keeps them on.
    2. Lipoprotein accumulation and oxidation. With chronic hyperlipidaemia, LDL accumulates in the intima and is aggregated and oxidised by free radicals from inflammatory cells. Hyperlipidaemia also impairs endothelial function directly by increasing reactive oxygen species and accelerating the decay of nitric oxide.
    3. Monocyte adhesion and foam cell formation. Monocytes adhere to the activated endothelium, migrate into the intima and become macrophages. These engulf modified LDL through scavenger receptors, which cannot be downregulated, and become lipid-laden foam cells (SMCs can become foam cells by a similar route). Uptake of modified lipid releases growth factors, cytokines and chemokines that sustain a vicious cycle of monocyte recruitment. The early lesion is the fatty streak.
    4. Inflammation. Cholesterol crystals and free fatty acids in macrophages activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, producing IL-1, which activates endothelium and recruits more macrophages and T cells. Activated T cells release interferon-γ, which further activates macrophages, endothelium and SMCs.
    5. Platelet adhesion at sites of injury, with release of PDGF and other factors.
    6. Smooth muscle proliferation and matrix synthesis. SMCs migrate from the media (or arise from circulating precursors), proliferate under the influence of PDGF, FGF and TGF, and synthesise collagen, elastin and proteoglycans. This converts the fatty streak into a mature atheroma with a fibrous cap. Lipid accumulates both within cells and extracellularly, and late calcification follows.

    Infection with herpesvirus, cytomegalovirus or Chlamydophila pneumoniae has been linked to atherosclerosis only circumstantially, and a causal role is not established.

    What are the risk factors of atherosclerosis?

    7DU25MDU22MDU18MDU17MDU08JuDU07JuDU05Ja

    The risk factors, identified largely from prospective studies such as the Framingham Heart Study, act with greater-than-additive effects and are grouped as follows (Table 11.3).

    A. Constitutional (non-modifiable) risk factors

    • Genetics: Family history is the most important independent risk factor. Mendelian disorders such as familial hypercholesterolaemia are strongly associated but account for only a small proportion of cases. The usual predisposition is polygenic.
    • Age: Atherosclerosis is a progressive disease that becomes clinically manifest in middle age or later. Between ages 40 and 60 the incidence of myocardial infarction increases fivefold. Age-related clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) with pro-inflammatory monocytes adds to the risk.
    • Sex: Premenopausal women are relatively protected compared with age-matched men. After menopause the incidence rises, eventually exceeding that in men, but oestrogen replacement has not been shown to be protective and in some cases has increased risk.

    B. Modifiable major risk factors

    • Hyperlipidaemia (especially hypercholesterolaemia): It can initiate lesions even in the absence of other risk factors. Raised LDL is the main atherogenic component, and HDL, which mobilises cholesterol from plaques to the liver, is protective. Raised lipoprotein(a) is an additional risk.
    • Hypertension: It increases the risk of ischaemic heart disease by about 60% and is the commonest cause of left ventricular hypertrophy.
    • Cigarette smoking: Prolonged smoking doubles the death rate from ischaemic heart disease.
    • Diabetes mellitus: It induces hypercholesterolaemia, doubles the incidence of myocardial infarction and increases the risk of lower-limb gangrene about 100-fold.

    C. Additional (emerging or less certain) risk factors

    • Inflammation, measured by C-reactive protein (a strong independent marker of risk).
    • Hyperhomocysteinaemia.
    • Metabolic syndrome (central obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, hypercoagulability).
    • Raised lipoprotein(a).
    • Haemostatic factors, such as raised plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and platelet-derived factors.
    • Physical inactivity, a competitive stressful lifestyle (type A personality) and obesity.

    Up to 20% of cardiovascular events occur without any of the major risk factors.

    Write in short the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.

    DU25MDU22M

    Atherogenesis is explained by the response-to-injury hypothesis, which regards the disease as a chronic inflammatory and reparative response of the arterial intima to endothelial injury. The principal steps follow in sequence.

    1. Endothelial injury or dysfunction, caused mainly by disturbed haemodynamics, hypercholesterolaemia and inflammation, increases permeability, leukocyte adhesion and thrombogenicity.
    2. LDL accumulates in the intima, where it is oxidised.
    3. Monocytes adhere to the endothelium, migrate into the intima and become macrophages and, after ingesting modified lipid through scavenger receptors, foam cells. SMCs can also become foam cells. Early lesions of foam cells are fatty streaks.
    4. Platelets adhere to injured endothelium.
    5. Macrophages, platelets and endothelium release PDGF, FGF, TGF, cytokines and chemokines, which attract SMCs from the media and also T cells.
    6. SMCs proliferate and synthesise collagen, elastin and proteoglycans, producing the fibrous cap, while lipid accumulates in cells and extracellularly and forms the necrotic core.
    7. Cholesterol crystals activate the inflammasome and IL-1 production, maintaining chronic inflammation
      Late in the process, calcification occurs.

    The result is a mature atheroma, which may then progress to stenosis or to acute plaque rupture, thrombosis and infarction.

    Atheroma: composition and sites

    B1

    Composition of an atheroma. Common sites of atheroma formation.

    An atheroma has four components: cells (smooth muscle cells, macrophages and T lymphocytes), extracellular matrix (collagen, elastic fibres, proteoglycans), intracellular and extracellular lipid, and calcification in late plaques. It typically has a superficial fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core. The commonest sites are the lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries, then the coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, internal carotid arteries and the circle of Willis.

    Composition. A typical atheroma consists of:

    • A fibrous cap at the luminal surface, made of SMCs and dense collagen, whose thickness and collagen content determine stability.
    • A cellular shoulder region beneath and lateral to the cap, containing macrophages, T lymphocytes and SMCs.
    • A necrotic core deep to the cap, containing lipid (mainly cholesterol and cholesterol esters, often crystalline and seen as empty clefts after processing), debris of dead cells, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages and SMCs), fibrin, organised thrombus in varying degrees and plasma proteins.
    • Neovascularisation at the periphery, and calcification in advanced lesions.

    Some plaques ("fibrous plaques") consist almost entirely of SMCs and fibrous tissue and may be heavily calcified.

    Sites. In descending order of severity: the lower abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries, the coronary arteries, the popliteal arteries, the internal carotid arteries and the vessels of the circle of Willis. Upper limb vessels are usually spared, as are mesenteric and renal arteries except at their ostia. Plaques favour the ostia of exiting vessels and branch points, where flow is turbulent.

    Draw and label a typical atheroma / give the morphology of an atheromatous plaque.

    DU26MDU23NDU17Nov

    Labelled diagram (cross-section of a muscular artery with an eccentric plaque):

    LUMEN (narrowed, eccentric) ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ENDOTHELIUM (may be eroded / ulcerated) │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ FIBROUS CAP │ │ <- SMCs + dense collagen │ │ (thin cap = vulnerable plaque) │ │ │ ├──────────────┬──────────────────────┤ │ │ │ SHOULDER: │ NECROTIC (ATHEROMATOUS)│ │ │ │ macrophages, │ CORE: cholesterol │ │ │ │ T cells, SMCs│ clefts, foam cells, │ │ │ │ │ debris, calcification │ │ │ └──────────────┴──────────────────────┘ │ │ Neovascularisation at plaque base │ └───────────────────────────────────────────┘ INTERNAL ELASTIC LAMINA (fragmented) MEDIA (thinned, SMC loss beneath plaque) EXTERNAL ELASTIC LAMINA ADVENTITIA (vasa vasorum) Plaque-free segment of wall (shows lesion is eccentric)

    Morphology

    Fatty streak. This earliest lesion consists of lipid-filled foamy macrophages. It begins as small flat yellow macules that coalesce into streaks 1 cm or longer, slightly raised and without flow disturbance. Fatty streaks are present in the aortas of infants and in virtually all adolescents, and coronary fatty streaks form at the same sites that later develop plaques.

    Atheromatous plaque, gross. Plaques are yellow-tan, raised lesions that may coalesce. Superimposed thrombus over an ulcerated plaque is red-brown. Lesions are patchy and rarely circumferential, so that on cross-section they are eccentric. Lesions at various stages coexist in one vessel.

    Microscopy. There are four components: cells (SMCs, macrophages, T cells), extracellular matrix (collagen, elastic fibres, proteoglycans), intracellular and extracellular lipid, and calcification in late stages. The superficial fibrous cap overlies the cellular shoulder and the necrotic core. Cholesterol crystals leave needle-shaped clefts, and neovascularisation appears at the periphery. The underlying media is thinned, with attenuation of the elastic laminae and loss of SMCs from pressure and ischaemia. Plaques enlarge through cell death, matrix remodeling, organisation of thrombus and calcification.

    Secondary changes. Rupture, ulceration or erosion with thrombosis, haemorrhage into the plaque, atheroembolism, and aneurysm formation.

    Name the blood vessels most frequently involved by atherosclerosis, with clinical consequences (common sites).

    DU23NDU18M

    Atherosclerosis affects the large elastic arteries (aorta, carotid and iliac arteries) and the large and medium-sized muscular arteries (coronary and popliteal arteries). In descending order of extent of involvement, the vessels are as follows.

    VesselPrincipal clinical consequences
    Lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteriesAbdominal aortic aneurysm with risk of rupture, thrombosis and embolism
    Occlusion causing claudication of the legs
    Coronary arteriesAngina pectoris, myocardial infarction, chronic ischaemic heart disease with heart failure, sudden cardiac death
    Popliteal and other leg arteriesIntermittent claudication, rest pain, ischaemic ulcers and gangrene of the lower limb (especially in diabetics)
    Internal carotid arteriesCerebral infarction (stroke), transient ischaemic attacks, from stenosis, thrombosis or embolism
    Circle of Willis (cerebral arteries)Ischaemic encephalopathy, infarction, multi-infarct dementia
    Renal and mesenteric arteries (mainly at the ostia)Renovascular hypertension and renal ischaemia
    Mesenteric occlusion with bowel ischaemia

    Upper-extremity vessels are usually relatively spared. Symptomatic disease most often involves the arteries supplying the heart, brain, kidneys and lower extremities, and the major consequences are myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, aortic aneurysm and peripheral vascular disease with gangrene.

    What are the complications of atherosclerosis / atheromatous plaque?

    5DU23NDU17MDU07JuDU06SDU05Ja

    The complications arise either from progressive luminal narrowing or from abrupt change in the plaque.

    1. Atherosclerotic stenosis (chronic ischaemia). Outward remodeling of the vessel (Glagov phenomenon) initially preserves the lumen. Eventually the expanding plaque produces critical stenosis, at about 70–75% loss of cross-sectional area. Consequences include stable angina, chronic ischaemic heart disease, intermittent claudication, mesenteric ischaemia with bowel infarction, and ischaemic encephalopathy. Slowly developing stenosis allows collateral circulation to compensate.

    2. Acute plaque change

    • Rupture or fissuring exposes highly thrombogenic plaque contents and activates coagulation, often producing a completely occlusive thrombus. This causes myocardial infarction, stroke, sudden cardiac death or acute limb ischaemia.
    • Erosion or ulceration exposes the thrombogenic subendothelial basement membrane, less often with occlusive thrombosis.
    • Haemorrhage into the plaque from rupture of the cap or of thin-walled neovascular channels expands the plaque and may precipitate rupture.

    Plaques with thin caps, large lipid cores and many inflammatory cells (vulnerable plaques) are most likely to rupture. Triggers include hypertensive surges, adrenergic stimulation (explaining the morning peak of infarction), vasospasm and emotional stress. Many culprit plaques were previously only mildly to moderately stenotic and asymptomatic.

    3. Atheroembolism. Cholesterol-rich plaque debris, or fragments of mural thrombus, embolise and obstruct small distal vessels.

    4. Aneurysm formation. Pressure atrophy and ischaemia of the underlying media, with loss of elastic tissue, weaken the wall. This leads to aneurysm (typically abdominal aortic), which may rupture, thrombose or embolise.

    Organisation of subclinical thrombi on disrupted plaques is also an important mechanism of lesion growth, and calcification can occur in late lesions.

    Atherosclerosis: diet

    A6

    How does dietary habit influence the development of atherosclerosis?

    A6

    Diet influences atherosclerosis mainly through its effect on blood lipids and on associated conditions such as obesity, hypertension and diabetes. A diet that raises LDL cholesterol (rich in cholesterol, saturated fat and trans fats) promotes atherosclerosis, whereas omega-3 fatty acids from fish are protective. Excess salt aggravates hypertension, and excess calories cause obesity, insulin resistance and diabetes.

    Cholesterol and LDL. Hypercholesterolaemia is sufficient on its own to initiate lesions, and the dominant lipids in plaques are cholesterol and cholesterol esters. Epidemiologic data show a strong correlation between the severity of atherosclerosis and plasma total and LDL cholesterol, and lowering cholesterol by diet or drugs slows progression, causes regression of some plaques and reduces cardiovascular events. In Robbins' account the contribution of most dietary fats is now regarded as minor, but diets that raise LDL (high in saturated animal fat and cholesterol) remain adverse in practice.

    Specific components

    • Trans-unsaturated fats (from artificial hydrogenation of oils, in baked goods and margarine) adversely alter the cholesterol profile.
    • Omega-3 fatty acids (abundant in fish oils) are beneficial.
    • Exclusive raising of HDL has not proved effective.

    Indirect effects. Heavy salt intake is strongly linked to hypertension, itself a major risk factor. Overnutrition produces obesity and the metabolic syndrome (central obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, hypercoagulability and a proinflammatory state) and type 2 diabetes. Diabetes induces hypercholesterolaemia and markedly increases atherosclerosis. Westernisation of diet explains the rising rates of coronary disease in lower-resource countries. Dietary and pharmacologic cholesterol lowering (statins, which also reduce plaque inflammation) is therefore a cornerstone of prevention.

    Vasculitis

    B1

    Define vasculitis. Types of vasculitis.

    Vasculitis is inflammation of the vessel wall. It may be infectious, from direct microbial invasion, or noninfectious and immune-mediated. Noninfectious forms are classified by the caliber of the vessel mainly involved: large-vessel (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis), medium-vessel (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease, thromboangiitis obliterans) and small-vessel vasculitis, which is either immune complex–mediated or ANCA-associated.

    Vasculitis can be systemic or confined to a single organ, and its manifestations include constitutional symptoms (fever, myalgia, arthralgia, malaise) together with organ-specific features that depend on the vessels involved. The two basic mechanisms are direct invasion of vessels by infectious agents (e.g., Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, Mucor), and noninfectious immune-mediated injury through immune complex deposition, ANCA, anti-endothelial cell antibodies, anti-GBM antibodies or autoreactive T cells. Distinguishing the two is essential, since immunosuppression helps immune forms but harms infectious ones.

    Tumors of Blood Vessels

    B1

    Classify vascular tumors.

    Vascular tumours are classified as benign tumours and tumour-like conditions (haemangiomas, lymphangiomas, glomus tumour, vascular ectasias and reactive proliferations such as bacillary angiomatosis), intermediate-grade or borderline tumours (Kaposi sarcoma, haemangioendothelioma), and malignant tumours, chiefly angiosarcoma.

    CategoryTypes
    Benign tumours and tumour-like conditionsHaemangiomas: capillary (including juvenile or strawberry type), cavernous, pyogenic granuloma. Lymphangiomas: simple (capillary), cavernous (cystic hygroma). Glomus tumour (glomangioma). Vascular ectasias: nevus flammeus (including port-wine stain), spider telangiectasia, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Rendu-Osler-Weber). Reactive vascular proliferation: bacillary angiomatosis

    Haemangioendothelioma (e.g., epithelioid haemangioendothelioma)
    Malignant tumoursAngiosarcoma (including lymphangiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphoedema)

    Benign tumours usually form obvious vascular channels lined by a monolayer of normal-looking endothelial cells. Malignant tumours are more solidly cellular with cytologic atypia and poor vessel formation, and their endothelial origin may need immunostaining for CD31 or von Willebrand factor.

    Ischemic Heart Disease

    Write a short note on angina pectoris.

    DU21M

    Angina pectoris (literally "chest pain") is characterised by paroxysmal, recurrent attacks of substernal or precordial discomfort caused by transient myocardial ischaemia (15 seconds to 15 minutes) that is not severe enough to cause myocyte necrosis. The pain results from ischaemia-induced release of adenosine, bradykinin and other molecules that stimulate sympathetic and vagal afferent nerves. It is classically described as crushing or squeezing, radiating down the left arm or to the left jaw. Not all ischaemia is felt as pain: "silent ischaemia" is common in the elderly and in diabetic neuropathy and may present as dyspnoea, nausea, diaphoresis or fatigue.

    Three overlapping patterns are recognised.

    • Stable (typical) angina is the most common. It is caused by an imbalance between perfusion (chronic stenosing atherosclerosis) and myocardial demand. It does not occur at rest, can be reliably reproduced by exertion, emotion or stress, and is relieved by rest or by nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers.
    • Prinzmetal variant angina is an uncommon form caused by coronary artery spasm. Attacks are unrelated to physical activity, heart rate or blood pressure and can occur at rest. They respond promptly to vasodilators, even though significant atherosclerosis may coexist.
    • Unstable (crescendo) angina is a pattern of increasingly frequent, prolonged (over 20 minutes) or severe attacks, precipitated by progressively lower levels of activity or at rest. It is associated with plaque disruption with superimposed thrombosis, distal embolisation or vasospasm, and it portends a high risk of complete occlusion and infarction.

    The Heart

    42 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Congenital Heart Disease

    Classification

    B1

    What are the major cardiac diseases? Classify congenital heart disease.

    The major cardiac diseases are heart failure, congenital heart disease, ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease, valvular heart disease, cardiomyopathies and myocarditis, pericardial disease, and cardiac tumours. Congenital heart disease is classified functionally into left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA), right-to-left shunts (tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous connection) and obstructive lesions (coarctation of the aorta, pulmonary stenosis or atresia, aortic stenosis or atresia).

    Major cardiac diseases. Heart disease reduces to six pathophysiologic mechanisms: pump failure, obstruction to flow, regurgitant flow, shunted flow, conduction disorders and rupture of the heart or a major vessel. The clinicopathologic groups are:

    1. Heart failure, which is the common end-point of most chronic heart disease.
    2. Congenital heart disease.
    3. Ischaemic heart disease (angina, myocardial infarction, chronic ischaemic heart disease, sudden cardiac death).
    4. Hypertensive heart disease (systemic, and pulmonary or cor pulmonale).
    5. Valvular heart disease (rheumatic heart disease, calcific aortic stenosis, mitral valve prolapse, infective and noninfective endocarditis).
    6. Cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive) and myocarditis.
    7. Pericardial disease.
    8. Cardiac tumours.

    Classification of congenital heart disease. CHD arises from faulty embryogenesis during weeks 3 to 8 and is broadly classified by the haemodynamic consequence into shunts and obstructions. About 1% of live births have a significant cardiovascular malformation, and ventricular septal defect (42%) is the most frequent.

    GroupLesionsHaemodynamics
    Left-to-right shunts (acyanotic at first; the most common group)Atrial septal defect (ASD), ventricular septal defect (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
    Also atrioventricular septal defect    		Increased pulmonary flow with right-sided volume overload and, with large shunts, pulmonary hypertension that may reverse the shunt (Eisenmenger syndrome)
    Right-to-left shunts (cyanotic CHD)Tetralogy of Fallot (most common in this group), transposition of the great arteries, persistent truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous connectionCyanosis from early postnatal life, polycythaemia, clubbing, paradoxical embolism

    Causes include chromosomal abnormalities (trisomy 21, 18, 13, Turner syndrome, 22q11.2 deletion in DiGeorge syndrome), single-gene mutations in transcription factors (NKX2.5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX1) and signalling molecules (Notch), and environmental factors such as congenital rubella, maternal diabetes and teratogens. The cause remains unknown in nearly 90% of cases.

    Tetralogy of Fallot

    B1

    Components of Fallot's tetralogy.

    Tetralogy of Fallot has four components: a ventricular septal defect, obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonic stenosis), an aorta that overrides the VSD, and right ventricular hypertrophy. It is the commonest cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease.

    The first three features arise embryologically from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum, and the right ventricular hypertrophy is secondary to the pressure overload. The VSD is large, with the aortic valve overriding it, so that both ventricles empty into the aorta. The severity of the right ventricular outflow obstruction determines the clinical picture. With mild stenosis the shunt may remain left-to-right with no cyanosis ("pink tetralogy"), whereas with more severe obstruction right-sided pressures reach or exceed left-sided pressures and a right-to-left shunt produces cyanosis.

    The heart is classically boot-shaped because of right ventricular hypertrophy, and a right aortic arch is present in about 25% of cases. The pulmonary stenosis protects the lungs from pressure overload, and right heart failure is rare because the right ventricle is decompressed through the VSD.

    Ischemic Heart Disease

    Overview

    B1

    What are the ischemic heart diseases?

    Ischaemic heart disease is myocardial ischaemia from an imbalance between myocardial blood supply and demand, caused in more than 90% of cases by obstructive atherosclerosis of the epicardial coronary arteries. It presents as angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, chronic ischaemic heart disease with heart failure, or sudden cardiac death.

    IHD comprises a group of related syndromes resulting from myocardial ischaemia. In practice the four clinical presentations are:

    1. Angina pectoris (stable, Prinzmetal variant and unstable), in which ischaemia is transient and insufficient to cause necrosis.
    2. Myocardial infarction (MI), in which prolonged ischaemia causes cardiac necrosis.
    3. Chronic ischaemic heart disease, progressive heart failure from accumulated ischaemic damage.
    4. Sudden cardiac death, usually from a lethal arrhythmia.

    Unstable angina, MI and sudden death due to acute plaque change with thrombosis are grouped as the acute coronary syndromes. In addition to coronary atherosclerosis (the dominant cause), ischaemia can result from coronary emboli, vasculitis, or spasm.

    Define ischemic heart disease.

    DU25N

    Ischaemic heart disease (IHD) is a group of related clinical syndromes resulting from myocardial ischaemia, which is an imbalance between the supply of oxygenated blood to the myocardium (perfusion) and the cardiac demand for it. Ischaemia reduces oxygenation and ATP generation and also impairs delivery of nutrients and removal of metabolic wastes, so that it is tolerated less well than hypoxaemia alone. In more than 90% of cases the cause is reduced coronary flow from obstructive atherosclerosis of the epicardial coronary arteries, for which reason IHD is often called coronary artery disease. It usually reflects decades of silent progression of atherosclerosis, which begins in childhood or adolescence.

    Write down the types of ischemic heart disease.

    7DU25NDU24MDU22NDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU12Ja

    Ischaemic heart disease presents in four clinical forms.

    1. Angina pectoris. Paroxysmal substernal chest discomfort from transient (15 seconds to 15 minutes) myocardial ischaemia insufficient to cause necrosis. Three patterns are recognised:

    • Stable (typical) angina: due to chronic stenosing coronary atherosclerosis. Pain is induced by exertion, emotion or stress, and is relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
    • Prinzmetal (variant) angina: due to coronary vasospasm. It occurs at rest, is unrelated to exertion, and responds to vasodilators.
    • Unstable (crescendo) angina: increasingly frequent, prolonged (over 20 minutes) or severe pain, occurring with progressively less exertion or at rest. It is caused by plaque disruption with thrombosis, embolisation or vasospasm and is a harbinger of infarction.

    2. Myocardial infarction. Death of cardiac muscle from prolonged ischaemia. It is either transmural (STEMI) or subendocardial (NSTEMI).

    3. Chronic ischaemic heart disease (ischaemic cardiomyopathy). Progressive congestive heart failure from accumulated ischaemic myocardial damage, usually after a prior infarct, with cardiomegaly and scars.

    4. Sudden cardiac death. Unexpected death from cardiac causes within 1 hour of symptom onset, usually from a fatal arrhythmia (ventricular fibrillation) in a heart with severe chronic coronary atherosclerosis.

    Angina pectoris (case)

    B10

    A 45-year-old male complained of left-sided chest pain, which was relieved by taking rest and spraying nitroglycerin under his tongue. What is your diagnosis? What are the other differential diagnoses? How will you diagnose a case of myocardial infarction in the laboratory?

    The history of exertional chest pain relieved by rest and sublingual nitroglycerin points to stable (typical) angina pectoris due to coronary atherosclerosis. The differentials are unstable angina, Prinzmetal angina and myocardial infarction, and noncardiac causes such as aortic dissection, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, oesophageal reflux and musculoskeletal pain. Myocardial infarction is diagnosed in the laboratory by raised cardiac troponin T or I, supported by CK-MB and the ECG.

    Diagnosis. Stable angina is caused by chronic stenosing coronary atherosclerosis, usually with a lesion obstructing more than 70% of the lumen, so that perfusion is inadequate when demand rises with exertion, emotion or stress. The transient ischaemia (usually less than 15 minutes) does not cause necrosis. The pain is classically a crushing or squeezing substernal sensation that radiates to the left arm or jaw, and it is relieved by rest (which lowers demand) or nitrates (which dilate vessels and improve perfusion). Pain provoked in a reproducible manner and relieved in this way distinguishes it from infarction.

    Differential diagnoses

    • Cardiac: unstable angina (pain at rest or crescendo and lasting longer), Prinzmetal angina (rest pain from spasm), acute MI (pain longer than 30 minutes, not relieved by rest or nitrates), acute pericarditis (pleuritic, positional, with a friction rub), aortic dissection (sudden tearing pain radiating to the back), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and aortic stenosis.
    • Pulmonary: pulmonary embolism, pleurisy, pneumothorax, pneumonia.
    • Gastrointestinal and others: gastroesophageal reflux or oesophageal spasm, peptic ulcer, biliary colic, costochondritis and other musculoskeletal pain, herpes zoster, anxiety.

    Laboratory diagnosis of myocardial infarction. MI is diagnosed by symptoms, the ECG (ST elevation in STEMI) and the detection of myocardial proteins in the blood. The test of choice is serum cardiac troponin T or I, which begins to rise within 2–4 hours, peaks at 24–48 hours and stays elevated for 7–10 days. CK-MB, which rises in 3–12 hours, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to normal in 48–72 hours, is useful for detecting early reinfarction.

    Myoglobin rises earliest but is nonspecific, and LDH (flipped LDH1 greater than LDH2) is now only of historical interest. Serial measurements are taken to document the rise and fall.

    Myocardial infarction: pathogenesis

    What is myocardial infarction?

    DU07Ju

    Myocardial infarction (MI), commonly called a heart attack, is the death of cardiac muscle due to prolonged ischaemia. It is usually caused by atherosclerotic coronary artery disease complicated by acute plaque rupture and occlusive thrombosis, and the dominant mechanism of cell death is ischaemic coagulative necrosis. Severe ischaemia (flow 10% or less of normal) lasting 20–30 minutes or longer causes irreversible injury, and necrosis is complete by 6–12 hours. When transmural it is called an ST-elevation MI (STEMI), and when confined to the subendocardium a non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI). Roughly 800,000 people in the United States have an MI each year.

    What are the risk factors of ischemic heart disease/MI?

    DU13JaDU12Ja

    The risk factors for IHD and MI are those of coronary atherosclerosis, since more than 90% of cases arise from it.

    • Non-modifiable: increasing age, male sex (women are protected until menopause), family history and genetic variation.
    • Major modifiable: hyperlipidaemia (raised LDL, low HDL, raised lipoprotein(a)), hypertension (which also causes left ventricular hypertrophy), cigarette smoking (which doubles the death rate from IHD) and diabetes mellitus (which doubles the incidence of MI).
    • Additional: inflammation (raised C-reactive protein), hyperhomocysteinaemia, metabolic syndrome and obesity, haemostatic abnormalities (raised PAI-1), physical inactivity and psychological stress.
    • Precipitants of the acute event: adrenergic surges (morning peak of MI between 6 a.m. and noon), emotional stress, cocaine use (vasospasm), and states of increased demand such as tachycardia, hypotension or severe anaemia.

    These factors act with greater than additive effect. Some 10% of MIs occur without typical atherothrombosis, through vasospasm, embolism or small-vessel disease.

    Describe the pathogenesis of myocardial infarction.

    4DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU19Nov

    1. Coronary arterial occlusion. In the great majority of cases the sequence is:

    1. An atheromatous plaque is eroded or suddenly disrupted by endothelial injury, intraplaque haemorrhage or mechanical forces, exposing subendothelial collagen and necrotic plaque contents. Vulnerable plaques have a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid core and many macrophages, and fissures typically occur at the cap's junction with the normal wall, where mechanical stress is highest.
    2. Platelets adhere, aggregate and become activated, releasing thromboxane A₂, ADP and serotonin, which promote further aggregation and vasospasm.
    3. Tissue factor activates coagulation, adding fibrin to the thrombus.
    4. Within minutes the thrombus can occlude the lumen completely.

    Angiography within 4 hours of onset shows coronary thrombosis in about 90% of cases. The culprit plaque is usually not critically stenotic beforehand. In about 10% of cases MI occurs without typical atherothrombosis, through vasospasm (cocaine, ephedrine), embolism (left atrial thrombus, endocarditis vegetations), small-vessel disease (vasculitis, sickle cell disease, amyloid), vessel dissection, severe hypertrophy or hypotension.

    2. Myocardial response. Within seconds aerobic metabolism ceases, ATP and creatine phosphate fall and lactate accumulates, and contractility is lost within about 2 minutes. Ultrastructural changes (myofibrillar relaxation, glycogen loss, mitochondrial swelling) are reversible at first. Only severe ischaemia lasting 20–40 minutes or more causes irreversible injury, and the earliest sign of necrosis is loss of sarcolemmal integrity, which allows proteins such as troponin to leak into the circulation.

    Microvascular injury follows after about an hour. Necrosis begins in the subendocardium (last to be perfused and exposed to high intramural pressure) and spreads as a wavefront toward the epicardium, so that a transmural infarct is complete by 6–12 hours. A thin rim of subendocardium (about 0.1 mm) survives by diffusion from the ventricular cavity.

    3. Determinants of size and pattern. The location, severity and rate of development of obstruction, the size of the vascular bed supplied, duration of occlusion, metabolic demand of the myocardium, collateral circulation, presence of spasm, and heart rate, rhythm and oxygenation all decide the outcome. Transmural infarcts follow occlusion of an epicardial vessel, subendocardial infarcts follow a thrombus that lyses early or global hypotension, and microinfarcts follow small-vessel occlusion.

    4. Reperfusion injury. Restoring flow can itself cause damage through mitochondrial dysfunction, myocyte hypercontracture (calcium influx), free radicals, leukocyte aggregation (no-reflow), and platelet and complement activation.

    Myocardial infarction: morphology

    Write the morphological changes in myocardial infarction.

    DU07Ja

    An infarct is generally localised to the territory of the occluded vessel (left anterior descending artery 40–50%, right coronary artery 30–40%, left circumflex artery 15–20%), and nearly all transmural infarcts involve part of the left ventricle. The characteristic change is ischaemic coagulative necrosis, followed by acute inflammation and repair, and the sequence is predictable.

    Early detection. Infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not visible grossly, but they can be shown after 2–3 hours by triphenyl tetrazolium chloride, which stains viable myocardium brick red because of intact lactate dehydrogenase activity and leaves the infarct pale. After reperfusion, infarcts are haemorrhagic and show contraction band necrosis (intense eosinophilic bands of hypercontracted sarcomeres). Healing proceeds from the border toward the centre, and a completely healed scar cannot be dated.

    Myocardial infarction: complications

    B1

    Complications of MI.

    The main complications of MI are arrhythmias (the commonest, and the cause of early sudden death), contractile dysfunction with heart failure and cardiogenic shock, papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation, myocardial rupture, pericarditis, mural thrombosis with embolism, ventricular aneurysm, right ventricular infarction, and progressive heart failure.

    Nearly three-quarters of patients have one or more complications, and their likelihood depends on infarct size, location and the fraction of wall thickness involved.

    1. Arrhythmias occur in up to 90% of patients (ventricular premature beats, ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation, bradyarrhythmias and heart block), are maximal in the first hour, and account for most out-of-hospital deaths.
    2. Left ventricular failure and cardiogenic shock. Pump function falls in proportion to the myocardium lost. Cardiogenic shock occurs in about 10% of transmural infarcts, usually when 40% or more of the left ventricle is damaged.
    3. Myocardial rupture (1–3%), most often 3 to 7 days after infarction when necrotic muscle is softest: free wall rupture causes haemopericardium and tamponade, septal rupture produces an acquired VSD, and papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation.
    4. Papillary muscle dysfunction with mitral regurgitation from ischaemia, later from fibrosis or ventricular dilation.
    5. Pericarditis, a fibrinous or fibrinohaemorrhagic reaction 2–3 days after a transmural infarct, and Dressler syndrome weeks later.
    6. Mural thrombosis with the risk of systemic embolism.
    7. Ventricular aneurysm, a late complication of a large anteroseptal infarct, with thrombi, arrhythmias and heart failure but no rupture.
    8. Right ventricular infarction accompanying posterior septal or inferior infarcts.
    9. Infarct expansion, ventricular remodeling and progressive heart failure (chronic ischaemic heart disease).

    Mention the complications/consequences of myocardial infarction.

    10DU25NDU24MDU22NDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU14JaDU12JaDU09JuDU03Ja

    Nearly three-quarters of patients experience at least one complication, and the risk depends mainly on infarct size, location and the fraction of wall thickness involved.

    1. Arrhythmias. About 90% of patients develop a rhythm disturbance, because of myocardial irritability and conduction disturbances: heart block, bradycardia, supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, ventricular premature contractions, ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Risk is greatest in the first hour, and arrhythmia accounts for most out-of-hospital deaths.
    2. Contractile dysfunction (left ventricular failure). Pump function falls in proportion to the volume damaged, causing hypotension, pulmonary congestion and oedema. Cardiogenic shock occurs in about 10% of patients with transmural MI, typically when 40% or more of the left ventricle is damaged.
    3. Myocardial rupture (1–3%). Left ventricular free wall rupture is most common and causes haemopericardium and cardiac tamponade. Rupture of the interventricular septum produces an acquired VSD with left-to-right shunt, and rupture of a papillary muscle causes severe acute mitral regurgitation. Rupture is commonest 3 to 7 days after infarction, when lysis of necrotic myocardium is maximal and the infarct is soft granulation tissue. Risk factors are age above 60, anterior or lateral infarcts, female sex, absence of left ventricular hypertrophy and a first MI.
    4. Papillary muscle dysfunction. Ischaemic papillary muscles are poorly contractile and cause postinfarct mitral regurgitation. Later, fibrosis and shortening or ventricular dilation may cause it.
    5. Right ventricular infarction. It is isolated in only 1–3% but accompanies posterior septal or left ventricular infarcts from right coronary occlusion, leading to right heart failure and hypotension.
    6. Pericarditis. Transmural infarcts cause fibrinohaemorrhagic pericarditis 2–3 days later (chest pain and friction rub). Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune pericarditis weeks after infarction.
    7. Chamber dilation and infarct expansion. Weakened necrotic muscle stretches and thins, especially in anteroseptal infarcts.
    8. Mural thrombus. Stasis, dilation and endocardial damage predispose to thrombus, with risk of systemic embolism (including stroke).
    9. Ventricular aneurysm. A late complication of a large anteroseptal transmural infarct that heals as a thin scar. It causes mural thrombi, arrhythmias and heart failure but does not rupture.
    10. Progressive heart failure and ventricular remodeling. Compensatory hypertrophy of the noninfarcted myocardium may eventually be overwhelmed by dilation and increased oxygen demand (chronic ischaemic heart disease).

    Posterior transmural infarcts are more often complicated by conduction block and right ventricular involvement, whereas anterior transmural infarcts carry the greatest risk of free wall rupture, dilation, thrombus and aneurysm. Subendocardial infarcts rarely cause pericarditis, rupture or aneurysm. Mortality within the first year is about 20%.

    Myocardial infarction: diagnosis and markers

    B1

    Mention important cardiac biochemical markers. Laboratory diagnosis of acute MI.

    The important cardiac biomarkers are the cardiac-specific troponins T and I (the best markers), CK-MB, myoglobin and, historically, LDH. Acute MI is diagnosed by combining typical symptoms, ECG changes and a rise and fall of troponin above the reference limit.

    The laboratory diagnosis rests on measuring proteins that leak from irreversibly injured myocytes after the sarcolemma loses integrity. Cardiac troponin T or I, regulatory proteins of calcium-mediated contraction, rise within 2–4 hours, peak at 24–48 hours and remain elevated for 7–10 days. With reperfusion they peak earlier and higher because of rapid washout. CK-MB rises in 3–12 hours, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to baseline by 48–72 hours, so it is useful for detecting reinfarction.

    Myoglobin rises within 1–3 hours but is not cardiac-specific. LDH rises at 24–48 hours with a flipped LDH1 greater than LDH2 ratio, peaking at 3–6 days. Low-level troponin elevation ("troponin leak") also occurs in heart failure, pulmonary embolism, renal failure and sepsis, and large acute rises occur in myocarditis and myocardial trauma, so the clinical context and serial values matter. Supporting tests are the ECG (ST elevation in STEMI), echocardiography for regional wall-motion abnormality and coronary angiography.

    Give the laboratory diagnosis of MI.

    DU07Ju

    The diagnosis of MI is made on clinical symptoms, electrocardiographic changes, and laboratory demonstration of myocardial proteins in plasma.

    1. Cardiac biomarkers (the cornerstone). The diagnosis of myocardial injury is established when troponin rises above the upper reference limit with a rise and/or fall pattern on serial samples. Cardiac troponin T or I is the preferred marker. CK-MB serves as a second marker, particularly for reinfarction. Myoglobin is an early but nonspecific marker, and LDH is of historic value.
    2. ECG. Transmural infarcts show ST-segment elevation (STEMI), and subendocardial infarcts show ST depression or T-wave changes without ST elevation (NSTEMI). Pathologic Q waves appear later. Small infarcts may be electrocardiographically silent.
    3. Imaging. Echocardiography shows regional wall-motion abnormality and measures ejection fraction. Coronary angiography demonstrates the occluding thrombus.
    4. Other findings. Neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised ESR and C-reactive protein reflect the inflammatory response, and hyperglycaemia is common.
