    Why is troponin the best indicator for MI?

    DU08JaDU06Ja

    Cardiac troponins T and I (cTnT and cTnI) are the most clinically useful markers of myocardial damage for the following reasons.

    1. Cardiac specificity. Cardiac troponins are encoded by genes distinct from those of skeletal muscle troponins and are expressed only in cardiac myocytes. CK-MB and myoglobin also occur in skeletal muscle and rise after trauma, exercise or myopathy.
    2. High sensitivity. Troponins are present in large amounts in the myocyte (part is free in the cytoplasm and the rest is bound to the contractile apparatus), so even minor myocardial necrosis, such as in NSTEMI, gives a measurable rise. A normal level makes MI very unlikely.
    3. Early rise with a wide diagnostic window. They begin to rise within 2–4 hours, peak at 24–48 hours and remain elevated 7–10 days, which allows the diagnosis even when the patient presents late, whereas CK-MB has normalised by 48–72 hours.
    4. Quantitative correlation. The magnitude of the rise correlates with the volume of damaged myocardium and with prognosis.
    5. Standardised. Reference values and assays are well established, and a rise and/or fall pattern fulfils the universal definition of MI.

    Its limitations are that small "troponin leaks" occur in heart failure, pulmonary embolism, renal failure and sepsis, and large rises in myocarditis, so serial values are interpreted in clinical context. Persistence of the elevation also limits its use for early reinfarction, where CK-MB is useful.

    Myocardial infarction (case)

    B10

    A 56-year-old male presented to you with sudden severe left-sided chest pain and sweating. The pain was not relieved by taking rest or by sublingual nitroglycerin. What is your probable diagnosis? What investigations should you advise, and what are their expected clinical results?

    My probable diagnosis is acute myocardial infarction, since severe chest pain with sweating that is not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin indicates prolonged ischaemia with myocardial necrosis, usually from plaque rupture with coronary thrombosis. I would order an ECG, serial cardiac troponins, CK-MB, echocardiography and coronary angiography, and I would expect ST-segment elevation and a rising troponin.

    Diagnosis. The pain is severe, lasts more than 30 minutes, is described as crushing and is accompanied by diaphoresis, and, unlike angina, it is unrelieved by rest or nitrates. This indicates acute MI, probably due to occlusive thrombosis over a disrupted atheromatous plaque (an acute coronary syndrome). Aortic dissection must be excluded, since it also causes severe pain.

    Investigations and expected results

    • ECG: ST-segment elevation in the leads overlying the infarct (STEMI) when transmural, with later T-wave inversion and pathologic Q waves. NSTEMI shows ST depression or T-wave changes.
    • Cardiac troponin T or I: raised from 2–4 hours, peaking at 24–48 hours and remaining high for 7–10 days (serial sampling, with a rise and fall).
    • CK-MB: raised at 3–12 hours, peaking at about 24 hours and normalising in 48–72 hours. Myoglobin is raised early.
    • Blood tests: neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised ESR and CRP, possible hyperglycaemia, and a lipid profile.
    • Echocardiography: regional wall-motion abnormality and reduced ejection fraction, and evidence of complications (mitral regurgitation, VSD, effusion, thrombus).
    • Chest radiograph: pulmonary congestion if left ventricular failure. Mediastinal widening if dissection is suspected.
    • Coronary angiography: shows the occluding thrombus and underlying atherosclerotic stenosis, and allows reperfusion by angioplasty and stenting.

    The goal of management is rapid reperfusion ("time is myocardium"), with antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, beta blockers and nitrates.

    A5

    50-year-old man with severe central chest pain and sweating followed by transient unconsciousness — Likely diagnosis? Laboratory investigations to confirm that diagnosis?

    A5

    The likely diagnosis is acute myocardial infarction, with the transient unconsciousness (syncope) most probably due to an arrhythmia such as ventricular tachycardia, heart block or asystole, or to hypotension from acute pump failure. It is confirmed by a raised cardiac troponin (with CK-MB), along with typical ECG changes.

    Severe central chest pain with diaphoresis is the classic presentation of acute MI. Syncope in this setting suggests a complication, the commonest being a ventricular arrhythmia (arrhythmias occur in about 90% of patients and are maximal in the first hour), or conduction block in a posterior (inferior) infarct, or hypotension from extensive myocardial damage with cardiogenic shock. Aortic dissection and massive pulmonary embolism, which can also present with pain and syncope, must be considered.

    Laboratory investigations. Serial cardiac troponin T or I is the key test and shows a rise from 2–4 hours, a peak at 24–48 hours and persistence for 7–10 days. CK-MB (rise at 3–12 hours, peak at 24 hours, normal by 48–72 hours) is a supporting test. The ECG will show ST elevation (STEMI), and the findings are supported by raised leukocyte count, ESR and CRP. Echocardiography and angiography are performed to define wall-motion abnormality and coronary occlusion.

    A patient has severe central chest pain, sweating, ± syncope. What is the probable diagnosis?

    5DU21MDU19MDU17NovDU12JaDU11Ja

    The probable diagnosis is acute myocardial infarction (an acute coronary syndrome, likely STEMI). Severe, prolonged (over 30 minutes) crushing central chest pain with profuse sweating (diaphoresis) is the classic presentation of infarction and implies myocardial necrosis, usually following rupture or erosion of a coronary atheromatous plaque with superimposed occlusive thrombosis. Nausea and vomiting, dyspnoea and a rapid weak pulse commonly accompany it, and syncope signals a complication such as a ventricular arrhythmia, heart block or hypotension from acute pump failure. In up to 25% of patients, particularly the elderly and those with diabetic neuropathy, the onset is atypical or painless.

    The differential diagnosis includes unstable angina, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, acute pericarditis and oesophageal causes, and these are excluded by the ECG, biomarkers and imaging.

    Same: what investigations/expected biochemical findings confirm it?

    5DU21MDU19MDU17NovDU12JaDU11Ja

    Confirmation is by the ECG and cardiac biomarkers, supported by imaging.

    Biochemical findings

    • Cardiac troponin T or I: raised above the reference limit, beginning at 2–4 hours, peaking at 24–48 hours and remaining elevated for 7–10 days. This is the most sensitive and specific marker.
    • CK-MB: rises in 3–12 hours, peaks at about 24 hours and returns to normal within 48–72 hours (useful for reinfarction).
    • Myoglobin: rises very early (1–3 hours) but is nonspecific.
    • LDH: rises at 24–48 hours with a flipped LDH1:LDH2 ratio, peaks at 3–6 days (historical).
    • Nonspecific: neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised ESR and C-reactive protein, hyperglycaemia.

    Other investigations. The ECG shows ST-segment elevation in STEMI (ST depression or T-wave changes in NSTEMI), followed by T-wave inversion and Q waves. Echocardiography shows regional wall-motion abnormality and reduced ejection fraction, and coronary angiography shows the occluded vessel.

    Hypertensive Heart Disease

    A 70y man has long-standing hypertension. What type of adaptive change may occur in his heart?

    DU24N

    The adaptive change is concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (systemic hypertensive heart disease). Chronic pressure overload increases wall stress, and the myocytes respond by increasing in size (cellular hypertrophy) with synthesis of new sarcomeres assembled in parallel to the long axis of the cell, so that the ventricular wall thickens concentrically while the cavity is initially not dilated. The heart weight rises disproportionately (it may exceed 500 g) and the wall thickness may exceed 2 cm. Hypertrophic myocytes show increased transverse diameter, enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei and often interstitial and perivascular fibrosis.

    Although initially compensatory, the change is eventually maladaptive. Capillary density does not increase in proportion to myocyte size, oxygen demand is increased and fibrosis stiffens the wall, so that the hypertrophied heart is vulnerable to demand ischaemia, diastolic dysfunction (with left atrial enlargement and atrial fibrillation), eventual dilation and congestive heart failure, and sudden death. Minimal criteria for the diagnosis of hypertensive heart disease are left ventricular hypertrophy in the absence of other cardiovascular pathology, together with a history or evidence of hypertension elsewhere (such as the kidney). Effective control of blood pressure can lead to regression of the hypertrophy.

    Same: mention physiological conditions where this change can occur.

    DU24N

    Cardiac hypertrophy can also be a physiologic adaptation to a sustained increase in workload, and the main examples are:

    1. Athletic training. Regular aerobic exercise (for example long-distance running) causes physiologic hypertrophy, generally with volume-load pattern and with an increase in capillary density. It is beneficial and lowers the resting heart rate and blood pressure. Static, isometric exercise such as weightlifting produces mild pressure hypertrophy with less beneficial remodeling.
    2. Pregnancy. The increased blood volume and cardiac output impose a volume load on the heart, producing a reversible increase in ventricular mass that regresses after delivery.
    3. Growth and manual labour. Hypertrophic growth of the heart in normal development of the child and adolescent, and in heavy physical work.

    The distinguishing feature of physiologic hypertrophy is that it is reversible, with preserved or improved function and normal capillary supply, whereas pathologic hypertrophy (pressure or volume overload) is associated with fibrosis, a relatively inadequate blood supply and a tendency to failure.

    Valvular Heart Disease

    Rheumatic fever

    B1

    What is the etiopathogenesis of rheumatic fever? Diagnostic criteria of rheumatic fever.

    Rheumatic fever is an acute, immunologically mediated multisystem inflammatory disease that follows group A β-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis by 2–3 weeks. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells directed against streptococcal M protein cross-react with host cardiac antigens (molecular mimicry). The diagnosis rests on the revised Jones criteria: evidence of preceding streptococcal infection plus two major manifestations, or one major and two minor manifestations.

    Aetiopathogenesis. Rheumatic fever (RF) is a hypersensitivity (autoimmune) reaction to group A streptococcal antigens, not an infection of the heart itself. Streptococci are absent from the lesions. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells against streptococcal M protein cross-react with pericardial, myocardial and valvular antigens. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits Fc-receptor–bearing cells such as neutrophils and macrophages, and T-cell cytokines activate macrophages (for example within Aschoff bodies).

    The 2–3 week delay (10 days to 6 weeks) reflects the time needed for the immune response. Only 0.3–3% of infected people develop RF, which points to genetic susceptibility. It mostly affects children aged 5–15 years and is favoured by overcrowding and poverty. The chronic valve deformity is the healing and scarring that follows repeated acute inflammation.

    Diagnostic criteria (revised Jones criteria). Evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection (a rising or raised ASO or anti-DNase B titre, positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or recent scarlet fever), plus:

    Major criteriaMinor criteria
    Migratory polyarthritis of large jointsFever
    Carditis (pancarditis)Arthralgia
    Subcutaneous nodulesRaised acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP)
    Erythema marginatumProlonged PR interval on ECG
    Sydenham chorea

    The diagnosis requires two major, or one major and two minor, criteria with evidence of preceding streptococcal infection. These criteria are applied differently in low-risk and high-risk populations. In high-risk populations, such as those with a high background incidence of RF, arthralgia may count as a major criterion and lower thresholds for fever and acute-phase reactants apply.

    B1

    Which valve is commonly affected by rheumatic fever? What is an Aschoff body?

    The mitral valve is the valve most commonly affected
    it is involved in virtually all cases of chronic rheumatic heart disease, alone in about two-thirds and together with the aortic valve in another 25%. An Aschoff body is the pathognomonic granulomatous lesion of rheumatic carditis, a focus of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells ("caterpillar cells").

    Valve involvement. The mitral valve is virtually always involved in chronic rheumatic heart disease, in isolation in about two-thirds of cases and with the aortic valve in another 25%. The tricuspid valve is infrequently affected and the pulmonary valve rarely. Rheumatic heart disease is virtually the only cause of mitral stenosis, producing "fish-mouth" stenosis with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and thickened, fused tendinous cords.

    Aschoff body. The Aschoff body is a distinctive lesion of acute rheumatic carditis, found in the interstitial connective tissue, often perivascular, in any of the three layers of the heart. It consists of an area of fibrinoid necrosis infiltrated by T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and large macrophages with abundant cytoplasm (Anitschkow cells). In longitudinal section the central chromatin of these cells condenses into a slender wavy ribbon ("caterpillar cells"), and in cross-section appears like an "owl-eye." Some Anitschkow cells fuse to form multinucleated Aschoff giant cells. Aschoff bodies are rarely seen in chronic rheumatic heart disease because of the long interval since the acute illness.

    B1

    Complications of rheumatic fever.

    The complications of rheumatic fever are acute carditis with heart failure, arrhythmias and pericardial effusion (fatal in 1–2%), recurrent attacks, and chronic rheumatic heart disease, whose complications include mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism, infective endocarditis and right-sided failure.

    Acute phase. Rheumatic carditis (pancarditis) can cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure, and 1–2% of patients die of fulminant cardiac involvement. Fibrinous pericarditis with friction rub and effusion may occur. The arthritis is self-limited and leaves no deformity, and Sydenham chorea and skin lesions resolve. After the first attack, each streptococcal pharyngitis can precipitate a recurrence, and the valve damage is cumulative.

    Chronic rheumatic heart disease (years to decades later). Healing by fibrosis produces leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickened, fused cords, causing mitral stenosis ("fish-mouth") and/or regurgitation and aortic valve disease. Consequent complications are left atrial dilation with atrial fibrillation and mural thrombi with systemic thromboembolism (stroke), pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular hypertrophy and failure, congestive heart failure, superimposed infective endocarditis, and valve calcification needing surgical repair or replacement.

    B10

    A 6-year-old boy develops fever, joint pain, a diffuse skin rash and a nodule 3 weeks after recovery from a sore throat. His ESR is 70 mm in the first hour, and his ASO titer is 500 IU/mL. What is your probable diagnosis? What are the changes in the heart in this case?

    The probable diagnosis is acute rheumatic fever. The history of a sore throat followed 3 weeks later by fever, migratory joint pain, a rash (erythema marginatum) and a subcutaneous nodule, together with a raised ESR and a raised ASO titre showing preceding streptococcal infection, fulfils the Jones criteria. In the heart there is pancarditis with Aschoff bodies, fibrinous pericarditis, myocarditis and verrucous endocarditis along the lines of closure of the mitral valve.

    Diagnosis. The child has major criteria (arthritis, erythema marginatum rash and a subcutaneous nodule, with carditis to be sought) and minor criteria (fever, raised ESR), and the ASO titre of 500 IU/mL documents a preceding group A streptococcal infection. The latent period of about 3 weeks is characteristic of an immune-mediated reaction.

    Cardiac changes. During acute rheumatic fever focal inflammatory lesions develop in the heart and the characteristic lesion is the Aschoff body, so that any of the three layers can be involved (pancarditis).

    • Pericarditis: fibrinous or serofibrinous pericarditis ("bread and butter" appearance), with a friction rub, which usually resolves without sequelae.
    • Myocarditis: scattered Aschoff bodies within the interstitial connective tissue, often perivascular, which may cause tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure.
    • Endocarditis (valvulitis): inflammation of the left-sided valves, especially the mitral, with fibrinoid necrosis in the cusps or tendinous cords. Small (1–2 mm), warty vegetations called verrucae form along the lines of closure. Subendocardial lesions exacerbated by regurgitant jets cause irregular thickenings in the left atrium called MacCallum plaques.

    With repeated attacks, healing leads to chronic rheumatic heart disease: leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickening and fusion of chordae, which produce the "fish-mouth" mitral stenosis.

    What are the criteria for diagnosis of rheumatic fever?

    DU12Ju

    The diagnosis is made using the revised Jones criteria, which require evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection together with either two major manifestations or one major and two minor manifestations.

    Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection: raised or rising antistreptolysin O (ASO) or anti-DNase B titre, positive throat culture or rapid streptococcal antigen test, or a recent history of scarlet fever. Pharyngeal cultures are usually negative by the time the illness begins.

    Major criteria

    1. Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints, in which one joint after another becomes painful and swollen for a few days and then settles without residual disability.
    2. Carditis (pancarditis): myocarditis, pericarditis or endocarditis, manifested by tachycardia, murmurs, pericardial friction rub and cardiac failure.
    3. Subcutaneous nodules, typically over extensor surfaces of the extremities.
    4. Erythema marginatum, an irregular circinate skin rash.
    5. Sydenham chorea, a neurologic disorder with involuntary rapid movements.

    Minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, raised acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) and a prolonged PR interval on ECG.

    The criteria are evolving and are applied differently in low-risk and high-risk settings. The first attack usually appears 10 days to 6 weeks after streptococcal infection.

    Give the pathogenesis of rheumatic fever.

    DU15JaDU12Ja

    Acute rheumatic fever results from host immune responses to group A streptococcal antigens that cross-react with host proteins. The following steps are involved.

    1. Preceding infection. Group A β-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis (occasionally skin infection) exposes the immune system to streptococcal antigens, particularly the M protein, a surface virulence factor.
    2. Genetic susceptibility. Only 0.3–3% of infected individuals develop RF, implying an intrinsic susceptibility (certain MHC haplotypes) that determines the cross-reactive response.
    3. Molecular mimicry. Antibodies and CD4⁺ T cells directed against streptococcal M protein recognise cardiac antigens in the pericardium, myocardium and valves.
    4. Effector mechanisms. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits Fc-receptor–bearing neutrophils and macrophages. Cytokines produced by stimulated T cells activate macrophages, which form the Aschoff bodies. Tissue damage is thus caused by a combination of antibody-mediated and T-cell–mediated reactions (type II and type IV hypersensitivity).
    5. Latent period. The 2–3 week delay reflects the time needed to generate the immune response, and streptococci are absent from the lesions.
    6. Chronic disease. Acute inflammation resolves by healing and scarring. With each recurrent attack the damage to the valves is cumulative, and turbulent flow through deformed valves causes further fibrosis in a positive feedback loop.

    Which valves are commonly involved in rheumatic fever?

    DU15Ja

    In chronic rheumatic heart disease the mitral valve is virtually always involved, in isolation in roughly two-thirds of cases, and together with the aortic valve in another 25%. The tricuspid valve is infrequently involved, and the pulmonary valve is only rarely affected. Thus the left-sided valves bear the brunt of the damage, probably because of the greater mechanical stress they sustain. In acute rheumatic fever, inflammation of the endocardium and left-sided valves produces fibrinoid necrosis in the cusps or tendinous cords with small verrucae along the lines of closure. Chronic disease produces leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickening and fusion of the cords. Rheumatic heart disease is responsible for 99% of acquired mitral stenosis.

    What are the complications of rheumatic fever?

    DU15JaDU11Ju

    Acute phase.

    • Acute rheumatic carditis (pancarditis) with tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac dilation, functional mitral insufficiency and heart failure. About 1–2% of patients die of fulminant cardiac involvement.
    • Pericarditis with friction rub, and effusion.
    • Arthritis (self-limited, leaving no deformity), Sydenham chorea and skin lesions.
    • Recurrences: after an initial attack there is increased vulnerability to reactivation with each subsequent streptococcal pharyngitis, and the damage to the valves is cumulative.

    Chronic rheumatic heart disease (appearing years or decades later).

    • Deforming fibrotic valvular disease: mitral stenosis ("fish-mouth") and/or regurgitation, and aortic stenosis or regurgitation.
    • Left atrial dilation, atrial fibrillation and mural thrombi with systemic thromboembolism (stroke).
    • Pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy and failure.
    • Congestive heart failure.
    • Infective endocarditis superimposed on the damaged valves.
    • Calcification of valves, requiring surgical repair or replacement.

    Write a short note on Aschoff nodule (myocardial changes, giant cell).

    DU14JuDU06MDU05Ja

    The Aschoff body (Aschoff nodule) is the characteristic and pathognomonic lesion of acute rheumatic carditis. It is a focal granulomatous inflammatory lesion found in the interstitial connective tissue of the heart, especially around small blood vessels, in the myocardium, endocardium and pericardium.

    Structure. A mature lesion has a central area of fibrinoid necrosis (collagen degeneration with deposits of fibrin and immune material), around which are collected T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells and large activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells (caterpillar cells). These have abundant cytoplasm and a round to ovoid nucleus in which chromatin is condensed into a central, slender, wavy ribbon (appearing as a "caterpillar" in longitudinal section and "owl-eye" in cross-section), and they are sometimes binucleate. Some Anitschkow cells fuse to form multinucleated Aschoff giant cells.

    Evolution. The lesion passes through an early exudative (fibrinoid) stage, a proliferative (granulomatous) stage with Anitschkow and giant cells, and a late healing stage in which fibrosis forms a perivascular scar. This is why Aschoff bodies are rarely seen in the chronic phase.

    Significance. Lesions in the myocardium contribute to rheumatic myocarditis, and Aschoff bodies in any of the layers define pancarditis. Nodules are accompanied by diffuse inflammation, and in the endocardium they underlie the verrucae. Streptococci are absent from the lesion because it is an immunologic reaction.

    A child has fever, migratory large-joint pain after sore throat. What is your provisional diagnosis?

    DU25NDU14Ju

    The provisional diagnosis is acute rheumatic fever. A child of school age with fever and migratory polyarthritis of the large joints developing about 2–3 weeks after a sore throat fits the picture of an immunologically mediated reaction to group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Migratory polyarthritis is a major Jones criterion (one large joint after another becomes painful and swollen for a few days, then resolves spontaneously without residual disability), and fever is a minor criterion. The diagnosis must be confirmed by looking for other manifestations, particularly carditis, and for evidence of the preceding infection. The differential diagnosis includes juvenile idiopathic arthritis, septic arthritis, reactive arthritis, SLE and leukaemia.

    Same: how will you diagnose the case?

    DU25N

    The diagnosis is established by applying the revised Jones criteria, which require evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection plus two major or one major and two minor manifestations. This is accomplished through history, examination and investigations.

    1. Clinical examination: look for carditis (new murmur, tachycardia, pericardial friction rub, cardiomegaly, signs of heart failure), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum and chorea.
    2. Evidence of streptococcal infection: ASO titre (raised or rising, with serial samples), anti-DNase B, throat swab culture or rapid antigen test (often negative by the time symptoms start).
    3. Acute-phase reactants: ESR and C-reactive protein raised, and leukocytosis.
    4. ECG: prolonged PR interval (a minor criterion), and other conduction abnormalities.
    5. Echocardiography: detects subclinical carditis, valvular regurgitation, effusion and ventricular function.
    6. Chest radiograph: cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion if in failure.
    7. Exclusion of other diseases: blood culture, rheumatoid factor and ANA, as indicated, to exclude septic arthritis, juvenile arthritis and SLE.

    Vegetations

    B1

    What is a vegetation? Name the vegetative heart diseases.

    A vegetation is an abnormal mass of thrombotic material, with or without microorganisms and inflammatory cells, attached to a heart valve or the endocardium. The vegetative (verrucous) endocardial diseases are rheumatic heart disease, infective endocarditis, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, and Libman-Sacks endocarditis of lupus.

    Robbins identifies four major forms of vegetative endocarditis.

    DiseaseVegetation featuresValve damage / nature
    Rheumatic heart diseaseSmall (1–2 mm), warty, firm vegetations (verrucae) along the lines of closure
    Sterile    		Fibrinoid necrosis of cusps
    Chronic scarring
    Infective endocarditisLarge, bulky, friable, irregular masses on the cusps that may extend onto the chordae
    Contain organisms    		Destructive, with ring abscess and perforation
    Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)Small (1–5 mm), bland, sterile thrombi loosely attached at the line of closure
    Single or multiple    		Nondestructive, no inflammation
    Libman-Sacks endocarditis (SLE)Small to medium (1–4 mm) sterile vegetations on either or both sides of the leaflets, chordae or mural endocardiumIntense valvulitis and fibrinoid necrosis
    Later scarring

    What is vegetation?

    DU26MDU19M

    A vegetation is a wart-like or friable mass attached to the surface of a heart valve (or less commonly the mural endocardium), composed of fibrin, platelets and other thrombotic debris, often with inflammatory cells and, in infective endocarditis, colonies of microorganisms. It forms where the endothelium has been damaged or the valve surface has become thrombogenic, so that thrombus builds up at the site, typically on the line of closure of the leaflets. Vegetations are a hallmark of vegetative (verrucous) endocarditis and may be infected (infective endocarditis) or sterile (rheumatic heart disease, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis and Libman-Sacks endocarditis).

    The principal consequences are valve damage with regurgitation, extension into adjacent myocardium (ring abscess), and embolisation. Infected vegetations cause septic infarcts and mycotic aneurysms where they lodge, and sterile vegetations of NBTE may cause bland infarcts in the brain, heart or elsewhere.

    Infective endocarditis

    B1

    What is infective endocarditis? Types and causative agents of infective endocarditis.

    Infective endocarditis is a microbial infection of the heart valves or mural endocardium that produces vegetations of thrombotic debris and organisms, often with destruction of the underlying cardiac tissue. It is classified clinically into acute and subacute forms. Acute endocarditis is caused by virulent organisms, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, and subacute endocarditis is caused by less virulent organisms, chiefly viridans streptococci, on previously damaged valves.

    Infective endocarditis requires a susceptible valve and organisms in the blood. The vegetations are made of platelets, fibrin, inflammatory cells and colonies of organisms, and they may destroy the valve and extend into adjacent myocardium.

    Types.

    • Acute IE: a virulent organism (chiefly Staphylococcus aureus) infects a previously normal valve, with rapid destruction, ring abscess and a stormy course.
    • Subacute IE: a low-virulence organism (chiefly viridans streptococci, 50–60% of native valve cases) infects a previously damaged valve (rheumatic, mitral valve prolapse, calcific stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, congenital defects), with an insidious course over weeks to months.
    • Special settings: prosthetic valve endocarditis (early: coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus
      Late: streptococci), endocarditis in intravenous drug users (S. aureus, usually right-sided), and culture-negative endocarditis (about 10%).

    Causative agents. S. aureus is the commonest cause overall. Viridans streptococci predominate in subacute disease. Other agents are enterococci, the HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), gram-negative bacilli and fungi (Candida, Aspergillus), the last two carrying about 50% mortality.

    What is subacute infective endocarditis?

    DU11Ju

    Subacute infective endocarditis is an insidious infection of previously abnormal (deformed) heart valves caused by organisms of low virulence, most characteristically viridans streptococci (Streptococcus viridans), a normal component of oral flora. The disease pursues a protracted course of weeks to months. The vegetations cause less valvular destruction than those of acute endocarditis, and microscopically they show granulation tissue at the base, indicating healing, with fibrosis, calcification and chronic inflammation developing later. The underlying valve abnormality is rheumatic heart disease, mitral valve prolapse, calcific valvular stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, prosthetic valves or congenital defects.

    Clinically the patient has low-grade fever, fatigue, weight loss, a flu-like illness and a murmur, and immune phenomena may appear (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis). Cure is often achieved by antibiotics alone (about 98% for low-virulence organisms such as viridans streptococci), usually with 6 weeks or more of therapy. The distinction from acute endocarditis is not absolute, and many cases lie between the two forms.

    Write the types/classification of infective endocarditis with infective agents.

    DU26MDU19M

    Infective endocarditis is classified clinically on the basis of severity and tempo (reflecting the virulence of the organism) and on the presence of underlying valve disease. Classification also recognises special settings.

    TypeValve and hostCommon organismsFeatures
    Acute IEPreviously normal valve, often with a recognised portal of entryStaphylococcus aureus (most cases overall)Stormy onset, rapid destruction, ring abscess, high mortality, often needs surgery
    Subacute IEPreviously damaged or deformed valve (RHD, MV prolapse, calcific stenosis, congenital defects)Viridans streptococci (50–60% of native valve cases)Insidious, weeks to months, less destruction, curable with antibiotics
    Prosthetic valve IEProsthetic (mechanical or bioprosthetic) valveEarly (within 1–2 months): skin flora, S. aureus and S. epidermidis. Late (over 1 year): streptococci, S. aureusVegetations at the prosthesis–tissue interface, ring abscess, paravalvular leak
    Cure rate poorer
    IE in intravenous drug usersRight-sided valves (tricuspid) mainly, though left-sided alsoS. aureusSeptic pulmonary emboli
    Other organismsNative valvesEnterococci, HACEK group (Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella), gram-negative bacilli, fungi (Candida, Aspergillus)Fungal and gram-negative infections have about 50% mortality
    Culture-negative IENative or prostheticNo organism isolated (about 10% of cases)Prior antibiotics, fastidious or deeply embedded organisms

    Noninfective (sterile) vegetations are a separate group: nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis and Libman-Sacks endocarditis.

    Give the pathogenesis of infective endocarditis.

    DU19M

    The development of infective endocarditis requires two ingredients, a susceptible valve and microorganisms in the bloodstream, and a series of events follows.

    1. Predisposing cardiac abnormalities. Valve damage creates a thrombogenic surface. Rheumatic heart disease was historically the commonest antecedent, now supplanted by mitral valve prolapse, degenerative calcific valvular stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve, prosthetic valves and congenital defects. Healthy valves can be infected by highly virulent organisms such as S. aureus.
    2. Bacteraemia or fungaemia. Organisms seed the blood from an infection elsewhere, dental or surgical procedures, injected drug use with contaminated needles, or even trivial breaks in the epithelial barriers of the gut, mouth and skin.
    3. Colonisation and vegetation formation. Organisms adhere to the damaged endothelium or the platelet-fibrin thrombus on the valve surface, and multiply within the growing mass of fibrin, platelets and inflammatory cells. Deeply embedded organisms are protected from host defences and antibiotics.
    4. Local and distant effects. The vegetation destroys the valve and may erode into the myocardium, forming a ring abscess. Fragments embolise, and immune complex deposition produces glomerulonephritis and other immune phenomena.

    Virulence determines the pattern: highly virulent organisms rapidly destroy even normal valves (acute IE), while low-virulence organisms infect deformed valves slowly (subacute IE). Antibiotic prophylaxis lowers risk in those with abnormal valves.

    Mention the complications of infective endocarditis.

    DU19M

    The complications of infective endocarditis generally begin within the first few weeks of illness.

    1. Cardiac: valve destruction with perforation and acute regurgitation, heart failure, ring abscess (invading the myocardium and conduction system, causing arrhythmias and heart block), pericarditis, and, with prosthetic valves, paravalvular leak.
    2. Embolic: systemic emboli from left-sided vegetations cause infarcts of the brain (stroke), spleen, kidney and heart, and septic emboli cause abscesses, septic infarcts and mycotic aneurysms (with risk of rupture and intracranial haemorrhage). Right-sided vegetations cause septic pulmonary infarcts.
    3. Immune-complex mediated: glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, Janeway lesions and rheumatoid factor.
    4. Septic: sepsis, and metastatic abscesses.

    Arrhythmias, invasion of the myocardium and systemic embolisation bode particularly ill. Untreated IE is generally fatal. With 6 or more weeks of antibiotics and/or valve replacement the cure rate is about 98% for low-virulence organisms, 60–90% for enterococci and S. aureus, and only about 50% for gram-negative bacilli or fungi.

    Cardiomyopathies

    B1

    What is cardiomyopathy? Types of cardiomyopathies.

    Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the heart muscle due to intrinsic myocardial dysfunction, excluding dysfunction secondary to coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular disease and congenital heart disease. They can be primary or secondary to systemic disease, and they are classified into three functional patterns: dilated (the most common, about 90%), hypertrophic and restrictive (the least common).

Myocarditis, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced apical ballooning), cardiotoxic drugs and radiation are other causes of myocardial disease.

    Pericardial Disease

    B1

    What is pericarditis? Important causes of pericarditis.

    Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, which occurs secondary to cardiac, thoracic or systemic disorders. Important causes are infections (viruses, pyogenic bacteria, tuberculosis), myocardial infarction and Dressler syndrome, uraemia, rheumatic fever, SLE and other immunologic disorders, cardiac surgery, neoplasms and radiation.

    Pericarditis is classified by the character of the exudate as serous, fibrinous or serofibrinous, purulent (suppurative), haemorrhagic, and caseous (tuberculous). The causes (Robbins Table 12.13) fall into groups:

    • Infectious: viruses (Coxsackie), pyogenic bacteria (by direct extension from empyema or pneumonia, or from blood), tuberculosis, fungi and parasites.
    • Immunologically mediated: rheumatic fever, SLE, scleroderma, postcardiotomy syndrome, post-MI (Dressler) syndrome and drug hypersensitivity.
    • Miscellaneous: acute myocardial infarction (2–3 days after infarction), uraemia, cardiac surgery, neoplasia (metastasis or direct extension, producing serous or haemorrhagic effusion), trauma and radiation.

    Symptoms of fibrinous pericarditis are pleuritic, positional chest pain and fever, with a loud friction rub that is lost if a large effusion separates the layers. Healing may leave adhesions, or scarring leading to constrictive pericarditis, and rapid accumulation of even 200–300 mL of fluid can cause cardiac tamponade.

    Diseases of White Blood Cells, Lymph Nodes, and Spleen (Haematolymphoid)

    6 questions, in the same order as the NMC viva list.

    B8

    WHO classification of Hodgkin lymphoma.

    The WHO classification recognises five subtypes of Hodgkin lymphoma—nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich and lymphocyte-depleted, which are grouped as classic Hodgkin lymphoma, and nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, which is a distinct non-classic type.

    The first four subtypes share a distinctive Reed-Sternberg cell immunophenotype (CD15⁺, CD30⁺, weakly PAX5⁺, usually negative for other B-cell markers, T-cell markers and CD45) and are lumped together as classic Hodgkin lymphoma. In the fifth, lymphocyte predominant type, the neoplastic cells have a B-cell immunophenotype that differs from the classic type. in the International Consensus Classification this entity has been renamed nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell lymphoma, dropping the Hodgkin designation.

    B8

    What is an R-S cell? Variants of the R-S cell. Morphology of a classical R-S cell.

    The Reed-Sternberg cell is the neoplastic giant cell of Hodgkin lymphoma, derived from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell. The classical cell is a large binucleate or multilobed cell with abundant cytoplasm and large, inclusion-like eosinophilic nucleoli, giving an "owl-eye" appearance.

    Definition and origin. The Reed-Sternberg (R-S) cell is the neoplastic cell of Hodgkin lymphoma and is essential for its diagnosis. Single-cell molecular studies show clonal IGH gene rearrangements and somatic hypermutation, establishing origin from a germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cell. Nevertheless, the R-S cells of classic Hodgkin lymphoma fail to express most B-cell–specific genes, including immunoglobulin genes.

    They constitute only a minority of cells (the tumour is more than 90% reactive lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils and plasma cells), recruited by cytokines and chemokines secreted by the R-S cells.

    Morphology of the classical (diagnostic) R-S cell. A large cell, 45 µm or more in diameter, with abundant, slightly basophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm. The nucleus is bilobed or multilobed—classically two mirror-image nuclei or lobes lying side by side—each with a thin, sharply defined nuclear membrane, vesicular, open (clear) chromatin, and a large, inclusion-like, eosinophilic or amphophilic nucleolus, about the size of a small lymphocyte (5 to 7 µm), surrounded by a clear halo, giving the "owl-eye" appearance.

    Variants

    1. Mononuclear (Hodgkin) variant: a single nucleus with a large inclusion-like nucleolus.
    2. Lacunar cell: a cell with a delicate, folded or multilobated nucleus and abundant pale cytoplasm that retracts during fixation, leaving the cell in an empty space (lacuna). Characteristic of nodular sclerosis.
    3. Lymphohistiocytic (L&H, "popcorn") variant: polypoid, multilobed nucleus with inconspicuous nucleoli, fine chromatin and moderately abundant cytoplasm. Characteristic of nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.
    4. Mummified cell: a shrunken, pyknotic cell with condensed eosinophilic cytoplasm, the result of a peculiar form of cell death in classic Hodgkin lymphoma.
    5. Pleomorphic or anaplastic variants: bizarre cells in lymphocyte-depleted (reticular) Hodgkin lymphoma.

    Immunophenotype. In classic Hodgkin lymphoma the R-S cells are CD15⁺, CD30⁺ and weakly PAX5⁺, and negative for CD45 and for most B and T-cell markers
    in nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma the L&H cells are CD20⁺, BCL6⁺, CD45⁺ and negative for CD15 and CD30.

    R-S–like cells may be seen in infectious mononucleosis, solid tumours and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, so diagnosis depends on identifying R-S cells in the appropriate inflammatory background with a confirmatory immunophenotype.

    B8

    What do you mean by generalized lymphadenopathy? Important causes of generalized lymphadenopathy.

    Generalised lymphadenopathy means enlargement of lymph nodes in two or more non-contiguous regions of the body. The important causes are systemic infections (viral, bacterial, protozoal), lymphoid and haematologic malignancies, autoimmune disorders, drug reactions and storage diseases.

    Meaning. Lymphadenopathy is an abnormality in the size (usually more than 1 cm), number or consistency of lymph nodes. It is called generalised when nodes are enlarged in two or more noncontiguous (non-adjacent) groups, in contrast to localised lymphadenopathy, in which a single region that drains a particular area is involved. The distinction is clinically important, since localised enlargement usually reflects a regional infection or tumour drainage, whereas generalised enlargement implies a systemic process.

    Mechanisms. Nodes enlarge because of (1) reactive hyperplasia of lymphoid follicles and paracortical T-cell zones in response to antigenic stimulation, (2) infiltration by inflammatory cells in lymphadenitis, (3) infiltration by neoplastic lymphoid or metastatic cells, and (4) accumulation of macrophages laden with storage material. In children, systemic viral infections and bacteraemia often produce acute generalised lymphadenopathy.

    Important causes

    • Infections: viral—infectious mononucleosis (EBV), cytomegalovirus, HIV (persistent generalised lymphadenopathy), rubella, measles, hepatitis B. Bacterial—tuberculosis, secondary syphilis, brucellosis, typhoid, plague. Protozoal and others—toxoplasmosis, kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), filariasis, histoplasmosis.
    • Neoplasms: non-Hodgkin lymphomas (especially follicular lymphoma and small lymphocytic lymphoma), Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, hairy cell leukaemia, angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Widespread metastases are an uncommon cause.
    • Autoimmune and inflammatory disorders: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, adult Still disease, sarcoidosis, dermatomyositis, Sjögren syndrome.
    • Drug reactions and serum sickness: phenytoin, allopurinol, carbamazepine, hydralazine, sulfonamides.
    • Others: lipid storage disorders (Gaucher and Niemann-Pick diseases), hyperthyroidism, Castleman disease, Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease, Rosai–Dorfman disease, amyloidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
    B8

    Differences between Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

    Hodgkin lymphoma arises in a single node or axial chain and spreads in an orderly contiguous manner, contains Reed-Sternberg cells in a predominantly reactive background and is mostly curable, whereas non-Hodgkin lymphoma commonly involves multiple peripheral nodes and extranodal sites, spreads noncontiguously and early, and is a monotonous proliferation of neoplastic lymphoid cells.

    Mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer ringRarely involvedCommonly involved

    B10

    A 60-year-old male presented to you with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. His ESR in the first hour was 100 mm. How will you approach the diagnosis? Important causes of cervical lymphadenopathy.

    In a 60-year-old with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and a very high ESR I think first of lymphoma or a lymphoid leukaemia, then tuberculosis and metastatic carcinoma from the head and neck. I would take a careful history and examine all node groups, do a blood count and smear, chest imaging, and establish the diagnosis by FNAC followed by excision biopsy of an entire node with histology and immunophenotyping.

    Interpretation of the case. A markedly raised ESR (100 mm in the first hour) indicates a significant systemic inflammatory or neoplastic process, since the ESR is raised by acute-phase proteins and by immunoglobulins. In an older adult the leading diagnoses are non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma (second incidence peak above 55 years), chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, tuberculous lymphadenitis, and metastatic carcinoma. Other possibilities include multiple myeloma, HIV infection, sarcoidosis, connective tissue disease and chronic infection.

    Approach

    1. History. Duration and rate of growth
      Painless or painful
      Constitutional (B) symptoms—unexplained fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss of more than 10%. Pruritus
      alcohol-induced node pain
      Contact with tuberculosis, cough, haemoptysis
      Sore throat, dental infection, dysphagia, hoarseness, nasal obstruction, epistaxis or deafness (nasopharyngeal and head and neck primary). Smoking and tobacco chewing
      Drug history
      HIV risk
      Bone pain.
    2. Examination. Size, number, consistency (hard, rubbery, soft), tenderness, matting, fixity and overlying skin changes of the nodes. Examination of all other node groups (axillary, inguinal, supraclavicular, epitrochlear). Hepatosplenomegaly
      Careful examination of the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx and larynx, thyroid, breasts and skin. Chest and abdominal examination.
    3. Initial investigations. Complete blood count with peripheral smear (lymphocytosis with smudge cells in CLL, anaemia, leukoerythroblastic picture, blasts)
      ESR and CRP
      Liver and renal function tests, serum LDH, uric acid, calcium. Serum protein electrophoresis
      HIV serology
      Mantoux test or interferon-gamma release assay
      Chest radiograph (mediastinal widening, hilar adenopathy, parenchymal tuberculosis). Ultrasound of the neck and abdomen.
    4. Tissue diagnosis. FNAC is a useful first step (caseating granuloma with acid-fast bacilli on ZN stain, metastatic carcinoma, or a monomorphic lymphoid population), but it is usually inadequate for diagnosing and subtyping lymphoma because architecture is lost. Excision biopsy of an entire, intact node (not a core or a node from an area of previous scarring) is the investigation of choice, with histology, immunohistochemistry (CD15, CD30, PAX5, CD20, CD3, CD5, CD23, cyclin D1, BCL2, BCL6, Ki-67), flow cytometry, and cytogenetic or molecular studies as required.
    5. Staging and further work-up if lymphoma is found. CT or PET-CT of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis
      Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy.
    6. If metastatic carcinoma is suggested. ENT examination with endoscopy and biopsy, thyroid assessment, chest imaging, and further evaluation for a primary.

    B8

    What are the types of lymphoma?

    Lymphomas are divided into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, and the non-Hodgkin group is subdivided according to the cell of origin into B-cell, T-cell and NK-cell lymphomas, many of which are further classified as indolent or aggressive.

    1. Hodgkin lymphoma: classic (nodular sclerosis, mixed cellularity, lymphocyte-rich, lymphocyte-depleted) and nodular lymphocyte predominant.

    2. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas (WHO classification of lymphoid neoplasms):

    • Precursor B-cell neoplasms: B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma.
    • Peripheral (mature) B-cell neoplasms: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma. Splenic and nodal marginal zone lymphoma, extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma. Mantle cell lymphoma

    • Peripheral T-cell and NK-cell neoplasms: T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia

    3. Clinical grouping by behaviour. Indolent (follicular lymphoma, CLL/SLL, marginal zone lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, mycosis fungoides). Moderately aggressive (mantle cell lymphoma)

The most common NHL is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, followed by follicular lymphoma. 85–90% of lymphoid neoplasms are of B-cell origin.
