    EsophagusCongenital Anomalies of GITStomachIntestines

    Esophagus

    Achalasia and reflux esophagitis

    B2

    What are achalasia and reflux esophagitis?

    Achalasia is a primary oesophageal motility disorder in which the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and the oesophageal body loses peristalsis because the inhibitory, nitric oxide–producing neurons of the myenteric plexus degenerate. it presents with dysphagia and a dilated oesophagus. Reflux oesophagitis is inflammation of the distal oesophageal squamous mucosa caused by repeated reflux of gastric contents through an incompetent lower oesophageal sphincter, and it is the clinical basis of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

    Achalasia. Achalasia is defined by a triad: incomplete relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) on swallowing, increased resting LES tone, and aperistalsis of the oesophageal body. The sphincter therefore behaves as a functional obstruction, food is retained, and the oesophagus above it dilates progressively.

    Aetiology and pathogenesis. Primary achalasia is rare and idiopathic. It results from degeneration of the nitric oxide–producing inhibitory neurons that normally relax the LES. The extra-oesophageal vagus nerve and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus may also show degenerative change. Rare familial cases are described, and an immune-mediated destruction of inhibitory neurons is suspected because some cases follow herpes simplex virus 1 infection, show linkage to immunoregulatory gene polymorphisms, or coexist with Sjögren syndrome or autoimmune thyroid disease.

    Secondary achalasia arises when the myenteric plexus is destroyed by another process. The classic example is Chagas disease, in which Trypanosoma cruzi infection destroys the myenteric plexus (and may involve the duodenal, colonic, and ureteric plexuses as well). Other causes include diabetic autonomic neuropathy, infiltrative disorders such as malignancy, amyloidosis, and sarcoidosis, systemic sclerosis, lesions of the dorsal motor nucleus (for example after poliomyelitis), and Down syndrome.

    Morphology and clinical features. The oesophagus above the sphincter is dilated, with hypertrophy of the muscularis in the early stage and thinning later. Histology shows a reduced number or absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus with a variable chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Patients have dysphagia for both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, difficulty in belching, and chest pain, and aspiration pneumonia may follow nocturnal regurgitation.

    A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus tapering to a "bird-beak" narrowing, and manometry confirms the diagnosis. Stasis oesophagitis and candidiasis may occur. There is a modestly increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma, but not enough to justify surveillance endoscopy. Treatment is directed at overcoming the obstruction: pneumatic balloon dilation, botulinum toxin injection to inhibit contraction-promoting cholinergic neurons, or surgical myotomy.

    Reflux oesophagitis. Reflux of gastric contents into the lower oesophagus is the commonest cause of oesophagitis and the most frequent outpatient gastrointestinal diagnosis in high-income countries. The stratified squamous epithelium is highly abrasion resistant but is sensitive to gastric acid and pepsin, and bile may add to the injury.

    Pathogenesis. The major mechanism is transient relaxation of the LES, mediated through vagal pathways and triggered by gastric distention. Reflux also follows abrupt rises in intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, straining, bending). Predisposing conditions include alcohol and tobacco use, obesity, central nervous system depressants, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, delayed gastric emptying, increased gastric volume, and drugs or foods that lower LES pressure.

    Morphology. Mild disease may show only hyperaemia, with unremarkable histology. More severe reflux produces erosions, basal zone hyperplasia, elongation of the lamina propria papillae, and infiltration of the squamous mucosa by eosinophils. Neutrophils appear later or when infection or chemical injury is superimposed. Chronic injury leads to ulceration, fibrosis, and stricture.

    Clinical features and complications. Symptoms are heartburn, regurgitation of sour-tasting fluid, and dysphagia, most often after meals, and they may be mistaken for ischaemic heart disease. Symptom severity correlates poorly with the histologic damage. Diagnosis is usually clinical
    Endoscopy is reserved for patients who fail proton pump inhibitor therapy or in whom complications are suspected.

    Proton pump inhibitors relieve symptoms in up to 90% of patients. The complications are erosive oesophagitis with bleeding, ulceration, peptic stricture, Barrett oesophagus, and, through Barrett oesophagus, oesophageal adenocarcinoma. A sliding hiatal hernia, in which the gastroesophageal junction herniates through the diaphragmatic hiatus, may impair LES competence and produce a similar syndrome.

    Esophageal varices

    B2

    What are esophageal varices? Mention their mechanism.

    Oesophageal varices are tortuous, dilated submucosal veins in the lower oesophagus (and proximal stomach) that develop as portosystemic collaterals when portal venous pressure is raised, most commonly because of cirrhosis. They matter because large varices can rupture and cause massive, life-threatening haematemesis.

    Mechanism. Portal hypertension, defined as increased resistance to portal blood flow, may be prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis or narrowing, splenic vein flow increase), intrahepatic (cirrhosis, which accounts for most cases; schistosomiasis, massive fatty change, sarcoidosis, nodular regenerative hyperplasia), or posthepatic (severe right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, hepatic vein outflow obstruction).

    In cirrhosis, resistance is raised at the level of the sinusoids by scarring and nodule formation, by contraction of sinusoidal smooth muscle cells and myofibroblasts, and by endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide and increased endothelin-1. At the same time, splanchnic arteriolar vasodilation, driven chiefly by nitric oxide, produces a hyperdynamic circulation that increases portal inflow.

    Because the portal system has no valves, blood seeks alternative pathways to the systemic venous circulation wherever the portal and caval systems communicate. At the gastroesophageal junction, blood from the left gastric (coronary) vein is diverted through the subepithelial and submucosal venous plexuses of the distal oesophagus into the azygos system. These thin-walled veins become congested and dilated, forming varices.

    Varices are most common in alcohol-associated cirrhosis but complicate cirrhosis of any cause. non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (presinusoidal as in schistosomiasis, sinusoidal as in amyloidosis, postsinusoidal as in Budd–Chiari syndrome) can also produce them. They are present in about 30% of patients with compensated cirrhosis and about 60% of those with decompensated cirrhosis.

    Morphology. Varices are dilated, tortuous veins within the mucosa and submucosa of the distal oesophagus and proximal stomach that bulge into the lumen under an intact, thinned mucosa. After rupture there may be mucosal ulceration, thrombosis, inflammation, and evidence of prior sclerotherapy or band ligation.

    B2

    What are esophageal varices? Mention their mechanism and complications.

    Oesophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins of the distal oesophagus that form as collateral channels when raised portal pressure, usually from cirrhosis, diverts blood through the left gastric–azygos connections. Their principal complication is variceal rupture with torrential haematemesis, which is a medical emergency with a high mortality.

    Definition and mechanism. Oesophageal varices are tortuous, dilated veins in the lower oesophageal submucosa and mucosa. They are caused by portal hypertension, which most often results from cirrhosis. Increased portal venous pressure opens collateral channels at sites where the portal and systemic venous beds communicate: the oesophagogastric junction, the anorectal junction (haemorrhoids), the falciform ligament (periumbilical veins, giving caput medusae), and the retroperitoneum.

    In the oesophagus the collateral flow passes from the left gastric vein through the oesophageal submucosal plexus to the azygos vein. The plexus has little connective tissue support and dilates under the high pressure. Two factors sustain portal hypertension: increased intrahepatic (sinusoidal) resistance from fibrosis, nodule formation, and vasoconstrictor mediators, and increased portal inflow from splanchnic vasodilation mediated by nitric oxide.

    Complications

    • Variceal haemorrhage is the major complication. Large or tortuous varices, high hepatic venous pressure gradient, red colour signs, previous bleeding, and advanced liver disease increase the risk of rupture. Each episode carries a mortality of roughly 15% to 20%, and more than half of survivors rebleed within one year.
    • Hypovolemic shock and death, directly from exsanguination or from precipitation of hepatic failure, since blood in the gut gives a large nitrogen load that provokes hepatic encephalopathy.
    • Infection (aspiration pneumonia, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) after a bleed.
    • Renal failure (hepatorenal syndrome) after haemorrhage.
    • Ulceration, thrombosis, and stricture of the oesophageal wall after rupture, banding, or sclerotherapy.

    Management comprises resuscitation, splanchnic vasoconstrictors, endoscopic variceal ligation or sclerotherapy, balloon tamponade, and, for prevention, non-selective beta-blockers and repeated ligation. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting is used for refractory bleeding.

    Barrett esophagus

    B2

    What is Barrett esophagus? Mention its clinical importance. How will you diagnose?

    Barrett oesophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux in which the normal squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus is replaced by metaplastic intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. Its importance is that it is the precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and it is diagnosed by endoscopy with biopsy showing columnar mucosa with goblet cells above the gastroesophageal junction.

    Definition and pathogenesis. Barrett oesophagus is intestinal metaplasia of the oesophageal squamous mucosa arising in the setting of long-standing GERD. Chronic exposure of the squamous epithelium to acid and bile reflux leads to replacement by a more acid-resistant columnar epithelium. It is estimated to occur in up to 10% of persons with symptomatic GERD and in about 2% of the general population
    it is most common in white men between 40 and 60 years of age, and obesity (central) is a recognised risk factor.

    Morphology. Endoscopically, tongues or circumferential bands of red, velvety mucosa extend upward from the gastroesophageal junction, alternating with residual pale, smooth squamous mucosa. The segment is classified as long (3 cm or more) or short (less than 3 cm). Histologically, the squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium of intestinal type, with goblet cells (the diagnostic feature) whose distended mucin vacuoles stain pale blue and give the cytoplasm the shape of a wine goblet, along with non-goblet columnar cells.

    Dysplasia, graded as low or high, is characterised by nuclear hyperchromasia, stratification, loss of polarity, irregular budding glands, and gland-within-gland architecture. Invasion into the lamina propria defines intramucosal carcinoma.

    Clinical importance

    1. It is the only recognised precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Most adenocarcinomas arise in Barrett oesophagus, although most patients with Barrett oesophagus never develop cancer.
    2. The cancer risk is greatest with goblet-cell metaplasia, long-segment disease, increasing age, male sex, and especially the presence and grade of dysplasia.
    3. Because dysplasia is a treatable preinvasive stage, Barrett oesophagus justifies surveillance endoscopy and biopsy, and dysplasia may be treated by radiofrequency ablation or endoscopic mucosal resection.
    4. It also signifies long-standing reflux disease and may be complicated by ulcer and stricture.

    Diagnosis. The diagnosis is made by upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, which demonstrates columnar-lined mucosa extending above the gastroesophageal junction, followed by systematic biopsy (four-quadrant biopsies at regular intervals along the segment plus targeted biopsies of any visible lesion). Histology confirms intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells (highlighted by Alcian blue at pH 2.5), and the biopsy must be assessed for dysplasia. a diagnosis of high-grade dysplasia is usually confirmed by a second pathologist. Chromoendoscopy or narrow-band imaging increases the yield of surveillance biopsies.

    What is Barrett esophagus?

    DU08JuDU06SDU06Ja

    Barrett oesophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease in which the stratified squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium of intestinal type, and it is associated with an increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma. The metaplastic mucosa is acquired as an adaptive response to chronic injury by gastric acid and bile, because columnar epithelium is more resistant to the refluxate than squamous epithelium.

    Grossly, it appears as tongues or patches of red, velvety mucosa extending upward from the gastroesophageal junction, interspersed with islands of residual pale squamous mucosa. a segment of 3 cm or more is called long-segment and one of less than 3 cm short-segment disease. Microscopically, the squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar cells, among which goblet cells, with their distended pale-blue mucin vacuoles, are the diagnostic cell type. gastric-type foveolar cells are also present. Dysplasia, if present, is graded as low or high.

    It occurs in about 10% of persons with symptomatic GERD, is commonest in white men aged 40 to 60 years, and is increasing in incidence. Its significance lies in its progression, through dysplasia, to adenocarcinoma, and it is diagnosed by endoscopy with biopsy.

    Mention the clinical importance of Barrett esophagus.

    DU08Ju

    The clinical importance of Barrett oesophagus rests on its malignant potential. It is the precursor lesion of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, the incidence of which has risen sharply in Western countries in parallel with GERD and obesity. Barrett epithelium acquires driver mutations (for example in TP53 and CDKN2A) in a stepwise fashion, progressing from metaplasia to low-grade dysplasia, high-grade dysplasia, intramucosal carcinoma, and invasive adenocarcinoma. Risk is highest with goblet-cell metaplasia, long-segment involvement, advancing age, male sex, white race, and dysplasia, whereas short-segment disease carries a lower risk.

    Its recognition therefore has several practical consequences. Patients are placed under endoscopic surveillance with a standardised biopsy protocol, although the effect of surveillance on survival remains debated. Dysplasia can be eradicated by radiofrequency ablation or endoscopic mucosal resection, and oesophagectomy is reserved for multifocal high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma that is unsuitable for endoscopic therapy.

    Early adenocarcinoma confined to the mucosa or submucosa has a 5-year survival of about 80%, compared with less than 25% once symptomatic. Barrett oesophagus also indicates long-standing reflux and may be complicated by ulceration, haemorrhage, and stricture, and it may be asymptomatic, particularly in short-segment disease.

    Esophageal carcinoma

    B2

    Mention the sites and types of esophageal cancer.

    Nearly all oesophageal cancers are either squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma, the commoner type worldwide, arises mainly in the upper and middle thirds of the oesophagus, whereas adenocarcinoma arises in the distal third on a background of Barrett oesophagus and may involve the gastric cardia.

    Gross patterns. Early lesions are small, grey-white, plaque-like thickenings. Advanced tumours are polypoid (fungating), ulcerated, or diffusely infiltrative, with thickening, rigidity, and luminal narrowing.

    Spread. The rich lymphatic network promotes longitudinal and circumferential spread with intramural satellite nodules.     Other types. Rare malignancies include undifferentiated carcinoma, neuroendocrine (small cell) carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, and sarcomas. Leiomyoma is the commonest benign tumour, arising in the oesophageal wall.

    Stomach

    Gastritis

    B2

    What is gastritis? What are the characteristics of Helicobacter pylori-associated and autoimmune gastritis?

    Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa, recognised histologically by the presence of neutrophils or chronic inflammatory cells (when inflammatory cells are scanty the lesion is called gastropathy). The commonest cause of chronic gastritis is Helicobacter pylori, which produces an antral-predominant gastritis with increased acid, whereas autoimmune gastritis is a body- and fundus-restricted atrophic gastritis with parietal cell loss, achlorhydria, hypergastrinaemia, and pernicious anaemia.

    Definition and classification. Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa. Acute gastritis (and gastropathy) results from agents that overwhelm mucosal defences (NSAIDs, alcohol, bile, chemotherapy, radiation, ischaemia, stress, uraemia) and shows oedema, congestion, foveolar hyperplasia, neutrophils, and in severe cases erosion and haemorrhage. In the gastrointestinal tract, "acute" refers to the duration of disease rather than to the pattern of inflammation.

    Chronic gastritis is caused most commonly by H. pylori
    Other causes include NSAIDs, autoimmune gastritis, radiation, chronic bile reflux, mechanical injury, and systemic disease such as Crohn disease, amyloidosis, and graft-versus-host disease. Symptoms of chronic gastritis are milder but more persistent than in acute disease: nausea, upper abdominal pain, and sometimes vomiting, with haematemesis uncommon.

    Helicobacter pylori–associated gastritis. H. pylori is a spiral, curved bacillus adapted to the gastric mucus niche. Infection is acquired in childhood by the fecal–oral route, is associated with poverty and crowding, and persists for life without treatment. Virulence depends on flagella (motility in mucus), urease (generates ammonia from urea and raises local pH), adhesins (attachment to foveolar cells), and toxins such as CagA and VacA. Host factors such as pro-inflammatory polymorphisms of TNF and IL-1 and reduced IL-10 influence the outcome.

    The infection typically causes a predominantly antral gastritis with normal or increased acid production. Inflammation enhances antral gastrin production, which expands the parietal cell mass and increases acid secretion, predisposing to peptic ulcer. Long-standing infection may extend to the body and fundus (pangastritis), causing patchy atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and reduced acid secretion, which increases the risk of adenocarcinoma.

    Histologically, organisms lie in the superficial mucus overlying foveolar cells (best seen with special stains or immunostains). The lamina propria contains numerous plasma cells, lymphocytes, and neutrophils, which cross the basement membrane to form pit abscesses. Lymphoid aggregates with germinal centres (induced MALT) are common and may give rise to MALT lymphoma. Diagnosis rests on biopsy, rapid urease test, culture, PCR, urea breath test, stool antigen, or serology
    Treatment is a proton pump inhibitor with antibiotics.

    Autoimmune gastritis. This accounts for less than 10% of chronic gastritis and is the second or third most frequent cause after H. pylori and NSAIDs. It is an autoimmune attack, mediated by CD4⁺ T cells and antibodies, on the parietal cells of the oxyntic mucosa, with antibodies to H⁺,K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) and to intrinsic factor. It affects the body and fundus and characteristically spares the antrum.

    The loss of parietal cells leads to achlorhydria, which stimulates antral G-cell hyperplasia and marked hypergastrinaemia, and to loss of intrinsic factor with defective ileal absorption of vitamin B₁₂, producing megaloblastic (pernicious) anaemia, atrophic glossitis, and neurologic complications such as subacute combined degeneration. Serum pepsinogen I is low. Morphologically, the oxyntic mucosa is thinned with loss of rugae, and there is a deep lymphocytic and plasma-cell infiltrate centred on the glands with lymphoid follicles. Intestinal metaplasia and endocrine cell hyperplasia are common, and the latter may progress to small multicentric neuroendocrine tumours.

    It occurs most often in older women, is associated with other autoimmune diseases (Hashimoto thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes mellitus, Addison disease), and carries an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

    Antrum spared
    Inflammatory infiltrateNeutrophils, subepithelial plasma cellsLymphocytes, macrophages
    Acid productionIncreased to slightly decreasedDecreased (achlorhydria)
    GastrinNormal to increasedMarkedly increased
    Other lesionsHyperplastic/inflammatory polypsNeuroendocrine hyperplasia

    Peptic ulcer disease

    B2

    Define ulcer. Mention the ulcers of stomach.

    An ulcer is a local defect or excavation of the surface of an organ or tissue produced by the sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue. In the stomach the principal ulcers are the chronic peptic ulcer, acute stress ulcers and erosions, drug (NSAID)-induced ulcers, and ulcerating malignancies.

    Definition. An ulcer is a break in the continuity of an epithelial surface, in which a defect extending at least into the submucosa results from sloughing of necrotic inflamed tissue. An erosion, by contrast, is a superficial defect confined to the mucosa.

    Ulcers of the stomach

    1. Chronic peptic (gastric) ulcer, usually solitary, on the lesser curvature at the junction of body and antrum, arising on a background of chronic H. pylori gastritis or NSAID injury.
    2. Acute stress-related mucosal ulcers, which are multiple, shallow, and found throughout the stomach in patients with shock, sepsis, severe trauma, or burns (Curling ulcers) or intracranial disease (Cushing ulcers).
    3. Drug-induced ulcers and erosions, notably NSAIDs and aspirin, alcohol, corticosteroids (potentiating NSAIDs), and cytotoxic drugs.
    4. Ulcers of Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), which are multiple and may involve the stomach, duodenum, and jejunum.
    5. Malignant ulcers, namely ulcerated gastric adenocarcinoma and occasionally lymphoma.
    6. Rarer lesions: ulcers in granulomatous gastritis (Crohn disease, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis), infectious ulcers (CMV, herpes simplex), ischaemic or radiation ulcers, and bleeding from a Dieulafoy lesion (abnormal submucosal artery eroding the mucosa).
    B2

    List the ulcers in the GIT.

    Ulcers occur throughout the gastrointestinal tract and are classified by site and cause: aphthous and herpetic ulcers in the mouth, reflux, viral, pill, and Barrett ulcers in the oesophagus, peptic and stress ulcers in the stomach and duodenum, typhoid, tuberculous, Crohn, and ischaemic ulcers in the small bowel, and ulcerative colitis, amoebic, bacillary, pseudomembranous, ischaemic, and malignant ulcers in the large bowel.

    What is PUD? Mention the common sites of peptic ulcer.

    Peptic ulcer disease is chronic mucosal ulceration of the stomach or duodenum caused by an imbalance between mucosal defences and acid–peptic injury, almost always associated with H. pylori infection, NSAID use, or smoking. The commonest site is the first part of the duodenum, followed by the lesser curvature of the stomach near the junction of the body and antrum.

    Definition. Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is a chronic, usually solitary, mucosal ulceration that arises in areas of the alimentary tract exposed to acid and pepsin. It is almost always associated with H. pylori infection, NSAIDs, or cigarette smoking, and it develops on a background of chronic gastritis. The commonest form arises in the gastric antrum or duodenum in association with H. pylori antral gastritis, which increases acid secretion and reduces duodenal bicarbonate secretion. Patients with gastric mucosal atrophy, who secrete little acid, are protected.

    Common sites

    1. First part (proximal duodenum), within a few centimetres of the pyloric valve, is the most frequent site. Duodenal ulcers outnumber gastric ulcers, and they occur typically on the anterior wall (tendency to perforate) or posterior wall (tendency to bleed).
    2. Stomach, predominantly the lesser curvature near the junction of the body and the antrum (the angularis).
    3. Less common sites: the pyloric channel, the margin of a gastrojejunostomy (marginal ulcer), the lower oesophagus (reflux ulcer and Barrett oesophagus, or acid secreted by an oesophageal inlet patch), the jejunum in Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, and an ileal Meckel diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa.
    B2

    What is PUD? What are the risk factors for PUD?

    Peptic ulcer disease is chronic, usually solitary ulceration of the duodenum or stomach resulting from an imbalance between mucosal defences and acid–peptic injury. The dominant risk factors are H. pylori infection and NSAID use, with smoking, corticosteroids, and other conditions contributing.

    Definition. PUD is chronic mucosal ulceration affecting the duodenum or stomach, sharply punched out, usually solitary, and developing on a background of chronic gastritis.

    Risk factors

    • *Helicobacter pylori* infection, the most important factor
      Antral gastritis increases acid secretion and gastrin, and reduces duodenal bicarbonate.
    • NSAIDs, including aspirin and selective COX-2 inhibitors, which inhibit prostaglandin E₂ and I₂ synthesis and so reduce mucus, bicarbonate, mucosal blood flow, and epithelial repair. The effect is potentiated by corticosteroids, and amplified in the elderly and in H. pylori–infected individuals.
    • Cigarette smoking, which synergises with H. pylori (particularly for gastric ulcers) and impairs mucosal blood flow and healing.
    • Hypersecretory states: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) and endocrine cell hyperplasia, which stimulate parietal cell growth and acid secretion.
    • Associated diseases: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, alcoholic cirrhosis (mainly duodenal ulcers), cardiovascular disease and other conditions with reduced mucosal blood flow, chronic renal failure, and hyperparathyroidism.
    • Drugs and toxins: illicit drugs such as cocaine that reduce mucosal blood flow. alcohol.
    • Other: psychological stress (may increase acid secretion), viral infections (CMV, herpes simplex virus), genetic susceptibility, and blood group O.
    B2

    What are the differences between benign and malignant ulcers?

    A benign (peptic) ulcer is typically small, round or oval, and sharply punched out with a clean smooth base and radiating mucosal folds, whereas a malignant ulcer is large, irregular, and has heaped-up, rolled everted margins, a shaggy necrotic base, and folds that are clubbed, fused, or amputated at the edge.

    Whatever the appearance, every gastric ulcer must be biopsied (multiple biopsies from the margin and base), because some malignant ulcers mimic benign ones and cure after medical therapy does not exclude cancer.

    B2

    How is PUD formed? What are the complications of PUD?

    Peptic ulcer forms when damaging forces (gastric acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overwhelm the protective mechanisms of the mucosa, on a background of chronic gastritis. The main complications are haemorrhage, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction, with penetration, intractable pain, and rarely malignant change.

    Formation. The gastric mucosa is protected by a mucus–bicarbonate barrier, tight epithelial junctions that limit back-diffusion of acid, rapid epithelial renewal, prostaglandin synthesis, and a rich mucosal blood supply that removes any acid that has diffused into the lamina propria. A peptic ulcer arises when these defences are impaired or the damaging factors are excessive.

    H. pylori is the principal cause. The organism lives in the gastric mucus and does not invade the tissues
    it injures the mucosa through urease-generated ammonia, CagA and VacA toxins, and the inflammatory response (neutrophils, TNF, IL-1). Antral gastritis increases gastrin and acid secretion and reduces duodenal bicarbonate secretion. The acid load produces gastric metaplasia in the duodenum, which becomes colonised and inflamed and finally ulcerates.

    NSAIDs cause ulceration by inhibiting COX-dependent prostaglandin synthesis. Smoking reduces mucosal blood flow and healing, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome produces massive acid hypersecretion. Peptic ulcers therefore arise on a background of chronic gastritis.

    Complications

    1. Haemorrhage: the most frequent complication (about 15% to 20% of patients)
      Erosion of a thickened vessel in the scarred base (the gastroduodenal artery in posterior duodenal ulcers) causes haematemesis, melaena, or chronic blood loss with iron deficiency anaemia, and it can be life threatening.
    2. Perforation: about 5% of patients, but it accounts for about two-thirds of ulcer-related deaths and is rarely the first indication of an ulcer
      it is commonest with anterior duodenal ulcers and causes peritonitis, with free air under the diaphragm on an upright abdominal radiograph.
    3. Obstruction (about 2%): from oedema or scarring, mostly with pyloric channel and duodenal ulcers, causing incapacitating pain, repeated vomiting, and rarely complete outlet obstruction with metabolic alkalosis.
    4. Penetration into adjacent organs (pancreas, causing back pain; liver) and fistula formation.
    5. Intractable pain and recurrence.
    6. Malignant transformation: rare, and almost exclusively a concern with gastric (not duodenal) ulcers, most of which were malignant from the outset.
    B2

    Tell the morphological features of PUD.

    A peptic ulcer is usually a solitary, round to oval, sharply punched-out defect with a smooth clean base and radiating folds, and microscopically its base shows four zones: fibrinous debris, neutrophilic exudate, granulation tissue, and fibrous scar.

    Gross. More than 80% of peptic ulcers are solitary. They are round to oval, usually less than 3 to 4 cm, with a sharply punched-out appearance. The mucosal margin is usually level with the surrounding mucosa, though it may overhang the base, particularly proximally. heaped-up margins suggest carcinoma. The base is smooth and clean because of peptic digestion of exudate and may be stained brown or black by altered blood.

    Scarring may involve the full thickness of the wall and draws the surrounding mucosa into folds that radiate outward like spokes of a wheel. The commonest sites are the first part of the duodenum and the lesser curvature of the stomach.

    Microscopic. The ulcer extends through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa or deeper, and the base has four layers: (1) a thin superficial layer of necrotic fibrinoid debris, often with neutrophils. (2) a zone of active, predominantly neutrophilic inflammation. (3) granulation tissue with immature vessels, neutrophils, and mononuclear cells. and (4) a deep fibrous or collagenous scar that may extend into or through the muscularis propria.

    Vessels within the scar are thickened (endarteritis obliterans) and occasionally thrombosed, and eroded vessels account for bleeding. The adjacent mucosa shows chronic gastritis, and foveolar metaplasia is common in duodenal disease, as a protective response.

    Ulcerative lesions of the gastrointestinal tract can be grouped by cause.

    What is peptic ulcer disease (PUD)?

    8DU26MDU24MDU19NovDU17NovDU14JaDU13JaDU11JaDU07Ja

    Peptic ulcer disease is chronic mucosal ulceration of the duodenum or stomach, caused by an imbalance between the protective mechanisms of the mucosa and the damaging action of gastric acid and pepsin. It is almost always associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, the use of NSAIDs, or cigarette smoking, and it develops on a background of chronic gastritis (Table 17.3).

    The ulcers are typically solitary, round to oval, sharply punched out, with a clean base, and they penetrate through the muscularis mucosae. They occur most frequently in the first part of the duodenum and on the lesser curvature of the stomach. The classic symptom is epigastric burning or gnawing pain, occurring one to three hours after meals, worse at night, and relieved by food or alkali.

    Haemorrhage, perforation, and gastric outlet obstruction are the main complications. Eradication of H. pylori, acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors, and withdrawal of NSAIDs heal most ulcers, and the recurrence rate after successful eradication is less than 20%.

    The commonest site of peptic ulcer is the proximal duodenum, within a few centimetres of the pyloric valve, usually the anterior or posterior wall of the first part. In the stomach, the commonest site is the lesser curvature near the junction of the body and the antrum. Less common sites include the pyloric channel, the gastrojejunal anastomotic margin, the lower oesophagus (in reflux disease or in Barrett oesophagus), the jejunum in Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, and a Meckel diverticulum containing gastric mucosa.

    Write down the predisposing factors for peptic ulcer.

    DU25MDU21MDU18Nov

    The predisposing factors for peptic ulcer disease are:

    1. Helicobacter pylori infection, the most important cause, through chronic antral gastritis, increased acid and gastrin, and reduced duodenal bicarbonate.
    2. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and aspirin, which inhibit protective prostaglandin synthesis. Their effect is potentiated by corticosteroids.
    3. Cigarette smoking, which synergises with H. pylori in gastric ulcer and impairs mucosal blood flow and healing.
    4. Zollinger–Ellison syndrome and other hypersecretory states, including endocrine cell hyperplasia.
    5. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, alcoholic cirrhosis (mainly duodenal ulcer), chronic renal failure, hyperparathyroidism, and cardiovascular disease.
    6. Illicit drugs such as cocaine that reduce mucosal blood flow, and alcohol.
    7. Psychological stress, which may increase gastric acid secretion.
    8. Viral infections (cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus), genetic predisposition, and blood group O.

    Write in short about the pathogenesis of PUD.

    DU24MDU22N

    Peptic ulcer results from an imbalance between damaging factors (gastric acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs, bile) and the defensive mechanisms of the mucosa (mucus and bicarbonate secretion, tight epithelial barrier, prostaglandins, mucosal blood flow, epithelial renewal), and it develops on a background of chronic gastritis.

    H. pylori is the principal cause. Residing in the mucus overlying the surface epithelium, it produces urease (ammonia, raising local pH), adhesins, flagella, and the CagA and VacA toxins, and it elicits a neutrophilic and lymphoplasmacytic response. Antral gastritis increases gastrin secretion and expands the parietal cell mass, so acid secretion rises, while duodenal bicarbonate secretion falls. Gastric metaplasia of the duodenal epithelium then allows colonisation of the duodenum and ulceration.

    NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase and so the synthesis of prostaglandins E₂ and I₂, which support mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow, and epithelial restitution. Smoking, ischaemia, and hypersecretory states add to the injury. Atrophic gastritis with low acid output protects against ulcer but predisposes to carcinoma.

    Explain: H. pylori does not invade the tissues but can cause peptic ulcer.

    DU08Ju

    Helicobacter pylori is a non-invasive organism that lives in the gastric mucus, attached to the surface of the foveolar epithelial cells and in the superficial mucus layer, and it is not found within the mucosal tissues. It nevertheless causes peptic ulcer through indirect mechanisms.

    First, it damages the epithelium and the mucus barrier from the luminal side: urease splits urea into ammonia, which neutralises acid locally to allow bacterial survival but is itself toxic to the epithelium and inhibits bicarbonate transport. The CagA protein (injected into epithelial cells) and the VacA cytotoxin disturb epithelial function. Second, the bacterium provokes a vigorous host inflammatory response, with neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and cytokines such as TNF and IL-1, that injures the mucosa.

    Third, antral inflammation raises gastrin and thus acid secretion and reduces duodenal bicarbonate secretion, so the acid–peptic load on the mucosa increases. The damaged mucosa, exposed to acid and pepsin, then breaks down into an ulcer. Thus the ulcer is the result of the interplay of the bacterial virulence factors, the host immune response, and acid, rather than of tissue invasion by the organism.

    Barium mealNiche projects beyond the lumen outlineCrater inside the lumen outline with an irregular filling defect
    HistologyInflammation and granulation tissue with fibrous scarAdenocarcinoma cells infiltrating the wall
    BehaviourHeals with acid suppression and H. pylori eradicationFails to heal
    Nodal and liver metastases

    Definitive differentiation is by endoscopic biopsy from the margins and base of the ulcer (multiple biopsies), and healing should be confirmed at follow-up endoscopy.

    Write the microscopic features/morphology of peptic ulcer.

    DU14JaDU13JaDU09Ju

    Microscopically, a chronic peptic ulcer extends through the muscularis mucosae and has a characteristic four-layered base. The superficial layer is a thin zone of necrotic fibrinoid debris containing neutrophils. Beneath it is a layer of active inflammation with a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate. Deeper is a zone of granulation tissue with proliferating, immature vessels, together with neutrophils and mononuclear leukocytes. At the bottom is a fibrous or collagenous scar, which may extend through the muscularis propria and sometimes to the serosa, drawing the surrounding mucosa into radiating folds. Vessels in the scar are thickened (endarteritis obliterans) and may be thrombosed
    Arteries eroded by the ulcer are the source of haemorrhage. The surrounding mucosa shows chronic gastritis, often with foveolar metaplasia in duodenal ulcers, and the epithelium at the margin shows regenerative change without dysplasia.

    Grossly, the ulcer is solitary, round to oval, sharply punched out, with a smooth, clean base and radiating folds.

    Mention the complications of PUD.

    9DU26MDU24MDU23NDU22NDU19NovDU15JaDU14JaDU13JaDU11Ja

    The complications of peptic ulcer disease are (Table 17.4):

    1. Haemorrhage, the commonest (about 15% to 20%), presenting as haematemesis, melaena, or chronic blood loss and iron deficiency anaemia. it may be life threatening and results from erosion of vessels in the ulcer base.
    2. Perforation (about 5%), accounting for about two-thirds of ulcer-related deaths. it produces acute peritonitis, shock, and free air under the diaphragm, and is most common with anterior duodenal ulcers.
    3. Gastric outlet obstruction (about 2%), due to scarring and oedema of pyloric channel or duodenal ulcers, causing incapacitating pain, vomiting, and, if prolonged, dehydration and hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.
    4. Penetration into the pancreas, liver, or other adjacent structures, with referred back pain, and fistula formation.
    5. Intractable pain and chronicity with recurrent ulceration.
    6. Malignant transformation, rare, and concerned chiefly with gastric ulcers.

    A patient with long-standing PUD has repeated/prolonged vomiting. What will be his electrolyte and acid-base status?

    6DU24MDU16JuDU10JuDU09JuDU08JaDU07Ja

    Repeated, prolonged vomiting in a patient with long-standing peptic ulcer disease indicates gastric outlet obstruction from pyloric or duodenal scarring, and it produces hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with dehydration and hyponatraemia.

    Vomiting removes gastric juice, which is rich in hydrochloric acid, so the body loses H⁺ and Cl⁻. Each H⁺ secreted into the stomach leaves a bicarbonate ion in the blood. Normally this bicarbonate is offset when acid reaches the duodenum and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion, but when the acid is vomited (or retained above an obstruction) this balancing step is lost, so plasma bicarbonate rises, giving metabolic alkalosis.

    Loss of fluid and sodium causes volume depletion, which stimulates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone axis. Aldosterone promotes sodium (and bicarbonate) reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions, so renal potassium loss produces hypokalaemia and a paradoxical aciduria develops even though the systemic pH is alkaline. Hypokalaemia itself promotes hydrogen ion shift into cells and renal H⁺ secretion, aggravating the alkalosis. Compensatory hypoventilation raises PCO₂ modestly. The reduction in ionised calcium that accompanies alkalosis may precipitate tetany.

    The biochemical profile is therefore low serum Cl⁻ and K⁺, low or low-normal Na⁺, high bicarbonate, arterial pH above 7.45, with low urinary chloride in the early stage.

    Same (40y): what test confirms it in the laboratory?

    DU24M

    The laboratory confirmation of the metabolic disturbance is by measurement of serum electrolytes and arterial blood gas analysis. Serum shows hypochloraemia, hypokalaemia, and raised bicarbonate (total CO₂), with hyponatraemia and a raised urea and creatinine from prerenal azotaemia. Arterial blood gas shows a raised pH (above 7.45) with raised bicarbonate and a compensatory modest rise in PCO₂, and urinary chloride is low (less than 10 mEq/L), indicating a chloride-responsive alkalosis. The cause of the vomiting, gastric outlet obstruction, is confirmed by upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (with biopsy of any gastric lesion to exclude carcinoma), a barium meal, or a saline load (succussion splash) test.

    Same (55y): what is the likely diagnosis of his present illness?

    DU16Ju

    The likely diagnosis is gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis) due to a chronic peptic ulcer, caused by fibrous scarring and oedema of a pyloric channel or duodenal ulcer. Obstruction occurs in about 2% of ulcer patients and is most often associated with ulcers of the pyloric channel. The result is persistent, often projectile vomiting of undigested food, weight loss, dehydration, and hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

    Acquired pyloric stenosis in adults may also be caused by antral gastritis or by carcinoma of the distal stomach or the pancreas, which narrows the pyloric channel by fibrosis or infiltration. Therefore, in a 55-year-old, endoscopy with biopsy is mandatory to exclude a malignant obstruction.

    A 30y man has epigastric pain after meals and at late night with nausea, vomiting. What is the likely diagnosis?

    DUno yr

    The likely diagnosis is peptic ulcer disease, most probably a duodenal ulcer. The characteristic pain is an epigastric burning or gnawing discomfort that occurs one to three hours after meals, is worse at night (typically between 11 p.m. and 2 a.m.), and is relieved by food or alkali. Nausea, vomiting, bloating, and belching may accompany it. The disease is usually caused by H. pylori–induced antral gastritis with increased acid secretion, and NSAID use, smoking, and stress contribute. The diagnosis is confirmed by upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy and testing for H. pylori (rapid urease test, histology, urea breath test, stool antigen).

    Same: what complications can occur?

    DUno yr

    The complications are those of peptic ulcer disease: haemorrhage (haematemesis, melaena, iron deficiency anaemia), perforation with peritonitis, gastric outlet obstruction from scarring (with persistent vomiting and hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis), penetration into the pancreas or adjacent organs, and intractable, recurrent pain. Malignant change is a concern only for gastric ulcers.

    H. pylori-related diseases

    B2

    Enumerate the H. pylori-related diseases of the stomach.

    Helicobacter pylori causes acute and chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease of the stomach and duodenum, gastric adenocarcinoma, and gastric MALT lymphoma, together with polyps and atrophic changes that link them.

    1. Acute gastritis: usually mild and self-limited, with nonspecific dyspeptic symptoms at the time of infection.
    2. Chronic gastritis: initially a superficial antral gastritis with plasma cells, lymphocytes, and neutrophils (pit abscesses), and lymphoid follicles with germinal centres. Later a pangastritis.
    3. Chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia (environmental metaplastic atrophic gastritis): patchy, without autoantibodies, with reduced acid output.
    4. Peptic ulcer disease: gastric ulcer and, through increased antral gastrin and acid, duodenal ulcer.
    5. Hyperplastic and inflammatory gastric polyps, which arise in the setting of chronic gastritis and may show dysplasia.
    6. Dysplasia and intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, through the sequence of atrophy, metaplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma. The risk is greatest with CagA-positive strains.
    7. Gastric MALT lymphoma (extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma), arising from induced mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Early tumours without translocation may regress after eradication.
    8. Less commonly, associations with hypertrophic gastropathy (Ménétrier disease), eosinophilic and granulomatous gastritis, and extragastric conditions such as iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia.

    Interestingly, H. pylori infection with atrophy lowers the risk of duodenal ulcer and of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, because of reduced acid secretion.

    Gastric carcinoma

    B2

    Tell the role of H. pylori in gastric carcinoma. What is linitis plastica?

    H. pylori is the commonest identifiable cause of gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type): chronic infection leads through atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia to dysplasia and carcinoma. Linitis plastica is the "leather bottle" stomach produced by diffuse infiltration of the gastric wall by signet-ring cell (diffuse-type) carcinoma, with a desmoplastic reaction, rigidity, and flattening of the rugae.

    Role of H. pylori. Most gastric cancers are associated with H. pylori infection, and the decline in gastric cancer incidence in high-income countries has been attributed largely to the decline in infection, chiefly of intestinal-type cancers. The mechanism is the long-standing chronic gastritis that causes multifocal mucosal atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, which is the field in which dysplasia and carcinoma arise (the Correa cascade: chronic gastritis, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma).

    Chronic inflammation exposes the epithelium to free radicals and to regenerative proliferative stimuli, including raised gastrin, which is mitogenic. Achlorhydria permits bacterial overgrowth and production of carcinogenic nitrosamines. Strains carrying the CagA pathogenicity island, present in about 90% of isolates in high-risk populations, colonise the body as well as the antrum and induce cytokine release, atrophy, and metaplasia more effectively.

    Host polymorphisms leading to high TNF and IL-1 and low IL-10 increase the risk. In diffuse gastric cancer the pathogenesis involves loss of E-cadherin (CDH1 mutation or promoter hypermethylation). A minority (about 10%) of gastric cancers are instead associated with Epstein–Barr virus. Eradication of H. pylori reduces the risk, and intestinal metaplasia may regress. Infection is also linked to gastric MALT lymphoma. The inverse relationship between duodenal ulcer (high acid) and gastric cancer (atrophy, low acid) is a notable feature.

    Linitis plastica. In diffuse-type gastric carcinoma, small clusters and individual discohesive signet-ring cells infiltrate the gastric wall. These cells contain large mucin vacuoles that push the nucleus to the periphery, and they provoke an intense desmoplastic reaction. Extensive infiltration produces diffuse thickening and rigidity of the stomach wall with flattening of the rugal folds and a contracted lumen, imparting a "leather bottle" appearance, without a discrete mass and often without an ulcer. It carries a very poor prognosis (5-year survival less than 20% in advanced disease).

    B2

    Mention the macroscopic and microscopic types of gastric carcinoma.

    Gastric adenocarcinoma is classified macroscopically as polypoid (exophytic), ulcerated, or diffusely infiltrative (linitis plastica), and microscopically into the intestinal type, which forms glands, and the diffuse type, composed of signet-ring cells.

    Early versus advanced. Early gastric cancer is limited to the mucosa and submucosa regardless of nodal status and has a 5-year survival exceeding 90% after resection
    Advanced cancer invades the muscularis propria or beyond.

    Macroscopic types (advanced cancer)

    1. Polypoid or fungating (exophytic): bulky, intraluminal mass, typical of intestinal-type tumours.
    2. Ulcerative (malignant ulcer): a crater with heaped-up, irregular margins and a necrotic base.
    3. Diffusely infiltrative: the wall is thickened and rigid
      with extensive involvement, linitis plastica ("leather bottle" stomach).
    4. Superficial spreading (early lesions) may be elevated, flat, or depressed.

    Most distal cancers occur in the antrum, and the lesser curvature is involved more often than the greater curvature.

    Microscopic types

    TypeGrowth and gross patternHistologyEpidemiology and genetics
    IntestinalBulky exophytic or ulcerated mass, cohesive frontsGlandular structures with apical mucin vacuoles
    Mucin lakes may occur    		Predominates in high-risk areas, mean age about 55, male:female 2:1
    Arises from dysplasia and adenomas
    CIN, MSI, and EBV molecular subtypes
    DiffuseInfiltrative thickening of the wall, linitis plasticaDiscohesive signet-ring cells without gland formation
    Desmoplasia    		Uniform incidence worldwide, no precursor
    Loss of E-cadherin (CDH1)
    May be hereditary

    Other recognised histologic patterns are tubular, papillary, mucinous (colloid), and poorly cohesive carcinomas. Extracellular mucin in either type may form mucin lakes.

    Spread. Direct extension to the duodenum, pancreas, and retroperitoneum. Lymph node metastases including the left supraclavicular (Virchow) node and periumbilical (Sister Mary Joseph) nodule. Haematogenous spread to the liver
    Peritoneal seeding with ovarian metastases (Krukenberg tumour) and pouch of Douglas deposits.

    Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)

    Write a short note on GIST.

    DU20NDU20Ju

    Gastrointestinal stromal tumour is the commonest mesenchymal tumour of the abdomen, with an annual incidence of about 11 to 20 per million. It arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal (the pacemaker cells of the gut) or their precursors, and it occurs most often in the stomach (more than half of cases), followed by the small intestine, and less commonly the colon, rectum, and oesophagus. The peak age is about 60 years, and it is uncommon before 40.

    Pathogenesis. About 75% of GISTs have gain-of-function mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT, and another 8% have activating mutations in PDGFRA
    The two are mutually exclusive and trigger the same downstream signalling. Tumours lacking these mutations often have loss of succinate dehydrogenase complex function (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD), which may be germline (Carney–Stratakis syndrome of GIST and paraganglioma).

    GIST is also associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 and the Carney triad (GIST, paraganglioma, pulmonary chondroma), and familial KIT mutations cause diffuse Cajal cell hyperplasia and multiple tumours.

    Morphology. The tumour forms a well-circumscribed solitary intramural or submucosal mass, with a whorled grey-white cut surface, that may be exophytic and may show haemorrhage, cystic change, or mucosal ulceration. Microscopically it is composed of spindle cells (most common), epithelioid cells, or a mixture, with uniform nuclei. The cells are characteristically immunoreactive for KIT (CD117) and DOG1, and often for CD34.

    Clinical behaviour. Symptoms are abdominal pain, a mass, gastrointestinal bleeding, anaemia, or obstruction. Many are found incidentally. The malignant potential depends on tumour size, mitotic rate, and site (small intestinal tumours behave worse than gastric tumours). Metastases are to the liver and peritoneum, and lymph node spread is rare. Treatment is surgical resection, and unresectable or metastatic disease responds to tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

    Congenital Anomalies

    B2

    What are the congenital anomalies of GIT?

    The principal congenital anomalies of the gastrointestinal tract are atresia, fistulae, and duplications (for example oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula and intestinal atresia), ectopia, Meckel diverticulum, congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and Hirschsprung disease.

    1. Atresia, fistulae, and duplications: failure of canalisation or abnormal septation of the foregut, producing oesophageal atresia (usually with a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula, causing choking, regurgitation, and aspiration at the first feed), intestinal atresia and stenosis (most frequent in the duodenum), and duplications
      Anorectal malformations (imperforate anus) also belong here.
    2. Ectopia: developmental rests of gastric mucosa (the oesophageal inlet patch) or pancreatic tissue in the oesophagus, stomach, or small intestine. They may cause dysphagia, peptic ulceration, or pyloric obstruction.
    3. Meckel diverticulum: the commonest congenital anomaly of the gut, a true ileal diverticulum from failed involution of the vitelline duct.
    4. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: hyperplasia of the pyloric muscularis presenting at 3 to 6 weeks with projectile nonbilious vomiting and a palpable "olive."
    5. Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): failure of neural crest migration, causing functional distal obstruction.
    6. Others: malrotation and volvulus, abdominal wall defects (omphalocele, gastroschisis), and diaphragmatic hernia.
    B2

    What is Meckel diverticulum and what is Hirschsprung disease?

    Meckel diverticulum is the commonest congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, a true diverticulum of the ileum caused by failure of involution of the vitelline duct, whereas Hirschsprung disease is a congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, causing functional obstruction with proximal megacolon.

    Meckel diverticulum. A true diverticulum includes all three layers of the bowel wall. Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, which connects the gut lumen to the yolk sac, and arises from the antimesenteric border of the ileum. The "rule of 2s" applies: it occurs in about 2% of the population, within about 2 feet (60 cm) of the ileocecal valve, is about 2 inches (5 cm) long, has a male:female ratio of 2:1, and is most often symptomatic by age 2 (although only about 4% ever become symptomatic).

    The lining may resemble normal small intestine, but ectopic gastric (acid-secreting) or pancreatic tissue may be present. The complications are peptic ulceration of the adjacent ileal mucosa with bleeding (occult or massive, particularly in children) and perforation, diverticulitis simulating acute appendicitis, intussusception, volvulus, and obstruction. A technetium-99m pertechnetate scan identifies ectopic gastric mucosa.

    Hirschsprung disease. Congenital aganglionic megacolon occurs in about 1 in 5000 live births, with a male predominance, and is associated with Down syndrome (about 10%) and other malformations. The enteric neural plexus develops from neural crest cells that migrate into the bowel wall in a craniocaudal direction. When migration is arrested prematurely or ganglion cells die prematurely, the distal segment lacks both Meissner (submucosal) and Auerbach (myenteric) plexuses.

    Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in RET account for most familial and about 15% of sporadic cases, and mutations in EDNRB and EDN3 have also been implicated. The aganglionic segment cannot relax and is hypercontracted, so peristalsis is absent and functional obstruction results, with dilatation of the proximal normally innervated colon (megacolon). The rectum is always involved. short-segment disease (rectosigmoid) is commoner than long-segment disease.

    Diagnosis requires histologic proof of absence of ganglion cells (rectal biopsy; acetylcholinesterase staining highlights hypertrophic nerve fibres). Infants fail to pass meconium in the first 48 hours and develop abdominal distention and bilious vomiting. The major risks are enterocolitis, fluid and electrolyte disturbance, perforation, and peritonitis. Treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with anastomosis of the normal colon to the rectum.

    List four congenital anomalies of GIT.

    DU17M
    1. Meckel diverticulum
    2. Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon)
    3. Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
    4. Oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula (other examples: intestinal atresia, imperforate anus, malrotation, ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue)

    Write a short note on Hirschsprung disease.

    DU12Ju

    Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) is a functional obstruction of the colon caused by failure of ganglion cells to migrate to the distal bowel wall. It occurs in about 1 in 5000 live births, affects boys more than girls, and may be isolated or associated with Down syndrome (about 10%) and other anomalies.

    Pathogenesis. The enteric neurons derive from neural crest cells that migrate caudally into the gut wall. Arrest of migration, or premature death of the ganglion cells, leaves the distal segment without the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase RET underlie most familial and about 15% of sporadic cases
    EDNRB and EDN3 mutations are also implicated.

    Morphology. The rectum is always affected, and the lesion extends proximally for a variable distance: short-segment (rectosigmoid), the commoner pattern, and long-segment disease. The aganglionic segment appears normal or contracted, whereas the proximal innervated colon is dilated and hypertrophic (megacolon), may be perforated, and may show shallow ulcers. Histology shows absence of ganglion cells with hypertrophic nerve bundles. Intraoperative frozen section confirms ganglion cells at the anastomotic site.

    Clinical features. Failure to pass meconium in the first postnatal days, followed by abdominal distention, constipation, and bilious vomiting. Complications are enterocolitis (in about 25% of cases), electrolyte disturbance, perforation, and peritonitis. Treatment is resection of the aganglionic segment and anastomosis of the normal colon to the rectum. Acquired megacolon (Chagas disease, obstruction, ulcerative colitis) differs because ganglion cells are present, except in Chagas disease.

    Small and Large Intestines

    Malabsorption

    List five causes of malabsorption syndrome.

    DU16JaDU14Ju

    Malabsorption results from a defect in intraluminal digestion, terminal (brush-border) digestion, transepithelial transport, or lymphatic transport. Five important causes are:

    1. Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy): villous atrophy from an immune reaction to gluten (terminal digestion and transepithelial transport).
    2. Chronic pancreatitis and cystic fibrosis: pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and defective intraluminal digestion.
    3. Crohn disease (and other extensive small-bowel or ileal disease, or resection): loss of absorptive surface and bile salt malabsorption.
    4. Whipple disease: infection with Tropheryma whipplei, with lymphatic obstruction by macrophages.
    5. Infectious and parasitic enteritis (for example giardiasis, environmental enteric dysfunction, tropical sprue) and lactase (disaccharidase) deficiency.

    Other causes include autoimmune enteropathy, abetalipoproteinaemia, bacterial overgrowth, bile salt deficiency (biliary obstruction), carcinoid syndrome, and graft-versus-host disease.

    Inflammatory bowel disease

    B2

    Name the inflammatory bowel diseases with macroscopic, microscopic and clinical features.

    Inflammatory bowel disease comprises two chronic relapsing disorders, Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Crohn disease may involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract, is segmental, transmural, and granulomatous, and causes fistulas and strictures, whereas ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and rectum, is continuous and limited to the mucosa and superficial submucosa, and presents with bloody diarrhoea.

    Definition and pathogenesis. IBD is a chronic condition composed of Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis (indeterminate colitis, up to 10% of cases, is the term for those that cannot be classified). It results from a combination of abnormal immune regulation (Th1 and Th17 activation), altered host–microbe interactions (dysbiosis), and epithelial barrier dysfunction in genetically susceptible individuals (NOD2 is the strongest association with Crohn disease
    ATG16L1 and IRGM affect autophagy). It most frequently presents in teenage years and the early twenties.

    Crohn disease

    Macroscopic. Any part of the tract may be involved, most commonly the terminal ileum, ileocecal valve, and caecum
    Small bowel only in about 40%, small bowel and colon in 30%, and colon only in the remainder. The hallmark is skip lesions with sharply delineated diseased segments. Early aphthous ulcers enlarge into deep, linear, serpentine ulcers oriented along the long axis, with oedema, loss of folds, and a cobblestone mucosa.

    The wall is thickened, rubbery, and stenotic from transmural inflammation, oedema, fibrosis, and muscular hypertrophy (strictures). Mesenteric fat extends over the serosa ("creeping fat")
    Deep fissures lead to abscesses, perforation, and fistulas to other loops, bladder, vagina, or skin.

    Microscopic. Transmural inflammation with neutrophilic crypt injury and crypt abscesses, ulceration, crypt distortion, pseudopyloric and Paneth cell metaplasia, and noncaseating granulomas (in about 35% of cases
    a hallmark). Lymphoid aggregates occur throughout the wall.

    Clinical. Intermittent diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and fever, with periods of remission. About 20% present acutely with right iliac fossa pain mimicking appendicitis. Blood loss and iron deficiency anaemia (colonic disease)
    Protein loss, hypoalbuminaemia, and malabsorption of vitamin B₁₂ and bile salts (small bowel disease). Fibrosing strictures, fistulas, perianal disease
    Extraintestinal manifestations (uveitis, migratory polyarthritis, sacroiliitis, ankylosing spondylitis, erythema nodosum, clubbing, primary sclerosing cholangitis). anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies
    Smoking is a risk factor
    Increased risk of colonic carcinoma with long-standing colonic disease.

    Ulcerative colitis

    Macroscopic. The rectum is always involved, and disease extends proximally in a continuous manner to variable extent (proctitis, left-sided colitis, pancolitis). The small bowel is spared, apart from mild backwash ileitis in severe pancolitis. The mucosa is red and granular with broad-based ulcers. Islands of regenerating mucosa form pseudopolyps
    in chronic disease the mucosa is atrophic and smooth. Because it is not transmural, the wall is not thickened, the serosa is normal, and strictures are not a feature. Severe cases may progress to toxic megacolon with perforation.

    Microscopic. Inflammation confined to the mucosa and superficial submucosa, with a lymphoplasmacytic and neutrophilic infiltrate, crypt abscesses, crypt distortion and atrophy, pseudopyloric and Paneth cell metaplasia. Granulomas are absent. Sharp demarcation between diseased and normal mucosa may be seen.

    Clinical. Relapsing attacks of bloody diarrhoea with stringy mucus, lower abdominal pain, and cramps relieved by defecation. Complications include toxic megacolon, perforation, haemorrhage, and colorectal carcinoma (risk increases sharply 8 to 10 years after onset, and is greatest with pancolitis). Extraintestinal manifestations overlap with Crohn disease, with primary sclerosing cholangitis markedly increased (about 5%)
    p-ANCA is positive in about 75%
    Smoking may be protective, and onset can follow smoking cessation.

    What is inflammatory bowel disease?

    DU11Ju

    Inflammatory bowel disease is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract comprising two related disorders, ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease. It results from a combination of abnormalities in immune regulation, host–microbial interactions (dysbiosis), and epithelial function in genetically susceptible individuals. Ulcerative colitis involves only the colon and rectum, is continuous, and is limited to the mucosa and submucosa. Crohn disease can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract (most often the terminal ileum and colon), is segmental, and is typically transmural. IBD usually presents in the teenage years and early twenties, and manifests with diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and, in ulcerative colitis, bloody diarrhoea. Both carry extraintestinal manifestations and an increased risk of colorectal carcinoma. Cases that cannot be assigned to either entity are called indeterminate colitis.

    Mention three important features of Crohn disease.

    DU17Ja
    1. Skip lesions: segmental involvement, with multiple separate sharply delineated diseased segments, most often in the terminal ileum and colon, separated by normal bowel.
    2. Transmural inflammation with noncaseating granulomas: the full thickness of the wall is inflamed, and noncaseating granulomas are found in about 35% of cases, a hallmark of the disease.
    3. Fissures, fistulas, and strictures: deep linear ulcers with cobblestoning, a thickened wall with fibrosis causing strictures, fistula formation to other loops, bladder, or skin, and creeping fat on the serosa.

    Name the inflammatory bowel diseases.

    DU26MDU24N

    The inflammatory bowel diseases are Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Cases showing features of both that cannot be classified are referred to as indeterminate colitis (up to 10% of patients).

    Polyps

    B2

    Define a polyp. Name the polyps of GIT.

    A polyp is a nodule or mass that projects above the level of the surrounding mucosa into the lumen. Gastrointestinal polyps are classified as nonneoplastic (inflammatory, hyperplastic, hamartomatous) or neoplastic (adenomas and sessile serrated polyps).

    Definition. A polyp is any mass projecting above the surrounding mucosal surface. Those without a stalk are sessile
    as they enlarge, traction and proliferation of adjacent cells may form a stalk, making them pedunculated. A polyp may arise from epithelial or stromal hyperplasia, inflammation, ectopia, or neoplasia, and any mass lesion of the tract, including carcinoma, neuroendocrine tumour, stromal tumour, lymphoma, or a metastasis, may form a polyp.
