    B2

    What is a polyp and what is a papilloma? What are the differences between them?

    A polyp is any mass that projects above a mucosal surface, irrespective of its nature, which may be hyperplastic, inflammatory, hamartomatous, or neoplastic. A papilloma is a specific benign epithelial neoplasm composed of finger-like (papillary) fronds with a fibrovascular connective tissue core, covered by the epithelium of the surface from which it arises.

    A polyp is a descriptive, gross term, defined by the shape of a lesion, whereas a papilloma is a histogenetic term, indicating a benign neoplasm of surface epithelium. (The definition of papilloma is not in this chapter
    The chapter mentions HPV-associated anal condyloma, which is a squamous papillary lesion.)

    FeaturePolypPapilloma
    NatureDescriptive term for any mucosal protrusion
    May be nonneoplastic or neoplastic    		Always a benign epithelial neoplasm
    ArchitectureSessile or pedunculated
    May be glandular (adenoma), cystic, or inflammatory    		Papillary, finger-like or villous fronds on a central fibrovascular core
    SurfaceSmooth, lobulated, or velvetyWarty or cauliflower-like
    EpitheliumGlandular (intestinal, gastric) epithelium in most GI polypsSquamous or transitional epithelium (skin, oral cavity, oesophagus, anal canal, bladder)
    ExamplesHyperplastic, juvenile, Peutz–Jeghers, adenomatous polypsSquamous papilloma of the oesophagus or oral cavity, anal papilloma, transitional cell papilloma of the bladder
    Malignant potentialPresent in adenomas, serrated polyps, syndromic hamartomatous polyps
    Absent in colonic hyperplastic polyps    		Generally low, though some (for example transitional papilloma, HPV-associated) may progress

    Write a short note on villous adenoma.

    DU16Ju

    Villous adenoma is an epithelial neoplasm of the colon and rectum (most often the rectosigmoid) characterised by dysplastic epithelium arranged on slender villi. It is one of the architectural patterns of adenoma, the others being tubular and tubulovillous. Adenomas are precursors to most colorectal carcinomas, and they arise from the APC/Wnt pathway.

    Gross. Villous adenomas are typically large, sessile, broad-based, with a velvety or cauliflower-like (shaggy) surface. They are usually less pedunculated than tubular adenomas, and may reach several centimetres in diameter.

    Microscopic. The lesion is covered by long, slender villi that extend straight down from the surface to the muscularis mucosae. The epithelium shows dysplasia: elongated, hyperchromatic, stratified nuclei, prominent nucleoli, reduced goblet cells, and, in high-grade dysplasia, glandular budding and a cribriform pattern.

    Clinical significance. Villous adenomas harbor invasive carcinoma more often than tubular adenomas, although this correlates chiefly with their larger size. Nearly 40% of adenomas larger than 4 cm contain invasive cancer. Invasion beyond the muscularis mucosae, including into the stalk, defines invasive adenocarcinoma. Clinically they present with rectal bleeding, mucus discharge, or occult blood loss with anaemia. Large rectal villous adenomas may secrete copious mucus, producing watery diarrhoea with hypokalaemia and hypoproteinaemia. Treatment is complete endoscopic or surgical excision, and surveillance colonoscopy follows.

    Define polyp.

    DU25NDU13Ju

    A polyp is a nodule or mass that projects above the level of the surrounding mucosa into the lumen of a hollow viscus. It is a descriptive term that implies nothing about the nature of the lesion. Polyps that arise directly from the mucosa without a stalk are described as sessile, and those with a stalk as pedunculated. They may be nonneoplastic (inflammatory, hyperplastic, or hamartomatous) or neoplastic (adenomas and serrated polyps).

    Write down the types/names of GI polyps.

    DU25NDU13Ju

    Gastrointestinal polyps are classified as nonneoplastic or neoplastic.

    Nonneoplastic polyps

    1. Inflammatory polyps (including inflammatory pseudopolyps of ulcerative colitis and the polyp of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome)
    2. Hyperplastic polyps (stomach and colon)
    3. Fundic gland polyps
    4. Hamartomatous polyps: juvenile polyps (sporadic or juvenile polyposis syndrome), Peutz–Jeghers polyps, and polyps of Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome), Cronkhite–Canada syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis

    Neoplastic polyps

    1. Adenomas: tubular, tubulovillous, and villous adenomas of the colon, and gastric adenomas
    2. Sessile serrated polyps (sessile serrated adenomas)
    3. Adenomas of polyposis syndromes: familial adenomatous polyposis (with its variants Gardner and Turcot syndromes) and MUTYH-associated polyposis

    Other lesions, such as neuroendocrine tumours, gastrointestinal stromal tumours, lymphomas, and carcinomas, can present as polyps.

    Mention the polyps having malignant potential.

    DU25N

    The polyps that carry malignant potential are:

    1. Adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, and villous)
      The risk rises with size (nearly 40% of lesions larger than 4 cm contain invasive cancer), villous architecture, and high-grade dysplasia.
    2. Sessile serrated polyps, which lack conventional dysplasia but have malignant potential (microsatellite instability, BRAF mutation, MLH1 methylation).
    3. Adenomas of polyposis syndromes: familial adenomatous polyposis (APC) with virtually 100% risk of carcinoma if untreated, and MUTYH-associated polyposis.
    4. Gastric adenomas (up to 30% when large) and large pedunculated gastric inflammatory or hyperplastic polyps more than 1 cm (dysplasia in 1% to 20%).
    5. Hamartomatous polyposis syndromes: juvenile polyposis syndrome (30% to 50% develop colonic adenocarcinoma by age 45) and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome (lifetime cancer risk of about 40% in multiple organs).
    6. Fundic gland polyps in familial adenomatous polyposis (may show dysplasia).

    Colonic hyperplastic polyps, sporadic fundic gland polyps, and sporadic juvenile polyps carry negligible risk.

    Carcinoid tumor

    B2

    What is carcinoid tumor and what is carcinoid syndrome?

    Carcinoid tumour, now called well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, is a neoplasm of the diffuse neuroendocrine cells of the gut that most often arises in the small intestine, appendix, and rectum and is composed of uniform cells with "salt and pepper" chromatin. Carcinoid syndrome is the constellation of flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis caused by vasoactive substances, mainly serotonin, released into the systemic circulation.

    Carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumour. Neuroendocrine tumours arise from the diffuse components of the endocrine system. The term carcinoid is still used in the gut. More than 40% occur in the small intestine
    The tracheobronchial tree and lungs are the next commonest site, and the appendix, rectum, and stomach are also important sites. Gastric tumours are associated with endocrine cell hyperplasia, autoimmune atrophic gastritis, MEN1, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. They occur most often in the sixth decade.

    Gross. Intramural or submucosal masses forming polypoid nodules with intact or ulcerated overlying mucosa, yellow-tan, and very firm because of intense desmoplasia, which may kink and obstruct the small bowel.

    Microscopic. Islands, trabeculae, strands, glands, and sheets of uniform cells with scant pink granular cytoplasm and round to oval nuclei with "salt and pepper" chromatin
    Positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin A. Grade is determined by mitotic rate and Ki-67 index. Poorly differentiated tumours are neuroendocrine carcinomas (small cell or large cell).

    Behaviour. Prognosis depends on differentiation, mitotic rate, Ki-67, size, and site. Gastric and duodenal tumours rarely metastasise
    Jejunal and ileal tumours are often multiple and aggressive. Appendiceal tumours (usually at the tip, less than 2 cm) are almost always benign. Rectal tumours are usually small and rarely metastasise.

    Carcinoid syndrome. It develops in fewer than 10% of patients, and is caused by vasoactive substances (serotonin, histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, tachykinins) secreted by the tumour into the systemic circulation. It occurs when the tumour products bypass the first-pass metabolism by the liver, so it is strongly associated with hepatic metastases (or tumours draining into a nonportal venous bed, such as bronchial carcinoids).

    Its features are cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and fibrosis of the right-sided cardiac valves (carcinoid heart disease). Biochemical confirmation is by raised urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), the metabolite of serotonin.

    Write a short note on carcinoid tumour.

    DU03Ja

    Carcinoid tumour, now termed well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, is a neoplasm of the diffuse neuroendocrine cells. Most are found in the gastrointestinal tract, with more than 40% in the small intestine, followed by the lungs and tracheobronchial tree. Other gastrointestinal sites include the appendix, rectum, and stomach. The peak incidence is in the sixth decade.

    Pathology. Grossly, they are firm, yellow to tan, intramural or submucosal polypoid masses, with a desmoplastic reaction that may kink and obstruct the small bowel. Microscopically, they are composed of islands, trabeculae, glands, or sheets of uniform cells with scant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and round nuclei with a "salt and pepper" chromatin pattern
    Immunostains for chromogranin A and synaptophysin are positive, and ultrastructurally the cells contain dense-core neurosecretory granules. Grade is based on mitotic count and Ki-67 index. high-grade tumours are neuroendocrine carcinomas.

    Clinical features. Many are silent or are found incidentally
    Others present with obstruction, pain, or bleeding. Hormone production may cause specific syndromes (gastrin: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome). The carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, right-sided valvular fibrosis) occurs in fewer than 10% of patients, usually with hepatic metastases, because intestinal tumour products are otherwise inactivated by the liver.

    Behaviour. Gastric and duodenal tumours rarely metastasise
    Jejunal and ileal tumours are often multiple and aggressive. Appendiceal tumours (distal tip, under 2 cm) are almost always benign. Rectal tumours are usually small and seldom metastasise.

    Malignant tumors of the GIT

    B2

    What are the common malignant tumors of GIT?

    The commonest malignant tumours of the gastrointestinal tract are adenocarcinomas, of which colorectal adenocarcinoma is the most frequent, together with squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus and anus, and, less commonly, lymphomas, neuroendocrine tumours, and gastrointestinal stromal tumours.

    SiteCommon malignant tumours
    OesophagusSquamous cell carcinoma (proximal and middle thirds)
    Adenocarcinoma (distal third, Barrett oesophagus)
    Rare small cell carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, sarcoma
    StomachAdenocarcinoma (more than 90%
    Intestinal and diffuse types)
    MALT lymphoma (about 5%)
    Gastrointestinal stromal tumour
    Neuroendocrine tumour
    Small intestineAdenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumours (about equal frequency), lymphoma (including enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma in celiac disease), sarcoma and GIST
    Colon and rectumAdenocarcinoma (the most common malignancy of the GI tract)
    Neuroendocrine tumours, lymphoma
    AppendixNeuroendocrine tumour (commonest, usually benign), mucinous neoplasms and adenocarcinoma (pseudomyxoma peritonei)
    Anal canalSquamous cell carcinoma (HPV related), adenocarcinoma, basaloid carcinoma

    Colorectal adenocarcinoma. It arises from adenomas and sessile serrated polyps along the chromosomal instability (APC/Wnt), microsatellite instability (mismatch repair deficiency), and CpG island methylator pathways. Right-sided tumours grow as polypoid exophytic masses and present with iron deficiency anaemia. left-sided tumours are annular "napkin-ring" constrictions that cause obstruction and altered bowel habit.

    Microscopically, they are composed of tall columnar cells forming glands with desmoplasia, and some are mucinous or signet ring in type. The most important prognostic factors are depth of invasion and lymph node metastasis. The liver is the commonest site of distant metastasis because of portal drainage.

    Appendix

    B10

    A 15-year-old boy came with acute abdominal pain, vomiting and fever. On examination, rebound tenderness is present in the right iliac fossa. The blood picture shows neutrophilic leukocytosis. What is your clinical diagnosis? How will you confirm it?

    The clinical diagnosis is acute appendicitis. It is confirmed by clinical scoring and imaging (ultrasound or computed tomography), and ultimately by histological examination of the removed appendix, which shows neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria.

    Diagnosis. Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency of adolescents and young adults, with a slight male predominance. The picture here is classic: periumbilical pain that localises to the right iliac fossa (McBurney point), nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever, localised tenderness with rebound (peritoneal irritation), and neutrophilic leukocytosis. It is thought to be initiated by increased intraluminal pressure with compromised venous outflow, most often following luminal obstruction (in 50% to 80% of cases) by a fecalith, or less commonly by a gallstone, tumour, worms (Enterobius), or by lymphoid hyperplasia, with bacterial proliferation, ischaemia, and inflammation.

    Differential diagnosis. Mesenteric lymphadenitis (often secondary to Yersinia or viral enterocolitis), Meckel diverticulitis, acute salpingitis, ectopic pregnancy, mittelschmerz (in females), Crohn disease, and typhoid.

    Confirmation

    1. Clinical assessment with a scoring system (for example, the Alvarado score), including signs of Rovsing, psoas, and obturator.
    2. Laboratory: complete blood count (neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised C-reactive protein) and urine examination (to exclude urinary tract infection or calculus). Pregnancy test in females.
    3. Imaging: graded-compression ultrasonography (noncompressible, blind-ending tubular structure more than 6 mm in diameter) in children and young patients, and contrast-enhanced computed tomography when needed. Plain abdominal radiography may show a fecalith.
    4. Diagnostic laparoscopy when doubt persists, which can proceed directly to appendectomy.
    5. Definitive confirmation: histopathology of the appendectomy specimen (neutrophils in the muscularis propria).

    A young male has acute abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, RIF tenderness, neutrophilic leukocytosis. What is your diagnosis?

    DU26MDU19NovDU15Ja

    The diagnosis is acute appendicitis. The pain typically begins in the periumbilical region and later localises to the right iliac fossa, with deep tenderness at McBurney point (two-thirds of the distance from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine), nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever, and neutrophilic leukocytosis. It is initiated by increased intraluminal pressure, usually from obstruction by a fecalith or lymphoid hyperplasia, which compromises venous outflow and allows bacterial proliferation, ischaemia, and inflammation. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by ultrasonography or computed tomography, and confirmed histologically. Treatment is appendectomy. Mesenteric lymphadenitis, Meckel diverticulitis, Crohn disease, acute salpingitis, and ectopic pregnancy must be considered.

    Same: write down the possible complications.

    DU26MDU19Nov

    The possible complications of acute appendicitis are:

    1. Gangrene and perforation, with release of fecal and purulent material into the peritoneal cavity.
    2. Peritonitis, localised or generalised.
    3. Periappendicular abscess and appendix mass (phlegmon), and subphrenic or pelvic abscess.
    4. Pylephlebitis (septic thrombophlebitis of the portal tributaries), portal vein thrombosis, and liver abscess.
    5. Bacteraemia and septicaemia.
    6. Intestinal obstruction from adhesions (paralytic ileus acutely, adhesive obstruction later).
    7. Wound infection and fecal fistula postoperatively.

    Same: what do you expect in the histopathology after operation?

    DU15Ja

    The histological diagnosis of acute appendicitis rests on neutrophilic infiltration of the muscularis propria. Neutrophils infiltrate the mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria, usually with mucosal ulceration and neutrophils within the lumen, which often contains pus (acute suppurative appendicitis). The wall is congested and oedematous, with dilated vessels and sometimes thrombosis. The serosa may show a fibrinopurulent exudate (periappendicitis). In more advanced cases there is transmural necrosis with haemorrhage and green-black discoloration (acute gangrenous appendicitis), which may perforate and form an abscess. A fecalith may be found in the lumen, and the appendix is grossly swollen, red, and tense, with a dull serosa covered by exudate.

    Laboratory Tests of the GIT

    Write a short note on occult blood test.

    DU10JaDU06S

    Occult (hidden) blood in the stool is blood present in such small amount that it is not visible to the naked eye or by colour changes in the stool. The test detects bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract, and its main use is in screening for colorectal neoplasia and in the investigation of unexplained iron deficiency anaemia.

    Principles

    1. Guaiac-based fecal occult blood test (gFOBT): the pseudoperoxidase activity of haem catalyses the oxidation of guaiac by hydrogen peroxide, producing a blue colour. It detects blood from any level of the gut, but is not specific for human blood.
    2. Fecal immunochemical test (FIT): uses antibodies to human globin
      it is specific for human blood, is more sensitive for lower gastrointestinal bleeding (globin is digested in the upper gut), and requires no dietary restrictions.
    3. Other methods are orthotolidine tests and quantitative fecal haem assays. Stool DNA tests combined with FIT are also used.

    Procedure. Stool samples from three consecutive days are tested (guaiac) after avoiding red meat, peroxidase-rich vegetables, and vitamin C for 3 days (false positives and negatives), as well as aspirin and NSAIDs, which may cause bleeding.

    Interpretation. A positive test indicates bleeding, in the absence of visible blood, from oesophagitis, peptic ulcer, gastritis, carcinoma of the stomach or colon, colorectal adenomas (large adenomas bleed), inflammatory bowel disease, angiodysplasia, hookworm infestation, haemorrhoids, and drugs. A positive result calls for colonoscopy (and upper endoscopy where indicated). A negative result does not exclude disease, since bleeding from polyps and tumours is intermittent.

    Infections

    What is pleocytosis?

    DU10Ju

    Pleocytosis is an increase in the number of cells in the cerebrospinal fluid above the normal value, which is up to 5 lymphocytes (mononuclear cells) per microlitre in adults. It reflects meningeal or parenchymal inflammation or the presence of tumour cells. The predominant cell type indicates the cause. A neutrophilic pleocytosis characterises acute bacterial meningitis. a lymphocytic pleocytosis is seen in viral, tuberculous, fungal and partially treated bacterial meningitis. Eosinophils appear in parasitic infections
    and malignant cells are seen in carcinomatous or leukaemic meningitis.

    The Liver and Biliary Tract

    CirrhosisViral HepatitisGallbladder

    Jaundice and Hyperbilirubinaemia

    What is jaundice?

    DU17NovDU16JaDU08Ju

    Jaundice (icterus) is the yellow discoloration of the skin, sclerae (icterus), and mucous membranes caused by retention of bilirubin in the blood and tissues. It becomes clinically evident when the serum bilirubin rises above 2 to 2.5 mg/dL (normal 0.3 to 1.2 mg/dL).

    Bilirubin is the end product of haem degradation. About 85% of the 0.2 to 0.3 g produced daily derives from the breakdown of senescent red cells by macrophages of the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, and the rest comes from turnover of hepatic haem proteins. It is released into the plasma, bound to albumin (as unconjugated, or indirect, bilirubin), taken up by hepatocytes, conjugated with glucuronic acid in the endoplasmic reticulum by UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT1A1), and excreted as water-soluble conjugated (direct) bilirubin into the bile canaliculi through the MRP2 transporter.

    In the gut, bacterial β-glucuronidases deconjugate it and degrade it to colourless urobilinogens, most of which are excreted in the feces (giving stool its colour), while about 20% is reabsorbed, recycled to the liver, and a small amount appears in the urine.

    Jaundice therefore results whenever bilirubin production exceeds the rate of hepatic uptake, conjugation, and biliary excretion: excess production (haemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis), impaired hepatic uptake or conjugation (immaturity, hereditary defects, hepatocellular disease), or impaired excretion (hepatocellular disease, bile duct obstruction). Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is not excreted in urine (acholuric), whereas conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is water-soluble and appears in the urine (bilirubinuria).

    Classify jaundice.

    DU05Ja

    Jaundice is classified according to the site of the defect in bilirubin metabolism and the type of bilirubin that accumulates.

    TypeMechanismPredominant bilirubinCauses
    Prehepatic (haemolytic)Excess bilirubin production overwhelming hepatic capacityUnconjugatedHaemolytic anaemias (hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency, autoimmune haemolysis, incompatible transfusion), ineffective erythropoiesis (pernicious anaemia, thalassaemia), resorption of large haematomas
    Hepatic (hepatocellular)Impaired uptake, conjugation, or excretion by hepatocytesUnconjugated, conjugated, or bothDefective uptake or conjugation: physiologic jaundice of the newborn, breast milk jaundice, Gilbert syndrome, Crigler–Najjar syndromes (types I and II)
    Defective excretion: Dubin–Johnson and Rotor syndromes
    Hepatocellular disease: viral and drug-induced hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure
    Posthepatic (obstructive, cholestatic)Impaired bile flowConjugatedExtrahepatic obstruction: gallstones (choledocholithiasis), carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, cholangiocarcinoma, strictures, biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, sclerosing cholangitis
    Intrahepatic cholestasis: primary biliary cholangitis, drug-induced, sepsis, cholestasis of pregnancy

    Alternatively, jaundice may be divided into predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (haemolytic, neonatal, hereditary conjugation defects) and predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (hepatocellular disease, bile duct obstruction, and canalicular transporter defects).

    What is physiological jaundice?

    DU14Ja

    Physiologic jaundice of the newborn is a transient, mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that occurs in nearly all newborns during the first week of life (usually appearing after 24 hours, peaking on days 3 to 5, and resolving by about 2 weeks). It is due to the immaturity of hepatic bilirubin metabolism: the activity of UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT1A1), the enzyme that conjugates bilirubin, is low at birth and does not reach adult levels until 3 to 4 months of age
    There is also a relatively increased bilirubin load from breakdown of foetal red cells, reduced hepatic uptake, and increased enterohepatic circulation (low gut flora and the presence of intestinal β-glucuronidase). Breastfeeding may exacerbate it because of bilirubin-deconjugating enzymes in breast milk. In most infants it is benign, and phototherapy with blue light, which converts bilirubin to a soluble isomer excreted in urine and bile, keeps the level within a safe range until the conjugating mechanism matures. It is considered pathological if jaundice appears within the first 24 hours, if the bilirubin rises rapidly or exceeds the phototherapy threshold, if it persists beyond 2 weeks, or if conjugated bilirubin is raised, because of the risk of kernicterus.

    Mention 2 important causes of obstructive jaundice.

    DU07Ju
    1. Gallstones in the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis).
    2. Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas (also other malignant neoplasms of the biliary tree, such as cholangiocarcinoma, and of the ampulla).

    Other causes include strictures after surgery or inflammation, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and, in infants, biliary atresia and choledochal cyst.

    What enzymes are elevated in hepatocellular and obstructive jaundice (AST, ALT, ALP interpretation)?

    DU21MDU13Ja

    Hepatocellular jaundice. The transaminases aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) are markedly raised (often 10 to 100 times normal in acute viral hepatitis, drug toxicity, or ischaemic hepatitis), as they leak from damaged hepatocytes. ALT is more specific for the liver, because AST is also found in the heart, skeletal muscle, kidney, and red cells. In most chronic liver diseases ALT exceeds AST. in alcohol-associated liver disease the AST:ALT ratio is 2:1 or greater. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is normal or only mildly raised (less than 3 times normal). In cirrhosis, the transaminases may be only modestly raised or normal, because few viable hepatocytes remain. Falling transaminases in acute liver failure with worsening jaundice and coagulopathy is an ominous sign.

    Obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice. Alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised (3 or more times normal), together with gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and 5′-nucleotidase, because biliary obstruction induces synthesis of these enzymes by the canalicular and ductal epithelium and impairs their excretion. The transaminases are normal or only mildly to moderately raised (usually less than 5 times normal), though they may rise transiently with acute obstruction by stones. Raised ALP with normal GGT suggests a bone source.

    Give the urinary findings of obstructive jaundice.

    DU21MDU16Ja

    In obstructive jaundice:

    1. Bile pigment (bilirubin) is present in the urine (bilirubinuria), because the conjugated bilirubin that regurgitates into the blood is water soluble and loosely bound to albumin and so is filtered by the glomeruli. it gives the urine a dark, tea- or brown-coloured appearance with a yellow froth on shaking.
    2. Bile salts are present (Hay's test positive) in the urine.
    3. Urobilinogen is absent or markedly reduced, because bile does not reach the intestine, so urobilinogen is not formed for reabsorption.

    What is acholuric jaundice?

    DU10Ja

    Acholuric jaundice is jaundice in which the urine is free of bile pigment ("acholuric" means without bile in the urine). It occurs when the raised serum bilirubin is predominantly unconjugated: unconjugated bilirubin is insoluble in water and tightly bound to albumin, so it cannot be filtered by the glomeruli and does not appear in urine. It is characteristic of haemolytic jaundice (the classic example being hereditary spherocytosis, formerly called "acholuric family jaundice") and of conjugation defects such as Gilbert and Crigler–Najjar syndromes and physiologic jaundice of the newborn. The urine contains increased urobilinogen (in haemolytic jaundice), and the stools are dark. It contrasts with obstructive and hepatocellular jaundice, in which conjugated bilirubin is raised and the urine is dark with bile pigment.

    How will you investigate a case of hemolytic jaundice?

    DU08Ju

    Investigation of haemolytic jaundice aims to confirm the haemolysis, establish its mechanism, and identify the cause.

    1. Confirm haemolysis: complete blood count with haemoglobin and red cell indices, reticulocyte count (raised), peripheral blood film (polychromasia, spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, target cells, parasites such as malaria), raised serum lactate dehydrogenase, reduced serum haptoglobin, raised indirect bilirubin, haemoglobinaemia and haemoglobinuria in intravascular haemolysis, and haemosiderinuria.
    2. Confirm that the jaundice is prehepatic: serum bilirubin fractionation (unconjugated predominates), urine examination (bilirubin absent, urobilinogen increased), stool (dark), and normal liver enzymes and liver function tests.
    3. Find the cause: direct Coombs (antiglobulin) test for autoimmune haemolysis
      Osmotic fragility test and eosin-5-maleimide binding for hereditary spherocytosis. Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC for sickle cell disease and thalassaemia. G6PD assay
      Pyruvate kinase assay
      Ham test or flow cytometry for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Peripheral smear and rapid tests for malaria
      and a drug and transfusion history.
    4. Imaging for splenomegaly and pigment gallstones (ultrasonography), and a bone marrow examination when needed, which shows erythroid hyperplasia.

    Write a short note on obstructive jaundice.

    DU13Ju

    Obstructive (cholestatic, posthepatic or surgical) jaundice results from impaired bile flow caused by obstruction of the extrahepatic or large intrahepatic bile ducts, with regurgitation of conjugated bilirubin into the blood.

    Causes. In adults the commonest causes are stones in the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis), malignant neoplasms of the head of the pancreas, biliary tree, and ampulla, and strictures from surgery or ischaemic injury. Primary sclerosing cholangitis may also produce an obstructive picture. In children the causes are biliary atresia, cystic fibrosis, and choledochal cysts.

    Pathology. Proximal duct dilatation develops. Liver biopsy shows portal expansion due to oedema, a prominent ductular reaction, and neutrophils around ductules. Canalicular and hepatocellular bile plugs (cholestasis) and "feathery degeneration" of hepatocytes (swollen, foamy cytoplasm from bile salt retention). Persistent obstruction leads to portal fibrosis and eventually secondary biliary cirrhosis. Ascending cholangitis (fever, chills, pain, jaundice) may supervene, and may cause abscesses and sepsis.

    Clinical features. Jaundice (greenish-yellow), pruritus (from retained bile salts), dark urine, pale bulky stools with steatorrhoea, malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (prolonged prothrombin time responsive to vitamin K; osteomalacia), xanthomas with prolonged cholestasis, and an enlarged gallbladder in malignant obstruction (Courvoisier sign).

    Laboratory. Raised conjugated bilirubin, markedly raised alkaline phosphatase and GGT, raised cholesterol, bilirubin and bile salts in the urine, absent urobilinogen, and normal or slightly raised transaminases.

    Investigation and treatment. Ultrasonography (dilated ducts), CT, MRCP, ERCP, or endoscopic ultrasonography to find the cause. Treatment is removal of the obstruction (endoscopic stone extraction, stenting, or surgery). Early relief of the obstruction reverses the changes, but persistent obstruction leads to fibrosis and biliary cirrhosis.

    Write a short note on unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

    DU12Ja

    Unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia results from excess bilirubin production, reduced hepatic uptake, or defective conjugation, so that unconjugated bilirubin accumulates in the blood. It is insoluble in water, tightly bound to albumin, and cannot be excreted in urine (acholuric jaundice)
    at high levels the free fraction rises and, particularly in infants, can cross the blood–brain barrier and cause kernicterus.

    Causes

    1. Excess production: haemolytic anaemias, ineffective erythropoiesis (pernicious anaemia, thalassaemia), and resorption of internal haemorrhage or haematoma.
    2. Reduced hepatic uptake: drug interference with membrane carriers and some cases of Gilbert syndrome.
    3. Impaired conjugation: physiologic jaundice of the newborn (low UGT1A1 activity), breast milk jaundice, and hereditary UGT1A1 deficiency: Crigler–Najjar syndrome type I (severe deficiency, fatal in infancy without liver transplantation
      no response to phenobarbital), type II (residual activity, milder, responds to phenobarbital), and Gilbert syndrome (mild reduction; benign intermittent jaundice during fasting, stress, or illness, which is common and harmless).

    Features. Mild to moderate jaundice with normal liver function tests and normal urine bilirubin, with increased urobilinogen in haemolysis. Treatment depends on the cause: phototherapy and exchange transfusion in neonatal disease, treatment of the haemolysis, or no treatment in Gilbert syndrome.

    Write a short note on kernicterus.

    DU11Ju

    Kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy) is the neurological damage that results from deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the brain, especially in the basal ganglia, in infants with severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid soluble and, when its concentration is high enough that the unbound (free) fraction rises, it crosses the immature blood–brain barrier and is toxic to neurons.

    Causes. Haemolytic disease of the newborn (Rh or ABO incompatibility), prematurity, severe physiologic or breast milk jaundice, Crigler–Najjar syndrome type I, G6PD deficiency, sepsis, and drugs (sulfonamides) that displace bilirubin from albumin, together with acidosis and hypoalbuminaemia.

    Pathology. The brain shows yellow staining (the term "kernicterus" means "yellow nucleus") of the basal ganglia, globus pallidus, subthalamic nuclei, hippocampus, brainstem nuclei, and cerebellum, with neuronal necrosis and gliosis.

    Clinical features. Lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry, hypotonia then hypertonia with opisthotonos and seizures. Survivors develop choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, upward gaze palsy, and intellectual deficits.

    Prevention and treatment. Monitoring of bilirubin in neonates, early phototherapy (blue light converts bilirubin to a water-soluble isomer), exchange transfusion for dangerous levels, and anti-D prophylaxis for Rh disease.

    A patient has jaundice, pruritus, bulky pale stool, raised ALP / gallstones with palpable gallbladder. What type of jaundice is this?

    DU25MDU14Ju

    This is obstructive (posthepatic, cholestatic, or surgical) jaundice. Jaundice with pruritus (retained bile salts), bulky pale clay-coloured stools (absence of bile pigment in the gut, with fat malabsorption), dark urine, and a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase indicates impaired bile flow through the extrahepatic bile ducts. The cause is most often stones in the common bile duct, or a malignant tumour such as carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.

    When the gallbladder is palpable, the cause must be considered carefully: according to Courvoisier's law, a palpable, nontender gallbladder with jaundice suggests malignant obstruction (pancreatic head or ampullary cancer), because a gallbladder with chronic stones is usually fibrotic and contracted and cannot distend, whereas a tender palpable gallbladder suggests acute cholecystitis or mucocele with stone impaction. Investigation is by ultrasonography, CT, MRCP, or ERCP.

    Name synthetic liver function tests.

    DU26M

    The synthetic liver function tests, which assess the capacity of the liver to synthesise proteins, are:

    1. Serum albumin (half-life about 20 days)
    2. Prothrombin time and INR, reflecting synthesis of clotting factors II (prothrombin), V, VII, IX, and X (factor VII has the shortest half-life)
    3. Serum fibrinogen and other clotting factors
    4. Serum pseudocholinesterase and serum cholesterol (to a lesser degree)

    Name two causes of raised prothrombin time.

    DU22MDU17Ja
    1. Hepatocellular disease or liver failure (acute liver failure, cirrhosis), because the hepatocytes synthesise the clotting factors II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII and fibrinogen. The prolongation is not corrected by parenteral vitamin K.
    2. Vitamin K deficiency, as in obstructive jaundice (bile salt deficiency causes malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins) or malabsorption syndromes. The prolongation is corrected by parenteral vitamin K.

    Other causes: warfarin therapy and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

    Why is prothrombin time more specific than total protein estimation?

    DU09Ja

    Prothrombin time is a more specific and sensitive indicator of hepatic synthetic function than total protein for the following reasons:

    1. The clotting factors measured by the prothrombin time (especially factor VII, with a half-life of about 4 to 6 hours) have a very short half-life, so the test reflects the current synthetic capacity of the liver and falls within hours to days of acute hepatocellular damage, whereas albumin has a half-life of about 20 days and so changes slowly.
    2. Total protein is the sum of albumin and globulins. In chronic liver disease albumin falls but globulins rise (polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia due to impaired clearance of antigens by the Kupffer cells and shunting), so the total protein may remain normal and mask the hepatic dysfunction.
    3. Total protein is also influenced by nutrition, protein-losing states (nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy), hydration, and chronic inflammation or myeloma, which are not related to liver function.
    4. The clotting factors are synthesised almost exclusively by the liver, and a prolonged prothrombin time that is not corrected by vitamin K indicates a severe hepatocellular defect and has prognostic value (it is part of the MELD and Child–Pugh scores).

    Viral Hepatitis

    B3

    Name the hepatotrophic viruses. Mention the serological markers of HBV infection.

    The hepatotropic viruses are hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E viruses. The serological markers of hepatitis B virus infection are HBsAg, anti-HBs, HBeAg, anti-HBe, anti-HBc (IgM and IgG), and HBV DNA, and the pattern of their appearance and disappearance defines acute, chronic, resolved, and vaccinated states.

    Typical patterns: acute hepatitis (HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBc IgM, HBV DNA). Recovery (anti-HBs and anti-HBc IgG, HBsAg negative). Chronic infection (HBsAg persisting with anti-HBc IgG, HBeAg or anti-HBe, HBV DNA). Vaccination (anti-HBs only). The "healthy carrier" has HBsAg and anti-HBe, without HBeAg, with normal transaminases and low or undetectable HBV DNA.

    B3

    Give the possible outcomes of hepatitis B virus infection.

    Hepatitis B infection may end in acute hepatitis with complete recovery, acute liver failure from massive necrosis, chronic hepatitis with or without cirrhosis, or an asymptomatic carrier state, and chronic infection carries a risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

    1. Acute hepatitis with recovery and viral clearance: the usual outcome in adults (acute infection is subclinical or mild in about two-thirds). HBsAg disappears and anti-HBs appears, conferring immunity.
    2. Acute liver failure (fulminant hepatitis) with massive hepatic necrosis, in about 0.1% to 0.5% of acute infections within 4 to 8 weeks
      The risk is increased by HDV co-infection.
    3. Chronic hepatitis, in 5% to 10% of infected adults, with persistent HBsAg for more than 6 months
      The risk is inversely related to age, being about 90% when infection is transmitted perinatally. It may progress to cirrhosis and its complications.
    4. Asymptomatic (healthy) carrier state: HBsAg positive, with anti-HBe, normal transaminases, low HBV DNA, and little liver injury
      Carriers are a reservoir of infection.
    5. Hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly in those infected perinatally and with chronic infection, even in the absence of cirrhosis.
    6. Superinfection with HDV, causing severe acute hepatitis or exacerbation, and progression to cirrhosis.
    7. Extrahepatic immune-complex disease: glomerulonephritis and polyarteritis nodosa.

    Name the hepatotropic viruses.

    DU26M

    The hepatotropic viruses are hepatitis A virus (HAV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), hepatitis D virus (HDV, the delta agent), and hepatitis E virus (HEV). HAV and HEV are transmitted by the fecal–oral route and cause only acute disease (HEV may be chronic in the immunocompromised), while HBV, HCV, and HDV are transmitted parenterally and can cause chronic hepatitis. Nonhepatotropic viruses such as Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, and yellow fever virus may also involve the liver.

    Discuss the clinical outcomes of hepatitis B virus infection.

    DU26M

    The outcome of HBV infection depends on the age at exposure, the immune competence of the host, and co-infection with other agents. Cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells directed against infected hepatocytes cause most of the injury, and a strong virus-specific CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T-cell response is associated with resolution.

    Acute infection. After an incubation period of 4 to 26 weeks, acute infection is mild or subclinical in about two-thirds of adults and may present with anorexia, fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, with a preicteric, icteric, and convalescent phase. Most patients clear the virus, with disappearance of HBsAg within about 12 weeks (up to 24), and appearance of anti-HBs. Immune-complex phenomena such as glomerulonephritis and polyarteritis nodosa may occur.

    Acute liver failure. Occurs in about 0.1% to 0.5% of acutely infected individuals, within 4 to 8 weeks, with massive hepatic necrosis, encephalopathy, and coagulopathy. HDV co-infection increases the risk.

    Chronic hepatitis. Develops in 5% to 10% of adults, but in about 90% of infants infected at birth, with persistence of HBsAg and HBV DNA. Persistent HBeAg indicates continued replication and probable progression. Chronic hepatitis is defined as symptomatic, biochemical, or serologic evidence of continuing or relapsing disease for more than 6 months, or the presence of fibrosis. Progression to cirrhosis occurs over years (average about 8), with portal hypertension, liver failure, and decompensation.

    Carrier state. An individual who harbors the virus but has no symptoms. The "healthy carrier" has HBsAg and anti-HBe, normal aminotransferases, low HBV DNA, and no significant liver damage.

    Hepatocellular carcinoma. Chronic HBV infection, especially acquired perinatally, carries a high risk of HCC, through the integration of viral DNA, the transcriptional activation by HBx, and chronic injury and regeneration. it may arise in noncirrhotic liver.

    HDV. Co-infection causes acute hepatitis that is usually self-limited, while superinfection of a chronic carrier causes severe acute hepatitis or exacerbation, with chronic HDV in more than 80%, and accelerates progression to cirrhosis and HCC.

    Antiviral therapy (interferon, entecavir, tenofovir) slows progression, and vaccination prevents infection (protective anti-HBs in 95%).

    Mention the microscopic features of liver in acute and chronic viral hepatitis.

    DU17M

    The microscopic changes in acute and chronic viral hepatitis due to the hepatotropic viruses are largely similar and overlap with those of autoimmune hepatitis, drug reactions, and Wilson disease.

    Acute viral hepatitis

    1. Lobular and portal inflammation, predominantly lymphocytes, with variable plasma cells and eosinophils, and activation of Kupffer cells.
    2. Hepatocyte injury: ballooning degeneration (swelling with clear cytoplasm) and necrosis or apoptosis. Apoptotic cells appear as shrunken, eosinophilic acidophil (Councilman) bodies. Pigmented macrophages scavenge dead cell debris.
    3. In severe cases, confluent necrosis of groups of cells that may become bridging necrosis (connecting portal tracts to central veins or portal tracts to each other) and, with massive necrosis, panlobular necrosis and collapse of the reticulin framework.
    4. Cholestasis (bile plugs) may be present, and regeneration (binucleate hepatocytes, thickened plates) is evident.

    Chronic viral hepatitis

    1. The defining feature is portal lymphocytic or lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis. Inflammatory cells cross the limiting plate and injure periportal hepatocytes (interface hepatitis, formerly piecemeal necrosis), with a variable degree of lobular inflammation.
    2. Fibrosis progresses from portal and periportal fibrosis to portoportal bridging fibrosis and finally cirrhosis.
    3. Chronic hepatitis B: "ground-glass" hepatocytes, with cytoplasm filled with HBsAg in swollen endoplasmic reticulum (confirmed by immunostaining for HBsAg and HBcAg).
    4. Chronic hepatitis C: prominent portal lymphoid aggregates or follicles, steatosis (marked with genotype 3), and focal bile duct injury.
    5. Biopsy is used to grade the inflammatory activity and stage the fibrosis.

    What alterations occur in liver function tests in acute viral hepatitis / chronic liver disease?

    DU17MDU11Ja

    Acute viral hepatitis

    • Serum aminotransferases (ALT and AST) are markedly raised (often several hundred to thousands of units per litre), and the rise precedes the jaundice. ALT is usually higher than AST. A fall in transaminases with worsening jaundice and coagulopathy is a sign of massive necrosis.
    • Serum bilirubin is raised (mixed conjugated and unconjugated), with bilirubinuria preceding the clinical jaundice. Urinary urobilinogen is increased early.
    • Alkaline phosphatase is normal or only mildly raised (cholestatic features in some cases of hepatitis A).
    • Prothrombin time is prolonged in severe disease
      This signifies a poor prognosis.
    • Serum albumin is usually normal because of its long half-life.

    Chronic liver disease (chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis)

    • Aminotransferases are mildly to moderately raised and fluctuate, and may be normal in cirrhosis.
    • Serum albumin is reduced (hypoalbuminaemia), while globulins are raised (hypergammaglobulinaemia), reversing the albumin:globulin ratio.
    • Prothrombin time is prolonged, and not corrected by vitamin K.
    • Serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are variably raised, and ammonia may be raised.
    • Haematologic changes of hypersplenism: thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and anaemia.
    • In advanced disease, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, and raised creatinine (hepatorenal syndrome).

    A 30y male with recent blood transfusion has jaundice, weakness. What are the possible fates/outcomes of such a case?

    DU20NDU20JuDU19Nov

    A jaundiced young adult with a recent history of blood transfusion most probably has acute viral hepatitis acquired parenterally, due to hepatitis B or hepatitis C. The possible outcomes are:

    1. Complete recovery with clearance of the virus and immunity (usual in acute HBV infection of adults
      HBsAg disappears and anti-HBs appears).
    2. Acute liver failure (fulminant hepatitis) from massive hepatic necrosis, with encephalopathy and coagulopathy. Rare (0.1% to 0.5% in HBV), and fatal without transplantation.
    3. Chronic hepatitis, in 5% to 10% of adults with HBV and in more than 80% of those with HCV (acute HCV is often asymptomatic).
    4. Cirrhosis, with portal hypertension, ascites, varices, encephalopathy, and liver failure, in about 20% of chronic HCV patients over 20 to 30 years.
    5. Hepatocellular carcinoma in chronic HBV or HCV, especially with cirrhosis.
    6. Asymptomatic carrier state in HBV, a reservoir of infection.
    7. Extrahepatic immune-complex disease (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia).

    Same (with anorexia, high SGPT): what is the provisional diagnosis?

    DU19Nov

    The provisional diagnosis is acute viral hepatitis, most likely hepatitis B (or C) acquired through the blood transfusion. The prodromal anorexia, malaise, and jaundice, with a markedly raised serum alanine aminotransferase (SGPT), indicate hepatocellular injury. It is confirmed by serology (HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM; anti-HCV and HCV RNA; anti-HAV IgM and anti-HEV IgM to exclude other viruses), liver function tests, and prothrombin time. a liver biopsy is not required in acute disease.

    Alcoholic Liver Disease

    Give an outline of the spectrum of liver diseases associated with alcohol abuse.

    DU10Ju

    Alcohol-associated liver disease has three distinctive, overlapping forms: hepatic steatosis, alcoholic (alcohol-associated) steatohepatitis, and fibrosis leading to cirrhosis. Short-term ingestion of about 80 g of alcohol per day produces mild reversible steatosis, the risk of severe injury becomes significant at 80 g or more per day, and 160 g or more daily for 10 to 20 years is frequently associated with severe injury
    Only 10% to 15% of persons with alcohol use disorder develop cirrhosis. Women are more susceptible, and genetic factors, iron overload, and HBV or HCV infection modify the risk. The injury begins in the centrilobular (zone 3) region.

    StagePathologyClinical features
    Alcoholic fatty liver (steatosis)Macrovesicular steatosis (small droplets coalescing to large), the liver is large (up to 4 to 6 kg), soft, yellow, and greasy
    Reversible with abstinence    		Often asymptomatic
    Hepatomegaly
    Mild elevation of bilirubin and ALP
    Alcoholic hepatitis (steatohepatitis)Ballooned hepatocytes with Mallory–Denk hyaline (keratin 8 and 18), neutrophilic infiltrate (satellitosis), lobular inflammation, spotty necrosis, steatosis, pericellular ("chicken-wire") perivenular fibrosisAcute illness after a heavy bout: malaise, anorexia, fever, tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, neutrophilic leukocytosis
    AST:ALT 2:1 or greater
    Mortality 10% to 20% per episode
