    Pathogenesis. Alcohol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetaldehyde (generating NADH, which promotes lipogenesis and suppresses fatty acid oxidation), and by CYP2E1, which generates reactive oxygen species. Acetaldehyde forms protein adducts and induces lipid peroxidation. Gut-derived endotoxin activates Kupffer cells through TLR4, with release of cytokines, and stellate cell activation causes fibrosis.

    Prognosis. The 5-year survival approaches 90% in abstainers without jaundice, ascites, or haematemesis but falls to 50% to 60% in those who continue to drink
    The death is due to hepatic coma, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, infection, hepatorenal syndrome, or hepatocellular carcinoma.

    Cirrhosis

    Cirrhosis: types and etiology

    B3

    Define cirrhosis of liver. Mention the types of liver cirrhosis.

    Cirrhosis is a diffuse, irreversible-in-its-established-form process of the liver in which fibrosis and the conversion of normal liver architecture into regenerative parenchymal nodules, surrounded by fibrous bands, is accompanied by vascular remodeling and shunting. It is classified by morphology into micronodular, macronodular, and mixed types, and by aetiology.

    Definition. Cirrhosis is a diffuse remodeling of the entire liver into parenchymal nodules (often regenerative) surrounded by fibrous bands, with a variable degree of vascular (often portosystemic) shunting. It is the end stage of many chronic liver diseases. The three hallmarks are diffuse involvement, bridging fibrous septa, and regenerative nodules, with disruption of the lobular architecture.

    It is not a specific diagnosis, and cirrhosis and liver failure are not synonymous: some cirrhotic patients, such as those whose hepatitis B is suppressed or whose hepatitis C is cured, may never progress to end-stage disease.

    Types

    1. Morphological classification (by nodule size):
      • Micronodular cirrhosis: nodules uniformly less than 3 mm
        Typical of alcohol-associated cirrhosis (Laennec cirrhosis), haemochromatosis, biliary obstruction, and hepatic venous outflow obstruction.
      • Macronodular cirrhosis: nodules larger than 3 mm (up to several centimetres), typical of post-necrotic or post-viral hepatitis cirrhosis, Wilson disease, and α₁-antitrypsin deficiency.
      • Mixed (micro-macronodular) cirrhosis.
    2. Aetiological classification: alcoholic, post-viral (post-necrotic), biliary (primary and secondary), cardiac (congestive), metabolic and inherited (haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), steatohepatitic (MASH), autoimmune, drug-induced, and cryptogenic (more than 90% of "cryptogenic" cirrhosis is probably burned-out MASH).
    3. Functional classification: compensated and decompensated cirrhosis.
    B3

    Mention the etiology of cirrhosis of liver.

    The leading causes of cirrhosis worldwide are chronic hepatitis B and C, alcohol-associated liver disease, and metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis, with biliary diseases, autoimmune hepatitis, and inherited metabolic disorders as other causes.

    1. Chronic viral hepatitis: hepatitis B (with or without D) and hepatitis C.
    2. Alcohol-associated liver disease (micronodular, Laennec).
    3. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH), the commonest cause in many Western countries, accounting for most "cryptogenic" cirrhosis.
    4. Chronic biliary disease: primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (secondary biliary cirrhosis), biliary atresia, and cystic fibrosis.
    5. Autoimmune hepatitis.
    6. Inherited and metabolic disorders: hereditary haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency, galactosaemia, tyrosinaemia, glycogen storage diseases.
    7. Vascular causes: chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction (Budd–Chiari syndrome), chronic right-sided heart failure (cardiac cirrhosis).
    8. Drugs and toxins: methotrexate, amiodarone, isoniazid, and others.
    9. Chronic parasitic disease: schistosomiasis (periportal fibrosis).
    10. Cryptogenic cirrhosis: no cause identified.
    B3

    A 40-year-old male had a history of jaundice, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy and ascites. What is the likely diagnosis? Name the liver function tests that are expected to be altered.

    The likely diagnosis is decompensated cirrhosis of the liver with portal hypertension, most probably alcohol-associated. Gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy reflect hyperoestrogenaemia and hypogonadism from impaired hepatic metabolism of oestrogen, and the liver function tests that are altered are bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, globulins, and prothrombin time.

    Diagnosis. A middle-aged man with jaundice (hepatic failure), gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy (impaired hepatic oestrogen metabolism, leading to hyperoestrogenaemia, and hypogonadism), and ascites (portal hypertension with hypoalbuminaemia) has cirrhosis of the liver in a decompensated stage. Other expected findings are palmar erythema, spider angiomas, loss of body hair, caput medusae, splenomegaly, variceal haemorrhage, and hepatic encephalopathy.

    The commonest cause in such a patient is alcohol, and chronic hepatitis B or C and MASH must be considered. The diagnosis is confirmed by ultrasonography, elastography, endoscopy for varices, and liver biopsy where indicated, and by testing for the cause.

    Liver function tests altered

    • Serum bilirubin raised (mixed hyperbilirubinaemia).
    • AST and ALT mildly to moderately raised (AST > ALT, ratio 2:1 or more in alcoholic cirrhosis).
    • Alkaline phosphatase (and GGT) variably raised.
    • Serum albumin reduced, with raised globulins (reversed A:G ratio).
    • Prothrombin time prolonged (reduced synthesis of clotting factors).
    • Others: raised serum ammonia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism).

    Define cirrhosis of liver.

    6DU25NDU24NDU22MDU17MDU13JuDU12Ja

    Cirrhosis is a diffuse process involving the entire liver, characterised by the conversion of the normal lobular architecture into parenchymal nodules (usually regenerative) surrounded by dense bands of fibrous tissue, with a variable degree of vascular, often portosystemic, shunting. It is the end stage of chronic liver injury of many causes. The liver surface becomes bumpy with depressed scars and bulging nodules. The key features are the diffuse nature, the bridging fibrosis, the nodule formation, and the disruption of the vascular architecture, which causes portal hypertension and impairs hepatocellular function.

    Name the etiology of cirrhosis.

    7DU24NDU18MDU16JuDU15JaDU13JuDU10JaDU07Ja

    The aetiology of cirrhosis includes:

    1. Chronic viral hepatitis (B, B with D, and C)
    2. Alcohol-associated liver disease
    3. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH)
    4. Chronic biliary disease: primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic biliary obstruction, biliary atresia
    5. Autoimmune hepatitis
    6. Inherited metabolic disease: haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency
    7. Chronic hepatic venous congestion: Budd–Chiari syndrome, right-sided heart failure
    8. Drugs and toxins
    9. Chronic schistosomiasis
    10. Cryptogenic (unknown cause)

    Write the etiopathogenesis of cirrhosis.

    DU25N

    Cirrhosis represents the common end point of repeated, prolonged hepatic injury, chronic inflammation, and the repair process, regardless of the underlying cause.

    Aetiology. The major causes are chronic viral hepatitis B and C, alcohol-associated liver disease, MASH, chronic biliary disease, autoimmune hepatitis, inherited metabolic diseases (haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency), venous outflow obstruction, and drugs.

    Pathogenesis

    1. Persistent hepatocellular injury and inflammation: Hepatocyte death by necrosis or apoptosis, with an inflammatory response by Kupffer cells and lymphocytes, releases cytokines and growth factors (TGF-β, PDGF, TNF, IL-1) and reactive oxygen species.
    2. Activation of hepatic stellate cells: The stellate cells in the space of Disse, which normally store vitamin A, are activated by these mediators and by injury to the sinusoidal endothelium. They transform into myofibroblast-like cells that proliferate and synthesise large amounts of collagen types I and III and other matrix proteins. Portal fibroblasts and bone marrow–derived cells contribute.
    3. Progressive fibrosis: The fibrosis begins in portal tracts or around the central veins (depending on the disease), progresses to bridging septa that link portal tracts to each other or to central veins, and finally subdivides the parenchyma. Capillarisation of the sinusoids (deposition of matrix in the space of Disse and loss of endothelial fenestrae) impairs exchange between blood and hepatocytes.
    4. Regeneration and nodule formation: Surviving hepatocytes regenerate as nodules, isolated from their blood supply by fibrous septa, with a ductular reaction and stem-cell activation. The nodular architecture compresses the vessels.
    5. Vascular derangement: Distortion and obliteration of the hepatic and portal vessels, with arterioportal anastomoses and shunts, increases the resistance to portal flow (portal hypertension) and decreases the perfusion of hepatocytes (hepatic failure).
    6. Failure of matrix degradation: The balance between matrix metalloproteinases and their tissue inhibitors (TIMPs) shifts toward matrix accumulation. Early fibrosis may regress when the cause is removed, but established cirrhosis with vascular remodeling rarely reverses completely.

    What are the complications of cirrhosis?

    DU25NDU24NDU12Ja

    About 40% of patients are asymptomatic until late. The complications result from portal hypertension and hepatocellular failure.

    Portal hypertension and its consequences

    1. Ascites, which may be complicated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and hydrothorax.
    2. Portosystemic shunts: oesophagogastric varices (haemorrhage), haemorrhoids, caput medusae, and retroperitoneal collaterals.
    3. Congestive splenomegaly with hypersplenism (thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, anaemia).

    Hepatic failure

    1. Hepatic encephalopathy and coma.
    2. Coagulopathy (bruising, bleeding, DIC).
    3. Jaundice and cholestasis with pruritus.
    4. Hepatorenal syndrome.
    5. Hyperoestrogenism: palmar erythema, spider angiomas, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, and hypogonadism.
    6. Hypoalbuminaemia and oedema
      Malnutrition and muscle wasting.
    7. Pulmonary complications: hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension.
    8. Infections (impaired Kupffer cell function and gut barrier loss).

    Neoplastic

    1. Hepatocellular carcinoma, which develops in many cirrhotic livers (1% to 6% annually in alcohol-associated cirrhosis).

    Others. Portal vein thrombosis and acute-on-chronic liver failure.

    How is ascites formed in cirrhosis of liver?

    5DU22MDU18MDU16JuDU12JaDU09Ja

    Ascites is the accumulation of excess fluid (usually serous, with less than 3 g/dL protein, and a serum-to-ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more) in the peritoneal cavity
    Cirrhosis causes 85% of cases, and it becomes clinically detectable when at least 500 mL has accumulated. Its pathogenesis is multifactorial:

    1. Sinusoidal (portal) hypertension. Raised hydrostatic pressure in the portal venous system and hepatic sinusoids increases the filtration of fluid into the space of Disse. The excess hepatic lymph (hepatic lymph flow can increase up to 20-fold) exceeds the capacity of the lymphatics and weeps from the surface of the liver into the peritoneal cavity. Increased splanchnic capillary pressure also adds to the transudation.
    2. Hypoalbuminaemia. Reduced hepatic synthesis of albumin lowers the plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid is retained in the interstitium and peritoneal cavity.
    3. Splanchnic arterial vasodilation (nitric oxide–mediated) and hyperdynamic circulation. Systemic arterial underfilling decreases the effective circulating volume and activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, sympathetic nervous system, and antidiuretic hormone, causing renal retention of sodium and water, which maintains and amplifies the ascites. Reduced hepatic inactivation of aldosterone contributes.
    4. Increased hepatic and splanchnic lymph production and renal sodium retention.

    The fluid may become infected (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, with neutrophils in the fluid), and long-standing ascites may cause hydrothorax (usually right-sided) by passage through diaphragmatic lymphatics.

    Write the mechanism of cirrhotic death.

    DU10Ja

    Death in cirrhosis results from the progressive loss of hepatocellular function and from the complications of portal hypertension. The common proximate causes are:

    1. Hepatic failure with hepatic encephalopathy and coma: failure of the liver to detoxify ammonia and other gut-derived toxins (and shunting of portal blood around the liver) leads to cerebral dysfunction and oedema, often precipitated by gastrointestinal bleeding, infection, electrolyte disturbance, or sedatives.
    2. Massive haemorrhage from oesophagogastric varices: about 40% of patients with advanced cirrhosis develop varices, and each bleeding episode carries a mortality of 15% to 30%
      The blood load in the gut also precipitates encephalopathy.
    3. Infections: sepsis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and pneumonia, caused by impaired Kupffer cell function, gut mucosal barrier damage, and immune dysfunction.
    4. Hepatorenal syndrome: renal failure due to splanchnic vasodilation, activation of the renin–angiotensin axis, and renal vasoconstriction.
    5. Hepatocellular carcinoma, developing in the cirrhotic liver.
    6. Coagulopathy and multiorgan failure, with acute-on-chronic liver failure precipitated by sepsis, drugs, or portal vein thrombosis.

    A male has jaundice, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy/abdominal distension, ascites. What is the likely diagnosis?

    DU15JaDU12Ja

    The likely diagnosis is cirrhosis of the liver (decompensated), with portal hypertension, most commonly alcohol-associated or post-viral. Jaundice reflects hepatocellular failure, gynaecomastia and testicular atrophy result from hyperoestrogenaemia and hypogonadism due to impaired hepatic oestrogen metabolism, and the abdominal distension with ascites results from portal hypertension, hypoalbuminaemia, and renal salt and water retention. Palmar erythema, spider angiomas, caput medusae, splenomegaly, and hepatic encephalopathy may coexist. The diagnosis is established by liver function tests, ultrasonography, endoscopy, ascitic fluid analysis, and, where appropriate, liver biopsy.

    Same (40y): name the liver function tests expected to be altered.

    DU12Ja

    In cirrhosis the following liver function tests are expected to be altered:

    1. Serum bilirubin is raised (conjugated and unconjugated).
    2. Aminotransferases (AST, ALT) are mildly to moderately raised (AST greater than ALT in alcohol-associated disease), and may be normal in advanced disease.
    3. Alkaline phosphatase and GGT are variably raised.
    4. Serum albumin is reduced and globulins are raised, so the albumin:globulin ratio is reversed.
    5. Prothrombin time (INR) is prolonged and is not corrected by vitamin K.
    6. Serum ammonia may be raised, and cholesterol low in advanced disease.

    Hepatic encephalopathy

    What is hepatic encephalopathy?

    DU18MDU16Ju

    Hepatic encephalopathy is a spectrum of potentially reversible neuropsychiatric disturbances of consciousness and behaviour, ranging from subtle changes in personality, sleep reversal, and confusion, through stupor, to deep coma and death, that complicates acute or chronic liver failure and portosystemic shunting.

    Pathogenesis. It is believed to be caused by elevated blood ammonia, which correlates with impaired neuronal function and cerebral oedema. The principal source of ammonia is the gastrointestinal tract, where it is produced by gut bacteria and by enterocytes during glutamine metabolism. Normally the ammonia travels in the portal vein to the liver, where it is converted to urea by the urea cycle. in severe liver disease, or when the portal blood bypasses the liver through shunts, this detoxification fails.

    In the brain, astrocytes metabolise ammonia to glutamine, which acts as an osmolyte and causes astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema. Ammonia also directly affects neurons and neurotransmission. Other contributors are false neurotransmitters, increased GABAergic tone, inflammation, and infection.

    Clinical features. Behavioural abnormalities, altered sleep rhythm, confusion, drowsiness, stupor, and coma. Fluctuating neurological signs including rigidity and hyperreflexia. Asterixis (flapping tremor: nonrhythmic rapid extension–flexion of the head and extremities, best seen with the arms outstretched and wrists dorsiflexed). Fetor hepaticus
    Raised blood ammonia
    and slowing of the electroencephalogram.

    Precipitating factors. Gastrointestinal haemorrhage, infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, alkalosis), a high-protein load, sedatives, diuretics, and renal failure.

    Management. Correction of precipitating factors, lactulose and rifaximin to reduce ammonia production and absorption, and protein-appropriate nutrition. Liver transplantation in refractory cases.

    Portal Hypertension

    B3

    Define ascites. What are the causes of ascites?

    Ascites is the accumulation of excess fluid in the peritoneal cavity. It is a transudate in most hepatic and cardiac causes and an exudate in infective or malignant causes, and the commonest cause overall is cirrhosis of the liver with portal hypertension.

    Definition. Ascites is the pathological accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, clinically detectable when at least about 500 mL has accumulated (shifting dullness, fluid thrill). In 85% of cases it is caused by cirrhosis. Cirrhotic ascites is serous with a low protein content (less than 3 g/dL) and a serum–ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more
    The fluid may contain scant mesothelial cells and mononuclear cells, neutrophils suggest infection, and red cells suggest disseminated intra-abdominal cancer.

    Causes

    MechanismCauses
    Portal hypertension (high SAAG, transudate)Cirrhosis
    alcohol-associated hepatitis
    Budd–Chiari syndrome
    Portal vein thrombosis
    Schistosomiasis
    right-sided heart failure and constrictive pericarditis
    Hypoalbuminaemia (low SAAG, transudate)Nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, severe malnutrition
    Exudative (peritoneal disease)Tuberculous peritonitis, secondary bacterial peritonitis, peritoneal carcinomatosis and mesothelioma, pseudomyxoma peritonei, pancreatitis
    OthersMyxoedema, Meigs syndrome and ovarian tumours, chylous ascites (lymphatic obstruction), and bile ascites

    The pathogenesis in cirrhosis is by sinusoidal hypertension, hypoalbuminaemia, increased hepatic lymph flow, and splanchnic vasodilation with renal sodium and water retention.

    Enumerate the important causes of ascites.

    DU21M

    The important causes of ascites are:

    1. Cirrhosis of the liver (commonest, 85% of cases), and other causes of portal hypertension: portal vein thrombosis, Budd–Chiari syndrome, and schistosomiasis.
    2. Cardiac: congestive cardiac failure and constrictive pericarditis.
    3. Renal: nephrotic syndrome and chronic kidney disease.
    4. Hypoalbuminaemia from malnutrition and protein-losing enteropathy.
    5. Peritoneal disease: tuberculous peritonitis, peritoneal carcinomatosis, and other causes of peritonitis.
    6. Malignancy: metastatic disease of the liver and peritoneum, and ovarian tumours (Meigs syndrome).
    7. Pancreatic disease (pancreatic ascites) and lymphatic obstruction (chylous ascites).
    8. Myxoedema.

    Tumours of the Liver

    Write down the etiology of hepatocellular carcinoma.

    DU07Ja

    Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for about 5.4% of all cancers worldwide. Most cases (more than 85%) occur in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, where chronic hepatitis B is common, and about 80% to 85% arise in a cirrhotic liver, although 15% to 20% arise in noncirrhotic liver. The unifying mechanism is chronic liver injury, with inflammation and repeated hepatocyte regeneration, leading to the acquisition of driver mutations. The aetiological factors are:

    1. Chronic hepatitis B virus infection, the leading cause worldwide, especially when acquired perinatally
      it acts through chronic inflammation and regeneration, integration of viral DNA, and the HBx protein, and may cause HCC without cirrhosis.
    2. Chronic hepatitis C virus infection, usually through cirrhosis (about one-third of HCC in the United States).
    3. Alcohol-associated liver disease and cirrhosis from any cause.
    4. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease/steatohepatitis, with obesity and diabetes, increasing in Western countries, which may cause HCC even without cirrhosis.
    5. Aflatoxin B₁, a mycotoxin produced by Aspergillus contaminating stored grain and groundnuts, which causes TP53 mutation (codon 249) and acts synergistically with hepatitis B.
    6. Inherited metabolic diseases: hereditary haemochromatosis, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency, tyrosinaemia, and, less often, Wilson disease and chronic biliary diseases.
    7. Hepatocellular adenoma (particularly with β-catenin mutation) and anabolic androgenic steroid use.
    8. Others: tobacco smoking, and male sex (up to 8:1 in high-incidence areas).

    Common driver mutations are activating mutations of CTNNB1 (β-catenin, about 40%), TERT promoter mutations (50% to 60%), and inactivating TP53 mutations (up to 60%)
    The fibrolamellar variant carries the DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion.

    A 59y male with HBV history has hepatomegaly, SOL in right lobe on USG. How will you proceed to diagnose?

    DU08Ju

    A 59-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B and a space-occupying lesion in the right lobe of the liver must be assumed to have hepatocellular carcinoma until proven otherwise (the other possibilities being a regenerative or dysplastic nodule, haemangioma, abscess, cholangiocarcinoma, and metastasis). The diagnosis proceeds as follows.

    1. History and examination: duration of HBV infection, alcohol, constitutional symptoms (weight loss, pain), and signs of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly, spider angiomas). a nodular hard liver.
    2. Serum α-fetoprotein (AFP): a markedly raised level (above 400 ng/mL) supports HCC, although it is not sensitive for early tumours and is not raised in the fibrolamellar variant. Des-γ-carboxy prothrombin may be added.
    3. Multiphase (triphasic) contrast-enhanced CT or MRI: the characteristic pattern in a cirrhotic liver is arterial-phase hyperenhancement with rapid venous-phase washout, which is diagnostic in an at-risk patient without biopsy
      it also shows the number and size of the lesions, vascular invasion (portal vein thrombosis), and extrahepatic spread.
    4. Image-guided percutaneous needle biopsy (or fine needle aspiration cytology) if imaging is indeterminate, with histology and immunostaining (glypican-3, HepPar-1, arginase-1). The risk is tumour seeding along the needle track and bleeding.
    5. Assessment of the underlying liver disease and function: liver function tests, prothrombin time, albumin, bilirubin (Child–Pugh score), HBV DNA, HBsAg, anti-HCV, upper endoscopy for varices, and platelet count.
    6. Staging: chest CT for lung metastases, bone scan if indicated, and staging systems such as BCLC to plan treatment (resection, transplantation, ablation, chemoembolisation, or systemic therapy).

    Same: what are your expected findings?

    DU08Ju

    Clinical. Abdominal pain or discomfort, weight loss, fatigue, anorexia, and a firm, nodular, tender hepatomegaly, sometimes with a bruit over the liver
    Features of underlying chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly, collaterals). Sudden deterioration of a known cirrhosis may signal the tumour. Complications are portal vein invasion, variceal bleeding, rupture with haemoperitoneum, and paraneoplastic syndromes (erythrocytosis, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia).

    Laboratory. Raised serum α-fetoprotein (a frequent finding in advanced disease), raised alkaline phosphatase and GGT, abnormal liver function tests reflecting the cirrhosis, positive HBsAg, and HBV DNA.

    Imaging. Ultrasonography shows a focal mass, usually hypoechoic or heterogeneous, and the multiphase CT or MRI shows arterial enhancement with early washout in the venous phase. There may be tumour thrombus in the portal or hepatic veins.

    Gross. A single mass, multiple discrete nodules, or a diffusely infiltrative tumour, pale yellow if fatty, green if cholestatic, often in a cirrhotic liver. Tumours larger than 2 cm are more likely to show vascular invasion and intrahepatic metastases, and invasion of veins may extend into the portal vein, inferior vena cava, and right heart.

    Microscopic. Well and moderately differentiated tumours resemble normal hepatocytes, growing as thick trabeculae (more than 3 cells thick), pseudoglandular structures with bile plugs, or sheets. The poorly differentiated tumours show marked atypia. Precursors are dysplastic nodules in a cirrhotic liver (large and small cell change). The fibrolamellar variant (adolescents and young adults, normal AFP) shows large polygonal oncocytic cells, prominent nucleoli, and lamellar collagen bundles.

    Spread. Haematogenous metastasis (lung, bone) late
    Lymph node spread in fewer than 5%. The 5-year survival is about 30% for localised disease and 5% to 10% with extrahepatic spread.

    Gallbladder

    Gallstones

    B3

    Mention the etiology, classification and complications of gallstones.

    Gallstones (cholelithiasis) are of two main types, cholesterol stones and pigment stones, formed when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol or unconjugated bilirubin with gallbladder stasis. Their complications include acute and chronic cholecystitis, obstruction with jaundice and cholangitis, pancreatitis, gallstone ileus, and carcinoma of the gallbladder.

    Classification

    FeatureCholesterol stonesPigment stones
    CompositionMore than 50% crystalline cholesterol monohydrateCalcium salts of unconjugated bilirubin with calcium carbonate and phosphate
    FrequencyAbout 90% in the United States and western EuropeCommon in Asia, haemolytic states
    TypesPure cholesterol stones (pale yellow, round or ovoid, with finely granular surface, radiating crystalline cut surface; solitary or several), and mixed stones (grey-white to black, lamellated, multiple, faceted)Black: small (under 1.5 cm), numerous, friable, spiculated, in sterile gallbladder bile, 50% to 75% radiopaque
    Brown: laminated, soft, greasy, in infected bile ducts, radiolucent
    RadiologyMostly radiolucent (10% to 20% radiopaque)Black often radiopaque

    Mucin glycoproteins form the scaffolding of all stones.

    Aetiology and risk factors

    • Cholesterol stones: age (middle to older), female sex and oestrogen (pregnancy, oral contraceptives), obesity and the metabolic syndrome, rapid weight loss, northern European and Native American ethnicity, ileal disease or resection (Crohn disease, cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency), gallbladder stasis, hereditary factors (ABCG8 variants), and hypertriglyceridaemia.
    • Pigment stones: chronic haemolysis (sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia), biliary infection with Escherichia coli, Ascaris lumbricoides, or Clonorchis sinensis liver flukes (β-glucuronidases deconjugate bilirubin), ileal dysfunction or bypass, and cirrhosis.

    Complications. About 70% to 80% of patients remain asymptomatic. Complications are biliary colic. Acute and chronic cholecystitis
    Empyema, gangrene, and perforation of the gallbladder. Obstruction of the cystic or common bile duct with obstructive jaundice and mucocele or hydrops. Ascending cholangitis
    Acute pancreatitis
    Cholecystoenteric fistula with gallstone ileus (Bouveret syndrome)
    and carcinoma of the gallbladder (gallstones are present in 95% of cases, although only 1% to 2% of patients with gallstones develop cancer)
    Porcelain gallbladder and xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis are other sequelae. The smallest stones ("gravel") are most dangerous because they enter the ducts.

    What are the factors that favour stone formation within gallbladder?

    DU09Ja

    Cholesterol stones. Four conditions contribute to the formation of cholesterol stones:

    1. Supersaturation of bile with cholesterol: cholesterol is rendered soluble by micelles formed with bile salts and lecithin. When cholesterol secretion exceeds the solubilising capacity (hypersecretion of cholesterol, or reduced bile salt pool), crystals can nucleate. This is favoured by oestrogen (female sex, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, which increase hepatic cholesterol uptake and HMG-CoA reductase activity), obesity, rapid weight loss, age, and ileal disease or resection with loss of bile salts.
    2. Gallbladder hypomotility (stasis): neurogenic or hormonal, as in pregnancy, prolonged fasting, parenteral nutrition, and rapid weight loss.
    3. Accelerated cholesterol crystal nucleation by pronucleating factors (mucin glycoproteins, calcium).
    4. Hypersecretion of mucus in the gallbladder, which traps the nucleated crystals and promotes their aggregation into stones.

    Pigment stones. Elevated unconjugated bilirubin in bile, due to chronic haemolysis, bacterial and parasitic infection of the biliary tree (β-glucuronidase release by E. coli, Ascaris, liver flukes), ileal dysfunction, and cirrhosis, with biliary stasis.

    Other factors: genetic variants of biliary lipid transporters (ABCG8), diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidaemia.

    Carcinoma of the gallbladder

    B3

    What type of carcinoma occurs in the gallbladder?

    The overwhelming majority of gallbladder carcinomas are adenocarcinomas, usually arising in the fundus on a background of chronic cholecystitis with gallstones.

    Carcinoma of the gallbladder is the commonest malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. The tumours are mainly adenocarcinomas, growing either as a firm, poorly circumscribed mass or as a diffuse infiltration of the gallbladder wall that simulates chronic cholecystitis. They are most often found in the fundus. Microscopically they consist of glands (of intestinal, biliary, or papillary pattern, and occasionally mucinous or signet-ring) in a desmoplastic stroma. in some, cytologic atypia and stromal response are minimal and perineural and vascular invasion help to establish the diagnosis. Rarely, other primary tumours occur, such as neuroendocrine tumours, squamous cell carcinoma, adenosquamous carcinoma, and sarcomas.

    The precursor lesions are flat dysplasia (carcinoma in situ), intracholecystic papillary-tubular neoplasms, and intestinal metaplasia. Gallstones are present in 95% of cases, with chronic inflammation the common thread. Other risk factors are female sex (at least twice as common), porcelain gallbladder and hyalinising cholecystitis, chronic Salmonella typhi carriage, anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction, and, in high-incidence areas (Chile, Bolivia, northern India, and Native American populations), ethnicity. Molecular changes include TP53 mutations and alterations of the EGFR family (HER2) and RAS.

    The tumour is diagnosed late (preoperative diagnosis in under 20%), spreading by direct extension into the liver and adjacent organs, along the peritoneum and biliary tree, and by metastasis to the liver and portahepatic nodes. The 5-year survival is less than 10%, but incidental carcinoma found early at cholecystectomy can be cured by resection.

    Glomerular Diseases

    Classification of glomerular diseases

    Classify glomerular disease.

    DU26M

    Glomerular diseases can be classified in three complementary ways: by origin, by the clinical syndrome they produce, and by the morphological pattern of injury.

    1. Classification by origin

    Primary glomerular diseases are those in which the kidney is the only or predominant organ involved. Some have a prominent inflammatory (proliferative) component and are therefore called glomerulonephritis
    Others, such as minimal change disease and membranous nephropathy, lack a cellular inflammatory component and are more correctly termed glomerulopathies.

    • Acute proliferative (postinfectious, e.g., poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis
    • Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis — anti-GBM antibody–mediated, immune complex–mediated, or pauci-immune (ANCA-associated)
    • Membranous nephropathy
    • Minimal change disease
    • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
    • Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (immune complex–mediated) and C3 glomerulopathies (dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis)
    • IgA nephropathy
    • Fibrillary glomerulonephritis
    • Hereditary glomerular diseases — Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane nephropathy
      Congenital nephrotic syndrome due to nephrin or podocin mutations

    Secondary glomerular diseases arise as one manifestation of a systemic disorder: systemic lupus erythematosus (lupus nephritis), diabetes mellitus (diabetic nephropathy), amyloidosis, Goodpasture syndrome, IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura), granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis, infective endocarditis, hepatitis B and C, HIV, malaria, syphilis and schistosomiasis, thrombotic microangiopathies (HUS/TTP), monoclonal immunoglobulin (myeloma-related) deposition disease, Fabry disease, and drug-induced lesions.

    Both the clinical manifestations and the histological changes of primary and secondary forms may be similar, which is why a systemic cause must always be sought.

    2. Classification by clinical syndrome

    SyndromePrincipal featuresTypical diseases
    Nephritic syndromeHaematuria, azotaemia, oliguria, mild–moderate proteinuria, hypertensionAcute postinfectious GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis
    Rapidly progressive GNNephritic picture with rapid loss of GFR over days to weeksCrescentic GN (anti-GBM, immune complex, ANCA)
    Nephrotic syndromeProteinuria >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia, lipiduriaMinimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, FSGS, diabetic nephropathy
    Isolated urinary abnormalitiesAsymptomatic haematuria and/or subnephrotic proteinuriaIgA nephropathy, Alport syndrome, thin basement membrane disease
    Chronic kidney diseaseAzotaemia progressing to uraemia over months to yearsEnd stage of any of the above

    3. Classification by morphology

    The glomerular lesion is described as diffuse (involving all or most glomeruli) or focal (involving only some)
    Global (the whole tuft affected) or segmental (only part of the tuft). It is further described as proliferative (endocapillary — endothelial, mesangial and leukocytic hypercellularity; or extracapillary — crescent formation) or nonproliferative (membranous change, minimal change). Membranoproliferative lesions combine capillary wall thickening with proliferation, and sclerosing lesions (FSGS, diabetic glomerulosclerosis) are characterised by obliteration of capillary lumens by matrix.

    Name the primary glomerular diseases.

    DU19NovDU11Ju

    The primary glomerular diseases are:

    1. Acute proliferative (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis
    2. Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis
    3. Membranous nephropathy
    4. Minimal change disease
    5. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
    6. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (immune complex–mediated)
    7. C3 glomerulopathy — dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis
    8. IgA nephropathy
    9. Fibrillary glomerulonephritis

    Hereditary disorders of the glomerulus, notably Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane nephropathy, are usually considered alongside these as glomerular diseases causing isolated haematuria.

    Nephrotic syndrome

    What is nephrotic syndrome?

    4DU26MDU17JaDU12JuDU08Ja

    Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical complex caused by a derangement of the glomerular capillary wall that makes it abnormally permeable to plasma proteins. It is defined by four features: (1) massive proteinuria, with loss of 3.5 g or more of protein in the urine per day (a lesser threshold, adjusted for body size, applies in children). (2) hypoalbuminaemia, with plasma albumin below 3 g/dL
    (3) generalised oedema
    and (4) hyperlipidaemia with lipiduria.

    These components are logically related. The glomerular filtration barrier, composed of fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and the podocyte slit diaphragm, normally restricts protein passage by size and charge. When structural or physicochemical injury to this barrier increases its permeability, albumin and other proteins escape into the urine. Urinary loss exceeds the compensatory synthetic capacity of the liver, so serum albumin falls.

    The reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure allows fluid to move into the interstitium, producing oedema, which is aggravated by secondary sodium and water retention. The hypoalbuminaemia and the resulting hepatic response also lead to hyperlipidaemia, and lipoproteins that leak through the capillary wall appear in the urine as lipiduria.

    What are the causes of nephrotic syndrome?

    DU17MDU12Ju

    Nephrotic syndrome results from any disorder that damages the glomerular filtration barrier. The causes are grouped into primary glomerular diseases and systemic diseases, and their relative frequency differs sharply with age.

    CauseChildren (%)Adults (%)
    Primary glomerular diseases≈95≈60
    Minimal change disease758
    Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis1035
    Membranous nephropathy330
    Membranoproliferative GN / dense deposit disease1010
    Other proliferative GN (focal, pure mesangial, IgA nephropathy)217
    Systemic diseases≈5≈40

    The systemic causes include diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis and systemic lupus erythematosus, which are the three commonest
    Drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold, captopril, heroin). Infections (malaria, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, HIV). Malignant disease (carcinoma, lymphoma)
    and miscellaneous conditions such as bee-sting allergy and hereditary nephritis. Minimal change disease is therefore the leading cause in children, membranous nephropathy in older adults, and FSGS can occur at any age. In adults a secondary cause must always be excluded before a lesion is labelled primary.

    Write a short note on nephrotic syndrome.

    DU24NDU15Ja

    Definition. Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome produced by increased permeability of the glomerular capillary wall to plasma proteins, characterised by massive proteinuria (≥3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminaemia (<3 g/dL), generalised oedema, and hyperlipidaemia with lipiduria.

    Causes. In children it is almost always due to a primary glomerular lesion, chiefly minimal change disease (about 75%) and FSGS. In adults membranous nephropathy and FSGS predominate, and about 40% of cases are secondary to systemic disease — most often diabetes, amyloidosis and systemic lupus erythematosus — or to drugs, infections and malignancy.

    Pathophysiology. Injury to the endothelium, basement membrane or podocytes (or loss of the negative charge of the basement membrane) allows albumin to leak across the filter. The proteinuria is called highly selective when it consists mainly of low-molecular-weight proteins such as albumin and transferrin, as in minimal change disease, and poorly selective when higher-molecular-weight globulins are also lost, as in membranous nephropathy and FSGS.

    Heavy proteinuria depletes serum albumin faster than the liver can replace it, and increased renal catabolism of filtered albumin contributes. The low plasma oncotic pressure causes generalised oedema. Hypovolaemia then stimulates renin and aldosterone secretion and the sympathetic nervous system, while natriuretic peptide secretion falls, so sodium and water retention further aggravates the oedema.

    Hyperlipidaemia results from increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis, abnormal transport of circulating lipid particles and decreased lipid catabolism. Lipoproteins also leak into the urine.

    Clinical features. The oedema is soft and pitting, most marked in the periorbital tissues and dependent parts, and in severe cases is accompanied by pleural effusion and ascites. Blood pressure and renal function are often normal initially, particularly in minimal change disease.

    Complications. Loss of immunoglobulins makes patients vulnerable to infection, especially staphylococcal and pneumococcal. Loss of endogenous anticoagulants such as antithrombin III in the urine produces a hypercoagulable state with thrombotic and thromboembolic complications. Renal vein thrombosis, once thought to be a cause of nephrotic syndrome, is usually a consequence of it, especially in membranous nephropathy. Other complications include accelerated atherosclerosis from persistent hyperlipidaemia, protein malnutrition, and progression to chronic kidney disease in FSGS and some other lesions.

    Investigation and outcome. Diagnosis rests on demonstrating the urinary and biochemical abnormalities, excluding secondary causes, and renal biopsy where indicated. Minimal change disease responds dramatically to corticosteroids. Membranous nephropathy and FSGS respond poorly and may progress to end-stage kidney disease.

    What are the urinary/biochemical findings of nephrotic syndrome?

    7DU26MDU18MDU16JuDU14JuDU12JaDU10JuDU06Ja

    Urinary findings

    • Proteinuria of 3.5 g or more per 24 hours (3+ to 4+ on dipstick)
      The urine protein–creatinine ratio is correspondingly high. The protein is predominantly albumin. The proteinuria is selective in minimal change disease and nonselective in membranous nephropathy and FSGS.
    • Lipiduria: free fat globules and oval fat bodies (renal tubular cells laden with reabsorbed lipoprotein), which show a characteristic "Maltese cross" birefringence under polarised light. Fatty casts and waxy casts may be present.
    • Hyaline and granular casts are common. Red cells and red cell casts are characteristically absent or few in pure nephrotic syndrome. Their presence suggests a mixed nephritic–nephrotic lesion such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
    • The urine is frothy and has a high specific gravity.

    Biochemical (blood) findings

    • Hypoalbuminaemia (serum albumin below 3 g/dL) with reduced total protein and a reversed albumin–globulin ratio. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a low albumin and gamma-globulin fraction with a relative rise in the α₂ and β fractions, because large molecules such as α₂-macroglobulin are retained.
    • Hyperlipidaemia: raised total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL, VLDL and lipoprotein(a), with HDL reduced in some patients.
    • Low total serum calcium, secondary to hypoalbuminaemia (ionised calcium is usually normal), and a raised ESR and fibrinogen.
    • Serum urea and creatinine are normal in minimal change disease and may be raised in FSGS, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and advanced disease.
    • Serum complement is normal in the primary nephrotic lesions (minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, FSGS) but may be low in membranoproliferative GN, C3 glomerulopathy and lupus nephritis.

    How will you investigate/diagnose a case of nephrotic syndrome?

    DU04JaDU03Ja

    The diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome is established clinically and biochemically, after which the cause is sought.

    1. Clinical assessment. History of oedema (periorbital, then generalised), frothy urine and reduced urine output. Enquiry about diabetes, drugs, infections, malignancy and systemic lupus erythematosus. Examination for oedema, ascites, effusions and blood pressure.

    2. Confirmation of the syndrome

    • Urine: dipstick protein, 24-hour urinary protein (≥3.5 g/day) or spot urine protein–creatinine ratio, urine microscopy for oval fat bodies, fatty casts and red cells.
    • Blood: serum albumin and total protein, lipid profile, serum urea, creatinine and electrolytes, and a complete blood count and ESR.

    3. Search for the cause. Fasting blood glucose or HbA1c
    Serum complement (C3, C4)
    Antinuclear antibody and anti-dsDNA
    HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV and syphilis serology
    Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (myeloma, amyloidosis). anti-PLA₂R antibody in suspected membranous nephropathy. and age-appropriate screening for an underlying malignancy in older adults. Ultrasonography assesses kidney size and echogenicity and may reveal renal vein thrombosis.

    4. Renal biopsy. Light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy provide the definitive diagnosis. Biopsy is indicated in adults, in children under 1 year or over about 10–12 years, in children with haematuria, hypertension, renal impairment or low complement, and in steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing disease. A child aged 2 to 6 years with typical selective proteinuria, normal complement and no nephritic features is usually given an empirical steroid trial, because minimal change disease is by far the most likely lesion.
