    Nephritic syndromes and glomerulonephritis

    What is nephritic syndrome (AGN)?

    6DU26NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU09JaDU08Ja

    Nephritic syndrome, of which acute glomerulonephritis is the classic example, is a clinical syndrome caused by inflammatory disease of the glomeruli. It is dominated by the acute onset of grossly visible or microscopic haematuria with red cell casts, a diminished glomerular filtration rate manifested by oliguria and azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria (usually subnephrotic), and hypertension, often with periorbital oedema.

    The lesions that produce it share proliferation of intrinsic glomerular cells, usually with infiltration by neutrophils and monocytes. This inflammatory reaction injures the capillary walls, allowing red cells to pass into the urine, and narrows or obliterates the capillary lumens, so that GFR falls. The reduced GFR produces oliguria, fluid retention and azotaemia, and hypertension results from the fluid retention together with renin release from the ischaemic kidneys.

    The commonest cause is acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis, typically poststreptococcal, in a child 1 to 4 weeks after a sore throat or skin infection. Other causes are rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, proliferative lupus nephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is the form in which GFR declines within hours to days.

    Write down the pathogenesis of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

    8DU25NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NDU17JaDU12JaDU09Ja

    Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex–mediated (type III hypersensitivity) disease that follows infection with a nephritogenic strain of group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus. The pathogenesis can be followed as a sequence of events.

    1. The infecting organism. Only certain strains are nephritogenic
    More than 90% of cases are traced to M-protein types 1, 4 and 12, which can be identified by typing of the M protein of the bacterial wall. The disease appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo), a latent period compatible with the time needed to produce antibodies and form immune complexes.

    2. The antigen. Streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B (SpeB), secreted by nephritogenic strains, is the principal antigen in most cases, and it has been localised to the "hump-like" subepithelial deposits characteristic of the disease.

    3. Formation and deposition of immune complexes. At the outset, the antigens are planted from the circulation in subendothelial positions in the glomerular capillary wall, where they combine with antibody to form immune complexes in situ. Subsequently, by mechanisms not fully understood, the antigen–antibody complexes dissociate, migrate across the basement membrane and re-form on its subepithelial side, producing the subepithelial humps. Circulating immune complexes may also contribute.

    4. Complement activation and inflammation. The deposited complexes activate complement, generating chemotactic fragments (C5a) and the membrane attack complex. Neutrophils and monocytes are recruited and release proteases, oxidants and cytokines, and the resident endothelial and mesangial cells proliferate and swell. The result is diffuse, global endocapillary hypercellularity.

    5. Functional consequences. Obliteration of capillary lumens by proliferation, swelling and leukocytes reduces GFR, causing oliguria, azotaemia, and salt and water retention, which together with renin release produce hypertension and oedema. Damage to the capillary wall allows red cells and some protein to enter the urine, producing haematuria with red cell casts and mild proteinuria.

    Supporting evidence. Antibody titers against streptococcal antigens (ASO, anti-DNase B) are raised in most patients
    Serum C3 and other complement components are low, indicating complement consumption. and immunofluorescence shows granular deposits of IgG and C3, the pattern of immune complex disease. Most children recover completely. a small minority progress to crescentic glomerulonephritis or chronic disease.

    What are the urinary findings of acute glomerulonephritis?

    19DU25NDU25MDU23NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU18NovDU17NovDU16JaDU16JuDU14JaDU14JuDU12JaDU11JuDU10JaDU10JuDU06Ja

    The urine in acute glomerulonephritis shows the following changes.

    Physical. The volume is reduced (oliguria). The urine is smoky, tea- or cola-coloured because of altered blood (acid haematin)
    The specific gravity is normal or raised, and the reaction is acid.

    Chemical

    • Proteinuria is mild to moderate, usually under 1 g/day (always below the nephrotic range in the typical case), and the dipstick is positive for blood and protein.
    • Urinary sodium excretion is low because of the reduced GFR.

    Microscopic

    • Red blood cells, many of which are dysmorphic (acanthocytes, cells with membrane blebs) because they have been deformed in passing through the damaged glomerular basement membrane.
    • Red cell casts, the hallmark of glomerular bleeding, formed when red cells become trapped in a Tamm–Horsfall protein matrix in the tubules.
    • Hyaline and granular casts, white cells, and renal tubular epithelial cells.
    • There are no oval fat bodies or fatty casts, unlike in nephrotic syndrome.

    These findings accompany a raised serum urea and creatinine, an elevated ASO titer in poststreptococcal disease, and a low serum C3.

    Mention the complications of acute glomerulonephritis.

    DU11Ju

    The complications of acute glomerulonephritis result from the fall in GFR and the resulting salt and water retention, and from failure of the lesion to resolve.

    Early (acute) complications

    • Acute kidney injury with severe oliguria or anuria and uraemia.
    • Hypertension and hypertensive encephalopathy, presenting with headache, vomiting, visual disturbance and convulsions.
    • Circulatory congestion: acute left ventricular failure and pulmonary oedema from fluid overload.
    • Hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, which may be life threatening.
    • Secondary infection.

    Late complications

    • Progression to rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, which occurs in a small minority (probably under 1%) of affected children and is more frequent in adults.
    • Chronic glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney disease, with persistent proteinuria, haematuria and hypertension, particularly in adults, in whom only about 60% of sporadic cases recover promptly.
    • Persistent heavy proteinuria and a reduced GFR mark patients with an unfavourable prognosis. More than 95% of affected children recover renal function with conservative management.

    A child has oliguria, cocoa-coloured urine, periorbital puffiness after sore throat/skin infection. What is the probable diagnosis?

    6DU25MDU23NDU18NovDU17NovDU14JaDU10Ja

    The probable diagnosis is acute poststreptococcal (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis, presenting as acute nephritic syndrome. The age of the patient, the preceding pharyngeal or skin streptococcal infection with a latent period of 1 to 4 weeks, the cola-coloured (smoky) urine from haematuria, oliguria from the fall in GFR, and periorbital puffiness from salt and water retention are characteristic. Hypertension is usually also present. The diagnosis is supported by red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells with mild proteinuria in the urine, a raised antistreptolysin O titer, and a low serum C3, and it is confirmed if necessary by biopsy, which shows diffuse endocapillary proliferation with subepithelial humps.

    Nephritic and nephrotic syndromes

    B4

    What is nephritic syndrome? Tell 3 microscopic differences between nephritic syndrome and nephrotic syndrome. How can you differentiate between them by serum complement level?

    Nephritic syndrome is a clinical syndrome of glomerular inflammation, characterised by haematuria with red cell casts, oliguria with azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension, whereas nephrotic syndrome is due to increased glomerular permeability and is characterised by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Microscopically, nephritic syndrome shows red cells and red cell casts in the urine and hypercellular, inflamed glomeruli, while nephrotic syndrome shows oval fat bodies and fatty casts in the urine and normal or only thickened glomeruli with podocyte foot process effacement. Serum complement is usually low in nephritic syndrome of the postinfectious type and normal in the common causes of nephrotic syndrome.

    Complete explanation

    Nephritic syndrome results from proliferative, inflammatory glomerular disease. The cellular proliferation and leukocyte infiltration injure the capillary wall, allowing blood into the urine, and reduce GFR, leading to oliguria, azotaemia, fluid retention and hypertension. The classic example is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Others are rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy and proliferative lupus nephritis.

    Nephrotic syndrome results from a derangement of the glomerular filter, structural or charge-related, that permits plasma proteins to leak. There is typically little inflammation.

    Microscopic differences

    FeatureNephritic syndromeNephrotic syndrome
    Urine microscopyDysmorphic red cells and red cell castsOval fat bodies, fatty and waxy casts
    Few or no red cells
    Glomerulus by light microscopyEnlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with leukocytic infiltration and endocapillary proliferation (crescents in RPGN)Normal (minimal change disease), diffusely thickened capillary walls (membranous), or focal segmental sclerosis
    Electron microscopy / immunofluorescenceSubepithelial humps and granular IgG and C3 (postinfectious GN)Diffuse foot process effacement without deposits (minimal change)
    Subepithelial deposits (membranous)

    Differentiation by serum complement. In acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis the serum C3 is low (with normal C4) because the alternative pathway is activated and complement consumed, and it returns to normal in about 2 months. Low complement is also found in membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, C3 glomerulopathy and lupus nephritis. In minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy and FSGS — the common causes of nephrotic syndrome — complement levels are normal. IgA nephropathy, a cause of nephritic presentations, also has normal complement.

    B4

    What is glomerulonephritis? Mention five primary glomerular diseases.

    Glomerulonephritis is a group of diseases, mostly immunologically mediated, in which the glomeruli are the primary site of injury, usually with proliferation of glomerular cells and an inflammatory reaction. The five main primary glomerular diseases are acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis, rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy complete the list.

    Complete explanation

    Glomerulonephritis denotes inflammatory disease of the glomerulus, most often caused by immunologic mechanisms: deposition or in situ formation of immune complexes, antibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane, or cell-mediated immunity. Because some of the glomerular diseases have no cellular inflammatory component (minimal change disease and membranous nephropathy, for example), the term glomerulopathy is used for them.

    Diseases in which the kidney is the sole or predominant organ affected are called primary
    Those that are a manifestation of systemic disease, such as lupus, diabetes, amyloidosis or vasculitis, are secondary.

    The primary glomerular diseases are:

    1. Acute postinfectious (poststreptococcal) glomerulonephritis — nephritic syndrome
    2. Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis — nephritic syndrome with rapid loss of function
    3. Membranous nephropathy — nephrotic syndrome
    4. Minimal change disease — nephrotic syndrome, the commonest cause in children
    5. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — nephrotic syndrome and progressive disease
    6. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and C3 glomerulopathies — mixed nephritic–nephrotic picture
    7. IgA nephropathy — recurrent haematuria, the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide
    B4

    What is nephritic syndrome? What are the complications that may arise from nephritic syndrome?

    Nephritic syndrome is the clinical presentation of inflammatory glomerular disease, with haematuria and red cell casts, oliguria and azotaemia, mild to moderate proteinuria and hypertension. Its complications include acute kidney injury with hyperkalaemia and uraemia, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary oedema, progression to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and eventually chronic kidney disease.

    Complete explanation

    The syndrome arises when proliferative inflammation of the glomeruli injures the capillary walls and reduces the glomerular filtration rate. Because of reduced filtration, salt and water are retained and nitrogenous waste accumulates. Hypertension arises from the volume expansion and from renin release by the ischaemic kidneys.

    Complications in the acute phase follow directly from these disturbances:

    • Acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria, azotaemia and uraemia, accompanied by hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, which may be life threatening.
    • Hypertensive encephalopathy, with headache, vomiting, visual disturbance and convulsions.
    • Circulatory overload, with acute left ventricular failure and pulmonary oedema.
    • Heavy proteinuria, occasionally reaching nephrotic range.

    Complications in the later course

    • Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, with extensive crescent formation and rapid loss of renal function over weeks. This is the most serious sequel and may follow postinfectious glomerulonephritis in a small minority of children and more often in adults.
    • Chronic glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney disease, which may end in end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplantation. Persistent proteinuria and an abnormal GFR mark patients with an unfavourable prognosis.

    Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

    B4

    Tell the pathogenesis of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. What is AGN? Mention the role of streptococcal infection in the pathogenesis of AGN.

    Acute glomerulonephritis is an acute nephritic syndrome caused by inflammatory proliferation of glomerular cells, of which acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is the prototype. It is an immune complex disease: after a pharyngeal or skin infection with a nephritogenic group A β-haemolytic streptococcus, streptococcal antigen, notably pyogenic exotoxin B, and its antibody form immune complexes in the glomerular capillary wall, activate complement, attract neutrophils and monocytes, and cause proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells, reducing the glomerular filtration rate.

    Complete explanation

    Definition. Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is a clinical syndrome of acute onset with haematuria, oliguria, azotaemia, mild proteinuria, hypertension and periorbital oedema, caused by diffuse proliferative inflammation of the glomeruli. In its classic form it appears 1 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection, mainly in children aged 6 to 10 years.

    Role of streptococcal infection in pathogenesis

    1. Nephritogenic strains. Only particular strains of group A β-haemolytic streptococci cause nephritis. Over 90% of cases are linked to M types 1, 4 and 12, which are typed by their cell wall M protein.
    2. Antigen–antibody complexes. Streptococcal antigen, most importantly streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B, is first planted in subendothelial sites in the capillary wall, where it forms immune complexes in situ with antibody. The complexes then dissociate, cross the basement membrane and re-form on the subepithelial side, appearing as humps. Circulating complexes may contribute.
    3. Latent period. The interval of 1 to 4 weeks matches the time required for antibody production and immune complex formation.
    4. Complement activation and inflammation. The complexes activate complement
      C5a and other mediators attract neutrophils and monocytes, and endothelial and mesangial cells proliferate, producing hypercellular glomeruli that obliterate the capillary lumens.
    5. Functional result. GFR falls, causing oliguria, azotaemia, fluid retention, oedema and hypertension. Damage to the capillary wall allows haematuria and mild proteinuria.

    Evidence of an immunological basis. The latent period, elevated antistreptococcal antibody titers, low serum C3 from complement consumption, and granular immunofluorescent deposits of IgG and C3 in the glomeruli, with subepithelial humps on electron microscopy, all point to an immune complex mechanism.

    B10

    A 7-year-old boy developed periorbital edema with high-colored scanty urination, following a history of a sore two weeks earlier. What is your clinical diagnosis? What do you expect in the microscopic findings of his urine?

    The clinical diagnosis is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis presenting as acute nephritic syndrome. The urine is expected to show red blood cells, many of them dysmorphic, together with red cell casts, along with mild proteinuria, white cells, and granular and hyaline casts.

    Complete explanation

    The age of the child, the periorbital oedema, the high-coloured (smoky) scanty urine and the history of a sore throat about two weeks earlier fit acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The latent period corresponds to the time needed for antibodies to form against nephritogenic streptococcal antigens and for immune complexes to deposit in the glomeruli, causing inflammation. Oliguria and oedema reflect the reduced glomerular filtration rate and salt and water retention, and the coloured urine reflects haematuria.

    Expected microscopic urine findings

    • Numerous red cells, many dysmorphic (acanthocytes), reflecting passage through damaged glomerular capillaries.
    • Red cell casts, indicating glomerular origin of the bleeding.
    • Granular and hyaline casts, a few white cells and tubular epithelial cells.
    • Mild to moderate proteinuria (usually less than 1 g/day) on chemical testing.

    Supporting tests are a raised antistreptolysin O titer, a low serum C3, and a raised serum urea and creatinine.

    Tubulointerstitial Diseases

    B4

    What is pyelonephritis? What are the predisposing factors for its development?

    Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney caused by infection, affecting the tubules, interstitium and renal pelvis, most often due to ascending bacterial infection from the lower urinary tract. It is predisposed to by urinary tract obstruction and stasis, vesicoureteral reflux, instrumentation or catheterisation, pregnancy, female sex, diabetes mellitus, preexisting renal lesions, and immunosuppression.

    Complete explanation

    Pyelonephritis is one of the commonest diseases of the kidney. Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation, usually bacterial, associated with urinary tract infection. Chronic pyelonephritis is chronic tubulointerstitial inflammation and scarring involving the calyces and pelvis, which results from recurrent episodes of infection in the presence of predisposing factors such as reflux and obstruction.

    More than 85% of infections are caused by enteric gram-negative bacilli, above all Escherichia coli, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella and Enterobacter. The kidney is reached either by the ascending route from the bladder (the commoner route) or by the bloodstream (as in infective endocarditis or in debilitated or obstructed patients).

    Predisposing factors

    • Urinary tract obstruction and stasis, whether congenital or acquired (stones, benign prostatic hyperplasia, tumours, neurogenic bladder), because residual urine allows bacteria to multiply unhindered.
    • Vesicoureteral reflux and intrarenal reflux, which carry infected bladder urine into the renal pelvis and parenchyma.
    • Instrumentation of the urinary tract, particularly catheterisation, and cystoscopy.
    • Pregnancy, in which 4% to 6% of women develop bacteriuria and 20% to 40% of these develop symptomatic infection if untreated.
    • Sex and age: infections are much more frequent in females up to about 40 years of age
      in older males the incidence rises because of prostatic enlargement and instrumentation. Congenital anomalies are important in infant boys.
    • Diabetes mellitus, through increased susceptibility to infection, neurogenic bladder and frequent instrumentation.
    • Immunosuppression and immunodeficiency, and preexisting renal lesions with scarring and obstruction.
    B4

    What is UTI? Who are commonly affected and why?

    Urinary tract infection is infection of any part of the urinary tract by microorganisms, usually bacteria, shown by significant bacteriuria and pyuria. it may involve the bladder (cystitis) or the kidney (pyelonephritis). It is most common in females, because of the short urethra and other anatomical and hormonal factors, and also in infants with congenital anomalies, elderly men with prostatic enlargement, pregnant women, diabetics, and patients with obstruction, stones, catheters or immunosuppression.

    Complete explanation

    Urinary tract infection (UTI) is characterised by bacteriuria and pyuria, the presence of bacteria and leukocytes in the urine. It may be symptomatic or asymptomatic and may involve the lower tract (urethritis, cystitis, prostatitis) or the upper tract (pyelonephritis). By convention a count of 10⁵ or more organisms per mL in a properly collected midstream sample is taken as significant. Over 85% of infections are caused by enteric gram-negative bacilli, most commonly E. coli.

    Who is commonly affected, and why

    • Females. After the first year of life and up to about 40 years of age, infection is much commoner in women. The reasons are the shorter female urethra, the close proximity of the urethral meatus to the anus and vagina, the absence of the antibacterial properties of prostatic fluid, hormonal changes that affect bacterial adherence to the mucosa, and urethral trauma during sexual intercourse.
    • Pregnant women, because of ureteric dilatation and stasis, with a risk of progression of asymptomatic bacteriuria to pyelonephritis.
    • Infants and young boys with congenital anomalies, such as obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux.
    • Older men, in whom prostatic hypertrophy causes obstruction and incomplete emptying, and in whom instrumentation is frequent.
    • Diabetics, who have increased susceptibility to infection and neurogenic bladder dysfunction.
    • Patients with obstruction, stones, neurogenic bladder, catheters or instrumentation, and those who are immunosuppressed.
    B10

    A 25-year-old female presented with complaints of dysuria, dribbling of micturition and fever for 5 days. What is your probable diagnosis? How will you investigate the case?

    The probable diagnosis is acute urinary tract infection, most likely acute cystitis with ascending involvement of the kidney, that is acute pyelonephritis, since fever accompanies the dysuria. It is investigated by urine routine examination and microscopy, midstream urine culture and sensitivity, a complete blood count, serum creatinine, and imaging of the urinary tract.

    Complete explanation

    Dysuria and difficulty with micturition indicate irritation of the bladder and urethra (cystitis and urethritis) in a young woman, in whom the shorter urethra predisposes to ascending infection by enteric bacteria, chiefly E. coli. Fever of five days' duration suggests spread to the upper tract and acute pyelonephritis, which is also suggested if there is loin pain and costovertebral angle tenderness.

    Investigations

    1. Urine examination. The urine contains many leukocytes (pyuria) and bacteria. Microscopy may show leukocyte casts, which indicate renal involvement because casts form only in the tubules. A dipstick may show a positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite test, and there may be microscopic haematuria.
    2. Urine culture and sensitivity on a clean-catch midstream specimen, the definitive diagnostic test, showing significant growth (10⁵ or more organisms/mL) of the causative organism and guiding antibiotic therapy.
    3. Blood tests: complete blood count (neutrophil leukocytosis), ESR/CRP, serum urea and creatinine. Blood culture if there is high fever or suspected septicaemia.
    4. Imaging. Ultrasonography of the kidneys and bladder to detect obstruction, stones and residual urine. Further imaging (CT, intravenous urography, voiding cystourethrography) if infection is recurrent or complicated, to look for reflux, obstruction or scarring.
    5. A pregnancy test should be done before imaging or treatment in a woman of this age.

    Why is UTI more common in females?

    DU09Ju

    Urinary tract infection is much more common in females than in males, except in infancy and in old age, for several reasons. The female urethra is short (about 4 cm), so bacteria colonising the introitus have only a short distance to travel to the bladder. The urethral opening lies close to the anus and the vagina, so it is readily colonised by coliform bacteria from the intestinal tract, which adhere to the urethral mucosa through P-fimbriae. Females lack the antibacterial properties of prostatic secretion, which protect the male urethra. Hormonal changes influence bacterial adherence to the mucosa. Urethral trauma during sexual intercourse introduces organisms into the bladder. Pregnancy, with dilatation and hypotonia of the ureters, and postmenopausal oestrogen deficiency, which alters the vaginal and periurethral flora, add further risk. In males the incidence rises only in the first year of life, as a result of congenital anomalies, and again in old age, when prostatic hypertrophy and instrumentation promote infection.

    What is recurrent UTI?

    DU09Ju

    Recurrent urinary tract infection is the occurrence of repeated symptomatic episodes of infection after the initial infection has apparently been eradicated, conventionally two or more episodes in six months or three or more in one year. It is of two kinds. A relapse is recurrence with the same organism within about two weeks of treatment, indicating persistence of a focus of infection in the urinary tract, such as a stone, a scarred kidney or chronic bacterial prostatitis. A reinfection is recurrence with a different organism, or with the same species after an infection-free interval, indicating fresh entry of bacteria from the periurethral flora. it is more common in females.

    Write the importance of recurrent UTI.

    DU09Ju

    The importance of recurrent urinary tract infection lies in what it signifies and in what it may cause.

    1. It indicates an underlying predisposing factor that must be sought: urinary tract obstruction (stones, prostatic hyperplasia, strictures, tumours), vesicoureteral reflux, incomplete bladder emptying, neurogenic bladder, diabetes, or an instrumented or catheterised tract. Unless the cause is corrected, the infection will continue to recur.
    2. Chronic pyelonephritis and reflux nephropathy. Repeated episodes of acute pyelonephritis lead to coarse, irregular scarring of the kidney with calyceal deformity, especially at the poles, chiefly in children with reflux.
    3. Renal damage and its consequences: tubular dysfunction with polyuria and nocturia, hypertension, secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with proteinuria, and progression to chronic kidney disease and end-stage kidney disease.
    4. Stone formation. Infection with urea-splitting organisms such as Proteus produces struvite stones, which in turn obstruct and perpetuate infection.
    5. Acute complications such as papillary necrosis, pyonephrosis, perinephric abscess and septicaemia, and considerable morbidity from repeated symptomatic episodes.

    What is pyelonephritis?

    DU11Ja

    Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney caused by infection, affecting the tubules, interstitium and renal pelvis. Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation of the kidney, usually bacterial and associated with urinary tract infection, which reaches the kidney by the ascending route from the lower urinary tract (more commonly, with vesicoureteral reflux) or by the haematogenous route. Chronic pyelonephritis is chronic tubulointerstitial inflammation and scarring that involves the calyces and pelvis, resulting from recurrent infection in the presence of predisposing factors, chiefly reflux and obstruction.

    Describe the pathogenesis of ascending infection in pyelonephritis.

    DU11Ja

    Ascending infection is the commonest route by which bacteria reach the kidney. The normal bladder and bladder urine are sterile, so a series of alterations must occur.

    1. Colonisation of the distal urethra and introitus by coliform bacteria from the intestine. The degree of adherence depends on adhesins, particularly those on the P-fimbriae of the bacteria, which bind to receptors on the urothelial cells.
    2. Entry into the bladder. Organisms reach the bladder through the urethra, more easily in the female because of the short urethra and urethral trauma during intercourse, or through catheterisation and instrumentation.
    3. Multiplication in the bladder. Normally the organisms are cleared by voiding and by antibacterial mechanisms. When there is outflow obstruction (benign prostatic hyperplasia, tumours, calculi) or bladder dysfunction (neurogenic bladder in diabetes or spinal cord injury), emptying is incomplete and residual urine allows the bacteria to multiply unhindered.
    4. Vesicoureteral reflux. The normal ureteral insertion is a one-way valve. In reflux, caused most often by congenital shortness or absence of the intravesical portion of the ureter, or acquired from infection or persistent bladder atony, contaminated bladder urine is carried up the ureter to the renal pelvis, and residual urine again favours bacterial growth.
    5. Intrarenal reflux. Infected urine is propelled through the open ducts at the papillary tips deep into the renal parenchyma. It is most common in the upper and lower poles, where the papillae are flattened or concave rather than convex.
    6. Parenchymal infection. Bacteria enter the tubules and cause neutrophilic tubulitis and interstitial suppuration, with abscess formation. Glomeruli are relatively resistant. In the absence of vesicoureteral reflux, the infection usually stays localised in the bladder as cystitis.

    What are the complications of acute pyelonephritis?

    DU11Ja

    The complications of acute pyelonephritis are:

    1. Papillary necrosis, seen mainly in diabetics, in sickle cell disease and in those with urinary tract obstruction. It is usually bilateral. The tips or distal two-thirds of the pyramids show grey-white to yellow areas of ischaemic coagulative necrosis, and it may cause acute renal failure.
    2. Pyonephrosis, when total or almost complete obstruction, particularly high in the urinary tract, prevents drainage, so that pus fills the renal pelvis, calyces and ureter.
    3. Perinephric abscess, extension of the suppurative inflammation through the renal capsule into the perinephric tissue.
    4. Septicaemia and bacteraemic shock from gram-negative organisms, particularly in the presence of unrelieved obstruction, diabetes or immunodeficiency. Repeated septicaemic episodes may occur.
    5. Acute kidney injury, especially when papillary necrosis or obstruction supervenes.
    6. Chronic pyelonephritis, with coarse scarring, calyceal deformity, hypertension and progressive renal insufficiency, after recurrent or persistent infection. Some patients later develop secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

    Acute Kidney Injury

    List the causes of acute renal failure.

    DUno yr

    Acute kidney injury (acute renal failure) is a rapid decline in GFR over hours to days with retention of urea and creatinine and dysregulation of fluid and electrolyte balance. Its causes are classified as prerenal, intrinsic renal and postrenal.

    Prerenal (renal hypoperfusion without parenchymal damage)

    • Hypovolaemia: haemorrhage, severe diarrhoea and vomiting, burns, excessive diuresis, dehydration.
    • Reduced effective circulating volume or cardiac output: shock (hypovolaemic, septic, cardiogenic), congestive heart failure, cirrhosis with hepatorenal physiology, nephrotic syndrome.
    • Renal vasoconstriction or loss of autoregulation: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, contrast agents.

    Intrinsic renal

    • Tubular: acute tubular injury (necrosis), which is by far the commonest, either ischaemic (shock, trauma, sepsis, major surgery, acute pancreatitis) or nephrotoxic (aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, radiographic contrast, heavy metals such as mercury, organic solvents, ethylene glycol), together with pigment injury from haemoglobinuria (mismatched transfusion, haemolysis) and myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis).
    • Glomerular: acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis.
    • Interstitial: acute drug-induced interstitial nephritis (penicillins, NSAIDs), acute pyelonephritis with papillary necrosis, acute uric acid nephropathy (tumour lysis), light-chain cast nephropathy.
    • Vascular: thrombotic microangiopathies (HUS, TTP), malignant hypertension, vasculitis, renal artery or vein occlusion, atheroembolic disease, bilateral cortical necrosis.

    Postrenal (obstruction)

    • Bilateral ureteric obstruction, or obstruction of a single functioning kidney, by calculi, blood clots or sloughed papillae, retroperitoneal fibrosis, or tumours of the cervix, bladder or prostate.
    • Bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia, urethral strictures or posterior urethral valves, and neurogenic bladder.

    A 6y girl has watery stool then cessation of micturition. What is the most likely mechanism?

    DU08Ja

    The most likely mechanism is acute tubular injury (acute tubular necrosis) of the ischaemic type, following prerenal azotaemia from hypovolaemia. Severe watery diarrhoea causes loss of salt and water and a fall in effective circulating volume and blood pressure. Renal perfusion falls, GFR declines and urine output drops
    if hypoperfusion is promptly corrected, the injury is reversible (prerenal azotaemia), but if it is prolonged and severe the tubular epithelium is damaged.

    The proximal tubular cells, with their high metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, are particularly sensitive to ischaemia. Ischaemia causes loss of cell polarity as Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase redistributes to the luminal surface, so that sodium delivery to the distal tubule rises and incites afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction through tubuloglomerular feedback. Renin–angiotensin activation and endothelial injury, with increased endothelin and reduced nitric oxide and prostacyclin, add to intrarenal vasoconstriction. Injured cells slough into the lumen and form casts that obstruct the tubule, while the filtrate leaks back through the damaged epithelium into the interstitium. All of these factors lower GFR, causing oliguria and then anuria, as in this child.

    In a child with diarrhoea followed by cessation of micturition, haemolytic uraemic syndrome from Shiga-like toxin–producing E. coli is an important consideration, but it usually follows bloody diarrhoea and is accompanied by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

    Cystic Diseases of the Kidney

    B4

    Classify cystic diseases of the kidney.

    Cystic diseases of the kidney are classified into hereditary, developmental and acquired types: autosomal dominant (adult) polycystic kidney disease, autosomal recessive (childhood) polycystic kidney disease, medullary sponge kidney, nephronophthisis (medullary cystic disease complex), multicystic renal dysplasia, acquired (dialysis-associated) cystic disease, and simple cysts.

    Complete explanation

    Cystic diseases of the kidney are a heterogeneous group of hereditary, developmental and acquired disorders. They are important because they are common and pose diagnostic problems for clinicians, radiologists and pathologists, because some, particularly adult polycystic kidney disease, are major causes of chronic kidney disease, and because they may be confused with malignant tumours.

    DiseaseInheritancePathological featuresClinical features / outcome
    Autosomal dominant (adult) polycystic kidney diseaseAutosomal dominant (PKD1, PKD2)Bilaterally enlarged kidneys replaced by multiple cysts
    Liver cysts, berry aneurysms    		Haematuria, flank pain, infection, stones, hypertension
    Chronic renal failure at 40–60 years
    Autosomal recessive (childhood) polycystic kidney diseaseAutosomal recessive (PKHD1)Enlarged smooth kidneys with small radially arranged collecting duct cysts
    Hepatic fibrosis    		Renal failure in infancy or childhood
    Portal hypertension
    Medullary sponge kidneyNoneCystic dilatation of medullary collecting ductsHaematuria, infection, stones
    Usually benign
    Nephronophthisis (familial juvenile)Autosomal recessive (NPHP genes)Small, shrunken kidneys with corticomedullary cysts and tubulointerstitial fibrosisPolyuria, salt wasting, progressive renal failure in childhood
    Multicystic renal dysplasiaNone (sporadic)Irregular cystic kidney with primitive mesenchyme and cartilageRenal failure if bilateral
    Curable by nephrectomy if unilateral
    Acquired (dialysis-associated) cystic diseaseNoneCortical and medullary cysts in end-stage kidneysHaemorrhage, erythrocytosis, renal cell carcinoma
    Simple cystsNoneSingle or multiple cortical cysts in normal-sized kidneysUsually benign and asymptomatic

    The major cystic diseases (polycystic kidney disease and nephronophthisis) are ciliopathies, caused by abnormalities of proteins localised to the primary cilium and basal body of tubular epithelial cells.

    Urolithiasis

    B4

    What are common types of renal calculi? Mention a single common test to diagnose renal calculi.

    The four common types of renal calculi are calcium stones (calcium oxalate with or without calcium phosphate), the commonest at about 70%
    Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones, formed after infection by urea-splitting bacteria. Uric acid stones
    and cystine stones. A single common diagnostic test is a plain X-ray of the kidneys, ureters and bladder, which shows radiopaque stones.

    Complete explanation

    Urolithiasis affects 5% to 10% of people during their lifetime, more often males, with peak onset between 20 and 30 years. The most important determinant of stone formation is a raised urinary concentration of the stone constituents that exceeds their solubility (supersaturation). Low urine volume, altered urinary pH, infection, and deficiency of crystal inhibitors (citrate, pyrophosphate, osteopontin, nephrocalcin) contribute.

    1. Calcium stones (about 70%) — calcium oxalate or calcium oxalate mixed with calcium phosphate. Most are associated with hypercalciuria, with or without hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, bone disease), and some with hyperuricosuria, hyperoxaluria or hypocitraturia. They are radiopaque.
    2. Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones (5–10%) — formed in alkaline urine after infection with urea-splitting bacteria such as Proteus. They can grow into large staghorn calculi that cast the pelvicalyceal system.
    3. Uric acid stones (5–10%) — occur in gout, leukaemia and other hyperuricaemic states, but over half of patients have no hyperuricaemia, only persistently acid urine (pH below 5.5). They are radiolucent.
    4. Cystine stones (1–2%) — caused by inherited defects in tubular reabsorption of amino acids (cystinuria), forming in acid urine.

    An organic mucoprotein matrix, forming 1% to 5% of the stone by weight, is present in all calculi.

    Diagnosis. Plain radiography of the abdomen (KUB) is the commonest single test because most stones (calcium and struvite) are radiopaque. Ultrasonography and non-contrast CT are alternatives, CT being the most sensitive, and uric acid stones, being radiolucent, may be missed on plain films. Urinalysis shows haematuria and crystals.

    Tumors of the Kidney

    Renal cell carcinoma

    B4

    Classify renal cell carcinoma. Tell the genetic association of renal cell carcinoma.

    Renal cell carcinoma is classified into clear cell carcinoma (70–80%), papillary carcinoma (10–15%), chromophobe carcinoma (5%), and rarer types including collecting duct carcinoma and Xp11 translocation carcinoma. Clear cell carcinoma is genetically associated with loss of the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p, and papillary carcinoma with trisomy 7 and 17 and MET mutations.

    Complete explanation

    Renal cell carcinoma accounts for 85% of renal cancers in adults. Classification is based on histological, cytogenetic and genetic features.

    TypeFrequencyCell of originGenetic features
    Clear cell70–80%Proximal tubular epitheliumDeletion of 3p25 containing the VHL gene in 98%
    Second VHL allele inactivated by mutation or hypermethylation in up to 80%
    Papillary10–15%Distal convoluted tubuleNo 3p loss
    Trisomies 7 and 17, loss of Y in males (sporadic)
    gain-of-function MET mutation in the familial form
    Chromophobe5%Intercalated cells of collecting ductsMultiple chromosome losses with extreme hypodiploidy
    Excellent prognosis
    Xp11 translocation (TFE3-rearranged)Uncommon—Translocations of TFE3 at Xp11.2
    Young patients
    Collecting duct carcinoma≤1%Collecting duct, medullaVariable losses
    Poor prognosis (medullary carcinoma is similar, in sickle cell trait)

    Genetic associations (familial syndromes, about 4% of cases)

    • von Hippel–Lindau syndrome: loss-of-function mutations of VHL
      a half to two-thirds of patients develop renal cysts and bilateral, often multiple, clear cell carcinomas.
    • Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma: loss of the FH gene encoding fumarate hydratase
      Aggressive high-grade papillary carcinoma, with cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas.
    • Hereditary papillary carcinoma: activating MET mutations
      Multiple bilateral low-grade papillary tumours.
    • Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome: BHD gene, encoding folliculin
      Skin tumours, lung cysts and renal tumours.
    • Tuberous sclerosis also carries an increased risk.

    The VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin ligase complex that degrades hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) in the presence of oxygen. When VHL is lost, HIF-1 persists even under normoxic conditions and drives the expression of genes such as VEGF (angiogenesis) and IGF-1 (growth).

    Write down the morphology of renal cell carcinoma (short note).

    DU10Ja

    Renal cell carcinomas may arise in any part of the kidney but more commonly in the poles.

    Gross appearance. The commonest, clear cell carcinoma, is usually a solitary, unilateral, spherical mass of variable size that distorts the kidney. The cut surface is bright yellow-grey-white, the yellow colour being the result of the lipid in the tumour cells, and there are commonly large areas of grey-white necrosis and foci of haemorrhagic discoloration, sometimes with cystic change.

    The margins are usually sharply defined and confined within the renal capsule. As the tumour enlarges it may bulge into the calyces and pelvis and extend into the ureter. A striking characteristic is its tendency to invade the renal vein, in which it may grow as a solid column of tumour that extends into the inferior vena cava and even into the right side of the heart. Papillary carcinomas are often multifocal and bilateral, and typically haemorrhagic and cystic.

    Microscopic appearance

    • Clear cell carcinoma: nests, tubules or sheets of round or polygonal cells with abundant clear or granular cytoplasm containing glycogen and lipid, with a delicate branching vasculature. Most are well differentiated, but some show nuclear atypia, bizarre nuclei and giant cells.
    • Papillary carcinoma: cuboidal or low columnar cells arranged in papillary or tubulopapillary formations with interstitial foamy histiocytes in the papillary cores, and often psammoma bodies.
    • Chromophobe carcinoma: solid sheets of cells with prominent cell membranes, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and a perinuclear halo, with the largest cells around blood vessels.
    • Collecting duct carcinoma: irregular channels lined by highly atypical hobnail epithelium in a desmoplastic stroma.

    Sarcomatoid change, which can occur in any type, carries a very poor prognosis.

    Spread. Besides direct invasion of the renal vein and perinephric fat, the tumour metastasises widely and early, most often to the lungs (over 50%) and bones, then regional lymph nodes, liver, adrenal glands and brain.

    A male has haematuria, loin pain, palpable lumbar mass. What is the likely diagnosis?

    DU18MDU09Ju

    The likely diagnosis is renal cell carcinoma. Haematuria, flank (loin) pain and a palpable renal mass constitute its classic clinical triad, although all three are present in only about 10% of cases. Haematuria is the most reliable clue, and the tumour often presents when large. Other considerations include polycystic kidney disease, hydronephrosis and Wilms tumour (in a child), but in a male adult the triad strongly suggests renal cell carcinoma.

    Same: what are the histologic types of this lesion?

    DU18M

    The histological types of renal cell carcinoma are:

    1. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (70–80%), the commonest
      Cells with clear cytoplasm containing glycogen and lipid.
    2. Papillary renal cell carcinoma (10–15%), with papillary or tubulopapillary growth, foamy macrophages in the cores and psammoma bodies.
    3. Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (about 5%), with pale eosinophilic cells with prominent membranes and a perinuclear halo.
    4. Xp11 translocation (TFE3-rearranged) carcinoma, occurring in young patients.
    5. Collecting duct carcinoma (1% or less), arising in the medulla, and the related medullary carcinoma of sickle cell trait.

    Same: how will you confirm it?

    DU09Ju

    The tumour is confirmed by a combination of imaging and histopathology.

    1. Imaging. Ultrasonography detects a solid renal mass and differentiates it from a simple cyst, which has a smooth outline, is avascular and gives a fluid signal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen is the principal investigation, showing an enhancing mass and delineating its extent, renal vein and caval involvement and lymph nodes. MRI helps to assess venous extension. Chest imaging, and bone scan if indicated, search for metastases.
    2. Histopathology. The definitive diagnosis is made by microscopic examination of the tumour, usually the radical nephrectomy specimen, which establishes the histological type and grade. a needle biopsy is used in selected cases when surgery is not planned.
    3. Supporting laboratory tests. Urine microscopy for red cells, complete blood count (anaemia or, less commonly, polycythaemia), ESR, serum calcium and liver function tests, which may reflect paraneoplastic effects or metastases.

    Classification of kidney tumours

    Classify tumours of kidney.

    DU10Ja

    Tumours of the kidney are classified as follows.

    Benign neoplasms

    • Renal papillary adenoma (under 1.5 cm, cortical)
    • Angiomyolipoma (vessels, smooth muscle and fat; associated with tuberous sclerosis)
    • Renal oncocytoma (arising from intercalated cells of the collecting ducts)

    Malignant neoplasms

    • Renal cell carcinoma (85% of adult renal cancers): clear cell, papillary, chromophobe, TFE3-rearranged (Xp11 translocation), collecting duct and medullary carcinoma
    • Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma), the commonest renal tumour of childhood
    • Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
    • Rare tumours: sarcomas, lymphoma, and metastatic tumours

    Wilms tumour

    Write a short note on Wilms' tumour/nephroblastoma.

    DU06M

    Definition. Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma) is the commonest primary renal tumour of childhood, arising from embryonal renal precursor cells (the metanephric blastema)
    Most cases occur between 2 and 5 years of age.

    Genetics. Most cases are sporadic, but three groups of congenital malformation syndromes carry an increased risk. The WT1 gene on chromosome 11p13 is involved in the WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumour, aniridia, genital anomalies, intellectual disability) through deletion, and in the Denys–Drash syndrome (gonadal dysgenesis, early renal failure from diffuse mesangial sclerosis) through dominant-negative missense mutations. Beckwith–Wioedemann syndrome (organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihypertrophy) is associated with abnormal imprinting of the 11p15.5 locus and overexpression of IGF2.

    Mutations of CTNNB1 (β-catenin) and WTX are found in some sporadic tumours. Precursor lesions called nephrogenic rests are frequently found in the adjacent kidney.

    Gross appearance. A large, solitary, well-circumscribed tumour with a pushing margin, sharply demarcated from the compressed renal tissue. The cut surface is soft, homogeneous and tan to gray, sometimes with cysts, haemorrhage and necrosis. It may extend into the renal vein.

    Microscopic appearance. The classic tumour is triphasic, containing varying amounts of: (1) blastemal cells, small, round and densely packed with scanty cytoplasm and high mitotic activity. (2) epithelial differentiation, in the form of abortive tubules and glomeruli. and (3) stromal cells, fibroblastic or myxoid, occasionally with skeletal muscle. Anaplasia, associated with TP53 mutation, identifies a subset of tumours with a worse prognosis.

    Clinical features. The commonest presentation is a large, palpable abdominal mass, often noticed by a parent, with abdominal pain, haematuria, fever and hypertension (from renin production). Metastasis is most often to the lungs.

    Prognosis. With nephrectomy, combination chemotherapy and, when indicated, radiotherapy, over 90% of children with the favourable histology are cured. Anaplastic tumours respond less well.

    Clinical Manifestations of Renal Disease

    Hematuria

    B4

    What is hematuria? Tell 4 renal causes and 4 post-renal causes of hematuria.

    Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine, either grossly visible or detected only on microscopy. Renal causes include glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, renal calculi and renal tumours such as renal cell carcinoma. post-renal causes include ureteric or bladder stones, cystitis, bladder carcinoma and benign prostatic hyperplasia or prostate carcinoma.

    Complete explanation

    Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine in excess of the normal, conventionally three or more red cells per high-power field in a centrifuged specimen. It is gross (macroscopic) when the urine is visibly red, smoky or cola-coloured, and microscopic when blood is detected only by dipstick or microscopy. It is one of the commonest manifestations of renal and urinary tract disease and, when painless, must always be investigated to exclude a neoplasm.

    Renal causes (any four of the following)

    1. Glomerulonephritis — acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, crescentic glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, Alport syndrome
    2. Acute pyelonephritis, and renal tuberculosis
    3. Renal calculi
    4. Renal tumours — renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumour, urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
    5. Polycystic kidney disease and medullary sponge kidney
    6. Renal trauma, papillary necrosis (diabetes, sickle cell disease, analgesic abuse), renal infarction, and vascular malformations

    Post-renal causes (any four of the following)

    1. Ureteric calculi
    2. Bladder calculi
    3. Cystitis, including schistosomal and haemorrhagic (cyclophosphamide, radiation, adenoviral) cystitis
    4. Bladder tumours — urothelial carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma
    5. Benign prostatic hyperplasia and carcinoma of the prostate. Prostatitis
    6. Urethritis, urethral trauma, and instrumentation or catheterisation

    Coagulation disorders and anticoagulant therapy can cause or unmask haematuria from any of these sources.

    Write a short note on haematuria.

    DU19NovDU08Ju

    Definition. Haematuria is the presence of an abnormal number of red blood cells in the urine. It may be macroscopic (gross), when the urine is visibly coloured, or microscopic, when red cells are found only on dipstick testing or microscopy of the sediment (conventionally three or more red cells per high-power field).

    Classification. By the timing of bleeding in the urinary stream, haematuria is initial (urethral or prostatic origin), terminal (bladder neck or prostate) or total (bladder, ureter or kidney). By the site of origin it is glomerular, when the red cells pass through damaged glomerular capillaries, or non-glomerular (urological), when bleeding arises from the tubules, the renal pelvis or the lower urinary tract.

    Causes

    • Glomerular: acute glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, Alport syndrome, thin basement membrane disease, lupus nephritis.
    • Renal, non-glomerular: pyelonephritis, renal calculi, tumours (renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumour), polycystic kidney disease, tuberculosis, papillary necrosis, trauma, infarction.
    • Lower urinary tract: ureteric and bladder stones, cystitis, bladder carcinoma, prostatic hyperplasia and carcinoma, urethritis, schistosomiasis.
    • Systemic: bleeding disorders and anticoagulants, sickle cell disease and trait, strenuous exercise.

    Distinguishing glomerular from non-glomerular bleeding. Glomerular haematuria is characterised by dysmorphic red cells (acanthocytes), red cell casts, and accompanying proteinuria
    The urine is brown, smoky or cola-coloured. Non-glomerular haematuria shows normal-shaped (isomorphic) red cells, the urine is bright red, clots may be present, and there are no red cell casts.

    Investigation. Urine microscopy and dipstick, urine culture, urine cytology for malignant cells, serum creatinine, a coagulation profile, ultrasonography and CT or intravenous urography of the urinary tract, and cystoscopy, with renal biopsy for suspected glomerular disease.

    Significance. Painless haematuria is the commonest presentation of bladder cancer and an important clue to renal cell carcinoma. Its causes range from trivial to life threatening.

    Enumerate the important causes of haematuria.

    4DU24MDU16JuDU13JuDU08Ju

    The important causes of haematuria are:

    A. Renal

    1. Glomerular: acute poststreptococcal and other glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, Alport syndrome and thin basement membrane disease, Goodpasture syndrome
    2. Tubulointerstitial and infective: acute pyelonephritis, tuberculosis of the kidney, acute interstitial nephritis, papillary necrosis
    3. Neoplastic: renal cell carcinoma, Wilms tumour, urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis, angiomyolipoma
    4. Cystic and vascular: polycystic kidney disease, medullary sponge kidney, renal infarction, renal vein thrombosis, arteriovenous malformation
    5. Calculi and trauma

    B. Ureter, bladder, prostate and urethra

    1. Ureteric and bladder calculi
    2. Cystitis (bacterial, tuberculous, schistosomal, radiation- or drug-induced)
    3. Bladder tumours
    4. Benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostate cancer, prostatitis
    5. Urethritis, urethral stricture and trauma, catheterisation

    C. Systemic and miscellaneous Bleeding diatheses (thrombocytopenia, haemophilia), anticoagulant therapy, sickle cell disease and trait, infective endocarditis (emboli), malignant hypertension, and strenuous exercise.

    Write a short note on microscopic haematuria.

    DU12Ju

    Microscopic haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine in excess of normal that can be detected only by dipstick or by microscopic examination of the urinary sediment, the urine appearing normal to the naked eye. It is conventionally defined as three or more red cells per high-power field, ideally confirmed on repeated, properly collected specimens, since transient haematuria may follow exercise, menstruation, fever or trauma.

    The first step is to determine its source. Dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and accompanying proteinuria indicate a glomerular origin. Uniformly shaped red cells without casts indicate bleeding from the urinary tract. Glomerular causes include IgA nephropathy, thin basement membrane disease, Alport syndrome and mild or resolving glomerulonephritis, which typically present as isolated urinary abnormalities. Non-glomerular causes include calculi, infection, tumours, polycystic disease, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and sickle cell trait.

    The evaluation comprises urine microscopy, culture and cytology, serum creatinine, assessment of proteinuria, ultrasonography and further imaging, cystoscopy in patients at risk of urothelial malignancy, particularly older adults and smokers, and renal biopsy when a glomerular cause is suspected. Microscopic haematuria is often asymptomatic, but it can be the only early sign of serious disease such as bladder or renal cancer, or of progressive glomerular disease, and it should never be dismissed without evaluation.

    Proteinuria

    What do you mean by massive proteinuria?

    5DU25MDU24MDU14JaDU11JaDU06S

    Massive proteinuria is the loss of 3.5 g or more of protein in the urine per 24 hours (a lesser amount, adjusted for body size, in children). This is the "nephrotic-range" proteinuria that is the cardinal feature of nephrotic syndrome. It is caused by a marked increase in permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier, so that large amounts of albumin, and in some diseases globulins, escape into the urine. It is much more than the mild to moderate proteinuria (usually under 1–2 g/day) of nephritic syndrome and the minor protein excretion (less than 150 mg/day) of the normal individual. It leads to hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia.

    What are the causes of massive proteinuria?

    5DU22NDU13JaDU11JuDU09JaDU07Ju

    Massive proteinuria is caused by diseases that severely damage the glomerular filtration barrier.

    Primary glomerular diseases

    • Minimal change disease (the commonest cause in children)
    • Membranous nephropathy (the commonest in older adults)
    • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
    • Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and dense deposit disease
    • IgA nephropathy and other proliferative glomerulonephritides, occasionally

    Systemic diseases

    • Diabetes mellitus (diabetic nephropathy)
    • Amyloidosis
    • Systemic lupus erythematosus
    • Multiple myeloma (light-chain deposition disease)

    Drugs, infections and malignancy

    • Drugs: NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold, captopril, heroin
    • Infections: malaria, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, HIV
    • Carcinoma and lymphoma

    Other: hereditary nephritis and congenital nephrotic syndrome, preeclampsia and, as a secondary process, glomerulosclerosis from loss of renal mass (reflux nephropathy, obesity).

    Name the tests we do for proteinuria.

    DU09Ju

    The tests for proteinuria are:

    1. Dipstick (reagent strip) test — based on the "protein error of indicators": albumin binds the indicator tetrabromophenol blue at an acid pH, changing its colour from yellow to green or blue. It is sensitive mainly to albumin and does not detect Bence Jones protein or low concentrations (microalbuminuria).
    2. Heat coagulation test (heat and acetic acid) — protein coagulates on boiling. Persistence of turbidity after adding dilute acetic acid confirms protein.
    3. Sulfosalicylic acid test — acid precipitation of all proteins, including albumin, globulins and Bence Jones protein, producing turbidity.
    4. Heller's nitric acid (ring) test — a white ring of precipitated protein at the junction of urine layered over concentrated nitric acid.
    5. Esbach's albuminometer — semi-quantitative estimation of protein.
    6. Quantitative tests — 24-hour urinary protein
      Spot urine protein–creatinine ratio
      Urine albumin–creatinine ratio (for microalbuminuria).
    7. Urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation — to characterise the protein, for example Bence Jones protein or glomerular versus tubular patterns.

    What are the causes of proteinuria?

    DUno yr

    Proteinuria is the excretion of more than 150 mg of protein in the urine per day. Its causes are classified by mechanism.

    1. Physiological (functional) proteinuria — transient and benign: strenuous exercise, fever, emotional stress, pregnancy, exposure to cold. and orthostatic (postural) proteinuria in adolescents.
    2. Glomerular proteinuria — due to increased permeability of the filtration barrier: minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, FSGS, proliferative glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis, lupus nephritis. It ranges from mild to massive, and may be selective or nonselective.
    3. Tubular proteinuria — low-molecular-weight proteins (β₂-microglobulin, retinol-binding protein) not reabsorbed by damaged proximal tubules: tubulointerstitial nephritis, pyelonephritis, acute tubular injury, Fanconi syndrome, heavy-metal toxicity, cystic kidney diseases. The amount is usually under 2 g/day.
    4. Overflow proteinuria — a raised plasma concentration of a low-molecular-weight protein exceeds tubular reabsorptive capacity: Bence Jones protein in multiple myeloma, myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis, haemoglobin in haemolysis, lysozyme in monocytic leukaemia.
    5. Post-renal proteinuria — protein added to urine in the lower tract from inflammation, calculi, tumours or prostatic disease.

    How do you perform the heat coagulation test of urine?

    DU05MDU03M

    Principle. Heat denatures and coagulates the proteins in urine, which appear as turbidity. Phosphates and carbonates of the urine, which are also precipitated by heat, are dissolved by dilute acetic acid, whereas coagulated protein is not, so persistence of turbidity after acidification establishes the presence of protein.

    Procedure

    1. The urine must be clear
      a cloudy specimen is centrifuged or filtered. Its reaction is tested, and if it is neutral or alkaline it is made faintly acid by adding a drop or two of dilute (about 5–10%) acetic acid.
    2. A test tube is filled about two-thirds with the urine. Holding the tube at its lower end, the upper portion is heated over a flame to boiling, while the lower portion serves as a control for comparison.
    3. Any turbidity appearing in the heated portion is noted.
    4. Two or three drops of dilute acetic acid are then added, and the urine is boiled again.

    Interpretation

    • Turbidity that disappears on adding acid is due to phosphates or carbonates: no protein.
    • Turbidity that persists indicates protein. It is graded by its appearance: a faint opalescence (trace). Definite cloudiness without granules (+)
      Granular turbidity (++)
      Dense flocculent turbidity (+++)
      and a solid coagulum (++++).
    • A very high salt concentration can redissolve protein and give a false negative, and a urine that was alkaline when heated may fail to coagulate.

    What is microalbumin? Write its importance.

    DU09Ju

    Definition. Microalbuminuria is the excretion of small amounts of albumin in the urine that are above the normal range but below the threshold of detection by the routine dipstick test or heat test, conventionally 30–300 mg per 24 hours (an albumin–creatinine ratio of about 30–300 mg/g) in an adult. The normal excretion is less than 30 mg/day. Above 300 mg/day is overt (macroalbuminuria) proteinuria.

    Importance

    1. It is the earliest detectable marker of diabetic nephropathy, at a stage when the lesion is still potentially reversible. Annual screening is therefore recommended in diabetic patients.
    2. It identifies patients with hypertension at risk of renal involvement, and it is an early indication of renal damage of other kinds.
    3. It is a marker of generalised endothelial dysfunction and of increased cardiovascular risk.
    4. Early identification allows intervention — strict glycaemic and blood pressure control and renin–angiotensin system blockade — that slows progression to overt nephropathy and renal failure.

    It is best measured as the albumin–creatinine ratio on a first morning urine, and a positive result should be confirmed on repeat samples, since fever, exercise, urinary infection and menstruation can cause transient elevation.

    Renal function tests

    B4

    Tell the important renal function tests. Why is serum creatinine a more specific renal function test?

    The important renal function tests are those of glomerular function — serum creatinine, blood urea, creatinine clearance and estimated GFR — and of tubular function, such as urine concentration, together with urinalysis for protein and sediment. Serum creatinine is more specific than blood urea because creatinine is produced at a constant rate from muscle, is freely filtered and not reabsorbed, and is largely unaffected by diet, hydration or liver function, whereas urea varies with all of these.

    Complete explanation

    Important renal function tests

    1. Glomerular filtration: serum creatinine and blood urea (BUN)
      Creatinine clearance
      Estimated GFR (derived from serum creatinine, age and sex). Cystatin C
      Inulin clearance (the reference method, used for research).
    2. Tubular function: urine specific gravity and osmolality, the concentration test after water deprivation, urinary acidification, and tests for specific tubular transport defects.
    3. Urinalysis: protein, albumin–creatinine ratio, and microscopy for red cells, casts and crystals.
    4. Serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate) and acid–base status. and imaging.

    Why serum creatinine is more specific than blood urea

    • Creatinine is produced from muscle creatine at a steady rate proportional to muscle mass, so its plasma level is stable. it is freely filtered at the glomerulus and not reabsorbed, with only slight tubular secretion. Its level therefore reflects GFR.
    • Urea production varies widely: it increases with high protein intake, gastrointestinal bleeding, catabolic states, tissue breakdown, fever and corticosteroids, and falls in liver disease and low protein intake. A large fraction of filtered urea is passively reabsorbed in the tubules, and this increases in dehydration and reduced flow, so blood urea rises in prerenal states without any parenchymal damage.
    • Creatinine is thus a more reliable index of GFR, although it is insensitive in early disease, since it rises above normal only after GFR has fallen by about half.

    Give the normal serum concentration of uric acid.

    DU03Ja

    The normal serum uric acid concentration is approximately 3.5–7.2 mg/dL (about 210–430 µmol/L) in adult males and 2.6–6.0 mg/dL (about 155–360 µmol/L) in adult females
    Values are lower in children and in premenopausal women, and the reference range varies slightly with the method and the laboratory.

    Give the normal serum albumin value.

    DU11Ja

    The normal serum albumin concentration is 3.5–5.0 g/dL (35–50 g/L), forming just over half of the total serum protein of 6.0–8.3 g/dL (60–83 g/L). A level below 3 g/dL is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome.

    Give the normal serum urea value.

    DU11Ja

    The normal serum (blood) urea concentration is approximately 15–40 mg/dL (2.5–6.5 mmol/L), corresponding to a blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of about 7–20 mg/dL
    Urea is converted to BUN by multiplying by 0.47 (BUN × 2.14 gives urea). It is higher with a high protein diet and in the elderly.

    Give the normal serum creatinine value.

    DU11Ja

    The normal serum creatinine concentration is approximately 0.7–1.3 mg/dL (62–115 µmol/L) in adult males and 0.6–1.1 mg/dL (53–97 µmol/L) in adult females, the difference reflecting muscle mass
    The value is lower in children.

    Name the important renal function tests with interpretation and normal values.

    10DU26MDU24NDU24MDU22MDU16JuDU14JaDU12JuDU12JaDU10JuDU09Ju

    Renal function tests assess glomerular filtration, tubular function and the integrity of the nephron. They are listed in the table below with interpretation.
