    The Endocrine System

    49 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Thyroid GlandPituitary GlandPancreas / Diabetes Mellitus

    Pituitary Gland

    B8

    Name two pituitary tumors. Mention their significance.

    Two important pituitary tumours are the prolactin-secreting lactotroph tumour (prolactinoma) and the growth hormone-secreting somatotroph tumour. Both are pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs, formerly pituitary adenomas) arising from the anterior lobe. Their significance lies in the hormone-excess syndromes they cause and in the local mass effects of an expanding sellar tumour.

    Complete explanation: PitNETs are the commonest cause of hyperpituitarism. They are classified by the hormone and lineage-specific transcription factor expressed by the tumour cells (POU1F1 for somatotroph, lactotroph and thyrotroph tumours. TBX19 for corticotroph tumours
    SF-1 for gonadotroph tumours). Histologically they are soft, circumscribed, composed of monotonous polygonal cells in sheets or cords with a sparse reticulin network, which distinguishes them from the mixed cell population and rich reticulin of normal anterior pituitary.

    The lactotroph tumour is the most common functioning PitNET. Hyperprolactinaemia produces amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido and infertility, and is detected earlier in females than in males. Serum prolactin tends to rise in proportion to tumour size. Hyperprolactinaemia is not always due to a tumour: it also occurs in pregnancy, with dopamine-blocking drugs, with hypothyroidism and renal failure, and when any suprasellar mass interrupts the dopaminergic inhibition travelling down the pituitary stalk. Treatment is usually with dopamine agonists (bromocriptine or cabergoline).

    The somatotroph tumour secretes growth hormone, which stimulates hepatic IGF-1. In children before epiphyseal closure it causes gigantism. in adults it causes acromegaly, with enlargement of the jaw, hands, feet and viscera, together with glucose intolerance, hypertension and cardiomyopathy. These tumours are often large at diagnosis because the clinical changes are insidious.

    Any PitNET may cause mass effects: erosion of the sella turcica, compression of the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia), headache, hypopituitarism through destruction of normal gland, and pituitary apoplexy after haemorrhage into the tumour. A corticotroph tumour causes Cushing disease.

    Thyroid Gland

    Hypothyroidism and goitre

    Mention four important causes of hypothyroidism.

    DU25N

    Hypothyroidism is a state of deficient thyroid hormone activity. Four important causes are:

    1. Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto thyroiditis), the most common cause in iodine-sufficient regions.
    2. Iodine deficiency, the most common cause worldwide and of congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism) in endemic areas.
    3. Iatrogenic causes: thyroidectomy, radioiodine therapy, external irradiation of the neck, and antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil) as well as lithium, amiodarone and iodides.
    4. Congenital causes: thyroid agenesis or hypoplasia (PAX8, FOXE1, TSH-receptor mutations) and dyshormonogenetic goitre due to enzyme defects in hormone synthesis.

    Less commonly, hypothyroidism is central (secondary or tertiary) from pituitary or hypothalamic disease, in which TSH is low or inappropriately normal rather than raised.

    What is goitre?

    DU17Nov

    Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland. It may be diffuse or nodular, and the patient may be euthyroid, hyperthyroid or hypothyroid. Most goitres result from a compensatory rise in TSH that causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the follicular epithelium when thyroid hormone output is inadequate.

    What are the causes of goitre?

    DU18MDU17Nov

    Goitre results from any condition that reduces hormone synthesis and so raises TSH, or that stimulates or infiltrates the gland.

    • Iodine deficiency (endemic goitre in mountainous areas such as the Himalayas and Andes).
    • Goitrogens: dietary substances (cassava thiocyanate, cabbage-family vegetables) and drugs (lithium, antithyroid drugs).
    • Dyshormonogenesis: hereditary enzymatic defects of hormone synthesis (autosomal recessive).
    • Autoimmune disease: Graves disease (diffuse toxic goitre) and Hashimoto thyroiditis.
    • Sporadic goitre, in which no cause can be found in most cases.
    • Multinodular goitre, a late complication of a long-standing simple goitre.
    • Neoplasms, thyroiditis (subacute granulomatous, Riedel) and infiltrative disease.

    Give the etiopathogenesis of multinodular goitre.

    DU18M

    Multinodular goitre is a late stage of long-standing simple (diffuse non-toxic) goitre, so it has the same background (iodine deficiency, goitrogens, or unknown causes) but affects older patients. Recurrent cycles of hyperplasia and involution, driven by raised TSH, produce a gland that is irregularly nodular and asymmetrically enlarged, sometimes exceeding 2000 g.

    The key concept is heterogeneity of the follicular cells. Some cells respond more vigorously to TSH and other stimuli, or acquire growth-promoting genetic changes, and so proliferate autonomously to form nodules. Both polyclonal and monoclonal nodules are found within the same gland. Activating mutations in the TSH-receptor signalling pathway have been identified in a subset of autonomous nodules, which explains why some goitres become hyperfunctioning (toxic multinodular goitre, Plummer disease).

    Morphologically the nodules contain colloid-rich follicles lined by flattened epithelium, areas of hyperplasia, and secondary haemorrhage, fibrosis, calcification and cystic change. There is no true capsule separating nodules from the compressed residual thyroid. Clinically the dominant features are mass effects: tracheal and oesophageal compression, substernal extension, and superior vena cava syndrome. A dominant nodule may mimic a neoplasm.

    Thyroiditis

    Write in short the pathogenesis of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

    DU25NDU18NovDU11Ja

    Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease in which a breakdown of self-tolerance leads to progressive immune destruction of the thyroid.

    Loss of tolerance. Defective regulatory T-cell function or exposure of normally sequestered thyroid antigens is thought to be the initiating event. Genetic susceptibility is shown by associations with polymorphisms in immune-regulatory genes, namely CTLA4, PTPN22 and IL2RA, all of which regulate T-cell responses. The disease is 10 to 20 times more common in females.

    Effector mechanisms. Three mechanisms contribute to loss of thyrocytes:

    1. CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells directly kill follicular cells.
    2. CD4⁺ Th1 cells release interferon-γ, which recruits and activates macrophages and damages the follicles.
    3. Autoantibodies to thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase may cause injury by antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity or complement activation, although they may be a consequence rather than a cause of injury.

    The result is progressive depletion of epithelial cells, replacement of parenchyma by lymphoid follicles with germinal centres, oncocytic (Hürthle cell) metaplasia of surviving follicles, and variable fibrosis. Clinically this leads to gradual hypothyroidism with a diffuse painless goitre, preceded in some patients by transient thyrotoxicosis (hashitoxicosis) as follicles rupture.

    What are the expected laboratory findings in Hashimoto's thyroiditis?

    DU06Ja

    Expected laboratory findings in Hashimoto thyroiditis

    • Thyroid function: raised serum TSH with low free T₄ and T₃ once hypothyroidism develops. Early in the disease, a transient thyrotoxic phase with high T₄ and low TSH may be seen.
    • Autoantibodies: high titres of anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies in most patients.
    • FNAC: a heterogeneous population of lymphocytes and plasma cells with oncocytes (Hürthle cells).
    • Histology: diffuse lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with germinal centres, atrophic follicles lined by oncocytes, and interstitial fibrosis confined within the gland.
    • Radioiodine uptake is low or patchy
      Other autoimmune markers may be positive.

    Graves disease (case)

    A 30y lady has diffuse thyroid enlargement with exophthalmos. What is your clinical diagnosis (Graves' disease)?

    6DU19MDU14JuDU13JuDU12JaDU12JuDU08Ju

    Provisional diagnosis: Graves disease (diffuse toxic goitre). A young woman with a diffusely enlarged thyroid, exophthalmos and (in addition) features of hyperthyroidism fits the classical triad of Graves disease: hyperthyroidism with diffuse goitre, infiltrative ophthalmopathy with exophthalmos, and, in a minority, localised infiltrative dermopathy (pretibial myxoedema).

    Immunological mechanisms. Graves disease is an autoimmune disorder. The principal autoantibody is thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), present in about 90% of patients. TSI binds the TSH receptor and mimics TSH, stimulating adenyl cyclase, thyroid growth and hormone release without feedback control. TSH-receptor blocking antibodies may also occur and cause hypothyroidism in a few patients. There is genetic susceptibility (concordance 30–40% in monozygotic twins
    CTLA4, PTPN22, IL2RA and TSHR variants).

    Ophthalmopathy arises because CD4⁺ T cells in the orbit release cytokines that stimulate fibroblast proliferation and synthesis of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans. Together with inflammation, oedema and fatty infiltration, this increases retro-orbital volume and pushes the eyeball forward.

    Morphology: the gland is symmetrically enlarged with a soft, beefy-red cut surface. The follicles are lined by tall crowded columnar cells forming papillae without fibrovascular cores, and the colloid is pale with scalloped margins. Lymphoid infiltrates with germinal centres are present.

    Same: what will be the status of thyroid hormone level?

    DU13Ju

    In Graves disease, the thyroid hormone profile shows elevated free T₄ and T₃ with suppressed TSH, because the autonomously raised hormone levels abolish pituitary TSH secretion by negative feedback. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) or TSH-receptor antibodies are detectable, and radioiodine scanning shows diffusely increased uptake. In occasional patients (T₃ toxicosis) only T₃ is raised.

    Thyroid tumours

    Enumerate the tumours of thyroid.

    DU07Ju

    Tumours of the thyroid are classified as follows.

    • Benign: follicular adenoma (including oncocytic variant).
    • Malignant epithelial (follicular cell): papillary carcinoma, follicular carcinoma (including oncocytic type), poorly differentiated carcinoma and anaplastic (undifferentiated) carcinoma.
    • Malignant (C-cell): medullary carcinoma.
    • Other: primary thyroid lymphoma (usually extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma arising in Hashimoto thyroiditis), sarcomas and metastases.
    • Borderline entity: noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP), which behaves in a benign fashion.

    Name the malignant tumours of thyroid.

    DU07Ja

    The malignant tumours of thyroid are papillary carcinoma (about 85% of cases), follicular carcinoma (5–15%), medullary carcinoma (about 5%), poorly differentiated and high-grade differentiated carcinoma (about 5%) and anaplastic carcinoma (under 5%). Rare malignancies include lymphoma and metastatic tumours. Papillary and follicular carcinomas are well differentiated and carry an excellent prognosis, whereas anaplastic carcinoma is one of the most lethal human cancers.

    Write a short note on papillary carcinoma of thyroid (microscopic morphology).

    DU17NovDU12Ja

    Papillary carcinoma is the commonest thyroid malignancy and is the typical radiation-associated thyroid cancer, occurring mainly between 25 and 50 years of age.

    Gross: it may be solitary or multifocal, circumscribed or infiltrative with ill-defined margins, often cystic, with areas of fibrosis and calcification, and sometimes grossly visible papillae.

    Microscopic hallmarks

    1. Branching, complex papillae with thin fibrovascular cores lined by cuboidal cells.
    2. Characteristic nuclei: enlarged, overlapping, with finely dispersed, optically clear chromatin ("ground-glass" or "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei), irregular contours with nuclear grooves ("coffee-bean") and intranuclear cytoplasmic pseudoinclusions.
    3. Psammoma bodies, concentrically calcified structures in papillary cores or stroma, virtually never seen in follicular or medullary carcinoma.
    4. Lymphatic invasion is common, and about half of patients have cervical nodal metastases, but blood-vessel invasion is uncommon.

    The diagnosis rests on nuclear features, not architecture, so that follicular variants with these nuclei are still papillary carcinoma. Genetically, BRAF V600E mutations or RET/NTRK fusions are typical. The 10-year survival exceeds 95%.

    Thyroid disease and tumors

    B8

    Tell two benign and four malignant tumors of the thyroid gland. Which malignancy is common in the thyroid gland? Mention its prognosis.

    Two benign thyroid tumours are follicular adenoma and oncocytic (Hürthle cell) adenoma. The four main malignant tumours are papillary carcinoma, follicular carcinoma, medullary carcinoma and anaplastic carcinoma. Papillary carcinoma is the most common, accounting for about 85% of thyroid cancers, and has an excellent prognosis with a 10-year survival above 95%.

    Complete explanation: Follicular adenoma is a solitary, encapsulated nodule of well-differentiated follicles that compresses adjacent gland. it is diagnosed only after the capsule has been examined and found to lack invasion. A minority are functioning (toxic adenoma).

    Among the malignant tumours, papillary carcinoma arises in young and middle-aged adults and spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes. Follicular carcinoma spreads by blood. Medullary carcinoma arises from calcitonin-secreting C cells, about 70% sporadic and the rest in MEN-2 with germline RET mutations. Anaplastic carcinoma arises in the elderly, often from a pre-existing differentiated tumour, and is almost uniformly fatal within a year.

    Prognosis of papillary carcinoma is influenced by age (worse above 55), extrathyroidal extension and distant metastasis. Local recurrence occurs in 5–20% and distant spread in 10–15%.

    B8

    What is follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma of thyroid gland? How will you differentiate them by FNAC?

    Follicular adenoma is a benign, encapsulated thyroid tumour of well-differentiated follicular cells, whereas follicular carcinoma is the malignant counterpart that shows capsular and/or vascular invasion. FNAC cannot separate them, because the cytology is identical. The distinction needs histological examination of the entire capsule.

    Complete explanation: Both tumours are composed of uniform follicles containing colloid, and both commonly harbour RAS mutations. Cytologically, an aspirate from either shows cellular smears of follicular cells in microfollicles without the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. The decisive feature of carcinoma is invasion: penetration of the tumour capsule, invasion of vessels within or beyond the capsule (usually veins), or invasion of adjacent thyroid.

    Because this can be assessed only by extensive sampling of the capsule in the resected specimen, FNAC results are reported as "follicular neoplasm" and the nodule is surgically excised (lobectomy), with molecular testing sometimes helping to stratify indeterminate nodules. Adenomas do not recur or metastasise
    Follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously to bone, lung and liver.

    B8

    What is hyperthyroidism? What are the types of hyperthyroidism?

    Hyperthyroidism is a hypermetabolic state caused by excess circulating thyroid hormone due to overactivity of the thyroid gland. Strictly, thyrotoxicosis is the broader term and includes causes in which hormone excess does not arise from gland hyperfunction. The commonest cause is Graves disease.

    Complete explanation: Types are as follows.

    Associated with increased gland function (true hyperthyroidism):

    • Primary: Graves disease (diffuse hyperplasia, about 85% of cases), toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer disease), toxic (hyperfunctioning) adenoma, iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, and neonatal thyrotoxicosis from maternal Graves disease.
    • Secondary: TSH-secreting pituitary tumour (rare)
      Here TSH is normal or raised.

    Thyrotoxicosis without increased gland function: granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, painless thyroiditis, struma ovarii and factitious thyrotoxicosis from exogenous thyroxine.

    In all except the pituitary type, TSH is suppressed. The clinical effects are heat intolerance, weight loss with increased appetite, tachycardia and atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, proximal myopathy, diarrhoea and osteoporosis, with a staring gaze and lid lag from sympathetic overactivity. Radioiodine uptake distinguishes diffuse increased uptake (Graves), a hot nodule (toxic adenoma) and low uptake (thyroiditis).

    B10

    A 30-year-old lady presented with diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland with exophthalmos. What is your clinical diagnosis? What will be the status of the thyroid hormone level in this case? What is hypothyroidism? Tell some common causes of hypothyroidism.

    A young woman with a diffusely enlarged thyroid and exophthalmos has Graves disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroidism. Her thyroid hormone status will show raised free T₄ and T₃ with suppressed TSH. Hypothyroidism is the opposite state of thyroid hormone deficiency, caused most often by Hashimoto thyroiditis, iodine deficiency and iatrogenic ablation.

    Complete explanation: Graves disease is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that stimulate the TSH receptor. Free T₄ and T₃ are elevated and TSH is suppressed. Radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased and TSI/TRAb are present. The gland shows diffuse hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the epithelium with lymphoid infiltrates.

    Hypothyroidism is a state of structural or functional derangement that interferes with thyroid hormone production. It is classified as primary (intrinsic thyroid disease), secondary (pituitary) or tertiary (hypothalamic). Common causes are Hashimoto thyroiditis (most common in iodine-sufficient regions), endemic iodine deficiency, surgical or radioiodine ablation, drugs (lithium, amiodarone, thionamides), congenital biosynthetic defects and thyroid dysgenesis.

    Serum TSH is raised in primary disease and is the most sensitive screening test. In infancy, deficiency produces cretinism with intellectual disability. in adults it causes myxoedema with slowing of mental and physical activity, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, non-pitting oedema from glycosaminoglycan accumulation, and hypercholesterolaemia.

    B8

    Define and classify goiter.

    Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland. It is classified by pattern into diffuse and multinodular, and by function into non-toxic (euthyroid or hypothyroid) and toxic (hyperthyroid).

    Complete explanation

    1. Diffuse non-toxic (simple) goitre: the whole gland is enlarged without nodules. It is endemic (iodine deficiency, goitrogens) or sporadic (goitrogenic drugs, dyshormonogenesis, usually unknown cause). It evolves from a hyperplastic phase to a colloid involution phase.
    2. Multinodular goitre: irregular nodular enlargement resulting from recurrent hyperplasia and involution. Usually euthyroid, but occasionally toxic (Plummer disease).
    3. Diffuse toxic goitre: Graves disease.
    4. Goitrous thyroiditis: Hashimoto thyroiditis with goitre.
    5. Neoplastic enlargement from a tumour.

    The common mechanism is raised TSH from reduced hormone output, producing hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the follicular epithelium. in most patients the enlarged functional mass restores euthyroidism, and only when the defect is severe does goitrous hypothyroidism result. Clinical features arise mainly from mass effect.

    Diabetes Mellitus (Endocrine Pancreas)

    Diabetes mellitus

    B8

    What is hypoglycemia? Which one is more dangerous: hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia? Explain.

    Hypoglycaemia is a fall in blood glucose to a level low enough to cause symptoms of neuroglycopenia and adrenergic activation, generally below about 3.0 mmol/L (50–54 mg/dL). In the acute situation hypoglycaemia is the more immediately dangerous, because the brain depends on a continuous glucose supply and prolonged hypoglycaemia causes irreversible neuronal injury and death within hours. Hyperglycaemia is dangerous mainly through chronic complications, although severe acute hyperglycaemia (ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar state) is also life-threatening.

    Complete explanation: The brain accounts for about 20% of the body's oxygen consumption and is strictly dependent on aerobic glucose metabolism, so the cellular effects of glucose deprivation resemble those of hypoxia. The cortical pyramidal neurons, the CA1 (Sommer) sector of the hippocampus and the cerebellar Purkinje cells are especially vulnerable. Clinically, hypoglycaemia presents with dizziness, confusion, sweating, palpitations and tachycardia, progressing to loss of consciousness and coma.

    It most often complicates insulin or sulfonylurea therapy (missed meals, excess exercise, over-dosage), and also occurs with insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency and severe liver disease. Patients with long-standing frequent episodes may lose warning symptoms ("hypoglycaemia unawareness"), so that neurological impairment is the first sign. Rapid correction with oral or intravenous glucose prevents permanent damage.

    Chronic hyperglycaemia, by contrast, damages vessels and nerves slowly over 15 to 20 years, causing nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy and accelerated atherosclerosis.

    B8

    What is glycosylated hemoglobin? Tell its importance.

    Glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) is haemoglobin A to which glucose has become non-enzymatically attached. Its level reflects the average blood glucose over the preceding two to three months, so it is the standard measure of long-term glycaemic control and is also used to diagnose diabetes.

    Complete explanation: Glucose combines non-enzymatically and irreversibly with the amino terminal valine of the β-chain of HbA, and the amount formed is proportional to the prevailing glucose concentration over the life span of the red cell (about 120 days), weighted towards the most recent weeks. It is not affected by day-to-day fluctuations or by fasting. A value of 6.5% or more is diagnostic of diabetes, 5.7–6.4% indicates prediabetes, and in most diabetic patients the treatment target is below 7%.

    Higher values correlate with a greater risk of microvascular complications. Results are unreliable in conditions altering red cell survival or haemoglobin structure (haemolytic anaemia, recent haemorrhage or transfusion, haemoglobinopathies, iron deficiency, chronic renal failure).

    B10

    A 50-year-old diabetic patient becomes unconscious following a chest infection. He did not take any antidiabetic drugs. He also developed a musty odor in the breath. What is the diagnosis? What may be the likely findings in urine analysis?

    A diabetic who becomes unconscious after a chest infection, omits insulin or antidiabetic treatment and has a fruity or musty odour on the breath has diabetic ketoacidosis. Urine analysis will show marked glycosuria and ketonuria.

    Complete explanation: Infection raises counter-regulatory hormones (epinephrine, glucagon, cortisol) that block insulin action while insulin is absent or insufficient. The combination of insulin deficiency and glucagon excess increases gluconeogenesis and lipolysis. Free fatty acids reach the liver and are converted to ketone bodies (acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid, with acetone, which causes the odour).

    Hyperglycaemia (usually 250–600 mg/dL) causes osmotic diuresis and dehydration
    Ketone accumulation causes metabolic acidosis with deep, laboured (Kussmaul) breathing, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, and eventually coma. In the urine one finds heavy glycosuria, positive ketones on nitroprusside testing, an acid reaction and a high specific gravity. Protein and pus cells may be present if there is renal involvement or infection.

    Blood shows high glucose, ketonaemia, low bicarbonate and pH, raised anion gap, and a total body potassium deficit even though serum potassium may be initially raised.

    B8

    What is OGTT? Discuss its procedure. Name the indications for OGTT. What are renal and alimentary glycosuria?

    The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) measures the body's ability to dispose of a standard oral glucose load. After a 75 g glucose load in an adult, a two-hour plasma glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more establishes diabetes, whereas 7.8–11.0 mmol/L defines impaired glucose tolerance. Renal glycosuria is glucose in urine despite normal blood glucose because of a low renal threshold, and alimentary glycosuria is transient glycosuria after a meal due to rapid absorption.

    Complete explanation

    Procedure. The patient eats an unrestricted, carbohydrate-adequate diet (at least 150 g daily) for three days and remains physically active, and fasts for 8–14 hours overnight with no smoking or exercise. A fasting blood sample is taken. The patient drinks 75 g anhydrous glucose dissolved in about 250–300 mL water within five minutes (1.75 g/kg up to 75 g in children). A further sample is taken at two hours, with additional samples at 30-minute intervals when a curve is wanted. Urine may be tested at each interval.

    Indications. Borderline fasting glucose (impaired fasting glucose)
    Suspected diabetes with a normal fasting value
    Screening for gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks
    Unexplained glycosuria
    Unexplained neuropathy, retinopathy or nephropathy. and assessment of high-risk individuals such as the obese and those with a family history.

    Interpretation.

    CategoryFasting2-h plasma glucose
    Normalbelow 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL)below 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL)
    Impaired fasting glucose / IGT5.6–6.9 / —— / 7.8–11.0
    Diabetes7.0 or more11.1 or more

    Renal glycosuria: the renal tubular threshold (about 10 mmol/L or 180 mg/dL) is abnormally low (familial, pregnancy, tubular disease), so glucose appears in urine although the OGTT curve is normal.

    Alimentary (lag-storage) glycosuria: rapid absorption after gastrectomy, gastroenterostomy or thyrotoxicosis produces a high early peak above the renal threshold with glycosuria, but fasting and 2-hour values are normal.

    B8

    Classify diabetes mellitus. What is gestational diabetes mellitus?

    Diabetes mellitus is classified by pathogenesis into type 1, type 2, other specific types and gestational diabetes. Gestational diabetes is glucose intolerance first recognised during pregnancy.

    Complete explanation

    1. Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune β-cell destruction leading to absolute insulin deficiency (5–10% of cases).
    2. Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance with inadequate β-cell compensation (90–95%).
    3. Other specific types:
      • Monogenic β-cell defects: maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY, HNF1A, HNF4A, GCK and others), neonatal diabetes (KCNJ11, ABCC8), maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (mitochondrial DNA), insulin gene mutations.
      • Genetic defects of insulin action (insulin receptor mutations, type A insulin resistance).
      • Exocrine pancreatic disease ("type 3c"): chronic pancreatitis, pancreatectomy or trauma, pancreatic cancer, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis.
      • Endocrinopathies: Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma, glucagonoma, hyperthyroidism.
      • Drug- or chemical-induced: glucocorticoids, thiazides, nicotinic acid, phenytoin, β-adrenergic agonists.
      • Infections (congenital rubella, cytomegalovirus) and genetic syndromes (Down, Turner, Klinefelter).
    4. Gestational diabetes mellitus: glucose intolerance first detected in pregnancy, which occurs because pregnancy is a diabetogenic state. it usually resolves after delivery but most affected women develop overt diabetes within 10 to 20 years.
    B8

    Name the ketone bodies. What are the causes of ketonuria?

    The ketone bodies are acetoacetic acid, β-hydroxybutyric acid and acetone. Ketonuria occurs whenever fat is being oxidised faster than the tissues can use the ketones formed, most importantly in uncontrolled diabetes, but also in starvation and prolonged vomiting.

    Complete explanation: Ketone bodies are produced in hepatic mitochondria from acetyl coenzyme A derived from fatty acids. β-hydroxybutyrate is quantitatively the main one in ketoacidosis, whereas the routine nitroprusside (Rothera) test detects acetoacetate and acetone only. They are normally used as fuel by muscle, heart and brain, and when production outstrips use they appear in blood (ketonaemia) and urine (ketonuria).

    Causes of ketonuria:

    • Diabetic ketoacidosis (insulin deficiency).
    • Starvation, prolonged fasting, very low carbohydrate diet.
    • Persistent vomiting (hyperemesis of pregnancy, pyloric stenosis) and severe diarrhoea.
    • Alcoholic ketoacidosis
      Febrile illness in children
      thyrotoxicosis.
    • Glycogen storage diseases, and treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors.
    B8

    What is diabetic ketoacidosis? How does diabetic ketoacidosis develop in a case of uncontrolled diabetes?

    Diabetic ketoacidosis develops when a profound deficiency of insulin, together with excess glucagon and other stress hormones, causes unrestrained lipolysis and hepatic ketone production, together with severe hyperglycaemia and osmotic dehydration. It is mainly a complication of type 1 diabetes.

    Complete explanation: The usual precipitant is omission of insulin, or infection, trauma or other stress. Epinephrine and other stress hormones antagonise residual insulin and stimulate glucagon secretion. The glucagon-to-insulin imbalance reduces peripheral glucose utilisation and increases hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, so that plasma glucose rises to 250–600 mg/dL. Glucose exceeds the renal threshold, causing osmotic diuresis, loss of water and electrolytes and dehydration.

    Insulin deficiency also activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, which releases free fatty acids. In the liver these are converted to fatty acyl coenzyme A and oxidised to acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid. The rate of formation exceeds peripheral use, causing ketonaemia and ketonuria. When dehydration limits renal excretion of ketones, systemic metabolic acidosis results. Protein catabolism supplies ketogenic amino acids and aggravates the process.

    Patients present with fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath and Kussmaul respiration, and become drowsy and comatose if untreated. Ketoacidosis is less frequent in type 2 diabetes because the higher portal insulin level restrains hepatic fatty acid oxidation. Type 2 patients are more liable to a hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state. Treatment consists of insulin, fluid and electrolyte replacement and correction of the precipitating cause.

    B8

    Tell the pathogenesis of type-2 diabetes mellitus.

    Type 2 diabetes results from the combination of insulin resistance in peripheral tissues and a failure of the pancreatic β cells to compensate, producing relative insulin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility and obesity, especially visceral obesity, are the main determinants.

    Complete explanation: There is no autoimmune basis.

    Genetic factors. Concordance in monozygotic twins exceeds 90%, and first-degree relatives have a 5- to 10-fold increased risk. Genome-wide studies have identified more than 30 loci (such as TCF7L2) of modest effect, many involved in β-cell function, adipose tissue function and obesity.

    Insulin resistance. Insulin resistance usually precedes hyperglycaemia. Its consequences are failure to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis (high fasting glucose), reduced glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis in skeletal muscle after meals (high postprandial glucose), and uncontrolled lipolysis in adipose tissue (high free fatty acids). Defects include reduced tyrosine phosphorylation of the insulin receptor and IRS proteins and decreased GLUT-4 translocation.

    Obesity contributes through several mechanisms: excess free fatty acids that generate toxic lipid intermediates (diacylglycerol, ceramides) and impair insulin signalling. Altered adipokines with lowered adiponectin
    Chronic inflammation, in which fatty acids activate the inflammasome and release IL-1β and other cytokines. and hepatic steatosis (MASLD).

    β-cell dysfunction. Initially the β cells hypersecrete and hyperinsulinaemia maintains euglycaemia. Eventually they fail, through lipotoxicity from excess fatty acids, glucotoxicity, a blunted incretin effect (reduced GIP and GLP-1 action), and islet amyloid deposition (found in over 90% of long-standing cases), together with genetic effects on insulin secretion.

    Other risk factors are a sedentary lifestyle, sleep disorders and circadian disruption. The combination of obesity, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia and hypertension is the metabolic syndrome.

    B8

    What are the macroscopic complications of diabetes mellitus? What is hypoglycemic coma?

    The macroscopic (macrovascular) complications of diabetes result from accelerated atherosclerosis of the aorta and large and medium-sized arteries, causing myocardial infarction, stroke and peripheral vascular disease with gangrene. Hypoglycaemic coma is unconsciousness from a fall in blood glucose, usually due to excessive insulin or sulfonylurea dosage.

    Complete explanation: Persistent hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance cause widespread endothelial dysfunction, which predisposes to atherosclerosis that is histologically identical to that in non-diabetics but occurs earlier and more severely. Hypertension and dyslipidaemia (high triglycerides and LDL, low HDL) potentiate it. Myocardial infarction is the most common cause of death in diabetes and is almost as common in diabetic women as in men. Cerebrovascular disease and renal artery atherosclerosis follow, and gangrene of the lower limbs is about 100 times more frequent than in the general population.

    Gross renal changes include diffuse granular, contracted kidneys from arteriolosclerosis and nephrosclerosis, and pyelonephritis with papillary necrosis.

    The microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) are due to diffuse basement-membrane thickening and increased capillary permeability.

    Hypoglycaemic coma follows missed meals, exertion or inappropriate dosing. The patient is cold, pale and sweating with tachycardia and hunger, then confused and unconscious. It requires immediate oral or intravenous glucose, since prolonged hypoglycaemia causes permanent neuronal damage, especially of the cortex and hippocampus.

    B8

    Define diabetes mellitus. Give the WHO diagnostic criteria of diabetes mellitus.

    Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders sharing the feature of hyperglycaemia caused by defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or most commonly both. By WHO and ADA criteria it is diagnosed by a fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more, a two-hour OGTT value or random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more with classic symptoms, or an HbA1c of 6.5% or more.

    Complete explanation: The chronic hyperglycaemia causes secondary damage in the kidneys, eyes, nerves and blood vessels, and diabetes is a leading cause of end-stage renal disease, blindness and non-traumatic amputation. Diagnostic criteria (any one; all except a symptomatic random glucose must be confirmed on a separate day, and if two tests disagree the more abnormal result is accepted):

    1. Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L).
    2. Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in a patient with classic symptoms.
    3. Two-hour plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL during a 75 g OGTT.
    4. HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.

    Acute stresses such as infection, burns or trauma can cause transient hyperglycaemia, so persistence after recovery is required.

    Define diabetes mellitus.

    4DU26MDU25MDU22MDU17Nov

    Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders characterised by chronic hyperglycaemia resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action or both, and associated with disturbances of carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism. The sustained hyperglycaemia leads to long-term damage of the eyes, kidneys, nerves, heart and blood vessels.

    How is diabetes mellitus classified?

    7DU25MDU22MDU18NovDU17NovDU17MDU17JaDU14Ju

    Diabetes mellitus is classified as follows (Table 24.6).

    1. Type 1 diabetes mellitus: autoimmune (immune-mediated) β-cell destruction with absolute insulin deficiency. Includes latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA).
    2. Type 2 diabetes mellitus: insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency.
    3. Other specific types:
      • Genetic defects of β-cell function (MODY, neonatal diabetes, mitochondrial diabetes, insulin gene mutations).
      • Genetic defects of insulin action.
      • Diseases of the exocrine pancreas (chronic pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, carcinoma, cystic fibrosis).
      • Endocrinopathies (Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma).
      • Drug- or chemical-induced (glucocorticoids, thiazides, phenytoin).
      • Infections and genetic syndromes.
    4. Gestational diabetes mellitus.

    KetoacidosisCommon without insulinRare
    Hyperosmolar state more common
    Islet pathologyInsulitis (T lymphocytes), β-cell depletion, islet atrophyNo insulitis
    Islet amyloid, mild β-cell depletion

    Give the WHO (diagnostic) criteria of diabetes mellitus.

    5DU23NDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU14Ju

    WHO/ADA diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus (any one):

    1. Fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more (fasting means no caloric intake for at least 8 hours).
    2. Two-hour plasma glucose 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more during a 75 g OGTT.
    3. Random plasma glucose 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycaemia.
    4. HbA1c 6.5% or more.

    Except for criterion 3, the test must be repeated and confirmed on a separate day. Prediabetes is defined by fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL (impaired fasting glucose), a two-hour OGTT value of 140–199 mg/dL (impaired glucose tolerance), or an HbA1c of 5.7–6.4%.

    Define gestational DM.

    DU09Ja

    Gestational diabetes mellitus is glucose intolerance of variable severity with onset or first recognition during pregnancy in a previously euglycaemic woman. Pregnancy is a diabetogenic state because the hormonal milieu favours insulin resistance, and the condition appears in women with other genetic and environmental susceptibility. It affects 5–9% of pregnancies, usually resolves after delivery, and may cause foetal macrosomia. Most affected women later develop overt diabetes. It is detected by an OGTT at 24–28 weeks.

    What are the clinical features of a diabetic patient?

    DU03Ja

    The clinical features of a diabetic patient depend on type and duration.

    Type 1: abrupt onset of the classic triad of polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia, with weight loss, fatigue and muscle weakness. The presentation may be diabetic ketoacidosis. The catabolic state arises because insulin deficiency impairs glucose assimilation, so glucose spills into urine and causes osmotic diuresis, thirst and increased appetite, while protein and fat breakdown cause wasting. Type 2: often asymptomatic and found on routine testing. Symptoms include fatigue, dizziness, blurred vision, recurrent skin and urinary infections, pruritus vulvae or balanitis, and delayed wound healing.

    Chronic features: retinopathy with visual loss, cataract, nephropathy with proteinuria and hypertension, peripheral and autonomic neuropathy, diabetic foot ulceration and gangrene, and accelerated atherosclerosis with ischaemic heart disease and stroke.

    OGTT and glucose tolerance

    What is OGTT? Write its procedure, indications and interpretation.

    8DU24MDU22NDU21MDU18NovDU17MDU15JaDU13JuDU11Ja

    The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) assesses the body's capacity to handle an oral glucose load.

    Procedure. Three days of an unrestricted carbohydrate diet and normal activity. Overnight fast of 8–14 hours
    a fasting plasma glucose sample
    Ingestion of 75 g anhydrous glucose in 250–300 mL of water over five minutes (1.75 g/kg to a maximum of 75 g in children). Further plasma glucose estimation at two hours, and if a curve is needed, at 30, 60 and 90 minutes. The patient must remain seated and not smoke.

    Indications. Borderline fasting glucose
    Suspected diabetes with normal fasting glucose
    Screening in pregnancy (gestational diabetes) and in high-risk groups. Glycosuria of uncertain cause
    Investigation of impaired glucose tolerance
    diabetic-type complications without proven hyperglycaemia.

    Interpretation (2-hour plasma glucose). Below 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL) is normal
    7.8–11.0 mmol/L is impaired glucose tolerance
    11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more is diabetes.

    What is the normal fasting blood glucose level?

    DU15Ja

    The normal fasting plasma glucose is 3.9–5.5 mmol/L (70–99 mg/dL). Values from 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L (100–125 mg/dL) constitute impaired fasting glucose, and 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more indicates diabetes.

    What is impaired glucose tolerance (IGT)?

    DU15JaDU12Ja

    Impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) is a state of dysglycaemia intermediate between normal and diabetes, in which the fasting glucose is below the diabetic level but the two-hour plasma glucose in a 75 g OGTT is 7.8–11.0 mmol/L (140–199 mg/dL). It is a form of prediabetes: about one-quarter of such persons develop overt diabetes within five years, and they are also at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, especially when obese or with a family history.

    Draw different types of diabetic curves.

    DU09Ja

    Typical OGTT curves (plasma glucose in mmol/L, illustrative values) are shown below.

    Time (min)NormalDiabeticImpaired glucose toleranceAlimentary (lag-storage)Flat curve (malabsorption)
    0 (fasting)4–5.57.0 or more5.6–6.9normalnormal
    30–60peak below 10, then fallsrises above 11.1rises to 9–11sharp peak above 10 (exceeds renal threshold)slight rise, below 1.5 above fasting
    120below 7.811.1 or more7.8–11.0returns to normal (below 7.8)normal

    The normal curve rises to a peak at 30–60 minutes and returns to the fasting level by two hours. The diabetic curve starts from a raised fasting level, rises to a high peak and remains above 11.1 mmol/L at two hours. The IGT curve is intermediate. The lag-storage curve shows an early high peak with glycosuria, but a normal two-hour value. The flat curve shows hardly any rise (coeliac disease, malabsorption). In renal glycosuria the curve is normal despite glycosuria.

    HbA1c

    A6

    What is HbA1c (glycosylated haemoglobin)?

    6A6DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU16JuDU04M

    Also asked as: What is HbA1c?

    HbA1c is glycated haemoglobin, formed by non-enzymatic attachment of glucose to the β-chain of haemoglobin A. It reflects mean blood glucose over the previous 8–12 weeks, and is used both to diagnose diabetes (6.5% or more) and to monitor long-term control (target below 7%).

    Complete explanation: Glycation proceeds continuously and irreversibly over the 120-day lifespan of the red cell, so that the HbA1c percentage is proportional to the average glucose exposure, weighted to the most recent month. Unlike a blood glucose it does not need fasting and is unaffected by day-to-day variation. Interpretation: below 5.7% normal
    5.7–6.4% prediabetes
    6.5% or more diabetes.

    Clinically, a lower HbA1c is associated with a reduced risk of retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy. Falsely low values occur in haemolytic anaemia, blood loss and recent transfusion, and falsely high or unreliable values in iron deficiency and some haemoglobinopathies. Continuous glucose monitoring has introduced "time in range" as an additional measure.

    A6

    Importance of HbA1c.

    A6

    The importance of HbA1c is that it gives an objective index of average glycaemia over two to three months, which makes it the best single test for assessing long-term control and the risk of complications. it is also an accepted diagnostic criterion for diabetes.

    Complete explanation: Its value rests on four uses. First, monitoring control: it shows whether treatment has been effective over the preceding months, independent of the day's meal or fast. Second, predicting complications: large trials have shown that sustained glycaemic control, with HbA1c maintained below 7%, reduces microvascular complications. Third, diagnosis and screening: 6.5% or more diagnoses diabetes and 5.7–6.4% identifies prediabetes.

    Fourth, it serves to separate transient stress hyperglycaemia from established diabetes, since a normal HbA1c in a hyperglycaemic patient suggests a short-lived rise. Its limitations are the effects of anaemia, haemoglobinopathy, transfusion and renal failure.

    Hyperglycaemia

    What is hyperglycaemia?

    DU12Ju

    Hyperglycaemia is an abnormally raised blood glucose concentration, above the normal fasting range of about 5.5 mmol/L (100 mg/dL). Diabetes mellitus is diagnosed when fasting plasma glucose is 7.0 mmol/L or more, or random glucose is 11.1 mmol/L or more with symptoms. Values in between define impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance.

    Mention the important causes of hyperglycaemia.

    DU05M

    Important causes of hyperglycaemia:

    1. Diabetes mellitus (type 1, type 2, gestational and secondary types), the commonest cause.
    2. Endocrine disease with insulin antagonism: Cushing syndrome, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, glucagonoma.
    3. Stress hyperglycaemia from acute illness: severe infection, myocardial infarction, stroke, burns, trauma and surgery, owing to catecholamines and cortisol.
    4. Drugs: glucocorticoids, thiazides, β-agonists, phenytoin, nicotinic acid.
    5. Pancreatic disease: pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, carcinoma, haemochromatosis, cystic fibrosis.
    6. Other: pregnancy, liver disease, intravenous glucose infusion, and sampling after a meal.

    What is hyperglycaemia sine glycosuria? Why is sugar absent in urine?

    4DU22NDU21MDU09JuDU08Ju

    Hyperglycaemia sine glycosuria is the finding of a raised blood glucose without glucose in the urine. This occurs because glucose appears in urine only when the plasma concentration exceeds the renal threshold of about 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL), and that threshold may be effectively raised. The usual causes are:

    • Blood glucose that is raised, but not above the renal threshold (mild hyperglycaemia).
    • A raised renal threshold from reduced glomerular filtration of glucose, as in elderly diabetic patients, in diabetic glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease) and in chronic renal failure. The kidney filters less glucose, so tubular reabsorption is able to cope.

    For this reason, urine testing alone must not be used to exclude diabetes in the elderly.

    Complications and ketoacidosis

    Write the complications of diabetes mellitus (macro- and microvascular).

    14DU26MDU25MDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18NovDU18MDU17NovDU17MDU17JaDU15JaDU13JuDU12Ju

    The complications of diabetes mellitus are acute and chronic.

    Acute metabolic complications: diabetic ketoacidosis (mainly type 1), hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (mainly older type 2 patients, glucose often 600–1200 mg/dL) and hypoglycaemia from treatment.

    Chronic complications are caused by sustained hyperglycaemia acting through advanced glycation end-products (AGEs binding RAGE), activation of protein kinase C, polyol pathway flux with NADPH depletion and oxidative stress, and the hexosamine pathway.

    1. Macrovascular disease: accelerated atherosclerosis causing myocardial infarction (the commonest cause of death), stroke, peripheral vascular disease and gangrene.
    2. Microangiopathy (basement-membrane thickening with increased permeability):
      • Nephropathy: capillary basement-membrane thickening, diffuse mesangial sclerosis and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson), arteriolosclerosis involving both afferent and efferent arterioles, and pyelonephritis with papillary necrosis. it progresses from microalbuminuria to overt proteinuria and end-stage renal disease.
      • Retinopathy: non-proliferative (microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, macular oedema) and proliferative (neovascularisation driven by VEGF), a leading cause of adult blindness.
      • Neuropathy: distal symmetric "glove and stocking" polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy and mononeuropathy.
    3. Eye: cataract and glaucoma.
    4. Infections: skin, tuberculosis, pneumonia and urinary tract infection, because of impaired neutrophil function and vascular compromise.
    5. Other: diabetic foot ulceration with osteomyelitis, MASLD, and pregnancy complications (macrosomia, malformations).

    What are ketone bodies (ketonuria)?

    DU16JuDU11JuDU10Ja

    Ketone bodies are acetoacetic acid, β-hydroxybutyric acid and acetone, produced in the liver from fatty acid oxidation when carbohydrate is unavailable or unutilizable, as in insulin deficiency or starvation. When their production exceeds tissue use they accumulate in blood (ketonaemia) and are excreted in urine (ketonuria), where they are detected by the nitroprusside (Rothera or dipstick) test. Ketonuria occurs in diabetic ketoacidosis, starvation, persistent vomiting and high-fat, low-carbohydrate diets, and in febrile illness in children.

    Write a short note on ketoacidosis / discuss the pathogenesis of DKA.

    7DU26MDU24NDU23NDU19MDU17JaDU11JuDU12Ju

    Diabetic ketoacidosis is a severe acute complication, chiefly of type 1 diabetes, characterised by hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis.

    Pathogenesis. A precipitant (omitted insulin, infection, trauma, certain drugs) raises epinephrine, glucagon and cortisol while insulin is deficient. Decreased glucose utilisation and increased gluconeogenesis produce marked hyperglycaemia, causing osmotic diuresis, dehydration and loss of electrolytes. Insulin deficiency stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase and so increases free fatty acids, which the liver oxidises via fatty acyl coenzyme A to acetoacetic and β-hydroxybutyric acids. Production overwhelms peripheral use, and dehydration impairs urinary excretion. Systemic ketoacidosis results, aggravated by ketogenic amino acids from protein catabolism.

    Clinical features. Fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity odour, Kussmaul breathing, dehydration, and progressive depression of consciousness to coma.

    Laboratory findings. Plasma glucose 250–600 mg/dL, ketonaemia and ketonuria, low pH and bicarbonate, raised anion gap and electrolyte disturbance.

    Management consists of insulin, fluid and electrolyte replacement, correction of acidosis and treatment of the precipitating cause. The lower frequency in type 2 diabetes is attributed to higher portal insulin levels, which restrain ketone formation.

    A 48y diabetic became unconscious after chest infection with musty odour in breath. What may be the likely urine finding?

    DU12Ju

    In a diabetic who is unconscious after a chest infection with a fruity or musty odour of the breath, the likely diagnosis is diabetic ketoacidosis. The urine will show heavy glycosuria and ketonuria (positive nitroprusside test), an acid pH and a high specific gravity
    There may also be proteinuria and pus cells from associated infection.

    Diabetes cases

    A 58y obese male has weight loss, FBS 6.6, RBS 10.0 mmol/L, raised lipids. What is the diagnosis?

    DU11Ju

    Probable diagnosis: an obese 58-year-old man with weight loss, a fasting glucose of 6.6 mmol/L, a random glucose of 10.0 mmol/L and a raised lipid profile has abnormal glucose regulation in the setting of the metabolic syndrome. His values fall just short of the diagnostic thresholds for diabetes (fasting 7.0 mmol/L, random 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms), so strictly he has impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes) and is a probable early type 2 diabetic, particularly given the weight loss, which should raise suspicion of evolving diabetes. Diagnosis must be confirmed by repeat fasting glucose, 75 g OGTT and HbA1c.

    The combination of central obesity, hyperglycaemia, increased cholesterol and triglycerides, and hypertension (to be sought) defines the metabolic syndrome and carries a high risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

    Same: how will you investigate the case?

    DU11Ju

    Investigation of this patient:

    1. Confirm glycaemic status: repeat fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour OGTT with 75 g glucose, HbA1c.
    2. Urine: glucose, ketones, protein
      albumin-to-creatinine ratio for microalbuminuria.
    3. Complication and risk assessment: lipid profile, serum creatinine and urea, electrolytes, liver function tests (MASLD), ECG, blood pressure measurement and fundoscopy.
    4. Other: thyroid function if weight loss is unexplained, and tests to exclude a pancreatic cause (amylase, imaging) and secondary diabetes.

    All topics / Ch 25

    The Skin

    16 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Terminology and Normal Skin

    B9

    Common terminology of skin: papule, pustule, vesicles, bulla, blister, wheal, macule, patch.

    These are the descriptive terms used for primary skin lesions. Macules and patches are flat lesions distinguished only by colour, the macule being less than 5 mm and the patch larger. Papules are solid elevations less than 5 mm. Vesicles and bullae are fluid-filled blisters, smaller and larger than 5 mm respectively. A pustule is a pus-filled elevation, and a wheal is a transient, oedematous, pale-pink raised plaque.

    Complete explanation: Dermatopathology begins with a precise clinical vocabulary, because the distribution and character of a lesion often point to the diagnosis before any tissue is examined.

    TermDefinition
    MaculeFlat, circumscribed area of colour change, less than 5 mm in diameter.
    PatchA flat lesion of altered colour larger than 5 mm.
    PapuleSolid, elevated, dome-shaped or flat-topped lesion less than 5 mm in diameter.
    VesicleFluid-filled, raised lesion less than 5 mm in diameter, lying within or just beneath the epidermis.
    BullaA fluid-filled, raised lesion larger than 5 mm.
    BlisterGeneral term for a fluid-filled lesion, covering both vesicle and bulla.
    PustuleDiscrete, raised lesion filled with pus, i.e. neutrophils and debris.
    WhealFirm, oedematous, pale-pink, transient plaque produced by dermal oedema and typically itchy, as in urticaria
    it resolves within hours without leaving a mark.

    A plaque is the larger counterpart of the papule: an elevated, flat-topped lesion greater than 5 mm in diameter, usually produced by confluent papules. The size limit of 5 mm is the conventional dividing line between each small and large pair.

    B9

    Structure of the skin. What are parakeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis and spongiosis?

    The skin consists of the epidermis, the dermis and the subcutis, with appendages such as hair follicles and sweat and sebaceous glands. The epidermis is a keratinising stratified squamous epithelium of basal, spinous, granular and cornified layers. Parakeratosis is retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum, hypergranulosis is thickening of the granular layer, acanthosis is thickening of the epidermis from hyperplasia of the spinous layer, and spongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis.

    Complete explanation

    Structure of the skin. The epidermis is a stratified squamous epithelium whose principal cell, the keratinocyte, matures as it moves upward from the basal layer. The deepest layer, the stratum basale, is a single row of cuboidal cells attached to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes. it contains the proliferating stem cells. Above it lies the stratum spinosum, whose cells are joined by desmosomes, giving the spiny appearance on fixation.

    Next is the stratum granulosum, with coarse basophilic keratohyalin granules that contribute to the cornified envelope. The outermost layer, the stratum corneum, consists of flattened, anucleate, keratin-filled squames that form the barrier. on the palms and soles a clear stratum lucidum may be identified. Interspersed among the keratinocytes are melanocytes in the basal layer, which transfer melanin to neighbouring keratinocytes and protect the nuclei from ultraviolet radiation, Langerhans cells, which are antigen-presenting dendritic cells in the spinous layer, and Merkel cells, which are touch-related neuroendocrine cells.

    The epidermis is separated from the dermis by the basement membrane zone, which anchors it and whose components (hemidesmosomal proteins, laminin, type VII collagen) are targeted in several blistering diseases. The dermis has a superficial papillary layer of loose connective tissue containing capillary loops, and a deeper, denser reticular layer of thick collagen bundles and elastic fibres, with blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves and sensory receptors.

    The subcutis is composed of lobules of fat separated by fibrous septa. The appendages (pilosebaceous units, eccrine and apocrine sweat glands, and nails) arise from the epidermis and extend into the dermis.

    Descriptive terms

    • Parakeratosis is the retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum. It indicates rapid epidermal turnover with incomplete maturation of keratinocytes, and it is accompanied by a thin or absent granular layer, as in psoriasis.
    • Hypergranulosis is an increase in the thickness of the stratum granulosum, usually a response to chronic rubbing or scratching, and a prominent feature of lichen planus.
    • Acanthosis is diffuse epithelial hyperplasia, with thickening of the stratum spinosum, and is a common response to chronic irritation or growth factors.
    • Spongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis. The oedema stretches the intercellular bridges so that the keratinocytes are pulled apart. it is the hallmark of eczematous dermatitis, and when severe it forms intraepidermal vesicles.

    Related terms that complete the group are hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum), acantholysis (loss of intercellular cohesion between keratinocytes, as in pemphigus), and dyskeratosis (premature, abnormal keratinisation of individual cells).

    Blistering (Vesiculobullous) Diseases

    B9

    What are the blistering diseases of the skin?

    The blistering diseases of the skin are classified by the level at which the blister forms. Pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus foliaceus form intraepidermal blisters through acantholysis. Bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis, epidermolysis bullosa and porphyria cutanea tarda form subepidermal blisters. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and impetigo produce subcorneal blisters.

    Complete explanation: In vesiculobullous disease, a blister arises either within the epidermis, from damage to desmosomes and keratinocyte cohesion, or beneath it, from damage to the basement membrane zone. The distinction is clinically important because intraepidermal blisters have a thin roof and rupture easily, producing erosions, whereas subepidermal blisters have a full-thickness roof and remain tense and intact.

    DiseaseLevel of splitMechanismCharacteristic findings

    "row of tombstones" basal cells

    Mucosa spared
    Bullous pemphigoidSubepidermalIgG to BP180 and BP230 (hemidesmosomal proteins) with complement activation and eosinophilsTense bullae in the elderly on flexures
