    MorphologyFine white granules or clumps, gritty
    Basophilic, amorphous and granular on H&E    		Resembles dystrophic calcification
    Noncrystalline amorphous deposits or hydroxyapatite crystals
    Clinical effectOften a cause of organ dysfunction, as in calcific valvular disease and atherosclerosisUsually no clinical dysfunction
    Massive lung involvement causes respiratory compromise and massive kidney deposits (nephrocalcinosis) may cause renal damage
    A1

    Sites of dystrophic calcification.

    A1Q28

    Areas of necrosis (coagulative, caseous, liquefactive, fat necrosis), atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis, and ageing or damaged heart valves.

    • Tuberculous lymph nodes (may become "stone")
      Fat necrosis of pancreatitis (calcium soaps).
    • Psammoma bodies in papillary cancers (e.g., thyroid)
      Asbestos bodies in lung.
    A1

    Common sites of metastatic calcification.

    A1Q4

    Interstitial tissues of the gastric mucosa, kidneys, lungs, systemic arteries and pulmonary veins.

    • Reason: all excrete acid and have an internal alkaline compartment, predisposing to calcification.
    • Massive deposits: lungs (radiographic changes, respiratory compromise) and kidney (nephrocalcinosis → renal damage).

    Dystrophic calcification

    Define dystrophic calcification.

    DU05S

    Dystrophic calcification is the local deposition of calcium salts in dying (necrotic) or damaged tissue. it occurs despite normal serum calcium levels and in the absence of derangements in calcium metabolism. In contrast, metastatic calcification affects normal tissues in hypercalcaemia.

    • Sites: areas of coagulative, caseous or liquefactive necrosis, foci of enzymatic fat necrosis, the atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis, and aging or damaged heart valves (Fig. 2.34), e.g. calcific aortic stenosis. A tuberculous lymph node may be virtually converted to stone.
    • Morphology: fine white granules or clumps, gritty on cutting. with H&E the salts are basophilic, amorphous and granular, intracellular, extracellular or both. Heterotopic bone may form in the focus.

    Write short note on: Dystrophic calcification

    DU06M

    Definition: Dystrophic calcification is the deposition of calcium salts locally in dying tissues. It occurs despite normal serum levels of calcium and in the absence of derangements in calcium metabolism.

    Pathogenesis

    • If necrotic cells and cellular debris are not promptly destroyed and reabsorbed, they provide a nidus for the deposition of calcium salts and other minerals, and tend to become calcified.
    • Single necrotic cells may constitute seed crystals that become encrusted by the mineral deposits.

    Sites

    • Areas of necrosis, whether of coagulative, caseous or liquefactive type.
    • Foci of enzymatic necrosis of fat.
    • Atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis, where calcification is almost always present.
    • Aging or damaged heart valves, as in calcific aortic stenosis.
    • Tuberculous lymph node, which may be virtually converted to stone.

    Morphology

    • Macroscopically: fine, white granules or clumps, often felt as gritty deposits.
    • On H&E: basophilic, amorphous granular, sometimes clumped calcium salts, intracellular, extracellular or in both locations.
    • Heterotopic bone may form in the focus of calcification.
    • Progressive acquisition of outer layers creates lamellated configurations called psammoma bodies, which are seen in some papillary cancers, for example of the thyroid.
    • In asbestosis, calcium and iron salts gather about long slender spicules of asbestos in the lung, creating beaded dumbbell forms known as asbestos bodies.

    Clinical significance

    • It may simply be a telltale sign of previous cell injury.
    • It is often a cause of organ dysfunction, as in calcific valvular disease and atherosclerosis.
    • Serum calcium is normal.

    Cellular Aging

    A1

    What do you mean by cellular aging?

    A1Q30

    Cellular ageing is the progressive decline in cellular function and viability caused by genetic abnormalities and accumulation of cellular and molecular damage from exogenous influences. it is genetically regulated, not merely cells "running out of steam."

    • Individuals age because their cells age
      Age is a major independent risk factor for cancer, Alzheimer disease and ischaemic heart disease.
    • Regulated by evolutionarily conserved genes (yeast → worms → mammals).
    A1

    How does cellular aging occur?

    A1Q30

    Cellular ageing results from accumulating DNA damage, replicative senescence (telomere shortening, p16/CDKN2A), defective protein homeostasis, and dysregulated nutrient sensing (IGF-1/mTOR, sirtuins), together with ROS and persistent low-level inflammation.

    MechanismDetails
    DNA damageExogenous agents and ROS damage nuclear/mitochondrial DNA
    Some persists and accumulates. Haematopoietic stem cells acquire ~14 new mutations/year. Premature-ageing syndromes: Werner (DNA helicase), Bloom, ataxia-telangiectasia
    Replicative senescenceFinite divisions → arrest. Telomere attrition (telomerase present in germ cells, low in stem cells, absent in most somatic cells; reactivated in cancer). CDKN2A/p16 activation controls G1→S progression and promotes senescence
    Defective protein homeostasisImpaired chaperones and autophagy–lysosome/ubiquitin–proteasome degradation → misfolded proteins → apoptosis. Rapamycin (mTOR inhibitor) extends lifespan in mice
    Dysregulated nutrient sensingCaloric restriction ↑ longevity by ↓ insulin/IGF-1 and mTOR signalling and ↑ sirtuins (NAD-dependent deacetylases)
    Other contributorsROS, persistent low-level inflammation, metabolic insults (Fig. 2.35)
    Morphologic markerLipofuscin ("wear-and-tear" pigment) accumulation

    Anti-ageing interventions are largely experimental
    Their long-term safety and efficacy in humans are not fully understood.

    All topics / Ch 3

    Inflammation and Repair

    16 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Overview of Inflammation

    A2

    Define inflammation.

    A2Q1DU06M

    Inflammation is the protective response of vascularised tissues to infection and tissue damage, in which circulating leukocytes, plasma proteins and other host-defence molecules are delivered to the site of injury so that the cause of cell injury and its consequences can be eliminated and repair can begin.

    Inflammation is a response of vascularised tissue. Its purpose is to bring the cells and molecules of host defence (phagocytic leukocytes, antibodies and complement proteins) out of the circulation, where they normally rest in an inactive state, and into the tissue where microbes, toxins or necrotic cells are located. It is therefore essential for survival: without inflammation infections would go unchecked, wounds would never heal and injured tissues would remain permanent festering sores.

    It is not itself a disease but a stereotyped response to injury, as John Hunter recognised in 1793. The suffix -itis attached to the name of an organ denotes inflammation at that site (appendicitis, meningitis, conjunctivitis).

    The response develops through a sequence of steps that can be remembered as the five R's: recognition of the injurious agent by sentinel cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells and epithelial cells) through receptors such as Toll-like receptors and the inflammasome-forming sensors of cell damage. recruitment of leukocytes and plasma proteins
    removal of the agent by phagocytosis and killing
    regulation (termination) of the reaction once its purpose is served. and repair of the damaged tissue by regeneration and scarring. The principal participants are blood vessels, leukocytes and plasma proteins, acting under the control of soluble chemical mediators.

    The same mechanisms that destroy microbes can injure normal tissue. Inflammation is therefore protective in most circumstances but becomes the cause of disease when it is misdirected (autoimmunity), directed against harmless environmental antigens (allergy), or inadequately controlled (chronic inflammation, septic shock). Depending on its kinetics and cellular character, inflammation is classified as acute or chronic.

    A2

    Types of inflammation.

    A2Q1

    Inflammation is of two basic types, acute and chronic. Acute inflammation is rapid in onset, short in duration and neutrophil-predominant. Chronic inflammation is prolonged, mononuclear-cell-predominant and accompanied by tissue destruction and fibrosis. Granulomatous inflammation is a special pattern of chronic inflammation.

    The distinction between acute and chronic inflammation was originally based on duration, but they are now known to differ in kinetics, dominant cell type, mediators and degree of tissue injury. Acute inflammation develops within minutes to hours, lasts hours to a few days, and is characterised by exudation of fluid and plasma proteins (oedema) and emigration of leukocytes, predominantly neutrophils.

    Chronic inflammation lasts weeks to months or longer. Inflammation, tissue destruction and attempted repair proceed side by side, and the infiltrate is composed of macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells. It may follow acute inflammation when the stimulus persists, or it may begin insidiously without a preceding acute phase, as in tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis or silicosis. A transitional or "subacute" stage with mixed neutrophilic and mononuclear infiltrates is often recognised clinically.

    Within each type, descriptive patterns are recognised on the basis of morphology and aetiology:

    Basis of classificationTypes
    Duration and kineticsAcute, (subacute), chronic
    Morphological pattern of acute inflammationSerous, fibrinous, purulent (suppurative, including abscess), ulcerative
    Special pattern of chronic inflammationGranulomatous (foreign-body and immune types)
    ExtentLocal versus systemic (sepsis, SIRS)
    CauseInfectious versus sterile (necrosis, trauma, crystals, immune reactions)
    A2

    Examples of each type of inflammation.

    A2Q1

    Acute inflammation is exemplified by acute appendicitis, bacterial pneumonia, acute meningitis and a skin abscess. Chronic inflammation by tuberculosis, chronic osteomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis and chronic peptic ulcer. and granulomatous inflammation by tuberculosis, leprosy, sarcoidosis and Crohn disease.

    Acute inflammation arises in response to agents that are readily eliminated, such as many bacteria and fungi, necrotic cells, and physical or chemical injury. Typical examples are acute appendicitis (suppurative inflammation), acute bacterial pneumonia and bronchopneumonia, acute pyogenic meningitis, a staphylococcal abscess or boil, acute pharyngitis and tonsillitis, a thermal burn or sunburn blister (serous inflammation), fibrinous pericarditis or pleuritis, and the early inflammatory reaction to myocardial infarction.

    Chronic inflammation arises when the stimulus persists or the immune system is inappropriately activated. Examples include persistent infections such as tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis and chronic osteomyelitis. immune-mediated diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis and bronchial asthma. Prolonged exposure to toxic substances such as silica (silicosis) and endogenous lipids (atherosclerosis). and unresolved acute inflammation such as a chronic lung abscess or chronic peptic ulcer, in which acute and chronic inflammation coexist.

    Granulomatous inflammation, a distinctive form of chronic inflammation, is seen in tuberculosis (caseating granulomas, or tubercles), leprosy, syphilis (gumma), cat-scratch disease, sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, schistosomiasis, and foreign-body reactions to talc, sutures or silica.

    A2

    Causes of inflammation.

    A2Q3

    Inflammation is caused by infections and microbial toxins, tissue necrosis from any cause, foreign bodies, trauma and physical or chemical agents, and immune (hypersensitivity) reactions.

    Inflammatory reactions are triggered by a variety of stimuli, which are recognised by sentinel cells and circulating proteins.

    Infections and microbial toxins (bacterial, viral, fungal and parasitic) are the most common and medically important causes. Different pathogens evoke very different responses, from mild self-limited acute inflammation, to fatal systemic reactions such as septic shock, to prolonged chronic reactions with extensive tissue injury. The outcome depends on the pathogen and on the host response.

    Tissue necrosis elicits inflammation regardless of how the cells die. Ischaemia (as in myocardial infarction), trauma, and physical or chemical injury (burns, frostbite, irradiation, environmental chemicals) all kill cells, and molecules released from the dead cells (uric acid, ATP, DNA, loss of intracellular potassium) trigger "sterile" inflammation through cytosolic sensors and the inflammasome, which generates interleukin-1.

    Foreign bodies such as splinters, dirt and sutures cause inflammation by themselves, by producing traumatic tissue injury, or by carrying microbes. Endogenous substances that deposit in tissues, including urate crystals in gout and cholesterol crystals in atherosclerosis, can also provoke inflammation.

    Immune reactions (hypersensitivity) are reactions in which the protective immune system damages the individual's own tissues. They may be directed against self antigens (autoimmune diseases), against environmental substances (allergies), or against microbes. Because the stimuli cannot be eliminated, these reactions tend to be persistent and chronic.

    Additional causes include hypoxia, which can itself trigger mediator release, and prolonged exposure to toxic agents such as silica.

    A2

    What are the cardinal signs of acute inflammation?

    4A2Q3DU26MDU13JaDU12Ja

    Also asked as: Cardinal signs of acute inflammation.

    The cardinal signs of acute inflammation are rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumour (swelling) and dolor (pain), first listed by Celsus. Virchow added a fifth, functio laesa (loss of function).

    Celsus, a Roman writer of the first century CE, described the four cardinal signs in his treatise De Medicina, and the fifth sign was added by Rudolf Virchow in the nineteenth century. They are the clinical expression of the vascular and cellular reactions of acute inflammation and are the hallmarks of the acute response.

    SignMeaningMechanism
    RuborRednessVasodilation of arterioles and postcapillary venules (mediated by histamine and other mediators) increases blood flow
    Later, slowing of flow and engorgement of small vessels with red cells (stasis/congestion)
    CalorHeatIncreased flow of warm blood from the body core into the dilated vessels of the inflamed area
    Most evident in the skin and extremities
    Fever (IL-1, TNF, PGE₂) contributes systemically
    TumourSwellingIncreased vascular permeability of postcapillary venules with exudation of protein-rich fluid (inflammatory oedema), plus accumulation of leukocytes and fibrin
    DolorPainProstaglandins (especially PGE₂, which sensitises nerve endings), bradykinin and substance P, together with tissue distension by oedema and injury to the tissue by leukocyte products
    Functio laesaLoss of functionResult of pain, swelling and the underlying tissue damage

    The increased blood flow and increased permeability together account for redness, warmth and swelling. Leukocytes activated by the offending agent and by endogenous mediators may release toxic metabolites and proteases extracellularly, which damages tissue. This damage, together with the prostaglandins, neuropeptides and cytokines liberated, produces pain, and the pain and tissue injury produce loss of function.

    A2

    How/why does rubor (redness) occur?

    A2Q3, Q13

    Rubor occurs because of vasodilation: histamine and other mediators dilate arterioles and postcapillary venules, the increased blood flow brings more oxygenated red cells into the area, and later slowing of flow with engorgement of small vessels adds to the redness.

    Vasodilation is among the earliest manifestations of acute inflammation. It is induced by several mediators acting on vascular smooth muscle, notably histamine (and also prostaglandins such as PGI₂, PGE₂ and PGD₂, nitric oxide, and anaphylatoxins that release histamine from mast cells). Histamine dilates arterioles. The vasodilation involves chiefly the arterioles and postcapillary venules and opens up the capillary beds, which causes active hyperaemia, that is, increased arterial blood flow to the part. The tissue becomes red because of the increased delivery of oxygenated blood.

    As vasodilation continues and permeability increases, protein-rich fluid leaves the vessels, the blood becomes more viscous and its flow slows (stasis), and red cells become concentrated in small vessels. These changes cause engorgement of small vessels with slowly moving red cells, which adds to the redness of the area and is seen histologically as vascular congestion. Redness in acute inflammation is therefore a combination of active hyperaemia followed by stasis and congestion.

    A2

    How does calor (heat) occur?

    A2Q3

    Calor results from the increased blood flow through the dilated vessels of the inflamed area, which delivers warm blood from the core of the body to the affected part. Systemic fever from endogenous pyrogens adds to the effect.

    Dilatation of arterioles and the opening of capillary beds under the influence of histamine and other mediators increase the volume of blood flowing through the inflamed region. Because the blood comes from the warmer core of the body, the temperature of the affected tissue rises toward core temperature. The effect is obvious in superficial tissues such as the skin, particularly of the extremities, which are normally cooler than the core. it is not perceptible in deeply placed organs that already operate at core temperature.

    In addition, the endogenous pyrogens IL-1 and TNF, acting through prostaglandin E₂ in the hypothalamus, reset the temperature set point and cause systemic fever when the inflammation is substantial, so the patient as a whole may be febrile.

    A2

    Why does swelling develop in inflammation?

    A2Q13

    Swelling in inflammation is mainly due to inflammatory oedema: increased permeability of postcapillary venules allows protein-rich fluid to escape into the extravascular tissue, and the accumulation of inflammatory cells and fibrin adds to the bulk.

    Several events act together. First, arteriolar dilation raises the hydrostatic pressure within the capillary bed. Second, and most important, mediators such as histamine, bradykinin and leukotrienes cause contraction of endothelial cells and open interendothelial gaps in postcapillary venules, while more severe injury causes endothelial necrosis and detachment. The vessel wall then becomes permeable to plasma proteins.

    The loss of protein from the plasma and its accumulation in the interstitium abolish the normal osmotic gradient that retains water within vessels, so fluid pours into the tissue. The result is an exudate, defined as an extravascular fluid with a high protein concentration. Third, lymphatic vessels attempt to drain the fluid and their flow increases, but when the rate of leakage exceeds drainage, fluid accumulates and the tissue swells.

    Finally, emigrated leukocytes, fibrin and, in purulent inflammation, pus further expand the inflamed tissue. In confined spaces such as the cranium or larynx, this swelling can be dangerous.

    A2

    What are the components of acute inflammation?

    A2Q13DU08JuDU07Ju

    Also asked as: Main components of acute inflammation.

    Acute inflammation has three major components: dilation of small vessels leading to increased blood flow, increased permeability of the microvasculature allowing plasma proteins and leukocytes to leave the circulation, and emigration of leukocytes from the microcirculation with their accumulation and activation at the site of injury.

    When a host encounters a microbe or dead cells, resident phagocytes try to eliminate them, while sentinel cells recognise the agent and liberate cytokines, lipid mediators and vasoactive amines. These mediators act on neighbouring small vessels and set in motion the three components of the response.

    1. Vascular changes. Vasodilation, mainly of postcapillary venules and arterioles, increases blood flow and causes heat and redness. It is followed by increased vascular permeability, with leakage of protein-rich fluid (exudation and oedema), which in turn causes slowing of blood flow (stasis), concentration of red cells and vascular congestion.
    2. Cellular events. As stasis develops, leukocytes, mainly neutrophils, marginate along the endothelium, roll, adhere firmly, transmigrate through interendothelial gaps and the basement membrane, and move to the site of injury along chemotactic gradients. At the site they are activated to phagocytose and kill microbes and clear necrotic debris.
    3. Mediators and regulation. The vascular and cellular changes are driven by chemical mediators (histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines and chemokines, complement and kinins) derived from cells and plasma proteins. The reaction is terminated by the short half-lives of mediators, neutrophil apoptosis, and active anti-inflammatory signals such as lipoxins, TGF-β and IL-10.

    The participants are therefore blood vessels, leukocytes and plasma proteins. The outcome is resolution, healing with scar, or progression to chronic inflammation.

    A2

    Hallmark of acute inflammation.

    A2Q15

    The hallmark of acute inflammation is increased vascular permeability of postcapillary venules, leading to exudation of protein-rich fluid (oedema) and the emigration of leukocytes, predominantly neutrophils, into the tissue.

    Robbins identifies the increased permeability of postcapillary venules as a hallmark of acute inflammation, because it underlies the exudate, which implies that an inflammatory process has increased vessel permeability. Together with dilation of small vessels and accumulation of leukocytes and fluid in the extravascular tissue, these are the morphological hallmarks of acute inflammatory reactions.

    Clinically, the hallmarks are the cardinal signs: rubor, calor, tumour and dolor, with loss of function. The characteristic cell of acute inflammation is the neutrophil, which predominates in the infiltrate during the first 6 to 24 hours.

    A2

    Name the acute inflammatory cells.

    A2Q2

    The principal cells of acute inflammation are the neutrophils, followed within 24 to 48 hours by monocytes and macrophages
    Mast cells and tissue macrophages act as sentinel cells, and eosinophils and lymphocytes predominate in particular settings.

    Neutrophils are the first and most numerous leukocytes to arrive and predominate during the first 6 to 24 hours
    They are more numerous than other leukocytes, respond more rapidly to chemokines and attach more firmly to endothelial P- and E-selectin. They are short lived and die by apoptosis within a few days. Monocytes arrive later, are replaced in tissues by macrophages and become the dominant population after about 48 hours.

    Tissue-resident sentinel cells (macrophages, dendritic cells and mast cells) recognise the offending agent and release the first mediators. Platelets, endothelial cells and epithelial cells also produce mediators. Eosinophils predominate in helminthic infections and allergic reactions. Lymphocytes may be the first cells to arrive in viral infections. and in some infections, for example with Pseudomonas, neutrophils continue to be recruited for several days. Th17 lymphocytes contribute to acute inflammation through IL-17, which induces chemokines that recruit neutrophils.

    A2

    Name the chronic inflammatory cells.

    A2Q2

    The cells of chronic inflammation are macrophages (the dominant cell), lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils and mast cells, with fibroblasts taking part in repair. Epithelioid cells and giant cells appear in granulomatous inflammation.

    Chronic inflammation is characterised by infiltration with mononuclear cells. Macrophages are the central cell, derived from blood monocytes and tissue-resident precursors. T lymphocytes (Th1, Th2 and Th17 subsets) and B lymphocytes with antibody-secreting plasma cells amplify and sustain the reaction, and they may organise into lymphoid follicles (tertiary lymphoid structures).

    Eosinophils are prominent in Th2-mediated reactions such as parasitic infection and allergy. Mast cells participate in both acute and chronic reactions through IgE-FcεRI-mediated degranulation and cytokine secretion. Neutrophils may persist in some chronic reactions, for example in chronic osteomyelitis and in smoking-related lung injury. In granulomas, activated macrophages become epithelioid cells and fuse to form multinucleate giant cells. Fibroblasts and endothelial cells proliferate as part of the attempted repair.

    A2

    What are the differences between acute and chronic inflammation?

    A2Q2DUno yr

    Also asked as: Differences between acute and chronic inflammation.

    Acute inflammation is rapid in onset, lasts hours to days, is characterised by oedema and neutrophil infiltration, and usually ends in resolution
    Chronic inflammation is of long duration, is characterised by mononuclear cells, tissue destruction and fibrosis, and arises from persistent agents or immune reactions.

    The distinction was originally based on duration, but the two forms differ in several respects.

    FeatureAcute inflammationChronic inflammation
    OnsetRapid, within minutes to hoursInsidious, or follows unresolved acute inflammation
    DurationShort: hours to a few daysLong: weeks, months or years
    Offending agentReadily eliminated: many bacteria and fungi, necrotic cells, physical and chemical injuryDifficult to eradicate: mycobacteria, some viruses, fungi, parasites
    Self and environmental antigens
    Toxic particles (silica)
    Dominant cellsNeutrophils, later monocytesMacrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells (mononuclear cells)
    Vascular changesProminent: vasodilation, exudation, oedemaLess prominent
    Angiogenesis is a feature of repair
    Tissue destructionUsually limited and self-limitedMarked, caused by the persistent agent and by the inflammatory cells themselves
    FibrosisAbsent or minimalProminent, with scarring
    Key mediatorsHistamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, complement, kinins, TNF, IL-1, chemokinesIFN-γ, IL-12, IL-17, TNF and growth factors, maintained by a macrophage–T-cell feedback loop
    Local and systemic signsProminent cardinal signs, fever, neutrophiliaLess florid
    Weight loss, anaemia, lymphocytosis, raised acute-phase proteins
    OutcomeResolution, scarring, or progression to chronicityFibrosis and loss of function
    Secondary amyloidosis
    Occasionally neoplasia

    Chronic inflammation may follow acute inflammation or arise de novo, and in conditions such as peptic ulcer the two coexist.

    Explain: "Inflammation is a protective response but may be potentially harmful."

    DU03S

    Inflammation is a defensive response of vascularised tissues whose purpose is to deliver leukocytes and plasma proteins to the site of infection or injury, eliminate the offending agent and its consequences (microbes, toxins, necrotic cells), and initiate repair. The statement that it is protective but potentially harmful reflects the fact that the very mechanisms that protect the host can also damage it.

    The protective role. Without inflammation infections would go unchecked, wounds would never heal and injured tissues would remain permanent festering sores. Vasodilation and increased permeability bring antibodies, complement and fibrin into the tissue and dilute toxins. Neutrophils and macrophages ingest and destroy microbes and necrotic debris. Lymphatic drainage carries antigen to lymph nodes to initiate adaptive immunity. Macrophages secrete growth factors and cytokines that induce angiogenesis, fibroblast proliferation and healing. and fever may contribute to defence.

    Metchnikoff concluded that the purpose of inflammation was to bring phagocytes to the site of injury, and John Hunter recognised that it is a stereotyped response with a salutary effect on its host.

    The potentially harmful role. Leukocytes, once activated, do not distinguish between offender and host. Reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and lysosomal proteases produced to kill microbes can leak into the extracellular space (particularly in "frustrated phagocytosis") and injure normal cells and matrix. This collateral damage is usually minor and self-limited, but harm may become the dominant feature of disease in several circumstances:

    • When the response is misdirected against self tissues, as in rheumatoid arthritis, glomerulonephritis and other autoimmune diseases.
    • When it is directed against harmless environmental antigens, as in asthma and allergy, with anaphylaxis as the most dramatic example.
    • When it is inadequately controlled or persists, as in chronic infections such as tuberculosis, atherosclerosis, silicosis, or when sustained systemic cytokine release produces septic shock, DIC and multiorgan failure.
    • When swelling occurs in a confined space (brain, larynx), or when fibrinous exudates organise into adhesions and constrictive scars, or when fluid loss is massive as in burns.
    • When it contributes to diseases regarded as primarily metabolic or degenerative, such as type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer disease and cancer.

    The clinical use of anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, corticosteroids, anti-TNF agents) rests on this duality, and their major drawback is that suppression of harmful inflammation also compromises host defence, as seen in the susceptibility of anti-TNF-treated patients to mycobacterial infection.

    Acute Inflammation: Vascular Events

    A2

    Vascular changes / reactions of blood vessels in acute inflammation.

    A2Q4, Q12, Q22

    The vascular reactions of acute inflammation are changes in blood flow and vessel caliber (vasodilation with increased flow, then slowing and stasis) and increased vascular permeability that lets protein-rich fluid and leukocytes leave the circulation. The escape of fluid is called exudation.

    These changes are designed to maximise the movement of plasma proteins and leukocytes out of the circulation and into the site of infection or injury.

    Changes in vascular flow and caliber begin early. A transient, inconstant vasoconstriction of arterioles may occur for a few seconds. This is followed by vasodilation, induced by histamine and other mediators acting on vascular smooth muscle, which involves mainly arterioles and postcapillary venules, opens new capillary beds and increases blood flow. This causes redness and heat.

    Vasodilation is quickly followed by increased permeability of the microvasculature, with outpouring of protein-rich fluid. The loss of fluid and the increased vessel diameter slow the blood flow (stasis) and increase the concentration of red cells in small vessels, producing vascular engorgement or congestion. With stasis, leukocytes, principally neutrophils, accumulate along the endothelium (margination). at the same time the endothelium is activated and expresses adhesion molecules, so that the leukocytes adhere and then migrate into the tissue.

    Increased vascular permeability occurs mainly in postcapillary venules and is the hallmark of acute inflammation. The mechanisms are endothelial cell contraction (immediate transient and delayed prolonged responses), endothelial injury with necrosis and detachment, and leukocyte-dependent endothelial injury. The escape of fluid, proteins and blood cells from the vascular system into the interstitial tissue is exudation. The fluid is an exudate with a high protein content, in contrast to a transudate, which is an ultrafiltrate of plasma with low protein content formed without increased permeability.

    Lymphatics also participate: lymph flow increases and drains the oedema fluid, microbes and debris. The lymphatics may become inflamed (lymphangitis), as may the regional lymph nodes (lymphadenitis).

    A2

    How does increased vascular permeability / vascular leakage occur in acute inflammation?

    A2Q15, Q21

    Increased vascular permeability occurs mainly in postcapillary venules, chiefly by chemically induced contraction of endothelial cells that opens interendothelial gaps, and also by direct or leukocyte-dependent endothelial injury with necrosis and detachment of endothelial cells.

    Several mechanisms are responsible, and all probably contribute in varying degrees to most inflammatory stimuli.

    1. Contraction of endothelial cells with opening of interendothelial gaps. This is the most common mechanism of leakage. It is elicited by histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes and other chemical mediators acting on postcapillary venules. Because it occurs rapidly after exposure to the mediator and lasts only 15 to 30 minutes, it is called the immediate transient response. In some forms of mild injury, such as burns, ultraviolet irradiation (sunburn) and certain bacterial toxins, leakage begins after a delay of 2 to 12 hours and lasts for several hours or even days
      This delayed prolonged leakage may be caused by endothelial contraction or mild endothelial damage. The two responses often occur along a continuum.
    2. Endothelial injury resulting in endothelial cell necrosis and detachment. Direct damage to the endothelium is encountered in severe injuries such as thermal burns and is induced by microbes and microbial toxins. Neutrophils adhering to the endothelium may also injure it (leukocyte-dependent injury) and thereby amplify the reaction. Leakage starts immediately and is sustained for hours until the damaged vessels are thrombosed or repaired.
    3. Additional mechanisms described in other texts are increased transcytosis of proteins through endothelial vesicular channels (promoted by VEGF) and leakage from newly formed vessels in healing tissue.

    At different stages of a thermal burn, leakage results from chemically mediated contraction, direct injury and leukocyte-dependent injury, and the resulting fluid loss can be life-threatening.

    A3

    How does edema (exudative edema) occur in acute inflammation?

    A3Q2, Q25

    Exudative oedema occurs because inflammatory mediators increase the permeability of postcapillary venules, so protein-rich fluid leaves the vessels. The loss of plasma protein removes the osmotic force that holds water in the vessels, and the fluid accumulates in the interstitium faster than lymphatics can drain it.

    In normal tissue, fluid movement across the capillary wall is governed by Starling forces. The hydrostatic pressure of about 32 mm Hg at the arterial end of a capillary bed and 12 mm Hg at the venous end tends to push fluid out, while the colloid osmotic pressure, which is approximately 25 mm Hg, holds fluid in
    The net flow is almost nil, and the small quantity that escapes is returned through the lymphatics.

    In acute inflammation this balance is upset in the following ways:

    • Vasodilation of arterioles raises the hydrostatic pressure in the capillary bed.
    • Endothelial gaps, or frank endothelial damage, permit plasma proteins, including albumin and later fibrinogen, to escape into the interstitium. The osmotic gradient across the vessel wall is therefore lost, and the increase of osmotic pressure in the interstitial fluid draws more water out of the vessels.
    • The volume of leaking fluid exceeds the capacity of lymphatic drainage, so fluid accumulates.

    The fluid so formed is an exudate: protein-rich, often cellular, with high specific gravity. It signifies an inflammatory process that has increased vascular permeability. A transudate, by contrast, is a low-protein ultrafiltrate that forms from hydrostatic or osmotic imbalance without a change in permeability, as in heart failure or hypoalbuminaemia. Oedema may therefore be either an exudate or a transudate. Inflammatory oedema is always an exudate.

    What are the vascular events in acute inflammation?

    DU14JuDU12JaDU08Ju

    The vascular events of acute inflammation consist of alterations in blood flow and in the permeability of vessels, both directed toward delivering plasma proteins and leukocytes to the site of injury. They occur in a recognisable sequence and are controlled by chemical mediators.

    1. Changes in vascular caliber and flow. After a brief and inconstant arteriolar vasoconstriction, vasodilation develops. It is induced by histamine, prostaglandins, nitric oxide and other mediators and involves the arterioles and postcapillary venules, opening up capillary beds. It increases blood flow (active hyperaemia), the cause of redness (rubor) and heat (calor), and it is one of the earliest manifestations of acute inflammation.

    2. Increased vascular permeability. Permeability of the postcapillary venules rises soon after vasodilation, leading to the escape of protein-rich fluid (exudate) into the extravascular space. The mechanisms are (a) endothelial cell contraction, which produces interendothelial gaps and is mediated by histamine, bradykinin and leukotrienes, giving an immediate transient response lasting 15 to 30 minutes, or a delayed prolonged response (2 to 12 hours, for example in sunburn)
    and (b) endothelial injury with necrosis and detachment, produced directly by burns and microbial toxins or by adherent neutrophils, leading to immediate sustained leakage. This produces swelling (tumour).

    3. Slowing of circulation (stasis). Loss of fluid raises the viscosity of the blood and the concentration of red cells. with dilated vessels, blood flow slows and the small vessels become engorged with red cells (vascular congestion). Stasis is one cause of persistent redness.

    4. Leukocyte margination. With slowing of flow, leukocytes leave the central axial stream and assume a peripheral position along the endothelium (margination). Endothelial cells activated by TNF and IL-1 express adhesion molecules, and the leukocytes roll, adhere and then migrate across the vessel wall, the beginning of the cellular phase.

    5. Lymphatic response. Lymph flow increases and drains the oedema fluid, microbes and cell debris. Lymphatic vessels and draining lymph nodes may become inflamed (lymphangitis, lymphadenitis), producing red streaks and tender enlargement of the nodes.

    The principal mediators responsible are histamine and serotonin, bradykinin, prostaglandins, leukotrienes C₄, D₄ and E₄, PAF, and the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a
    TNF and IL-1 cause endothelial activation. Vascular leakage ends when the damaged vessels have thrombosed or been repaired, or when mediators have decayed. The loss of fluid can be life-threatening in severe burns.

    Acute Inflammation: Cellular Events

    Leukocyte recruitment and chemotaxis

    A2

    Steps of cellular events in acute inflammation.

    A2Q19

    The cellular events of acute inflammation are leukocyte recruitment (margination, rolling, adhesion and transmigration), chemotaxis to the site of injury, leukocyte activation with phagocytosis and intracellular killing of the offending agent, and finally termination of the response.

    After the vascular changes, leukocytes, principally neutrophils, are recruited from the blood to the extravascular site, where they eliminate the offending agent.

    1. Recruitment from the vessel lumen. In the dilated postcapillary venules with slowed flow, leukocytes marginate along the endothelium
      They roll on it through weak, rapidly reversible selectin interactions. They adhere firmly through integrins binding to their ligands on activated endothelium. and they transmigrate (diapedesis) through interendothelial junctions, using CD31 (PECAM-1), and pierce the basement membrane.
    2. Chemotaxis. In the tissue, leukocytes migrate along a chemical gradient of chemoattractants (bacterial peptides, IL-8 and other chemokines, C5a and LTB₄) toward the focus of injury.
    3. Activation. Recognition of microbes and dead cells by Toll-like receptors, G protein-coupled receptors, mannose and scavenger receptors, and opsonin receptors activates the leukocytes, which produce arachidonic acid metabolites, cytokines, reactive oxygen species and lysosomal enzymes.
    4. Phagocytosis and killing. The agent is recognised, engulfed into a phagosome, and destroyed in the phagolysosome by reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and lysosomal enzymes. Neutrophils may also extrude nuclear contents to form extracellular traps.
    5. Termination. The response subsides as mediators decay, neutrophils undergo apoptosis, and anti-inflammatory signals (lipoxins, TGF-β, IL-10) become active.

    Neutrophils predominate in the first 6 to 24 hours and are replaced by monocytes and macrophages in 24 to 48 hours.

    A2

    Steps of the journey of leucocytes from the vessel lumen to the tissue space.

    A2Q16

    The journey of leukocytes from lumen to tissue is a multistep process: margination, rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins), transmigration or diapedesis through the endothelium (PECAM-1/CD31), penetration of the basement membrane, and chemotaxis in the tissue.

    The process is controlled by adhesion molecules and cytokines, and has three phases: events in the lumen, migration across the vessel wall, and migration in the tissue.

    1. Margination. In normal venules, red cells are confined to a central axial column, which displaces leukocytes toward the wall. With dilation and stasis, more leukocytes assume a peripheral position.
    2. Rolling. Tissue macrophages, mast cells and endothelial cells that encounter microbes secrete TNF, IL-1 and chemokines. Within 1 to 2 hours endothelium begins to express E-selectin and the ligands for L-selectin, and histamine and thrombin cause P-selectin to move from Weibel-Palade bodies to the cell surface. Leukocytes carry L-selectin and ligands (sialyl-Lewis X) for E- and P-selectin. These low-affinity, fast-off-rate interactions are broken by the flowing blood, so the cells bind, detach and bind again, rolling along the endothelium.
    3. Firm adhesion. TNF and IL-1 induce endothelial expression of ICAM-1 and VCAM-1. Chemokines displayed on endothelial proteoglycans activate the rolling leukocytes and convert the integrins LFA-1 and MAC-1 (β2) and VLA-4 (β1) to a high-affinity state. Firm binding to ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 stops the cell, which then spreads on the surface.
    4. Transmigration (diapedesis). Chemokines stimulate the adherent cells to pass through interendothelial gaps, mainly in postcapillary venules, using CD31 (PECAM-1) at the junctions.
    5. Penetration of the basement membrane. Leukocytes cross the basement membrane probably by secreting collagenases, which is then repaired.
    6. Chemotaxis. The cells move to the focus of injury along the chemoattractant gradient.
    A2

    What is chemotaxis?

    A2Q16, Q23DU11Ja

    Also asked as: Define chemotaxis.

    Chemotaxis is the movement of leukocytes in the tissues toward the site of injury after they exit the circulation. it is defined as locomotion along a chemical gradient, mediated by chemoattractants that bind specific G protein-coupled receptors on the leukocyte surface.

    After leaving the circulation, leukocytes move in tissue toward the injury by chemotaxis. Both exogenous and endogenous substances act as chemoattractants:

    • Exogenous: bacterial products, including peptides with N-formylmethionine terminal amino acids, and some lipids.
    • Endogenous: (1) cytokines of the chemokine family, such as IL-8 (CXCL8)
      (2) complement components, particularly C5a
      and (3) arachidonic acid metabolites, mainly leukotriene B₄.

    All of these bind to specific seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors on leukocytes. Signals from the receptors activate second messengers that induce polymerisation of actin at the leading edge of the cell and localisation of myosin filaments at the back. The leading edge extends filopodia which pull the back of the cell forward, so the leukocyte crawls toward the highest concentration of the attractant. The chemoattractants also increase the avidity of integrins and activate the leukocyte.

    The nature of the infiltrate depends on the stimulus and on its age: neutrophils predominate during the first 6 to 24 hours, being more numerous, responding faster to chemokines and attaching more firmly to P- and E-selectin. Monocytes follow in 24 to 48 hours
    Eosinophils respond to eotaxin in allergy and helminthic infection. and lymphocytes may be first in viral infection.

    A2

    Name the chemotactic substances.

    A2Q23

    Chemotactic substances include exogenous bacterial products such as N-formylmethionine peptides, and endogenous chemoattractants: chemokines such as IL-8, complement fragment C5a, and leukotriene B₄.

    GroupExamplesCells attracted
    Bacterial products (exogenous)N-formylmethionyl peptides, some lipidsNeutrophils, monocytes
    ChemokinesIL-8 (CXCL8)Neutrophils
    MCP-1 (CCL2), MIP-1α (CCL3)Monocytes, lymphocytes, basophils, eosinophils
    Eotaxin (CCL11)Eosinophils (selective)
    Lymphotactin (XCL1), fractalkine (CX3CL1)Lymphocytes
    Monocytes and T cells
    ComplementC5a (also C3a)Neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils
    Arachidonic acid metabolitesLTB₄, 5-HETENeutrophils
    CytokinesTNF, IL-1 (indirectly through chemokines), IL-17Neutrophils and monocytes
    OthersPAFLeukocytes

    What are the cellular events of acute inflammation?

    DU23N

    The cellular events of acute inflammation comprise the recruitment of leukocytes from the blood to the extravascular focus of injury, their activation, and the removal of the offending agent.

    Leukocyte recruitment. The important leukocytes in typical inflammatory reactions are neutrophils and macrophages, which are capable of phagocytosis. Their journey from the lumen is a multistep process controlled by adhesion molecules and cytokines. With stasis, leukocytes marginate. Selectins (L-selectin on leukocytes; E- and P-selectin on activated endothelium) mediate rolling. Chemokines bound to endothelial proteoglycans activate integrins (LFA-1, MAC-1, VLA-4) so that they bind firmly to ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 whose expression is increased by TNF and IL-1; and transmigration through interendothelial junctions occurs under the influence of chemokines and CD31 (PECAM-1). The cells penetrate the basement membrane, probably by collagenases.

    Chemotaxis. Leukocytes move along chemical gradients created by bacterial peptides, chemokines such as IL-8, C5a and LTB₄, which act on G protein-coupled receptors and drive actin polymerisation. Neutrophils predominate during the first 6 to 24 hours, then give way to monocytes within 24 to 48 hours
    Neutrophils are short lived and die by apoptosis.

    Leukocyte activation. Recognition of microbes and dead cells by Toll-like receptors, G protein-coupled receptors, opsonin receptors and cytokine receptors activates the cells for phagocytosis, production of arachidonic acid metabolites, cytokine secretion, degranulation, and generation of reactive oxygen species.

    Phagocytosis and intracellular killing. Phagocytosis involves recognition and attachment, engulfment with formation of a phagosome that fuses with a lysosome, and killing by reactive oxygen species (phagocyte oxidase and myeloperoxidase), reactive nitrogen species derived from nitric oxide, and lysosomal enzymes. Neutrophils can also release extracellular traps (NETs) of nuclear chromatin laden with antimicrobial proteins.

    Tissue injury and termination. Products of activated leukocytes may be released extracellularly and injure normal tissue. The reaction ends when the stimulus is removed, mediators decay, neutrophils undergo apoptosis, and lipoxins, TGF-β and IL-10 and cholinergic signals exert anti-inflammatory effects.

    What are the steps of leukocyte extravasation?

    DU09Ju

    Leukocyte extravasation is the multistep exit of leukocytes from the circulation into the extravascular tissue, which takes place mainly in postcapillary venules. The sequential phases are margination, rolling, adhesion, transmigration, and migration in the tissue by chemotaxis.

    1. Margination. In normal flow, red cells occupy a central axial column and leukocytes are displaced toward the wall. In inflammation, vasodilation and increased permeability slow flow, and more white cells assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface.
    2. Rolling. This is mediated by selectins and their sialylated oligosaccharide ligands. TNF and IL-1, secreted by sentinel cells, induce the endothelial expression of E-selectin within 1 to 2 hours and ligands for L-selectin
      Histamine and thrombin cause redistribution of P-selectin from Weibel-Palade bodies to the surface. The interactions are of low affinity and fast off-rate, so the leukocytes bind, detach and rebind, thereby rolling.
    3. Firm adhesion. TNF and IL-1 induce endothelial ICAM-1 and VCAM-1. Chemokines presented on endothelial proteoglycans activate the leukocytes and convert integrins (LFA-1, MAC-1, VLA-4) to a high-affinity state, so that the leukocytes adhere firmly, stop rolling, reorganise their cytoskeleton and spread.
    4. Transmigration (diapedesis). Chemokines drive the adherent cells through interendothelial gaps toward the source of the chemokines. Adhesion molecules at the junctions, notably CD31 (PECAM-1), participate.
    5. Penetration of the basement membrane and chemotaxis. Leukocytes pierce the basement membrane, probably through collagenases, which is then restored, and migrate toward the chemotactic gradient to accumulate at the site.
    StepPrincipal molecules
    RollingSelectins (L, E, P) and sialyl-Lewis X ligands
    ActivationChemokines (e.g., IL-8)
    Firm adhesionIntegrins (LFA-1, MAC-1, VLA-4) with ICAM-1 and VCAM-1
    TransmigrationCD31 (PECAM-1), chemokines

    Genetic deficiencies in leukocyte adhesion molecules result in increased susceptibility to bacterial infection, which proves their importance. Therapeutic antagonists of integrins and TNF control harmful inflammation but may compromise host defence.

    Phagocytes and phagocytosis

    A2

    What are phagocytes?

    A2Q8, Q20

    Phagocytes are cells capable of ingesting and destroying microbes, dead cells and foreign particles. The two professional phagocytes are neutrophils and macrophages.

    Neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes, or "microphages") are the first phagocytes recruited to acute inflammation and are short-lived. Macrophages, derived from circulating monocytes or from embryonic yolk-sac and foetal liver precursors, are the long-lived "macrophages" of the mononuclear phagocyte system. The two cell types share phagocytosis, migration through vessels and chemotaxis, but differ in several respects:

    FeatureNeutrophilsMacrophages
    OriginBone marrow haematopoietic stem cellsBone marrow (inflammatory)
    Yolk sac or foetal liver (many tissue-resident cells)
    Life span in tissueSeveral daysDays to weeks (recruited)
    Years (resident)
    ResponsesRapid, short-lived, mainly degranulation and enzymatic activityProlonged, slower, usually dependent on new gene transcription
    Reactive oxygen speciesRapid respiratory burstLess prominent
    Nitric oxideLow or noneProduced by iNOS
    Degranulation, lysosomal enzymesMajor responseLess
    Cytokine productionLowMajor functional activity
    NET formationYesNo

    Eosinophils and dendritic cells have limited phagocytic functions. Phagocytes recognise their targets using mannose receptors, scavenger receptors, integrins and receptors for opsonins.

    A2

    Organs where cells of the MPS are found.

    A2Q20Highlighted

    Cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system are found in the liver as Kupffer cells, in the spleen and lymph nodes as sinus histiocytes, in the central nervous system as microglia, in the lungs as alveolar macrophages, and diffusely in connective tissues.

    The mononuclear phagocyte system, an older (and inaccurate) name for which is the reticuloendothelial system, consists of monocytes and tissue macrophages. Macrophages are diffusely scattered in most connective tissue and are present in specific locations in organs:

    Organ or siteName of the cell
    LiverKupffer cells
    Spleen and lymph nodesSinus histiocytes (sinusoidal macrophages)
    Central nervous systemMicroglia
    LungsAlveolar macrophages
    Connective tissueHistiocytes
    BoneOsteoclasts
    KidneyMesangial cells
    Serosal cavities and synoviumPeritoneal and pleural macrophages
    Type A synoviocytes
    Skin and intestineMacrophages of dermis and lamina propria (derived from monocytes)

    Microglia, Kupffer cells and alveolar macrophages arise from yolk-sac or foetal liver progenitors early in embryogenesis and persist throughout life as stable populations. Macrophages at inflammatory sites generally derive from blood monocytes. The half-life of blood monocytes is about 1 day, while tissue macrophages may live for months or years.

    A2

    Define phagocytosis.

    A2Q24DU25NDU19N

    Phagocytosis is the process by which phagocytic cells, mainly neutrophils and macrophages, recognise, engulf and destroy microbes, dead cells and other particulate material by enclosing them in a membrane-bound vesicle (phagosome) that fuses with lysosomes.

    Phagocytosis was discovered by Elie Metchnikoff in the 1880s, who observed the ingestion of rose thorns by amoebocytes of starfish larvae and of bacteria by mammalian leukocytes. It is, together with intracellular killing, the most important functional response of activated leukocytes for destroying microbes and removing necrotic tissue. It involves three sequential steps: (1) recognition and attachment of the particle to the leukocyte, (2) engulfment with formation of a phagocytic vacuole, and (3) killing of the microbe and degradation of the ingested material in the phagolysosome.

    The efficiency of the process is greatly enhanced by opsonins (IgG, C3b and plasma lectins) for which phagocytes express high-affinity receptors. Killing depends on reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species and lysosomal enzymes, all of which are sequestered within the phagolysosome to protect the phagocyte itself.

    A2

    Three sequential steps of phagocytosis.

    A2Q24

    The three sequential steps of phagocytosis are recognition and attachment of the particle to the phagocyte, engulfment with formation of a phagocytic vacuole, and killing and degradation of the ingested material.

    1. Recognition and attachment. Phagocytes bind particles through receptors: the mannose receptor (a lectin binding terminal mannose and fucose of microbial glycoproteins and glycolipids, but not host molecules, which end in sialic acid), scavenger receptors, and macrophage integrins such as MAC-1. Binding is greatly enhanced by opsonins, which are IgG antibodies, the complement fragment C3b (and iC3b), and plasma lectins such as mannose-binding lectin and collectins, recognised by Fc receptors, complement receptors and lectin receptors.
    2. Engulfment. After binding, cytoplasmic extensions flow around the particle and the plasma membrane pinches off to form an intracellular vesicle, the phagosome. This involves actin polymerisation and membrane remodelling. The phagosome fuses with a lysosomal granule to form a phagolysosome, into which the lysosomal contents are discharged.
    3. Killing and degradation. Within the phagolysosome, microbes are destroyed by reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species and lysosomal enzymes.
    A2

    How is phagocytosed material degraded?

    A2Q8

    Phagocytosed material is degraded in the phagolysosome by reactive oxygen species generated by phagocyte oxidase and myeloperoxidase, by reactive nitrogen species derived from nitric oxide, and by lysosomal enzymes and antimicrobial proteins.

    Killing and digestion are most efficient after phagocyte activation, and all the lethal mechanisms are normally sequestered in lysosomes, so that the cell's cytoplasm and nucleus are protected.

    • Reactive oxygen species. NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase) assembles in the phagosomal membrane and converts oxygen to superoxide anion. Superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide
      and, in neutrophils, myeloperoxidase uses H₂O₂ and chloride to generate hypochlorite (bleach), the most potent bactericidal system. Hydroxyl radical is another destructive product.
    • Reactive nitrogen species. Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), induced in macrophages by cytokines such as IFN-γ, generates nitric oxide, which reacts with superoxide to form peroxynitrite.
    • Lysosomal enzymes and proteins. Acid hydrolases (active in the acidified phagolysosome) degrade bacteria and debris. Neutral proteases (elastase, cathepsin G, collagenases, proteinase 3) degrade extracellular matrix. and lysozyme, defensins, cathelicidins and lactoferrin kill or inhibit microbes. Major basic protein of eosinophils damages helminths.
    A2

    Outline of the oxygen-dependent mechanism of bacterial killing.

    A2Q25

    In the oxygen-dependent mechanism, activated phagocytes assemble NADPH oxidase, which converts oxygen to superoxide in the respiratory burst. Superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase converts H₂O₂ with chloride to hypochlorite, which kills the bacterium.

    Activation of the phagocyte causes the cytosolic components of phagocyte oxidase to translocate to the phagosomal membrane, where they assemble with the membrane components. The assembled enzyme oxidises NADPH and reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide anion (O₂•⁻), accompanied by a burst of oxygen consumption (the respiratory burst) in neutrophils. Superoxide dismutes, mostly spontaneously, to H₂O₂.

    H₂O₂ alone is not an efficient killer, but azurophil granules fuse with the phagosome and deliver myeloperoxidase, which in the presence of a halide such as chloride converts H₂O₂ to hypochlorite (ClO⁻). This kills microbes by halogenation of cell constituents and by oxidation of proteins and lipids (lipid peroxidation). H₂O₂ is also converted to hydroxyl radical. Inherited deficiency of phagocyte oxidase components causes chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent infection.

    Name the cells causing phagocytosis.

    DU19Nov

    The cells that perform phagocytosis are called phagocytes. The two major (professional) phagocytes are neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes), which dominate in the early phase of acute inflammation, and macrophages, derived from circulating monocytes and tissue precursors, which dominate later and in chronic inflammation. Macrophages are tissue cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system and include the Kupffer cells of liver, sinus histiocytes of spleen and lymph nodes, alveolar macrophages of the lung, microglia of the central nervous system, and connective-tissue histiocytes. Dendritic cells and, to a limited extent, eosinophils also have phagocytic capacity.

    What are the steps/mechanism of phagocytosis?

    11DU25NDU24NDU23NDU22NDU19NovDU18NovDU17NovDU12JuDU08JuDU08JaDU07Ja

    Phagocytosis is the engulfment and destruction of microbes, necrotic cells and other particles by neutrophils and macrophages. It is the key effector mechanism by which inflammation removes the offending agent and follows leukocyte recruitment and activation. It proceeds through three sequential steps.

    Step 1: Recognition and attachment of the particle. Phagocytes recognise particles through several classes of receptors.

    • The macrophage mannose receptor is a lectin that binds terminal mannose and fucose residues of microbial glycoproteins and glycolipids. Mammalian glycoproteins end in sialic acid or N-acetylgalactosamine, so host cells are not recognised.
    • Scavenger receptors, originally defined by their ability to bind oxidised or acetylated LDL, also bind many microbes.
    • Macrophage integrins, notably MAC-1 (CD11b/CD18), may also bind microbes.
    • Opsonin receptors. Phagocytosis is greatly enhanced by opsonisation of microbes with IgG antibodies, the C3b (and iC3b) fragments of complement, and plasma lectins (mannose-binding lectin, collectins). Phagocytes express high-affinity receptors for these opsonins (Fc receptors and complement receptors).

    Leukocyte activation through Toll-like receptors and other receptors (including G protein-coupled receptors for N-formylmethionine peptides, and cytokine receptors) enhances the process.

    Step 2: Engulfment. After binding, signals integrated from the receptors cause remodelling of the membrane and polymerisation of actin filaments. Extensions of the cytoplasm (pseudopods) flow around the particle and the plasma membrane pinches off, forming an intracellular vesicle, the phagosome. The phagosome fuses with one or more lysosomal granules, and the contents of the granules are discharged into the resulting phagolysosome. During this process the phagocyte may release lysosomal contents into the extracellular space.

    Step 3: Killing and degradation. Killing is achieved by reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species and lysosomal enzymes within the phagolysosome. These are most efficient when the phagocytes are activated, and they are sequestered in lysosomes to protect the cell.

    • Reactive oxygen species (oxygen-dependent mechanism). Phagocyte oxidase (NADPH oxidase), a multicomponent enzyme of at least seven proteins, assembles at the phagosomal membrane. It oxidises NADPH and converts oxygen to superoxide anion (the respiratory burst). Superoxide is dismutated to H₂O₂, and in neutrophils myeloperoxidase from azurophil granules converts H₂O₂ and Cl⁻ to hypochlorite, which kills microbes by halogenation and by oxidation of proteins and lipids. H₂O₂ also generates hydroxyl radical.
    • Reactive nitrogen species. iNOS in activated macrophages generates nitric oxide from arginine. NO reacts with superoxide to form peroxynitrite, which damages microbial lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.
    • Lysosomal enzymes. Acid hydrolases in the acidified phagolysosome degrade bacteria and debris. Neutrophil specific (secondary) granules contain lysozyme, collagenase, gelatinase, lactoferrin. Azurophil (primary) granules contain MPO, defensins, lysozyme, acid hydrolases and neutral proteases (elastase, cathepsin G, proteinase 3). Lysozyme hydrolyses the bacterial cell wall, defensins and cathelicidins are antimicrobial peptides, and lactoferrin sequesters iron.

    Other points. Neutrophils may in addition extrude nuclear chromatin laden with antimicrobial proteins as extracellular traps (NETs) to trap microbes too large to phagocytose. If the phagocyte cannot engulf a target (for example immune complexes on a basement membrane, "frustrated phagocytosis"), or if crystals such as urate damage the phagolysosome, lysosomal enzymes and ROS are released extracellularly and injure host tissue. Host tissues are protected by antioxidants (superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, ceruloplasmin, transferrin) and by antiproteases (α₁-antitrypsin, α₂-macroglobulin).

    Clinical correlates. Deficiency of phagocyte oxidase causes chronic granulomatous disease. Deficiency of MPO alone causes minimal susceptibility because of redundancy. and deficiency of α₁-antitrypsin permits unrestrained elastase activity and emphysema.

    Write the mechanism of oxygen-dependent microbial killing (role of oxygen in phagocytic killing).

    6DU23NDU22MDU18NovDU17NovDU16JuDU12Ju

    Killing of ingested microbes by phagocytes is achieved by reactive oxygen species (ROS), reactive nitrogen species, and lysosomal enzymes. The oxygen-dependent mechanism is the most important and is produced by the following sequence.

    1. Assembly of phagocyte oxidase. Reactive oxygen species are produced by the rapid assembly and activation of a multicomponent enzyme, phagocyte oxidase (NADPH oxidase), consisting of at least seven proteins. In resting neutrophils, some components lie in the plasma membrane and others in the cytoplasm. In response to activating stimuli, the cytosolic components translocate to the membrane of the phagosome, where they assemble into the functional enzyme complex. As a result, ROS are generated within the phagolysosome, where they act on the ingested particle without damaging the host cell.

    2. Respiratory burst and generation of superoxide. The assembled enzyme oxidises NADPH (supplied by the hexose monophosphate shunt, which accelerates) and reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide anion (O₂•⁻): NADPH + 2O₂ → NADP⁺ + 2O₂•⁻ + H⁺. In neutrophils, this is accompanied by a sharp increase in oxygen consumption, called the respiratory burst.

    3. Conversion to hydrogen peroxide. Superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), mostly by spontaneous dismutation (also accelerated by superoxide dismutase).

    4. Myeloperoxidase-halide system. H₂O₂ is not by itself able to kill microbes efficiently. The azurophil granules of neutrophils contain myeloperoxidase (MPO), which, in the presence of a halide such as chloride, converts H₂O₂ to hypochlorite (HOCl or ClO⁻), the active ingredient of household bleach. Hypochlorite destroys microbes by halogenation (covalent binding of the halide to cellular constituents) and by oxidation of proteins and lipids (lipid peroxidation). The H₂O₂-MPO-halide system is the most potent bactericidal system of neutrophils.

    5. Hydroxyl radical. H₂O₂ is also converted to the hydroxyl radical (•OH), a further powerful destructive agent that damages microbial lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

    Reactive nitrogen species act in parallel: iNOS, induced mainly in macrophages by IFN-γ or microbial products, produces nitric oxide, which reacts with superoxide to give peroxynitrite. Because of the overlapping action of ROS and RNS, mice that lack both phagocyte oxidase and iNOS succumb to infection by otherwise harmless commensal bacteria, while those lacking only one are mildly susceptible.

    Protection of the host. ROS may leak extracellularly and cause tissue damage. The host is protected by superoxide dismutase, catalase (detoxifies H₂O₂), glutathione peroxidase, ceruloplasmin and the iron-free fraction of transferrin.

    Clinical significance. Inherited deficiency of components of phagocyte oxidase produces chronic granulomatous disease, an immunodeficiency in which phagocytes cannot generate ROS, causing recurrent infections and granuloma formation. By contrast, inherited MPO deficiency causes minimal increase in susceptibility to infection, which shows the redundancy of the microbicidal mechanisms.

    Write a short note on opsonin.

    DU06JaDU04Ja

    Opsonins are molecules that coat microbes or other particles and make them more readily recognised and ingested by phagocytes. The process of coating is called opsonisation. Phagocytes express high-affinity receptors for opsonins, so the efficiency of phagocytosis is greatly enhanced when microbes are opsonised. The term comes from a Greek word meaning "to prepare for eating".

    Major opsonins and their receptors:

    OpsoninReceptor on phagocyte
    Immunoglobulin G antibody (Fc portion)Fcγ receptors
    C3b and its breakdown product iC3b (complement)Complement receptors (including MAC-1 / CR3)
    Plasma lectins: mannose-binding lectin and collectinsLectin receptors
    Acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein and serum amyloid ABind microbial walls and fix complement

    Mechanism. Antibody binds through its Fab region to a microbial antigen and presents the Fc tail to Fc receptors. Complement activation by the classical, alternative or lectin pathways deposits C3b covalently on the microbial surface. mannose-binding lectin binds microbial sugars. The bridge formed between the microbe and the phagocyte receptor triggers signalling that leads to engulfment and also activates the phagocyte.

    Significance. Opsonisation is the mechanism by which adaptive immunity (antibodies) and innate immunity (complement, lectins) direct phagocytes against microbes. Deficiencies of antibody or complement (and, clinically, absence of the spleen) predispose to infections with encapsulated bacteria. Opsonin-coated microbes are also recognised by macrophages through opsonin-independent receptors such as the mannose and scavenger receptors, but with lower efficiency.

    Chemical Mediators of Inflammation

    A2

    Name the chemical mediators of inflammation.

    A2Q26

    The chemical mediators of inflammation are either cell-derived (vasoactive amines such as histamine and serotonin, arachidonic acid metabolites, platelet-activating factor, cytokines and chemokines, reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, lysosomal enzymes, neuropeptides) or plasma-derived (the complement system, kinins and the coagulation system).

    The most important mediators of acute inflammation are vasoactive amines, lipid products (prostaglandins and leukotrienes), cytokines including chemokines, and products of complement activation.

    A2

    General principles of action of chemical mediators.

    A2Q26

    Mediators are produced only in response to offending stimuli, are either cell-derived or plasma-derived, usually act briefly, and can stimulate the release of other mediators, with considerable redundancy in their actions.

    1. The vascular and cellular reactions are triggered by soluble factors that are produced by cells or derived from plasma proteins, and are generated or activated in response to the inflammatory stimulus.
    2. Cell-derived mediators are sequestered in intracellular granules and rapidly secreted by exocytosis (for example histamine in mast cell granules), or synthesised de novo (prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines). The main producers are sentinel cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells), but platelets, neutrophils, endothelium and epithelia may also elaborate them.
    3. Plasma-derived mediators (complement, kinins) are produced mainly in the liver and circulate as inactive precursors that must be activated by a series of proteolytic cleavages.
    4. Active mediators are produced only in response to stimuli such as microbial products and substances released from necrotic cells, which ensures that inflammation is triggered only when and where it is needed.
    5. Most mediators are short lived. They decay quickly, are inactivated by enzymes (for example kininase for bradykinin), scavenged or inhibited, giving a system of checks and balances.
    6. One mediator can stimulate the release of others. For example, complement products stimulate histamine release and TNF stimulates endothelial cells to produce IL-1 and chemokines. Such cascades amplify or, in some instances, counteract the initial action.
    7. There is redundancy: several mediators act on the same target, so the response is robust and not readily subverted
      Yet their actions are sufficiently distinct that inhibiting each has been therapeutically useful.
    8. Most mediators act by binding to specific receptors, usually G protein-coupled, on target cells. Some have direct enzymatic activity (lysosomal proteases) or mediate oxidative damage (ROS).
    A2

    Principal actions of arachidonic acid metabolites.

    A2Q27

    Arachidonic acid metabolites (eicosanoids) are produced by cyclooxygenases (prostaglandins and thromboxane) and lipoxygenases (leukotrienes and lipoxins). Prostaglandins cause vasodilation, pain and fever, leukotrienes cause chemotaxis, increased permeability and bronchospasm, and lipoxins inhibit inflammation.

    Arachidonic acid (AA), a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid, is released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A₂ in response to mechanical, chemical or physical stimuli or mediators such as C5a. It is metabolised along two pathways.

    COX-1 is constitutive (gastric cytoprotection, renal function), while COX-2 is induced at inflammatory sites. Aspirin and NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenases. Corticosteroids reduce transcription of COX-2 and phospholipase A₂. Leukotriene receptor antagonists and 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors are used in asthma.

    A2Q27

    A2

    Write the functions of vasoactive amines.

    A2Q28DU10Ja

    Also asked as: Functions of vasoactive amines.

    The vasoactive amines are histamine and serotonin
    They are preformed and stored in cells, so they are among the first mediators released, and they cause vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, with histamine the principal mediator of the immediate transient phase of increased permeability.

    Sources. Histamine is richest in mast cells located in connective tissue adjacent to blood vessels, and is also found in basophils and platelets. Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is present in platelets and in neuroendocrine cells such as those in the gastrointestinal tract, where its primary function is as a neurotransmitter.

    Release. Histamine is released from mast cell granules by degranulation in response to (1) physical injury (trauma, cold, heat), (2) binding of antigen to IgE antibodies on mast cell surfaces (immediate hypersensitivity), (3) the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a, and (4) neuropeptides such as substance P and cytokines (IL-1, IL-8).

    Functions of histamine

    • Dilates arterioles and increases the permeability of venules by producing interendothelial gaps in postcapillary venules. it is the principal mediator of the immediate transient phase of increased permeability (15 to 30 minutes), leading to redness, warmth and swelling.
    • Contracts some smooth muscles (for example bronchial).
    • Activates endothelium (P-selectin expression).
    • Acts mainly through H1 receptors on microvascular endothelium. Four receptor types exist (H1 in allergic responses, H2 in gastric acid secretion, H3 in neurotransmitter modulation, H4 in immune function), all G protein-coupled
      H1 blockers treat allergy, H2 blockers reduce gastric acid.

    Functions of serotonin. Serotonin is a vasoconstrictor, but its importance in inflammation is unclear. It is released from platelets during aggregation and contributes to increased permeability in some species.

    A2

    How is the complement system activated?

    A2Q28

    The complement system is activated by three pathways, classical (antigen-bound IgM or IgG), alternative (microbial surfaces without antibody) and lectin (mannose-binding lectin), all of which converge on C3 convertase, which cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b
    C3b leads to C5 convertase, and the late components form the membrane attack complex.

    The complement system consists of more than 20 plasma proteins, some numbered C1 to C9, present as inactive precursors and activated in an enzymatic cascade capable of great amplification. The critical step is proteolysis of C3, the most abundant component.

    • Classical pathway: triggered by binding of C1 to antibody (IgM or IgG) that has combined with antigen, followed by sequential binding of C4 and C2 and formation of a multiprotein enzyme (C3 convertase).
    • Alternative pathway: triggered by microbial surface molecules (endotoxin/LPS), complex polysaccharides, cobra venom and other substances in the absence of antibody. Spontaneous C3 cleavage is amplified and stabilised on the microbe.
    • Lectin pathway: plasma mannose-binding lectin binds microbial carbohydrates and activates a C1-homologous protease. Subsequent steps are those of the classical pathway.

    C3 convertase splits C3 into C3a (released) and C3b (deposited on the microbe). More C3b binds to form C5 convertase, which cleaves C5 into C5a (released) and C5b, which binds C6 to C9 to form the membrane attack complex (MAC), made of multiple C9 molecules.

    Activation is controlled by regulatory proteins on host cells and in plasma: C1 inhibitor (deficiency causes hereditary angioedema), decay-accelerating factor (CD55) and CD59 (GPI-anchored
    Deficiency causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria), and factor H (defects cause atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and are linked to macular degeneration).

    What chemical mediators are responsible for the vascular events/features of acute inflammation?

    4DU26MDU14JuDU13JaDU10Ja

    The vascular events of acute inflammation (vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and the later endothelial activation that promotes leukocyte adhesion) are driven by several mediators with overlapping actions, which ensures a robust response (Table 3.5).

    Vasodilation (cause of redness and warmth):

    • Histamine, acting on H1 receptors of vascular smooth muscle, is the principal early mediator.
    • Prostaglandins PGI₂ (prostacyclin), PGE₁, PGE₂ and PGD₂ are vasodilators. PGD₂ is the major prostaglandin of mast cells.
    • Nitric oxide, produced by endothelial and inducible NOS, relaxes vascular smooth muscle.
    • Bradykinin (kinin system), PAF (at low concentrations), and the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a (by releasing histamine from mast cells) contribute.

    Increased vascular permeability (cause of oedema):

    • Histamine and serotonin, the immediate transient response through endothelial contraction.
    • Bradykinin, which has effects similar to those of histamine, and is rapidly inactivated by kininase.
    • Leukotrienes C₄, D₄ and E₄, produced by 5-lipoxygenase in mast cells and leukocytes.
    • C3a and C5a, by liberating vasoactive amines from mast cells.
    • PAF, substance P and prostaglandins (which potentiate permeability).
    • Cytokines (TNF, IL-1) and reactive oxygen species and lysosomal enzymes from leukocytes mediate delayed and sustained leakage by endothelial activation and injury.

    Vasoconstriction (transient, minor): thromboxane A₂, leukotrienes C₄, D₄, E₄ and serotonin.

    Leukocyte adhesion and recruitment: TNF and IL-1 induce E-selectin and the integrin ligands ICAM-1 and VCAM-1
    Histamine and thrombin mobilise P-selectin
    Chemokines, C5a and LTB₄ attract and activate leukocytes.

    Increased permeabilityHistamine, serotonin, C3a, C5a, leukotrienes C₄/D₄/E₄, bradykinin, PAF
