    A3

    Common sources of emboli.

    A3Q6

    The commonest source of emboli is thrombus: deep vein thrombosis of the legs for pulmonary emboli, and cardiac mural thrombi (after myocardial infarction or in atrial fibrillation) for systemic emboli.

    • Pulmonary emboli: 70% to 80% originate from deep vein thrombosis of the legs (popliteal, femoral and iliac veins). Pelvic veins and upper limb veins are less common sources.
    • Systemic emboli: 80% arise from intracardiac mural thrombi, two-thirds of which are associated with left ventricular wall infarcts and one-fourth with left atrial dilation and fibrillation (as in rheumatic mitral stenosis). The remainder come from aortic aneurysms, atherosclerotic plaques, valvular vegetations, or venous thrombi (paradoxical emboli). 10% to 15% are of unknown origin.
    A3

    Other sources of emboli.

    A3Q6

    Other sources are fractures of long bones (fat and marrow), sudden decompression (nitrogen), intravenous procedures and trauma (air), obstetric tears (amniotic fluid), atherosclerotic plaques (cholesterol), tumours, and foreign bodies.

    • Fat and bone marrow: fractures of long bones, soft tissue trauma, burns, rarely orthopaedic procedures.
    • Air: neck and chest wall injuries, intravenous lines, surgery in a sitting position, obstetric and laparoscopic procedures, mechanical ventilation.
    • Nitrogen: rapid ascent in divers, unpressurised aircraft.
    • Amniotic fluid: tear in the placental membranes or rupture of uterine veins during labour or delivery.
    • Atheromatous debris: ulcerated plaques of the aorta, especially after catheterisation or surgery.
    • Tumour fragments: tumours invading veins (renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma).
    • Foreign bodies: bullets, catheter fragments, talc and other particles in intravenous drug use.
    • Infected vegetations of the heart valves (septic emboli), and parasites.
    A3

    How does fat embolism occur?

    A3Q7

    Fat embolism occurs when trauma, usually fracture of long bones, ruptures the vascular sinusoids or small venules of the marrow, allowing droplets of marrow fat (sometimes with haematopoietic marrow) to enter the venous circulation and travel to the lungs.

    Fat embolism is the presence of microscopic fat globules, sometimes with haematopoietic bone marrow, in the vasculature, typically after fractures of long bones or, rarely, in soft tissue trauma and burns. It is common, occurring in about 90% of individuals with severe skeletal injuries, but only a minority have the clinical fat embolism syndrome. The injury ruptures vascular sinusoids or small venules in the marrow, allowing marrow and adipose tissue to herniate into the vascular space and travel to the lung.

    Small globules may pass through pulmonary capillaries to reach the systemic circulation (brain, kidney, skin). The embolic fat also causes biochemical injury, because free fatty acids released from the globules damage endothelium.

    A3

    What is fat embolism syndrome?

    A3Q7

    Fat embolism syndrome is the symptomatic condition seen in a minority of patients with fat embolism, characterised by pulmonary insufficiency, neurological symptoms, anaemia and thrombocytopenia, with a petechial rash, appearing 1 to 3 days after injury and fatal in 5% to 15% of cases.

    Typically, 1 to 3 days after injury, there is sudden onset of tachypnoea, dyspnoea and tachycardia, with irritability and restlessness that may progress to delirium or coma. Thrombocytopenia is attributed to platelet adhesion to fat globules and aggregation or splenic sequestration, and anaemia to red cell aggregation or haemolysis. A diffuse petechial rash (20% to 50%) is a useful diagnostic clue.

    Pathogenesis. Mechanical obstruction by fat microemboli and associated red cell and platelet aggregates occludes the pulmonary and cerebral microvasculature. Biochemical injury follows because free fatty acids released from the fat globules cause toxic injury to endothelium, with platelet activation and granulocyte recruitment releasing free radicals, proteases and eicosanoids.

    Diagnosis. Because paraffin processing dissolves lipids, demonstration of fat microglobules (in the absence of marrow elements) requires frozen sections with fat stains (Oil red O, Sudan).

    A3

    What is decompression sickness / caisson disease?

    A3Q8, Q9

    Decompression sickness is a form of gas embolism caused by sudden decrease in atmospheric pressure, in which nitrogen dissolved in blood and tissues at high pressure comes out of solution as bubbles. Caisson disease is the chronic form, in which persistent gas emboli in bone cause multiple foci of ischaemic necrosis.

    Scuba and deep-sea divers, underwater construction workers and people in unpressurised aircraft who ascend rapidly are at risk. When air is breathed at high pressure, increased amounts of gas (especially nitrogen) dissolve in blood and tissues
    with too rapid ascent, nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles.

    • The bends: rapid formation of gas bubbles in skeletal muscle and supporting tissues around joints causes severe pain (named from the arched posture of those afflicted, like the "Grecian bend").
    • The chokes: bubbles in the lung vasculature cause oedema, haemorrhage and focal atelectasis or emphysema, producing respiratory distress.
    • Central nervous system bubbles cause memory loss, ataxia, visual disturbances, even coma.
    • Caisson disease (named after the pressurised vessels used in bridge construction) is the chronic form: persistence of gas emboli in the skeletal system leads to multiple foci of ischaemic necrosis, commonly in the femoral heads, tibia and humeri.

    Small intravascular bubbles also evoke inflammatory and thrombogenic responses. Treatment is recompression in a chamber under high pressure to force the bubbles back into solution, followed by slow decompression.

    A3

    How much air is needed to produce a clinical effect?

    A3Q8

    More than about 100 mL of air is needed to produce a clinical effect in the pulmonary circulation, and 300 to 500 mL introduced over several seconds may be fatal.

    A large volume of air, generally more than 100 mL, is necessary to produce a clinical effect in the pulmonary circulation. This volume can inadvertently be introduced during obstetric or laparoscopic procedures, or through chest wall injury. Air in the pulmonary vasculature not only blocks perfusion of downstream regions but also induces an intense inflammatory response with release of cytokines that may injure the alveoli.

    Air embolism requires communication between the vasculature and outside air and a negative pressure gradient that sucks in air. in the cerebral circulation much smaller volumes can be dangerous.

    A3

    Clinical effects of caisson disease.

    A3Q9

    The clinical effects of decompression sickness and caisson disease are the bends (painful joints and muscles), the chokes (respiratory distress with pulmonary oedema and haemorrhage), neurological manifestations, and, in the chronic form, ischaemic bone necrosis, especially of the femoral heads, tibia and humeri.

    • Acute decompression sickness: rapid bubble formation in muscles and tissues around joints causes the painful bends. Bubbles in the lungs cause oedema, haemorrhage and focal atelectasis or emphysema, leading to respiratory distress (the chokes). Bubbles in the central nervous system cause headache, memory loss, ataxia, visual disturbances and the sudden onset of coma. Even small bubbles cause inflammatory and thrombogenic responses.
    • Chronic (caisson disease): persistence of gas emboli in the skeletal system causes multiple foci of ischaemic (avascular) necrosis, most commonly of the femoral heads, tibia and humeri, leading to joint pain and degenerative arthritis.
    • Treatment: recompression, then slow decompression.
    A3

    Why is amniotic fluid embolism so dangerous?

    A3Q10

    Amniotic fluid embolism is dangerous because, although rare, it has a mortality up to 60%, and the morbidity arises less from mechanical obstruction than from activation of coagulation and the innate immune system with release of vasoactive substances, causing sudden pulmonary hypertension, shock, DIC and neurological injury.

    It is the fifth most common cause of maternal mortality worldwide (about 10% of maternal deaths in the United States) and occurs in about 2 to 6 per 100,000 deliveries. About half of survivors have permanent neurologic dysfunction. Amniotic fluid or foetal tissue enters the maternal circulation through a tear in the placental membranes or rupture of uterine veins.

    The onset is sudden: severe dyspnoea, cyanosis and shock, followed by neurologic impairment (headache, seizures, coma) and DIC. The reasons for the danger are:

    1. Amniotic fluid contains many procoagulants (activated factors II, VII, X and tissue factor), causing DIC with massive haemorrhage.
    2. Activation of components of the innate immune system and release of vasoactive substances cause acute pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure, leading to hypoxia, left heart failure, pulmonary oedema and diffuse alveolar damage.
    3. The onset is abrupt and unpredictable during labour, and the features differ from those of thromboembolism.

    At autopsy, squamous cells shed from foetal skin, lanugo hair, fat from vernix caseosa and mucin from the foetal respiratory or gastrointestinal tract are found in the maternal pulmonary microvasculature.

    A3

    Sources of pulmonary embolism.

    A3Q26

    Pulmonary emboli originate in 70% to 80% of cases from deep vein thrombosis of the leg veins (popliteal, femoral, iliac), and less commonly from pelvic and upper limb veins, the right heart, and non-thrombotic emboli.

    • Deep veins of the lower limbs at or above the knee, the source of the great majority.
    • Other venous sources: periprostatic and ovarian/periuterine (pelvic) venous plexuses, upper limb veins (especially with central catheters), inferior vena cava.
    • Right atrial or ventricular mural thrombi (atrial fibrillation, right ventricular infarction), and right-sided valve vegetations.
    • Non-thrombotic emboli: fat and bone marrow (fractures), air, amniotic fluid, tumour (renal cell carcinoma), foreign material.

    The risk factors are the same as for DVT: immobilisation, surgery, trauma, malignancy, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, heart failure, and inherited thrombophilia.

    A3

    Clinical consequences of pulmonary embolism.

    A3Q26

    The consequences of pulmonary embolism depend on the size of the embolus and the vessel blocked: most are silent, but a large embolus causes sudden death or acute right heart failure, medium-sized emboli may cause haemorrhage or infarction, and multiple emboli over time cause pulmonary hypertension.

    • Silent emboli: 60% to 80% are clinically silent because they are small
      They become organised and incorporated into the vessel wall, sometimes leaving a delicate fibrous web.
    • Massive embolism: obstruction of 60% or more of the pulmonary circulation (large embolus, or saddle embolus at the bifurcation) causes sudden death, acute right heart failure (cor pulmonale) or cardiovascular collapse.
    • Medium-sized arteries: rupture of vessels can cause pulmonary haemorrhage, but infarction usually does not occur because of the dual supply from the bronchial arteries. if bronchial flow is compromised (left heart failure), infarction occurs.
    • Small end-arteriolar branches: often produce haemorrhage or infarction (wedge-shaped haemorrhagic infarct, with pleuritic chest pain, cough, dyspnoea and haemoptysis).
    • Recurrent emboli: pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure (chronic cor pulmonale).
    • Paradoxical embolism: if an interatrial or interventricular septal defect exists, the embolus can reach the systemic arterial circulation.
    A3

    Fate of pulmonary embolism.

    A3Q26

    A pulmonary embolus may cause sudden death, or be lysed, or become organised and incorporated into the vessel wall. Patients are at high risk of recurrent emboli.

    The embolus may (1) cause immediate death or acute right heart failure when large. (2) fragment and move into smaller branches
    (3) be dissolved by fibrinolysis
    (4) become organised, with ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts, and be incorporated into the vessel wall, sometimes leaving a bridging fibrous web. (5) cause haemorrhage or infarction, which heals by scarring

    (6) recur, because the patient who has had one embolus is at high risk for more, leading to pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure. The source thrombus in the leg may remain and re-embolise unless treated with anticoagulation.

    Classify emboli on the basis of their composition.

    DU03S

    An embolus is a detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass carried by the blood to a distant site. On the basis of composition emboli are classified as follows:

    ClassTypeSource or setting
    SolidThromboembolus (most common
    The great majority of emboli)    		Dislodged thrombus: DVT, cardiac mural thrombi
    Atheromatous (cholesterol) embolusUlcerated atherosclerotic plaque, often after vascular procedures
    Tumour embolusTumour invading veins (renal cell carcinoma)
    Bone marrow embolusFractures, resuscitation
    Foreign body embolusBullets, catheter fragments, talc
    Septic embolusInfected vegetations or thrombi
    LiquidFat embolusLong bone fractures, burns, soft tissue trauma
    Amniotic fluid embolusLabour and postpartum period
    GasAir embolusVein injury, intravenous or surgical procedures
    Nitrogen embolusDecompression sickness

    Write in short the pathogenesis/effects of systemic embolism.

    DU04M

    Systemic (arterial) thromboembolism refers to emboli that enter the arterial circulation.

    Sources. About 80% arise from intracardiac mural thrombi, two-thirds of which are associated with left ventricular wall infarcts and another quarter with left atrial dilation and fibrillation (for example in rheumatic mitral stenosis). The remainder come from aortic aneurysms, atherosclerotic plaques, valvular vegetations, or venous thrombi crossing a septal defect (paradoxical emboli)
    10% to 15% are of unknown origin.

    Pathogenesis. A fragment of the thrombus detaches, enters the arterial stream and travels until it lodges in a vessel too small to allow passage. In contrast to venous emboli, which lodge in the lung, arterial emboli can travel to a wide variety of sites. The point of arrest depends on the source and on the relative amount of blood flow received by downstream tissues. Most (75%) come to rest in the lower extremities and 10% in the brain. Other sites are the intestines, kidneys, spleen and upper extremities.

    Effects. The consequences depend on the vulnerability of the affected tissue to ischaemia, the caliber of the occluded vessel and whether there is a collateral blood supply. in general, tissue infarction results: gangrene of the lower limb, cerebral infarction (stroke), mesenteric infarction, renal and splenic infarcts. Septic emboli cause abscesses or mycotic aneurysms.

    Write a short note on embolism / emboli.

    DU19NovDU18Nov

    Definition. An embolus is a detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass that is carried by the blood from its point of origin to a distant site, where it often obstructs blood flow and causes tissue dysfunction or infarction. The phenomenon is called embolism.

    Types. Most emboli (more than 90%) are dislodged thrombi (thromboembolism). Others are fat droplets, air or nitrogen bubbles, atherosclerotic debris (cholesterol emboli), tumour fragments, bone marrow, amniotic fluid and foreign bodies.

    Venous and arterial emboli. Emboli of venous origin lodge in the pulmonary arteries (pulmonary embolism, from deep leg vein thrombosis in 70% to 80%). Emboli of cardiac or arterial origin lodge in systemic arteries, most commonly in the lower limbs (75%) and brain (10%). Paradoxical embolism occurs when a venous embolus passes through an interatrial or interventricular defect into the arterial circulation.

    Consequences. These depend on the size and site of the embolus and the vascular bed: partial or complete vascular occlusion, ischaemia and infarction (when collateral supply is absent), sudden death (massive pulmonary embolism), pulmonary hypertension (recurrent emboli), and DIC (amniotic fluid embolism). Septic emboli spread infection.

    Special forms. Pulmonary embolism, fat embolism and fat embolism syndrome, air embolism and decompression sickness, amniotic fluid embolism.

    Write a short note on fat embolism.

    DU05S

    Definition. Fat embolism is the presence of microscopic fat globules, sometimes with haematopoietic bone marrow, in the lung and other vasculature.

    Cause and incidence. It typically follows fractures of long bones, or rarely soft tissue trauma and burns, and is found in about 90% of individuals with severe skeletal injuries
    Injuries rupture vascular sinusoids or small venules in the marrow, allowing marrow and adipose tissue to enter the circulation and travel to the lung.

    Fat embolism syndrome affects the minority who become symptomatic. About 1 to 3 days after injury there is sudden tachypnoea, dyspnoea and tachycardia, with irritability and restlessness progressing to delirium or coma. Thrombocytopenia (platelet adhesion to fat globules, sequestration), anaemia (red cell aggregation, haemolysis) and a diffuse petechial rash (20% to 50%) occur. The syndrome is fatal in 5% to 15% of cases.

    Pathogenesis. Mechanical obstruction of the pulmonary and cerebral microvasculature by fat globules and platelet and red cell aggregates, plus biochemical injury: free fatty acids released from the globules injure endothelium, with platelet activation and granulocyte recruitment (free radicals, proteases, eicosanoids).

    Diagnosis. Frozen sections stained for fat (Oil red O, Sudan), as routine processing dissolves fat. Bone marrow elements may be seen in the pulmonary vessels.

    Write a short note on air embolism.

    DU16Ja

    Definition. Air (gas) embolism is the presence of gas bubbles within the circulation that coalesce to form frothy masses obstructing vascular flow and causing distal ischaemic injury.

    Causes. Air embolism occurs when there is communication between the vasculature and outside air and a negative pressure gradient that sucks air in: injuries of the neck or chest wall veins, neurosurgery in the sitting position, endovascular and interventional procedures, central venous catheters, mechanical ventilation, and obstetric or laparoscopic procedures.

    Volume. More than about 100 mL of air is generally needed to produce a clinical effect in the pulmonary circulation, and 300 to 500 mL over several seconds may be fatal.

    Effects. In the pulmonary vasculature air blocks perfusion and induces an intense inflammatory response with cytokine release and alveolar injury (right heart "air lock" with sudden dyspnoea, hypotension, a churning "mill-wheel" murmur). In the central nervous system, bubbles cause memory loss, ataxia, visual disturbances and sudden coma.

    Decompression sickness. A particular form of gas (nitrogen) embolism seen when sudden decreases in atmospheric pressure occur (divers, caisson workers, rapid ascent in unpressurised aircraft): the bends (painful bubbles in muscles and joints), the chokes (pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage and atelectasis), and the chronic caisson disease (ischaemic bone necrosis of femoral heads, tibia and humeri).

    Treatment. Recompression in a hyperbaric chamber with slow decompression. For venous air embolism, left lateral decubitus and head-down position and aspiration.

    Pulmonary embolism

    Write a short note on pulmonary embolism.

    DU08Ju

    Definition and incidence. Pulmonary embolism (PE) is occlusion of the pulmonary arterial vasculature by emboli, almost always thromboemboli from deep vein thrombosis. Incidence is estimated at 60 to 120 per 100,000 in the United States. it is somewhat more common in males
    it causes 60,000 to 100,000 deaths per year, and about 20% of individuals with PE die before or shortly after diagnosis.

    Source and risk factors. In 70% to 80% of cases the embolus originates from leg DVT, so the risk factors are those of DVT: prolonged bed rest and immobilisation, heart failure, trauma, surgery, burns, pregnancy and the puerperium, malignancy, oral contraceptives, inherited thrombophilias, and advanced age.

    Pathogenesis and morphology. Fragmented thrombi are carried through progressively larger veins and the right side of the heart and impact in the pulmonary arterial tree. Depending on size, an embolus may occlude the main pulmonary artery, straddle the bifurcation (saddle embolus), or pass into smaller branching arteries. Multiple emboli are common, sequentially or as a shower. Rarely a venous embolus passes through a septal defect into the systemic circulation (paradoxical embolism).

    Consequences

    • 60% to 80% are small and clinically silent
      They organise and are incorporated into the wall.
    • Occlusion of 60% or more of the circulation causes sudden death, acute right heart failure (cor pulmonale) or cardiovascular collapse.
    • Occlusion of medium-sized arteries causes haemorrhage but usually not infarction, because of the bronchial arterial supply (infarction occurs if bronchial flow is compromised, as in left heart failure).
    • Occlusion of small end-arteriolar branches often causes haemorrhage or infarction.
    • Multiple emboli over time cause pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure.

    Clinical features. Sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, haemoptysis, tachycardia. Diagnosis by CT pulmonary angiography
    Raised D-dimer
    Treatment with anticoagulation, thrombolysis or embolectomy.

    Pulmonary embolism (case)

    A5

    Male (30 or 38 years) hospitalised for femur fracture. After two weeks sudden chest pain, cough and haemoptysis — Most probable diagnosis? Cause of this complication?

    A5

    The most probable diagnosis is pulmonary thromboembolism with pulmonary infarction, caused by a thrombus from deep vein thrombosis of the leg veins that developed because of immobilisation and trauma and embolised to the lung.

    Diagnosis. Sudden chest pain, cough and haemoptysis in a patient immobilised in hospital for a femoral fracture indicate pulmonary embolism with infarction. The delay of two weeks favours thromboembolism. Fat embolism syndrome would present 1 to 3 days after injury with respiratory distress, neurological signs, thrombocytopenia and a petechial rash.

    Cause. The cause is deep vein thrombosis of the deep veins of the leg or pelvis. The trauma and fracture, together with immobilisation and bed rest, provide all three elements of Virchow's triad: endothelial injury and release of procoagulants from injured tissue and surgery (hypercoagulability), and stasis from immobility (loss of the muscle pump). A fragment of the thrombus detaches, travels through the venous system and the right heart and lodges in a branch of the pulmonary artery.

    Embolic obstruction of small end-arteriolar branches produces haemorrhage or a wedge-shaped haemorrhagic infarct, causing pleuritic pain and haemoptysis. Many DVTs are asymptomatic and recognised only after embolisation.

    A 38y male with femur fracture develops chest pain, cough and haemoptysis after 2 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?

    DU16Ju

    The most likely diagnosis is pulmonary thromboembolism with pulmonary infarction. Sudden chest pain, cough and haemoptysis in a patient immobilised after a femoral fracture are the typical features of pulmonary embolism with infarction of lung tissue. The interval of about two weeks is consistent with deep vein thrombosis of the leg that has embolised, whereas fat embolism syndrome appears 1 to 3 days after the fracture with tachypnoea, neurologic changes, thrombocytopenia and a petechial rash. Embolic obstruction of small end-arteries causes a wedge-shaped haemorrhagic (red) infarct, accounting for the pleuritic pain and blood-stained sputum. Confirmation is by CT pulmonary angiography, with raised D-dimer and demonstration of DVT by Doppler ultrasound.

    Same patient: what is the cause of this complication?

    DU16Ju

    The cause is deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the leg veins, with detachment of the thrombus and embolisation to the pulmonary arteries. Following a femoral fracture, all components of Virchow's triad are present:

    1. Stasis, because of immobilisation and enforced bed rest, which abolishes the milking action of the calf muscles on the deep veins.
    2. Endothelial injury, from direct trauma and surgery (fixation) to the vessels at the fracture site.
    3. Hypercoagulability, from release of tissue procoagulants (tissue factor) from injured tissue, increased hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and decreased t-PA production after trauma and surgery.

    The thrombus forms in the deep veins (popliteal, femoral, iliac) and extends toward the heart. Its poorly attached propagating portion fragments and is carried through the right heart into the pulmonary arterial circulation, causing embolic obstruction, haemorrhage and infarction. About 70% to 80% of pulmonary emboli arise in this way, and DVT is often asymptomatic until embolisation occurs.

    Infarction

    A3

    What is an infarct?

    A3Q11, Q27

    An infarct is an area of ischaemic necrosis caused by occlusion of either the arterial supply or the venous drainage of a tissue.

    Infarction is a common and extremely important cause of clinical illness. Roughly 40% of all deaths in the United States are caused by cardiovascular disease, and most of these are attributable to myocardial or cerebral infarction. Pulmonary infarction is a common complication in many clinical settings, bowel infarction is frequently fatal, and ischaemic necrosis of the extremities (gangrene) is a serious problem in diabetic patients.

    Most infarcts are due to arterial thrombosis or embolism. The characteristic histological change is coagulative necrosis (liquefactive necrosis in the brain), and most infarcts are eventually replaced by scar. Infarcts are classified as red (haemorrhagic) or white (anaemic), and as bland or septic.

    A3

    Underlying causes of infarction.

    A3Q11

    Infarction is most commonly caused by arterial thrombosis or arterial embolism. Less common causes are local vasospasm, haemorrhage into an atheromatous plaque, extrinsic compression, torsion of a vessel, and venous occlusion.

    • Arterial thrombosis (commonly on an atherosclerotic plaque, as in coronary and cerebral arteries) and arterial embolism underlie most infarctions.
    • Local vasospasm, haemorrhage into an atheromatous plaque, and extrinsic compression of a vessel (for example by a tumour).
    • Torsion of a vessel, as in testicular or ovarian torsion and volvulus of the bowel. Entrapment in a hernia sac.
    • Traumatic vascular rupture, and vascular compromise by oedema (anterior compartment syndrome of the leg).
    • Venous thrombosis: more often causes only congestion, since bypass channels open and permit outflow, but it can cause infarction in organs with a single efferent vein (testis, ovary).
    • Contributing factors are hypotension (shock), hypoxaemia, and sickle cell disease.
    A3

    Sites where white infarct occurs.

    A3Q12

    White (anaemic) infarcts occur with arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation and dense tissue, namely the heart, spleen and kidney.

    White infarcts occur where arterial occlusion affects solid organs with end-arterial circulation (heart, spleen, kidney) and where tissue density limits the seepage of blood from adjoining capillary beds into the necrotic area. The brain also develops pale infarcts, which undergo liquefactive necrosis. With time such infarcts become progressively paler and more sharply demarcated, and are eventually replaced by a scar (the remote renal infarct is a depressed fibrous scar).

    A3

    Factors that influence the development of an infarct.

    A3Q12

    Whether vascular occlusion causes infarction depends on the anatomy of the vascular supply, the rate of occlusion, the vulnerability of the tissue to hypoxia, and the oxygen content of the blood.

    1. Anatomy of the vascular supply. The availability of an alternative blood supply is the most important determinant. The lungs (pulmonary and bronchial arteries), the liver (hepatic artery and portal vein), and the hand and forearm (radial and ulnar arteries) are relatively resistant. Renal and splenic circulations are end-arterial, so obstruction generally causes tissue death.
    2. Rate of occlusion. Slowly developing occlusions are less likely to cause infarction because collateral pathways of perfusion have time to develop (for example interarteriolar anastomoses between coronary arteries).
    3. Vulnerability of the tissue to hypoxia. Neurons undergo irreversible damage after only 3 to 4 minutes of ischaemia
      Myocardial cells die after 20 to 30 minutes
      Fibroblasts remain viable after many hours.
    4. Blood oxygen content (hypoxaemia). Abnormally low oxygen content, whatever the cause, increases the likelihood and extent of infarction.
    A3

    Organs where red infarct occurs, and why.

    A3Q27

    Red (haemorrhagic) infarcts occur in the lung, small intestine, testis and ovary, and brain in some circumstances, because of venous occlusion, dual circulation, loose spongy tissue, previous congestion, or reperfusion.

    Red infarcts occur:

    1. With venous occlusions (testicular torsion, ovarian torsion).
    2. In loose, spongy tissues such as the lung, where blood can collect in the infarcted zone.
    3. In tissues with dual circulations (lung, small intestine), which allow blood from an unobstructed parallel supply to flow into the necrotic zone.
    4. In tissues previously congested by sluggish venous outflow.
    5. When flow is re-established to a site of previous arterial occlusion and necrosis (for example after angioplasty), including haemorrhagic transformation of cerebral infarcts.

    The lung is the typical organ: haemorrhagic wedge-shaped infarcts are the rule. In the infarcted zone, extravasated red cells are phagocytosed by macrophages and converted into haemosiderin.

    What are the factors that influence formation of infarct?

    DU16JuDU12Ju

    Vascular occlusion may have effects ranging from virtually nothing to tissue necrosis sufficient to cause death. The variables determining the outcome are:

    1. Anatomy of the vascular supply. The availability of an alternative (collateral or dual) blood supply is the most important determinant. The lung has a dual pulmonary and bronchial artery supply that protects against thromboembolic infarction. The liver, with its hepatic artery and portal vein, and the hand and forearm, with radial and ulnar arteries, are likewise resistant. Renal and splenic circulations are end-arterial, and obstruction generally causes infarction. Organs with a single efferent vein (testis, ovary) infarct with venous occlusion.
    2. Rate of development of occlusion. Slowly developing occlusions are less likely to cause infarction since there is time for development of collateral pathways. For example, small interarteriolar anastomoses connect the three major coronary arteries and, if one is occluded slowly by an encroaching atherosclerotic plaque, collateral flow may increase enough to prevent infarction.
    3. Tissue vulnerability to hypoxia. Neurons suffer irreversible damage after 3 to 4 minutes of ischaemia
      Myocardial cells are hardier but die after 20 to 30 minutes. Fibroblasts survive many hours.
    4. Hypoxaemia. Low oxygen content of the blood, whatever its cause (anaemia, cardiac failure, lung disease), increases the likelihood and extent of infarction.
    5. In addition, the caliber of the occluded vessel, the nature of the occlusion (embolus versus slowly progressive thrombosis), and the presence of shock or poor perfusion influence the result.

    Write a short note on red infarct / red and white infarct.

    4DU25MDU22MDU17JaDU15Ja

    Definition. An infarct is an area of ischaemic necrosis caused by occlusion of the arterial supply or venous drainage. Infarcts are classified by colour and by the presence of infection: they are either red (haemorrhagic) or white (anaemic), and either bland or septic.

    FeatureRed (haemorrhagic) infarctWhite (anaemic) infarct
    CauseVenous occlusion
    Arterial occlusion in tissues with dual circulation
    in loose tissue
    in previously congested tissue
    Reperfusion    		Arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation
    TissueLung, small intestine, testis, ovary, brain (reperfusion)Heart, spleen, kidney (and brain)
    MechanismBlood seeps into the necrotic area from parallel or collateral supply or from the congested veinsDense tissue limits seepage of blood from neighbouring capillary beds
    ColourRed-dark, haemorrhagic
    Later brown (haemosiderin)    		Pale, yellow-white, sharply demarcated
    ExamplesPulmonary infarct, testicular torsion, intestinal volvulusMyocardial infarct, splenic infarct, renal infarct

    Morphology. Infarcts tend to be wedge-shaped, with the occluded vessel at the apex and the periphery of the organ forming the base. When the base is a serosal surface, a fibrinous exudate may overlie it. Fresh infarcts are poorly defined and slightly haemorrhagic. Within a few days the margins become better defined by a narrow rim of congestion due to inflammation. White infarcts become progressively paler and more sharply defined. in the lung haemorrhagic infarcts are the rule.

    Extravasated red cells are phagocytosed by macrophages and converted to haemosiderin, leaving a firm brown residuum if haemorrhage is extensive.

    Histology and evolution. The dominant histological feature is coagulative necrosis (liquefactive necrosis in the brain). Microscopic changes take 4 to 12 hours to appear
    Acute inflammation is present along the margins within a few hours and well defined in 1 to 2 days. Repair begins in the preserved margins, and most infarcts are replaced by scar.

    Septic infarcts arise when infected valve vegetations embolise or microbes seed necrotic tissue, converting the infarct to an abscess.

    What types of infarct are seen in heart and lungs?

    DU12Ju

    Heart: white (anaemic) infarct. Myocardial infarction results from occlusion of a coronary artery (usually by thrombosis on an atherosclerotic plaque). The heart is a solid organ with end-arterial type supply, so the arterial occlusion produces a pale (white) infarct, in which tissue density limits seepage of blood into the necrotic area. Histologically it is coagulative necrosis, which takes 4 to 12 hours to be visible (cardiac myocytes die after 20 to 30 minutes of ischaemia), with neutrophilic infiltration at the margins within 1 to 2 days and eventual replacement by a fibrous scar. Reperfusion (angioplasty, thrombolysis) may make the infarct haemorrhagic (red). The infarct may be subendocardial or transmural.

    Lung: red (haemorrhagic) infarct. Pulmonary infarcts result from occlusion of small peripheral branches of the pulmonary artery, usually by emboli, and are haemorrhagic (red) because the lung is a loose spongy tissue with dual (pulmonary and bronchial) circulation, so blood flowing from the bronchial arteries collects in the necrotic zone, and because pulmonary congestion is often present.

    They are wedge-shaped with the base on the pleural surface, which may be covered by fibrinous exudate (pleuritic pain), and cause haemoptysis. Pulmonary infarction is uncommon with embolic occlusion of medium arteries because of the bronchial supply, unless the bronchial circulation is compromised (left heart failure).

    Shock

    A3

    What are the types of shock?

    A3Q28DU20NDU20Ju

    Also asked as: Classify shock.

    The three major types of shock are cardiogenic, hypovolaemic and septic shock
    Less commonly shock occurs in neurogenic and anaphylactic forms, in which acute vasodilation causes hypotension.

    Shock is a state of circulatory failure that impairs tissue perfusion and leads to cellular hypoxia. Its causes fall into three general categories:

    TypeClinical examplesPrincipal mechanisms
    CardiogenicMyocardial infarction, ventricular rupture, arrhythmia, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolismFailure of the myocardial pump from intrinsic myocardial damage, extrinsic compression, or obstruction to outflow
    Low cardiac output
    HypovolemicHaemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhoea, burns, traumaInadequate blood or plasma volume
    SepticOverwhelming bacterial and fungal infections (also superantigens, toxic shock syndrome)Activation of cytokine cascades, peripheral vasodilation and pooling of blood, endothelial activation and injury, leukocyte-induced damage, DIC
    NeurogenicSpinal cord injury, anaesthesiaLoss of vascular tone, peripheral vasodilation
    AnaphylacticIgE-mediated hypersensitivity (drugs, venoms, foods)Systemic vasodilation and increased vascular permeability

    SIRS (systemic inflammatory response syndrome) is a sepsis-like state triggered by non-infectious insults such as burns, trauma and pancreatitis. Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is a subset with particularly profound circulatory, cellular and metabolic abnormalities and higher mortality.

    A3

    What type of shock occurs in severe burn?

    A3Q28

    Severe burns cause hypovolaemic shock, due to massive loss of plasma and fluid from the burned surface.

    Thermal injury of the skin produces direct endothelial damage and increased vascular permeability, with outpouring of protein-rich plasma into the tissues and loss of fluid by evaporation and exudation from the burned surface. This causes inadequate blood and plasma volume and low cardiac output. Burn patients may subsequently develop septic shock from infection of the burn wound, and SIRS may complicate burns.

    A3

    Why do the skin become cool and pale in the early non-progressive phase of shock?

    A3Q13

    In the early non-progressive phase, reflex neurohumoral mechanisms (baroreceptor reflex, catecholamines, ADH, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, sympathetic stimulation) cause cutaneous vasoconstriction, which shunts blood from the skin to vital organs such as the heart and brain, making the skin cool and pale.

    In this stage the reflex compensatory mechanisms maintain cardiac output and blood pressure. The net effect is tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction and renal fluid conservation. Cutaneous vasoconstriction produces the characteristic "shocky" skin coolness and pallor (in the cold, clammy skin). Coronary and cerebral vessels are less sensitive to sympathetic signals and maintain relatively normal caliber, flow and oxygen delivery, so blood is shunted away from the skin to the vital organs. In septic shock, the skin may initially be warm and flushed because of cutaneous vasodilation.

    A3

    Changes that occur in the progressive phase of shock.

    A3Q14

    The progressive phase is characterised by widespread tissue hypoxia, with a switch to anaerobic glycolysis, lactic acidosis, loss of vasomotor tone and pooling of blood in the microcirculation, worsening cardiac output, endothelial injury with DIC, and onset of failure of vital organs.

    If the underlying causes are not corrected, shock passes to the progressive phase:

    1. Persistent oxygen deficit changes intracellular aerobic respiration to anaerobic glycolysis with excessive production of lactic acid.
    2. The resultant metabolic lactic acidosis lowers the tissue pH and blunts the vasomotor response. Arterioles dilate and blood begins to pool in the microcirculation.
    3. Peripheral pooling worsens cardiac output and exposes endothelial cells to anoxic injury with subsequent DIC.
    4. With widespread hypoxia, vital organs fail: the kidneys (oliguria), brain (confusion), heart (reduced contractility), lungs and gut.
    5. Hypotension worsens, the pulse is weak and rapid, and skin is cold, clammy and cyanotic.

    If untreated the process enters the irreversible stage, with lysosomal enzyme leakage, further myocardial depression (partly through NO), bacterial translocation from ischaemic gut, acute renal failure and death.

    Define shock.

    6DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU09JuDU08JuDU07Ju

    Shock is a state of systemic tissue hypoperfusion resulting from reduced cardiac output and/or reduced effective circulating blood volume, which leads to circulatory failure, impaired delivery of oxygen and nutrients to the tissues, and cellular hypoxia. At the outset the cellular injury is reversible, but prolonged shock leads to irreversible tissue injury, multiorgan failure and death.

    Causes. Shock may complicate severe haemorrhage, extensive trauma or burns, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism and microbial sepsis. The three major categories are cardiogenic shock (failure of the myocardial pump), hypovolaemic shock (loss of blood or plasma volume) and septic shock (systemic microbial infection with dysregulated host response). Less common forms are neurogenic and anaphylactic shock, in which acute vasodilation causes hypotension.

    Course. Shock evolves through three stages: nonprogressive (compensated), progressive, and irreversible.

    Features. Hypotension, weak rapid pulse, tachypnoea, cool, clammy, cyanotic skin (warm and flushed in early septic shock), oliguria, altered sensorium, and lactic acidosis. Morphologically the changes are those of hypoxic injury, with involvement of brain, heart, kidneys, adrenals and the gastrointestinal tract.

    What is anaphylactic shock?

    DU15Ja

    Anaphylactic shock is an acute, life-threatening systemic type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction, in which a sudden widespread vasodilation with increased vascular permeability causes hypotension and tissue hypoperfusion.

    Pathogenesis. In a previously sensitised individual, re-exposure to the antigen (penicillin and other drugs, insect venom, foods such as peanuts and shellfish, latex, contrast media) causes cross-linking of the antigen to IgE bound to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils. Degranulation releases histamine, and newly synthesised mediators (leukotrienes C₄, D₄, E₄, prostaglandin D₂, platelet-activating factor) and cytokines. Bradykinin and complement anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a) may contribute.

    Effects. Systemic arteriolar and venous dilation, increased vascular permeability with loss of plasma into the tissues (angioedema, laryngeal oedema), bronchospasm and mucus secretion (respiratory distress), urticaria, and hypotension with circulatory collapse.

    Clinical features. Within minutes of exposure: itching, urticaria, flushing, swelling of lips and larynx, wheezing, abdominal cramps, tachycardia, hypotension and collapse. it may be fatal. Treatment is immediate intramuscular epinephrine, with airway support, intravenous fluids, antihistamines and corticosteroids.

    Name the stages of shock.

    4DU25NDU16JuDU15JaDU10Ju

    Shock is a progressive disorder that leads to death if the underlying problems are not corrected. Unless the insult is massive and rapidly lethal (exsanguination from a ruptured aortic aneurysm), it evolves through three somewhat artificial stages, described most clearly in hypovolaemic shock but common to other forms:

    1. Initial nonprogressive (compensated) stage. Reflex compensatory mechanisms are activated and vital organ perfusion is maintained. These include baroreceptor reflexes, release of catecholamines and antidiuretic hormone, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, and generalised sympathetic stimulation. The net effect is tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction and renal fluid conservation. Cutaneous vasoconstriction causes cool, pale skin (in septic shock the skin may be warm and flushed from vasodilation). Coronary and cerebral vessels remain of normal caliber, so blood is shunted to the heart and brain.
    2. Progressive stage. Characterised by tissue hypoperfusion and the onset of worsening circulatory and metabolic derangement, including acidosis. Anaerobic glycolysis produces lactic acidosis, tissue pH falls, arterioles dilate and blood pools in the microcirculation, cardiac output falls further, endothelial anoxic injury causes DIC, and vital organs begin to fail (oliguria, confusion).
    3. Irreversible stage. Cellular and tissue injury is so severe that even if the haemodynamic defects are corrected, survival is not possible. There is widespread cell injury with lysosomal enzyme leakage, worsening myocardial function (partly from nitric oxide), intestinal ischaemia with bacteraemia, and renal failure (acute tubular necrosis), leading to multiorgan failure and death.

    Write a short note on hemorrhagic shock (pathophysiology of severe hemorrhage after RTA).

    DU20NDU20JuDU10Ju

    Haemorrhagic shock is hypovolaemic shock due to acute loss of a large volume of blood, as in severe haemorrhage after a road traffic accident, ruptured organs or fractures.

    Pathophysiology. The clinical significance of haemorrhage depends on the volume, the rate and the site. Rapid loss of up to about 20% of blood volume may have little impact in healthy adults. Greater losses cause haemorrhagic (hypovolaemic) shock.

    1. Reduced circulating volume. Loss of blood volume reduces venous return and cardiac preload, so cardiac output and arterial pressure fall.
    2. Compensatory stage (nonprogressive). Baroreceptor reflexes, release of catecholamines and antidiuretic hormone, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis and sympathetic stimulation produce tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction and renal fluid conservation. The skin becomes cool and pale, and blood is shunted to the heart and brain. Fluid shifts from the interstitium into the vessels partly restore volume.
    3. Progressive stage. If bleeding continues, persistent tissue hypoperfusion shifts metabolism to anaerobic glycolysis, with lactic acidosis. Acidosis blunts vasomotor tone, arterioles dilate and blood pools in capillaries, cardiac output falls further, and endothelium is injured, which may cause DIC. Trauma adds tissue injury and release of inflammatory mediators (SIRS), and massive transfusion, hypothermia and acidosis aggravate coagulopathy.
    4. Irreversible stage. Widespread cell injury, lysosomal enzyme release, myocardial failure, ischaemic gut with bacteraemia, acute tubular necrosis and multiorgan failure lead to death.

    Morphology and clinical features. Hypoxic injury of brain, heart, kidneys (acute tubular necrosis), adrenals (lipid depletion) and gut, with centrilobular hepatic necrosis. The lungs are relatively resistant to hypoxic injury in hypovolaemic shock after haemorrhage, though trauma may cause diffuse alveolar damage (shock lung). The patient is pale, with cold clammy skin, weak rapid pulse, hypotension, tachypnoea and oliguria. More than 90% of young, otherwise healthy patients with hypovolaemic shock survive with appropriate management (control of bleeding, volume replacement).

    Write the pathogenesis/mechanism of septic shock.

    7DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU13JuDU09JuDU08JuDU07Ju

    Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is a subset of sepsis with particularly profound circulatory, cellular and metabolic abnormalities and a greater risk of death. It is most frequently triggered by gram-positive bacterial infections, followed by gram-negative bacteria and fungi, and also by viruses. Superantigens (toxic shock syndrome) cause a similar syndrome. Mortality remains around 40%. It represents a failure of the normal control mechanisms that evolved to contain infection, when the response becomes generalised and injures normal tissues remote from the site of infection.

    Initiators. Microbial constituents such as endotoxin (LPS), staphylococcal enterotoxin B and M protein of streptococci. Macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and endothelial cells recognise pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) through Toll-like receptors, G protein-coupled receptors and C-type lectin receptors.

    Major pathogenic mechanisms

    1. Inflammatory and counter-inflammatory responses. Engagement of the receptors activates NF-κB and increases expression of cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-12, IL-18, IFN-γ) and other mediators (HMGB1, reactive oxygen species, prostaglandins, PAF)
      CRP and procalcitonin are elevated. These mediators induce endothelial adhesion molecules and further cytokine and chemokine release. Complement is activated, generating anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a), chemotactic C5a and opsonin C3b. Microbial products also activate coagulation through factor XII and altered endothelial function. The hyperinflammatory state triggers counterregulatory immunosuppression (shift from Th1 to antiinflammatory cytokines, IL-10, IL-1 receptor antagonist, soluble TNF receptor, lymphocyte apoptosis, anergy), so patients may oscillate between hyperinflammatory and immunosuppressed states.
    2. Endothelial activation and injury. Cytokines loosen endothelial tight junctions, causing widespread vascular leakage and protein-rich oedema that impairs perfusion, aggravated by intravenous fluids. Activated endothelium produces nitric oxide and other vasoactive mediators (C3a, C5a, PAF), causing vascular smooth muscle relaxation and systemic hypotension. Microvascular dysfunction (intermittent capillary flow, loss of autoregulation) produces a mismatch of oxygen delivery and need.
    3. Procoagulant state and DIC. Proinflammatory cytokines increase tissue factor on monocytes (and possibly endothelium) and decrease endothelial anticoagulants (TFPI, thrombomodulin, protein C), and increase PAI-1, dampening fibrinolysis. NETs may promote coagulation. Vascular leak and stasis reduce washout of activated factors. Systemic thrombin activation produces fibrin-rich thrombi in small vessels, further compromising perfusion. Up to half of septic patients develop DIC
      with consumption of platelets and factors, bleeding follows.
    4. Metabolic abnormalities. Insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia (TNF, IL-1, glucagon, growth hormone, glucocorticoids and catecholamines drive gluconeogenesis while cytokines impair insulin release and GLUT-4 expression)
      Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function. Initial surge in glucocorticoids may be followed by adrenal insufficiency, including adrenal haemorrhagic necrosis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome). Cellular hypoxia and impaired oxidative phosphorylation cause lactic acidosis.
    5. Organ dysfunction. Hypotension, interstitial oedema, microvascular dysfunction and microthrombi reduce oxygen delivery. Mitochondrial damage from oxidative stress impairs oxygen use. High cytokine levels depress myocardial contractility. Increased permeability leads to ARDS
      The result is failure of kidneys, liver, lungs and heart, culminating in death.

    Clinical aspects. Hypotension with warm, flushed skin early (vasodilation), tachycardia, fever or hypothermia, tachypnoea, leukocytosis or leukopenia, lactic acidosis and oliguria. Therapeutic attempts to block individual mediators have failed because of the multiplicity of mediators and concurrent anti-inflammatory activation. The standard of care is antibiotics, intravenous fluids, pressors and oxygen.

    A 40y male lost consciousness with cold clammy skin after severe bleeding in RTA. What is your probable diagnosis?

    DU25M

    The probable diagnosis is hypovolaemic (haemorrhagic) shock due to acute massive blood loss after the road traffic accident. Loss of a large volume of blood reduces circulating volume, venous return and cardiac output. The compensatory sympathetic and neurohumoral response causes cutaneous vasoconstriction, giving cold, clammy, pale skin, with tachycardia, weak thready pulse and hypotension. Loss of consciousness indicates cerebral hypoperfusion, and suggests progression beyond the compensated stage. Immediate management is control of haemorrhage, airway and oxygen, and rapid intravenous fluid and blood replacement.

    Same patient: what complications may occur?

    DU25M

    If shock is not rapidly reversed, tissue hypoxia leads to the following complications:

    • Acute kidney injury from acute tubular necrosis (ischaemic renal injury), with oliguria, acidosis and electrolyte disturbances. This is the commonest late complication.
    • Lactic (metabolic) acidosis from anaerobic glycolysis.
    • Disseminated intravascular coagulation, from endothelial anoxic injury, with microthrombi (visible in glomeruli) and bleeding.
    • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (shock lung), from diffuse alveolar damage following trauma.
    • Myocardial ischaemia and failure
      Hypoxic encephalopathy with neuronal loss
      Ischaemic bowel with mucosal necrosis and bacterial translocation, which can superimpose septic shock. Centrilobular hepatic necrosis
      Adrenal cortical lipid depletion and necrosis.
    • Multiorgan failure and death. Prognosis depends on the cause and duration
      More than 90% of young healthy patients with hypovolaemic shock survive if treated promptly.
    • Other complications related to trauma and resuscitation: infection, coagulopathy from massive transfusion, hypothermia, and iron deficiency anaemia if chronic.

    A 25y male has high fever, sore throat, gum/mandibular swelling after tooth extraction, then collapses with feeble pulse and unrecordable BP. What is your clinical diagnosis?

    DU18Nov

    The clinical diagnosis is septic shock (bacteraemic shock) secondary to an odontogenic (post-extraction) infection, with cellulitis of the gum and mandibular region (deep neck space infection such as Ludwig angina or abscess). High fever, sore throat and swelling after tooth extraction indicate acute pyogenic infection and spread. The subsequent collapse with feeble pulse and unrecordable blood pressure indicates circulatory failure due to systemic spread of infection with release of bacterial products and cytokines (TNF, IL-1), producing widespread vasodilation, vascular leakage, hypotension, and tissue hypoperfusion. Disseminated intravascular coagulation and multiorgan failure may follow. Management consists of immediate resuscitation with intravenous fluids and vasopressors, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical drainage of the focus.

    Same patient: what may be the etiology?

    DU18Nov

    The aetiology is bacterial infection introduced at tooth extraction into the gum and the soft tissues of the mandibular region, followed by bacteraemia. Septic shock is most frequently triggered by gram-positive bacterial infections, followed by gram-negative bacteria and fungi. The likely organisms in an odontogenic infection are:

    • Streptococci (viridans group and Streptococcus pyogenes) and Staphylococcus aureus, which may produce superantigens (toxic shock syndrome toxin, enterotoxins, streptococcal M protein) that cause polyclonal T-cell activation, massive cytokine release, rash, vasodilation, hypotension and shock.
    • Oral anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides), often with mixed flora, and gram-negative bacilli whose endotoxin (LPS) triggers TLR-mediated cytokine release.

    Predisposing factors include poor oral hygiene, poorly controlled diabetes, immunosuppression and non-sterile technique. The microbial constituents (endotoxin, enterotoxin B, M protein) engage Toll-like receptors on macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and endothelium, and trigger the inflammatory cascade of sepsis.

    Fluid, Electrolyte and Acid–Base Disorders

    Normal serum electrolytes

    A3

    Normal serum levels of Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻.

    A3Q16

    The normal serum values are sodium 135 to 145 mmol/L, potassium 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L, chloride 98 to 106 mmol/L and bicarbonate 22 to 28 mmol/L.

    ElectrolyteNormal serum level (adult)
    Sodium (Na⁺)135 to 145 mmol/L (mEq/L)
    Potassium (K⁺)3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L
    Chloride (Cl⁻)98 to 106 mmol/L
    Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)22 to 28 mmol/L
    Calcium (total)8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL (2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L)

    The anion gap, calculated as Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), is normally about 8 to 12 mmol/L. Reference ranges vary slightly between laboratories.

    Sodium

    A3

    What is hyponatraemia?

    A3Q18

    Hyponatraemia is a serum sodium concentration below 135 mmol/L, which usually reflects an excess of water relative to sodium and is a state of hypo-osmolality.

    Because sodium is the principal extracellular cation and determinant of plasma osmolality, hyponatraemia causes water to move into cells, producing cellular swelling. The brain is most vulnerable, and cerebral oedema produces headache, nausea, lethargy, confusion, seizures and coma, especially when the fall is acute and severe (below about 120 mmol/L). Chronic hyponatraemia is often better tolerated, and too rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis).

    It is classified as hypovolaemic, euvolaemic or hypervolaemic according to the volume status. Pseudohyponatraemia (hyperlipidaemia, hyperproteinaemia) and hypertonic hyponatraemia (hyperglycaemia) must be distinguished.

    A3

    Causes of hyponatraemia.

    A3Q18

    The causes of hyponatraemia are classified by volume status: loss of sodium and water (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhoea, adrenal insufficiency), water retention with normal volume (SIADH, hypothyroidism, polydipsia), and oedematous states (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure).

    Volume statusCauses
    Hypovolemic (loss of Na⁺ greater than water)Renal: thiazide and loop diuretics, adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), salt-losing nephropathy, osmotic diuresis. Extrarenal: vomiting, diarrhoea, sweating, burns, third spacing
    EuvolemicSyndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH: small cell carcinoma of lung, CNS disease, drugs, pulmonary disease), hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid deficiency, primary polydipsia, beer potomania, postoperative
    Hypervolemic (water retention greater than sodium)Congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, acute or chronic renal failure
    Spurious or redistributivePseudohyponatraemia (severe hyperlipidaemia, hyperproteinaemia), hyperglycaemia, mannitol
    A3

    What is hypernatraemia?

    A3Q19

    Hypernatraemia is a serum sodium concentration above 145 mmol/L, which indicates a deficit of water relative to sodium and always represents a hyperosmolar state.

    The raised osmolality draws water out of cells, causing cellular shrinkage. in the brain this may tear bridging veins and cause intracranial haemorrhage. The clinical features are thirst, irritability, weakness, restlessness, muscle twitching, confusion, seizures and coma. The condition occurs in patients who cannot respond to thirst (infants, elderly, unconscious), or who have excessive water loss. Correction should be gradual to avoid cerebral oedema.

    A3

    Causes of hypernatraemia.

    A3Q19

    The causes of hypernatraemia are pure water loss (diabetes insipidus, fever, sweating, inadequate intake), loss of hypotonic fluids (vomiting, diarrhoea, osmotic diuresis, burns), and, less commonly, sodium excess (hypertonic saline, sodium bicarbonate, mineralocorticoid excess).

    MechanismCauses
    Water loss without sodiumCentral or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
    Insensible loss (fever, burns, sweating, hyperventilation)
    Inadequate water intake (elderly, infants, unconscious patients, no access to water)
    Hypotonic fluid lossOsmotic diuresis (hyperglycaemia, mannitol, urea), diarrhoea and vomiting, loop diuretics
    Sodium gainAdministration of hypertonic saline or sodium bicarbonate, salt poisoning, primary hyperaldosteronism and Cushing syndrome (mild)

    Potassium

    A3

    What is hypokalaemia?

    A3Q16

    Hypokalaemia is a serum potassium concentration below 3.5 mmol/L.

    It is a common electrolyte disturbance, and its clinical importance is in cardiac and neuromuscular effects. Features are muscle weakness and cramps, paralysis in severe cases (below 2.5 mmol/L), constipation and paralytic ileus, polyuria from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, rhabdomyolysis, metabolic alkalosis, and cardiac arrhythmias. The ECG shows flattened T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves and prolonged QT interval
    Arrhythmias are particularly dangerous in patients taking digoxin. Hypokalaemia is often associated with hypomagnesaemia.

    A3

    Causes of hypokalaemia.

    A3Q16

    The causes of hypokalaemia are inadequate intake, excessive loss through the gut or kidneys (vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, hyperaldosteronism), and shift of potassium into cells (insulin, β-agonists, alkalosis).

    MechanismCauses
    Decreased intakeStarvation, anorexia, alcoholism, potassium-poor intravenous fluids
    Gastrointestinal lossVomiting and nasogastric suction (also causes renal loss through alkalosis), diarrhoea, laxative abuse, villous adenoma
    Renal lossDiuretics (loop and thiazide), primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), Cushing syndrome, renal tubular acidosis, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, hypomagnesaemia, amphotericin B, osmotic diuresis
    Transcellular shiftInsulin, β₂-agonists, metabolic alkalosis, thyrotoxic or familial periodic paralysis, rapid cell growth (treatment of megaloblastic anaemia)
    OtherExcess sweating
    Dialysis
    A3

    What is hyperkalaemia?

    A3Q17

    Hyperkalaemia is a serum potassium concentration above 5.0 to 5.5 mmol/L, and is dangerous because it can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias.

    Clinical features include muscle weakness and paralysis, paraesthesia, nausea, and, most importantly, cardiac conduction abnormalities. The ECG progresses from tall peaked T waves, to prolonged PR interval and loss of P waves, widened QRS complex, sine-wave pattern, ventricular fibrillation and asystole. It is a medical emergency when the potassium is above about 6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes are present.

    Treatment includes intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium, insulin with glucose, β-agonists, sodium bicarbonate, potassium-binding resins, loop diuretics and dialysis. Pseudohyperkalaemia from haemolysis of the specimen should be excluded.

    A3

    Causes of hyperkalaemia.

    A3Q17

    The causes of hyperkalaemia are reduced renal excretion (renal failure, adrenal insufficiency, potassium-sparing drugs), shift of potassium out of cells (acidosis, tissue breakdown), and excessive intake. Pseudohyperkalaemia from haemolysis must be excluded.

    MechanismCauses
    Decreased renal excretionAcute and chronic renal failure (most common), adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), hypoaldosteronism, potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, NSAIDs, heparin, trimethoprim
    Transcellular shiftMetabolic acidosis, insulin deficiency, β-blockers, digoxin toxicity, hyperosmolality, periodic paralysis
    Tissue breakdown (release)Rhabdomyolysis, crush injury, burns, tumour lysis syndrome, massive haemolysis, gastrointestinal haemorrhage
    Increased intakePotassium supplements, rapid transfusion of stored blood, potassium-containing salt substitutes
    ArtefactPseudohyperkalaemia from haemolysis in vitro, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis

    Calcium

    A3

    What is hypocalcaemia?

    A3Q20

    Hypocalcaemia is a serum total calcium concentration below about 8.5 mg/dL (2.1 mmol/L), corrected for the serum albumin, or a low ionised calcium. it causes neuromuscular irritability and tetany.

    Features include perioral and fingertip paraesthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm and tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, positive Chvostek sign (facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve) and Trousseau sign (carpal spasm with a blood pressure cuff), prolonged QT interval and arrhythmias, and in chronic cases cataracts, dry skin and basal ganglia calcification. Because about half of calcium is bound to albumin, a low albumin lowers total calcium without lowering the ionised fraction (pseudohypocalcaemia).

    A3

    Causes of hypocalcaemia.

    A3Q20

    The causes of hypocalcaemia are hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, chronic renal failure, hypomagnesaemia, acute pancreatitis and massive transfusion. Hypoalbuminaemia causes a spurious fall.

    CauseMechanism
    HypoparathyroidismPost-thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy, autoimmune, DiGeorge syndrome, radiation
    Pseudohypoparathyroidism (end-organ resistance)
    Vitamin D deficiency or resistanceMalnutrition, malabsorption, lack of sunlight, rickets and osteomalacia, liver disease, anticonvulsants
    Chronic renal failureImpaired activation of vitamin D, phosphate retention
    HypomagnesaemiaImpaired PTH secretion and action
    Acute pancreatitisSaponification of calcium in fat necrosis
    OthersMassive blood transfusion (citrate binding), hyperphosphataemia, rhabdomyolysis, bisphosphonates, osteoblastic metastases, sepsis, "hungry bone" syndrome
    SpuriousHypoalbuminaemia (low total but normal ionised calcium)
    A3

    What is hypercalcaemia?

    A3Q21

    Hypercalcaemia is a serum total calcium concentration above about 10.5 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L), corrected for albumin, and its commonest causes are primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy.

    Clinical features are summarised as "stones, bones, groans and psychic moans": renal stones, polyuria with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and dehydration, nephrocalcinosis, bone pain and fractures, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea, peptic ulcer and pancreatitis, fatigue, depression, confusion and coma, shortened QT interval, and arrhythmias. Metastatic calcification of soft tissues may occur. Severe hypercalcaemia is a medical emergency.

    A3

    Causes of hypercalcaemia.

    A3Q21

    The causes of hypercalcaemia are primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy (bone metastases and tumours that produce PTH-related protein), which account for most cases, followed by vitamin D excess, granulomatous disease, drugs and immobilisation.

    GroupCauses
    PTH-mediatedPrimary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma, hyperplasia, carcinoma)
    Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
    Lithium
    MalignancyOsteolytic bone metastases (breast, lung), myeloma, humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy (PTH-related protein from squamous cell carcinomas of lung and others), lymphoma (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D)
    Vitamin D-mediatedVitamin D intoxication, granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis)
    Increased bone turnoverHyperthyroidism, immobilisation, Paget disease, vitamin A excess
    Drugs and othersThiazide diuretics, milk-alkali syndrome, calcium supplements, adrenal insufficiency, acute renal failure (recovery of rhabdomyolysis)

    Acid–base disorders

    A3

    What is metabolic acidosis?

    A3Q22

    Metabolic acidosis is an acid-base disorder in which a primary fall in plasma bicarbonate lowers the blood pH below 7.35, caused by gain of acid or loss of bicarbonate, and compensated by hyperventilation.

    The arterial blood gas shows a low pH, a low HCO₃⁻ (below 22 mmol/L) and a compensatory fall in PCO₂. It is classified by the anion gap into high anion gap (accumulation of unmeasured acids) and normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic, from bicarbonate loss) types. The respiratory compensation produces deep, rapid, sighing breathing (Kussmaul respiration). Other features are hypotension, peripheral vasodilation, hyperkalaemia (potassium shifts out of cells), cardiac arrhythmias, reduced cardiac contractility, confusion, stupor and coma.

    A3

    Causes of metabolic acidosis.

    A3Q22

    The causes of metabolic acidosis are divided into high anion gap (lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis, renal failure, poisoning by salicylates, methanol and ethylene glycol) and normal anion gap (diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, acetazolamide, ureteral diversion).

    TypeCauses
    High anion gap (acid gain)Lactic acidosis (shock, hypoxia, sepsis, metformin), diabetic ketoacidosis, alcoholic and starvation ketosis, renal failure (uraemia: retention of phosphates and sulfates), toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, paraldehyde, isoniazid and iron), rhabdomyolysis (mnemonic MUDPILES)
    Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic; bicarbonate loss)Diarrhoea and intestinal fistulae, renal tubular acidosis, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide), ureterosigmoidostomy, early renal failure, hypoaldosteronism, excess saline infusion
    A3

    What is metabolic alkalosis?

    A3Q23

    Metabolic alkalosis is an acid–base disorder in which a primary rise in plasma bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻ above 28 mmol/L) raises the blood pH above 7.45, caused by loss of acid or gain of alkali, and compensated by hypoventilation.

    Compensation. Hypoventilation raises PCO₂
    This is limited by hypoxia, so compensation is incomplete. The kidney normally excretes excess bicarbonate, so metabolic alkalosis persists only when renal bicarbonate excretion is impaired, as in volume depletion, chloride depletion and potassium depletion.

    Classification and causes

    • Chloride-responsive (urine chloride low): vomiting, nasogastric suction, gastric outlet obstruction, diuretic therapy.
    • Chloride-resistant (urine chloride high): primary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, severe potassium depletion.
    • Alkali gain: excess bicarbonate or antacid intake.

    The arterial blood gas shows a high pH, high HCO₃⁻ (above 28 mmol/L) and compensatory rise in PCO₂. Alkalosis reduces the ionised calcium by increasing its binding to albumin, causing tetany, paraesthesias, muscle cramps and seizures. it also causes hypokalaemia (potassium shifts into cells and is lost in urine), hypoventilation, confusion, arrhythmias and, if severe, coma. It is maintained by volume depletion, chloride depletion and hypokalaemia, and is classified as chloride-responsive (urine chloride low) or chloride-resistant (urine chloride high).

    A3

    Causes of metabolic alkalosis.

    A3Q23

    The causes of metabolic alkalosis are loss of gastric acid (vomiting, nasogastric suction), diuretic therapy, mineralocorticoid excess, severe potassium depletion, and ingestion or administration of alkali.

    TypeCauses
    Chloride-responsive (urine chloride below 20 mmol/L)Vomiting and nasogastric suction (loss of HCl), pyloric stenosis, diuretics (thiazide and loop; contraction alkalosis), post-hypercapnic state, villous adenoma, cystic fibrosis
    Chloride-resistant (urine chloride above 20 mmol/L)Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), Cushing syndrome, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, severe hypokalaemia, licorice ingestion, renal artery stenosis
    Alkali administrationSodium bicarbonate, antacids (milk-alkali syndrome), citrate in massive blood transfusion, acetate

    Genes and Human Diseases

    16 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Genes, Mutations and Classification

    A7

    Define gene.

    A7Q1, Q4, Q8

    A gene is a segment of DNA that carries the coded information for making a specific functional product, usually a polypeptide and sometimes a functional RNA. It is the basic physical and functional unit of heredity.

    The human genome contains about 3 billion base pairs distributed over 23 pairs of chromosomes and about 20,000 protein-coding genes. Exons make up only about 1.5% of the genome. A typical protein-coding gene has these parts:

    • Regulatory sequences (promoter and enhancers) that control when and in which cells the gene is transcribed.
    • Exons, which are the coding segments.
    • Introns, which are removed by splicing.
    • 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions.

    Transcription produces a pre-mRNA, splicing yields mature mRNA, and translation yields the protein. Many genes instead specify functional noncoding RNAs, such as microRNAs and long noncoding RNAs (for example, XIST, which silences the inactive X). The position of a gene on a chromosome is its locus, and the alternative forms present at a locus are alleles. An individual who has two identical alleles is homozygous, and one who has two different alleles is heterozygous. These terms underlie every description of Mendelian inheritance.

    A7

    What is mutation?

    4A7Q2, Q8DU03SDU19M

    Also asked as: Define mutation.

    A mutation is a permanent change in the DNA sequence. If it occurs in germ cells it can be passed to offspring and cause inherited disease. if it occurs in somatic cells it is not transmitted and cannot cause hereditary disease.

    Germline mutations are present in every cell of the offspring and are the basis of hereditary disorders. Somatic mutations are restricted to a cell and its progeny. They drive cancer, produce clonal expansions such as clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, and, when they arise early in development, give rise to mosaic overgrowth syndromes. Mutations arise from errors in DNA replication or repair, or from mutagens such as ionising radiation, ultraviolet light and chemicals.

    A common DNA variant present in more than 1% of the population is called a polymorphism rather than a mutation. Polymorphisms rarely cause disease on their own but contribute additively to complex multigenic disorders.

    Gene mutations are grouped by their location and nature:

    • Point mutations in coding sequences. One base pair is substituted for another. The change may substitute a different amino acid (missense) or create a stop codon (nonsense).
    • Mutations in noncoding sequences. Changes in promoters or enhancers reduce or abolish transcription, and changes at intron-exon junctions disturb mRNA splicing.
    • Deletions and insertions. If the number of bases lost or gained is a multiple of three, the reading frame is preserved. Otherwise a frameshift results, usually ending in a premature stop codon.
    • Structural alterations. These include copy number changes (amplification or deletion) and rearrangements. The 22q11.2 microdeletion in the germline and the t(9;22) BCR-ABL translocation in chronic myeloid leukaemia are examples.
    • Trinucleotide-repeat expansions. These are dynamic mutations. In fragile X syndrome the CGG repeat in FMR1 expands from an average of about 29 copies to 250–4000, silencing the gene.

    Mutations interfere with gene function at every level. Deletions and promoter mutations compromise transcription, splice-site mutations abnormal RNA processing, nonsense and frameshift mutations translation, and missense mutations the function of the finished protein. Functionally, a mutation may cause loss of function (the common outcome) or, less often, gain of function.

    A7

    Types of mutation.

    A7Q2

    Mutations are classified into point mutations, which include missense, nonsense and silent changes, mutations of noncoding sequences, deletions and insertions (in-frame or frameshift), structural alterations of genes, and trinucleotide-repeat expansions.
