    A4

    What is cancer?

    A4Q4

    Cancer is the common term for a malignant neoplasm, that is, a tumour whose cells can invade and destroy adjacent tissues and spread to distant sites by metastasis.

    The word is derived from the Latin for crab, because malignant tumours tend to adhere to any tissue they seize on in an obstinate manner, like a crab. Cancer is not a single disease but a collection of disorders with widely different pathogeneses, natural histories and responses to treatment. Some, such as Hodgkin lymphoma, are highly curable, while others, such as pancreatic adenocarcinoma, are almost invariably fatal.

    In biologic terms, a cancer is a clonal expansion of a cell that has acquired a series of driver mutations and epigenetic changes in proto-oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes, apoptosis-regulating genes and DNA repair genes, and that has consequently acquired the hallmarks of cancer: self-sufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to growth inhibition, altered cellular metabolism, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replicative potential, sustained angiogenesis, the ability to invade and metastasise, and the ability to evade the host immune response.

    Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States, exceeded only by cardiovascular disease. The designation "malignant" always raises a red flag, although not every cancer pursues a lethal course, since some are found early enough for surgical excision and others respond well to drugs, antibodies or cellular therapies.

    A4

    What is carcinoma?

    A4Q2, Q4, Q6

    A carcinoma is a malignant neoplasm of epithelial cell origin.

    Carcinomas may arise from epithelium derived from any of the three germ layers (for example, squamous carcinoma of the skin from ectoderm, renal cell carcinoma from mesoderm-derived tubular epithelium and adenocarcinoma of the gastrointestinal tract from endoderm). They are qualified according to the pattern of growth or the cell they resemble. In squamous cell carcinoma the tumour cells resemble stratified squamous epithelium and often make keratin, whereas in adenocarcinoma the neoplastic epithelial cells grow in a glandular pattern.

    Other examples are transitional (urothelial) cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma and renal cell carcinoma. When the tissue or organ of origin can be identified it is added as a descriptor, as in bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma. In about 2% of cases the cells are so primitive that their origin cannot be determined and the tumour is called an undifferentiated malignant neoplasm
    Immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratins is then used to establish epithelial origin.

    Carcinomas are the commonest form of cancer in adults, and the carcinomas of the lung, breast, prostate and colorectum together account for more than half of cancer diagnoses and deaths in the United States. They develop through a sequence of premalignant change (dysplasia and carcinoma in situ) before they invade, and their initial dissemination is most commonly by the lymphatic route.

    A4

    What is sarcoma?

    A4Q2, Q4, Q6

    A sarcoma is a malignant tumour arising from mesenchymal tissue, such as connective tissue, fat, cartilage, bone, muscle and blood vessels.

    The name comes from the Greek sar, meaning fleshy, because sarcomas typically have little connective tissue stroma and so present as soft, fleshy tumours on cut section. They are named by attaching the suffix "-sarcoma" to the cell type that they resemble, for example fibrosarcoma, liposarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteogenic sarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma and angiosarcoma.

    Sarcomas are much less common than carcinomas in adults but form a significant proportion of malignant tumours in children and young adults. They tend to spread by the haematogenous route, although they may sometimes use the lymphatic channels. Several sarcomas are characterised by specific translocations, for instance the t(11;22)(q24;q12) of Ewing sarcoma, which are useful for diagnosis.

    A4

    Common examples of carcinoma.

    A4Q4

    The common carcinomas are squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, basal cell carcinoma and transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma, and by organ the carcinomas of the lung, breast, prostate, colon and rectum, stomach, cervix and liver are the most frequent.

    Examples by type and site include squamous cell carcinoma of the skin, oral cavity, oesophagus, larynx, lung and uterine cervix. Adenocarcinoma of the colon, stomach, pancreas, breast, prostate, endometrium and lung. Basal cell carcinoma of the skin
    Transitional cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder. Hepatocellular carcinoma of the liver
    Renal cell carcinoma of the kidney
    Bronchogenic carcinoma of the lung
    Serous and mucinous cystadenocarcinomas of the ovary. and choriocarcinoma of the placenta and embryonal carcinoma of the testis among the germ cell group.

    A4

    Common examples of sarcoma.

    A4Q4

    Common sarcomas are fibrosarcoma, liposarcoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma and angiosarcoma.

    These tumours arise from fibrous tissue, fat, cartilage, bone, smooth muscle, skeletal muscle and blood vessels respectively. Additional examples are lymphangiosarcoma (lymph vessels), Ewing sarcoma (a small round blue cell tumour of bone and soft tissue in children and young adults) and Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular tumour associated with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) infection and immunodeficiency.

    Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour in adolescents, rhabdomyosarcoma is one of the common soft tissue sarcomas of childhood and leiomyosarcoma may arise in the uterus, gastrointestinal tract and retroperitoneum.

    A4

    What is a hamartoma?

    A4Q18

    A hamartoma is a disorganised mass composed of mature cells indigenous to the tissue in which it arises.

    It was long regarded as a developmental malformation rather than a true tumour, but most hamartomas have been found to carry clonal chromosomal aberrations acquired through somatic mutation, and they are therefore now considered benign neoplasms. The mass is made up of the same cell types that are normally present at the site but they are arranged in a haphazard way and in abnormal proportions.

    A familiar example is the pulmonary hamartoma, a "coin lesion" on chest imaging that is composed of disorganised cartilage, fat, connective tissue and bronchial epithelium. The polyps of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, which is caused by germline loss-of-function mutations of the STK11 tumour suppressor gene, are also hamartomatous.

    A choristoma is different: it is a heterotopic (misplaced) rest of normal tissue, such as a nodule of well-developed pancreatic tissue in the submucosa of the stomach or small intestine. Like hamartoma, the name sounds neoplastic and conveys a gravity that far exceeds the actual significance of these lesions.

    A4

    Write a short note on teratoma.

    5A4Q18DU17NovDU16JaDU15JaDU14Ja

    Also asked as: What is a teratoma?

    A teratoma is a germ cell tumour composed of mature or immature tissues derived from more than one germ layer, and sometimes from all three, which arises from totipotential germ cells. The commonest example is the cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) of the ovary.

    Definition and origin. Most neoplasms, including mixed tumours, are composed of cells from a single germ layer. Teratoma is the exception. It originates from totipotential germ cells that are normally present in the ovary and testis and are sometimes found in abnormal midline embryonic rests, such as the sacrococcygeal region, mediastinum, retroperitoneum and pineal region. Because these cells can differentiate into any cell type of the body, the tumours contain, in a haphazard fashion, tissues such as skin, hair, sebaceous glands, teeth, bone, cartilage, muscle, fat, nerve, respiratory and gastrointestinal epithelium and even thyroid tissue.

    Types

    • Mature teratoma (benign). The best-known form is the cystic teratoma of the ovary, or dermoid cyst, which differentiates mainly along ectodermal lines. Grossly it is a unilocular cyst lined by skin-like squamous epithelium and filled with sebaceous material and hair, with a tooth or bone frequently projecting from a nodule of the wall. Microscopically it shows skin with sebaceous glands, fat cells and neural tissue, often with cartilage, bone, respiratory or intestinal epithelium. Mature teratomas of the ovary are nearly always benign.
    • Immature teratoma (malignant). It contains immature, embryonic-appearing tissue, most often primitive neuroectodermal elements, and behaves as a malignant tumour, its grade depending on the amount of immature tissue.
    • Teratocarcinoma. A teratoma that contains a carcinomatous (e.g., embryonal carcinoma) component.
    • Monodermal teratoma. A teratoma that is composed predominantly of one tissue, such as struma ovarii (thyroid tissue).

    Sites and age. In females the ovary is the commonest site, and the tumour is seen usually in reproductive-age women. In infants, the sacrococcygeal region is a characteristic site. In the testis, teratomas of adults are generally regarded as potentially malignant, in contrast to the ovarian counterpart.

    Clinical significance. Complications of ovarian dermoid cysts include torsion, rupture with chemical peritonitis, infection, and rarely malignant transformation of one component (usually a squamous cell carcinoma). Immature teratomas and teratocarcinomas may secrete alpha-fetoprotein or human chorionic gonadotropin, which are useful tumour markers for diagnosis and for monitoring response to therapy.

    Define neoplasia with example.

    DU24N

    Neoplasia means "new growth", and a neoplasm is defined as a disorder of cell growth that is triggered by acquired or, less commonly, inherited mutations affecting a single cell and its clonal progeny. These mutations alter the function of genes that regulate proliferation, survival, differentiation and DNA repair, and they give the neoplastic cells a growth advantage that results in excessive proliferation, independent of physiologic growth signals and controls. In Willis's classic words, a neoplasm is an abnormal mass of tissue whose growth exceeds and is uncoordinated with that of normal tissues and persists in the same excessive manner after cessation of the stimulus that evoked the change.

    A neoplasm consists of the proliferating neoplastic cells (the parenchyma) and a supporting stroma of connective tissue, vessels and immune cells. Neoplasms are either benign, remaining localised and amenable to surgical removal, or malignant, with the capacity to invade surrounding tissues and metastasise.

    Examples. A lipoma is a benign neoplasm of fat cells that closely resembles normal adipose tissue, grows as a discrete encapsulated mass and does not metastasise. An adenoma of the colon is a benign epithelial neoplasm that forms glandular structures and often presents as a polyp. A colonic adenocarcinoma is the corresponding malignant neoplasm, in which irregular glands invade the muscular layer of the colon wall and may metastasise to regional lymph nodes and the liver.

    Differentiation, Anaplasia and Dysplasia

    Benign vs malignant tumours

    What are the characteristics of a malignant tumour/cell?

    DU13JaDU12JaDU11Ju

    Malignant tumours differ from benign ones in the structure and behaviour of their cells, in their pattern of growth and in their capacity to invade and metastasise. Their characteristics can be considered under the following headings.

    1. Loss of differentiation (anaplasia). Malignant cells show a variable lack of differentiation
    The greater the anaplasia the more poorly the tumour resembles its tissue of origin and the more aggressive it is likely to be. In well-differentiated cancers, such as a well-differentiated thyroid adenocarcinoma that forms normal-looking follicles, the features may be subtle, and malignancy is then recognised by invasion and metastasis. Highly anaplastic tumours show the following cytologic changes:

    • Pleomorphism: variation in the size and shape of cells and nuclei within the same tumour, ranging from small undifferentiated cells to tumour giant cells many times larger than their neighbours, some with a single huge nucleus and others with multiple hyperchromatic nuclei.
    • Abnormal nuclear morphology: nuclei are disproportionately large, so that the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio approaches 1:1 instead of the normal 1:4 to 1:6
      The nuclear shape is irregular, the chromatin is coarse and clumped along the nuclear membrane or hyperchromatic, and the nucleoli are abnormally large.
    • Mitoses: often numerous, reflecting rapid proliferation, and importantly atypical and bizarre, including tripolar or multipolar spindles.
    • Loss of polarity: cells lose their orientation to one another and to the basement membrane, and they grow in sheets or masses in a disorganised fashion.
    • Ischaemic necrosis: the vascular supply is often inadequate for the rapidly growing tumour, so that areas of necrosis (and haemorrhage) are common.

    2. Altered function. Well-differentiated cancers may retain the function of their parent cells (for example, keratin production by squamous carcinomas, bile production by hepatocellular carcinoma). Highly anaplastic tumours lose specialised function but may acquire new properties, such as the production of foetal proteins or ectopic hormones that give rise to paraneoplastic syndromes.

    3. Growth. The rate of growth is erratic and may be slow or rapid, and in general it correlates with the level of differentiation. Growth is progressive and autonomous, and the tumour continues to grow in an excessive manner. The rate of growth alone is not a reliable discriminator of malignancy, since many benign tumours, and some cancers, deviate from the rule.

    4. Local invasion. Cancers are usually poorly demarcated from surrounding tissue and lack a well-defined cleavage plane. Their cells infiltrate and destroy adjacent tissues and do not respect anatomic boundaries. A slowly growing cancer may be surrounded by a pseudocapsule, but careful histologic examination shows tumour cells infiltrating beyond it. Invasiveness makes complete surgical removal difficult and requires wide margins.

    5. Metastasis. The capacity to spread to physically discontinuous sites, by seeding of body cavities, lymphatics or blood vessels, unequivocally identifies a tumour as malignant. About 30% of newly diagnosed solid tumours already have metastases. Metastasis is more likely with large, undifferentiated, rapidly growing and aggressively invasive primaries.

    6. Molecular characteristics. The cells carry driver mutations and epigenetic changes that confer the hallmarks of cancer: self-sufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to growth inhibitors, altered metabolism, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replicative potential, sustained angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis, and evasion of the host immune response. They are also genomically unstable and show genetic heterogeneity.

    7. Effects on the host. Malignant tumours cause local destruction, bleeding and infection, and also systemic effects such as cachexia and paraneoplastic syndromes. They usually recur after incomplete excision and may be fatal if untreated.

    Mention the characteristics of a benign neoplasm.

    DU22N

    A benign neoplasm remains localised at its site of origin, has no capacity to invade or metastasise and can usually be cured by surgical excision. Its characteristics are as follows.

    1. Differentiation. Benign tumours are well differentiated, and their cells closely resemble the normal cells of origin. A lipoma, for example, may be almost indistinguishable from normal adipose tissue microscopically, and is recognised as a tumour only because it forms a discrete mass. Anaplasia is absent.
    2. Cytology. The nuclei are uniform and normal in size and shape, with a normal nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Mitoses are rare and, when present, are of normal configuration. There is no pleomorphism and no tumour giant cells.
    3. Rate of growth. Growth is usually slow and progressive
      The tumour may come to a standstill or even regress.
    4. Mode of growth. The tumour grows as a cohesive, expansile mass that pushes aside the surrounding tissue. Because the expanding tumour compresses its surroundings, the stromal cells deposit a rim of compressed fibrous tissue, which forms a capsule. This tissue plane makes the tumour discrete, palpable, movable and easily removed. The exceptions include haemangiomas, which are often unencapsulated and permeate the tissues in which they arise.
    5. Invasion and metastasis. The tumour does not invade adjacent tissues and never metastasises.
    6. Vascularity. There is usually an adequate blood supply, so necrosis and haemorrhage are uncommon.
    7. Function. Benign tumours often retain the functions of their cell of origin, so that benign endocrine tumours may secrete hormones. A benign islet β-cell adenoma less than 1 cm in diameter may produce enough insulin to cause fatal hypoglycaemia.
    8. Behaviour and prognosis. Recurrence after complete excision is unusual and the prognosis is good. However, a benign tumour may cause serious morbidity or even death because of its location (as in the brain, or by compressing a vital structure such as the pituitary gland) or through hormone production, obstruction (such as intussusception in the gut), ulceration and bleeding. Most benign tumours transform rarely (leiomyoma, pleomorphic adenoma) or never (lipoma), but some, such as the colonic villous adenoma, progress to cancer in about half of untreated cases.

    Give the differences between benign and malignant tumour.

    DU20NDU20JuDU14Ja

    Distinguishing a benign from a malignant tumour is one of the most important decisions a pathologist makes, since nothing is more important to a patient with a tumour than being told that it is benign. The distinction rests on differentiation, local invasion and metastasis, and also on a range of cytologic and gross features.

    Of all these criteria, invasion and metastasis are the most reliable discriminators. Growth rate is not reliable, since there are many exceptions. Leukaemias and lymphomas are always considered malignant, because they arise from cells that normally circulate and are frequently disseminated at diagnosis.

    Anaplasia and carcinoma in situ

    A4

    What do you mean by differentiation?

    A4Q7

    Differentiation refers to the extent to which the neoplastic parenchymal cells resemble the corresponding normal parenchymal cells, both morphologically and functionally. Lack of differentiation is called anaplasia.

    Differentiation is the single most useful concept in the morphologic assessment of a tumour, because it links the appearance of the tumour cells to their likely behaviour. Benign tumours are, as a rule, well differentiated. The cells of a lipoma, for example, may so closely resemble normal adipocytes that the lesion can be recognised as a tumour only because the cells have grown into a discrete mass, and a follicular adenoma of the thyroid is made up of normal-looking colloid-filled follicles.

    Malignant tumours range from well differentiated, through moderately differentiated, to poorly differentiated or undifferentiated (anaplastic). In a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma of the thyroid the cells still form follicles, and some squamous cell carcinomas contain cells that look identical to normal squamous epithelium and produce keratin pearls. in a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, gland formation is still present but the glands are irregular in shape and size. in an anaplastic tumour the cells have lost almost all resemblance to the tissue of origin.

    Differentiation has a functional as well as a morphologic dimension. Well-differentiated cells tend to retain the specialised functions of their normal counterparts: well-differentiated endocrine tumours secrete hormones, squamous cell carcinomas synthesise keratin and hepatocellular carcinomas elaborate bile. Highly anaplastic tumours lose these specialised functions, although they may acquire unexpected ones, such as the expression of foetal proteins or the ectopic secretion of hormones. In general, the less differentiated a cancer, the more aggressive it tends to be, and this relationship is the basis of histologic grading.

    A4

    Define anaplasia.

    6A4Q7DU26MDU24MDU20NDU20JuDU09Ja

    Also asked as: What do you mean by anaplasia?

    Anaplasia means lack of differentiation. It is the failure of neoplastic cells to resemble their normal counterparts, in form or in function, and in its fully developed state it is a morphologic hallmark of malignancy.

    The word is derived from the Greek for "to form backward", reflecting the old belief that cancer cells were mature cells that had undergone "dedifferentiation". It is now generally held that most cancers arise from tissue stem cells or from progenitor cells whose maturation is arrested, although in some tumours mature cells may revert to a stem-like state through lineage plasticity. Whatever the origin, the cancer cell fails to complete the program of maturation that characterises the normal cell of that lineage.

    Anaplasia exists in degrees. Tumours range from well differentiated, in which the malignant nature is revealed only by invasion and metastasis, to highly anaplastic, poorly differentiated tumours in which the cell of origin cannot be identified on morphologic grounds alone and ancillary methods such as immunohistochemistry are needed. Highly anaplastic tumours are characterised by pleomorphism, abnormal nuclear morphology with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, numerous and often atypical mitoses, tumour giant cells, and loss of polarity with disorganised growth (these features are set out in the next question).

    Functionally, anaplastic tumours lose the specialised activities of their parent tissue. The degree of anaplasia correlates with biologic aggressiveness, so that a highly anaplastic appearance is highly predictive of malignant behaviour, and it forms the basis for histologic grading of the tumour.

    A4

    What are the features of anaplasia (anaplastic cell)?

    8A4Q7DU26MDU25MDU24MDU22MDU17NovDU16JuDU06Ja

    Also asked as: Features of anaplasia.

    The cardinal features of anaplasia are pleomorphism, abnormal nuclear morphology (hyperchromatic, enlarged, irregular nuclei with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and prominent nucleoli), numerous and atypical mitoses, loss of polarity, and tumour giant cells, usually accompanied by areas of ischaemic necrosis and loss of specialised function.

    1. Pleomorphism. There is variation in the size and shape of both cells and nuclei. Cells within the same tumour are not uniform but range from small, primitive-looking cells to tumour giant cells many times larger than their neighbours.
    2. Tumour giant cells. Some possess a single huge, bizarre nucleus, whereas others have two or more large hyperchromatic nuclei. They must not be confused with Langhans or foreign body giant cells, which derive from macrophages and contain many small, normal-appearing nuclei.
    3. Abnormal nuclear morphology. The nuclei are disproportionately large, so that the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, normally 1:4 to 1:6, approaches 1:1. The nuclear shape is irregular, the chromatin is coarsely clumped and distributed along the nuclear membrane, or the nucleus stains more darkly than normal (hyperchromasia), and the nucleoli are abnormally large and prominent. These changes reflect disturbed organisation of chromatin, which is now known to stem in part from acquired defects in epigenetic regulators.
    4. Mitoses. Undifferentiated cancers often contain many cells in mitosis, reflecting a high proliferative rate. The mere presence of mitoses does not indicate malignancy, because they are also seen in rapidly turning-over normal tissues and in hyperplasias. The more significant finding is the presence of atypical, bizarre mitotic figures, such as tripolar or multipolar spindles.
    5. Loss of polarity. The orientation of the anaplastic cells to one another and to supporting structures such as the basement membrane is disturbed, and the cells grow in sheets or masses in a disorganised fashion. Cell cohesion is lowered, which is the reason shed cells can be recognised in cytologic smears.
    6. Vascular supply and necrosis. The blood supply of rapidly growing anaplastic tumours is often insufficient, and areas of ischaemic necrosis are therefore common.
    7. Functional changes. Anaplastic tumours typically lose the specialised functions of their tissue of origin. Some acquire new properties, such as the production of foetal proteins or ectopic hormones that cause paraneoplastic syndromes.
    A4

    Types of dysplasia.

    A4Q8

    Epithelial dysplasia is graded as mild, moderate or severe according to the proportion of the epithelial thickness that shows disordered maturation, and in practice these are condensed into low-grade and high-grade dysplasia. Severe dysplasia involving the full thickness is carcinoma in situ.

    By grade. In mild dysplasia the cytologic and architectural abnormalities are confined to the lower third of the epithelium, in moderate dysplasia they involve up to two-thirds, and in severe dysplasia they extend through more than two-thirds up to the full thickness, at which point the lesion merges with carcinoma in situ. This is exemplified in the uterine cervix by cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) grades 1 to 3, which correspond to low-grade and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions.

    Mild dysplasia may regress when the cause is removed, whereas severe dysplasia carries a high probability of progression to invasive cancer.

    By tissue and site. Dysplasia is encountered mainly in epithelia, and the common settings are squamous dysplasia (cervix, oral mucosa as leukoplakia, bronchus, skin as actinic keratosis, oesophagus) and glandular dysplasia (Barrett oesophagus, adenomatous polyps of the colon, gastric intestinal metaplasia, endometrium).

    Non-neoplastic usage. The term is also used for developmental disorders of tissue structure that are not premalignant, such as fibrous dysplasia of bone, fibromuscular dysplasia of arteries and ectodermal dysplasia.

    A4

    What is carcinoma in situ (and locally malignant tumour)?

    A4Q8DU17JaDU15Ja

    Also asked as: What is carcinoma in situ?

    Carcinoma in situ is a cancer that has not yet invaded: the epithelium shows severe dysplasia involving its full thickness, with all the cytologic features of malignancy, but the basement membrane is intact and there is no penetration into the underlying stroma. A locally malignant tumour is one that invades and destroys surrounding tissue but rarely or never metastasises, as exemplified by basal cell carcinoma of the skin and gliomas of the central nervous system.

    Carcinoma in situ. When dysplasia is severe and involves the entire thickness of the epithelium but the lesion does not penetrate the basement membrane, it is called carcinoma in situ. Microscopically the epithelium is replaced by atypical cells showing no orderly differentiation, marked nuclear and cellular pleomorphism and numerous mitotic figures extending toward the surface, while the basement membrane remains intact and there is no tumour in the subepithelial stroma.

    Carcinoma in situ is seen in the skin, breast, bladder and uterine cervix. In situ cancers display all the cytologic features of malignancy, and unless treated they have a high probability of progression to invasive cancer. Because the lesion has not breached the basement membrane, it has no access to lymphatics and blood vessels and cannot metastasise, and so complete excision or ablation is curative.

    This is why detection of precursor lesions by Pap smear has been so effective in reducing cervical cancer mortality. An in situ carcinoma may persist for years before becoming invasive, the interval reflecting the time required for the accumulation of the further mutations and epigenetic changes needed for a fully malignant phenotype.

    Locally malignant tumours. Invasiveness and metastasis are separable properties. Some malignant tumours invade early and destroy surrounding tissue but metastasise rarely, and are therefore sometimes described as locally malignant. The two examples given are basal cell carcinoma of the skin, which infiltrates and ulcerates the surrounding tissue (the "rodent ulcer") but almost never spreads to distant sites, and gliomas of the brain, which invade the neuropil diffusely but seldom metastasise outside the central nervous system.

    Such tumours may be fatal or disabling because of local destruction or because of their location, and they require wide local excision with adequate margins.

    A4

    Two examples of carcinoma in situ.

    A4Q8

    Two examples are carcinoma in situ of the uterine cervix (squamous CIN 3) and ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast.

    Carcinoma in situ is also encountered in the skin (Bowen disease, a squamous carcinoma in situ) and in the urinary bladder (urothelial carcinoma in situ), and in the cervix it often precedes invasive squamous cell carcinoma by years.

    Define dysplasia.

    DU19MDU13Ju

    Dysplasia is a term that literally means "disordered growth". It is encountered principally in epithelial cells.

    Mention the clinical importance of dysplasia.

    DU13Ju

    The clinical importance of dysplasia lies in its relationship to cancer and in the opportunity it provides for early intervention.

    1. Precancerous lesion. Dysplastic changes are often found adjacent to foci of invasive carcinoma, and in some situations, such as the uterine cervix, severe epithelial dysplasia or carcinoma in situ frequently antedates the appearance of invasive cancer. Dysplasia in Barrett oesophagus, in oral leukoplakia, in the bronchial epithelium of smokers, in the colon in inflammatory bowel disease and in adenomatous polyps carries a corresponding risk.
    2. Molecular significance. Mutations associated with full-blown cancer may be present even in mild dysplasias, so that dysplasia marks a field of epithelium in which carcinogenesis is already under way.
    3. Reversibility. Progression to cancer is not inevitable. With removal of the inciting cause, such as cessation of smoking or treatment of chronic irritation or infection, moderately severe dysplasia may regress completely. Even carcinoma in situ may persist for years before becoming invasive.
    4. Basis of screening. Cytologic smears can distinguish normal, dysplastic and malignant cells. The Papanicolaou smear detects cervical precursor lesions and early curable cancers, and the marked fall in cervical cancer deaths in highly resourced countries is attributed largely to this test.
    5. Grading and management. The grade of dysplasia guides management. Low-grade lesions may be followed by surveillance, whereas high-grade dysplasia and carcinoma in situ generally require excision or ablation, because the time interval for evolution of a full-blown cancer from an in situ lesion relates to the time required to accumulate the necessary mutations.
    6. Surgical margins. Residual dysplasia at a resection margin signals a field defect and a risk of recurrence.

    It should also be remembered that dysplasia often occurs in metaplastic epithelium, but not all metaplastic epithelium is dysplastic.

    Write down the features of dysplasia.

    DU16Ju

    The features of dysplasia may be grouped into cytologic and architectural changes.

    Cytologic features

    • Pleomorphism, with variation in the size and shape of cells and nuclei.
    • Enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, irregular nuclear contours, coarse chromatin and enlarged nucleoli.
    • Increased mitotic activity, with mitoses seen above the basal layer rather than being confined to it, and occasionally abnormal mitotic figures.

    Architectural features

    • Disarray of the epithelium, with loss of the normal orderly maturation. In dysplastic squamous epithelium the progressive maturation of tall basal cells into flattened surface squames fails in part or entirely, so that the epithelium is replaced by basal-like cells with hyperchromatic nuclei.
    • Loss of polarity of the cells.

    Other features

    • The basement membrane is intact and there is no stromal invasion.
    • The severity is graded by the proportion of the epithelium involved, the full-thickness form being carcinoma in situ.
    • The process is potentially reversible when the cause is removed, but it may progress to invasive cancer.
    • Dysplasia occurs predominantly in epithelia and frequently, though not invariably, in metaplastic epithelium.

    How does dysplasia differ from anaplasia?

    DU07Ja

    Both terms describe disturbances of differentiation, and the cytologic features overlap, since dysplastic cells may show pleomorphism, hyperchromasia and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. They differ in meaning and in significance.

    FeatureDysplasiaAnaplasia
    MeaningDisordered growth, with abnormal cell appearance and loss of orderly maturationLack of differentiation of the tumour cells
    NatureA premalignant alteration of epitheliumA feature of malignant neoplasms
    TissuePrincipally epithelialSeen in any malignant tumour (carcinoma, sarcoma, lymphoma)
    ArchitectureEpithelial layering is disordered, but the epithelium is still recognizableOrderly arrangement is lost, and the cells grow in sheets without polarity
    InvasionAbsent
    The basement membrane is intact    		Usually accompanied by invasion and potential metastasis
    ReversibilityMay regress when the inciting cause is removed (mild and moderate forms)Irreversible, since it is a property of the cancer cell

    Invasion and Metastasis

    A4

    Define metastasis (short note).

    6A4Q1, Q9, Q14DU25NDU10JaDU09Ju

    Also asked as: What is metastasis?

    Metastasis is the spread of a primary tumour to physically discontinuous sites, and it unequivocally marks a tumour as malignant.

    Metastasis is the process whereby cells separate from the primary tumour, are carried to a distant site and there establish a secondary growth of the same histologic type. It is made possible by the invasiveness of cancers, which allows them to penetrate blood vessels, lymphatics and body cavities. All malignant tumours can metastasise, but some do so very infrequently. Gliomas and basal cell carcinomas, for example, invade early but rarely metastasise, which shows that invasiveness and metastasis are separable properties.

    Leukaemias and lymphomas are a special case. Because they are derived from cells that normally circulate, they are often disseminated at diagnosis and are always considered malignant, unlike the solid tumours.

    About 30% of solid tumours (excluding skin cancers other than melanoma) present as metastatic disease, and in general the likelihood of metastasis correlates with lack of differentiation, aggressive local invasion, rapid growth and large size, although there are innumerable exceptions. Metastatic spread follows three pathways: seeding of body cavities, lymphatic spread and haematogenous spread.

    The process is a multistep cascade that is divided into two phases: invasion of the extracellular matrix (loosening of intercellular contacts, degradation of the matrix, attachment to modified matrix components and migration), followed by vascular dissemination, homing and colonisation (intravasation, survival in the circulation, arrest, extravasation and growth at the new site).

    The cascade is highly inefficient, since although many tumour cells enter the circulation daily, very few produce metastases. Metastasis is the major cause of cancer deaths, and it strongly reduces the possibility of cure.

    A4

    Mention the routes/pathways of spread of a malignant tumour.

    12A4Q1DU25NDU24MDU22MDU19NovDU17NovDU17JaDU16JuDU14JuDU13JaDU12JaDU09Ju

    Also asked as: Routes of spread of a malignant tumour.

    A malignant tumour spreads by direct local invasion of adjacent tissues, and its dissemination to distant sites occurs by three pathways: seeding of body cavities and surfaces, lymphatic spread and haematogenous spread. Iatrogenic implantation on surgical instruments is a rare additional route.

    1. Local invasion (direct extension). Cancer cells infiltrate and destroy contiguous tissues, penetrating the wall of an organ and crossing anatomic boundaries, and may eventually fungate through the skin. This is the first step in all other forms of spread.

    2. Seeding of body cavities and surfaces. This occurs when a malignant neoplasm penetrates into a natural "open field" lacking physical barriers. The peritoneal cavity is most often involved, but any cavity or surface, including the pleura, pericardium, meninges and joint spaces, may be affected. It is particularly characteristic of ovarian carcinoma, which spreads over the peritoneal surfaces and the omentum to produce a heavy cancerous coating without invading the deeper tissues.

    Mucus-secreting carcinomas of the appendix or ovary may fill the peritoneal cavity with a gelatinous neoplastic mass called pseudomyxoma peritonei.

    3. Lymphatic spread. Transport through lymphatic vessels is the most common pathway for the initial dissemination of carcinomas. Sarcomas may also use it. Tumours do not contain functional lymphatics, but lymphatic vessels at the margins of invading cancers are sufficient for lymphatic spread. The pattern follows the natural routes of lymphatic drainage: carcinomas of the breast, which usually arise in the upper outer quadrant, spread first to the axillary nodes and then to the infraclavicular and supraclavicular nodes, and carcinomas of the lung spread first to the perihilar tracheobronchial and mediastinal nodes.

    Sometimes the regional nodes are bypassed (skip metastasis). The sentinel lymph node, the first node in the regional basin that receives lymph from the primary tumour, is identified by radiolabeled tracers or dyes and examined to determine whether the tumour has spread, as in breast cancer and melanoma. Regional nodes may serve for a while as barriers, and enlarged nodes near a cancer do not always contain metastasis, because reactive hyperplasia in response to tumour antigens can enlarge them. Only microscopic examination is definitive.

    4. Haematogenous spread. This is typical of sarcomas but is also seen with carcinomas. Penetration of small veins at the site of the primary tumour is an ominous feature. Arteries, with their thicker walls, are more resistant, but arterial spread may occur when tumour cells pass through pulmonary capillaries or arteriovenous shunts. Blood-borne cells tend to lodge in the first capillary bed they encounter, so that the liver and lungs are the most frequent sites of metastasis, since they filter the blood from the portal vein and from the vena cavae respectively.

    Cancers close to the vertebral column, such as carcinomas of the thyroid and prostate, may embolise through the paravertebral venous plexus and produce vertebral metastases. Some cancers have a propensity to grow within large veins: renal cell carcinoma invades the renal vein and grows up the inferior vena cava, sometimes as far as the right atrium, and hepatocellular carcinoma grows into the portal and hepatic veins.

    A4

    Common organs where metastasis occurs.

    A4Q9

    The commonest sites of haematogenous metastasis are the liver and the lungs, followed by the bones and brain, and the adrenal glands are also frequently involved
    Regional lymph nodes are the commonest site of lymphatic metastasis.

    The liver and lungs are involved most often because their capillary beds act as filters for the blood carried by the portal vein and by the vena cavae. The pattern is also influenced by the site of the primary tumour and by tissue tropism. Colonic carcinomas metastasise to the liver, the first organ downstream of the tumour. Carcinomas of the prostate and breast preferentially spread to bone. Lung carcinomas tend to involve the adrenals and brain. Neuroblastoma spreads to liver and bones
    and melanoma of the eye has a remarkable tendency to spread to the liver.

    Some tissues, such as skeletal muscle and spleen, are rarely the site of metastasis despite a rich blood supply, and are regarded as nonpermissive.

    A4

    Carcinomas that prefer haematogenous spread.

    A4Q2, Q9

    Although carcinomas spread initially by lymphatics, renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, follicular carcinoma of the thyroid and choriocarcinoma are the classic examples that prefer the haematogenous route.

    Renal cell carcinoma has a characteristic propensity to invade the renal vein and to grow as a snake-like column up the inferior vena cava, sometimes reaching the right atrium, and hepatocellular carcinoma invades the portal and hepatic venous radicles and grows into the main venous channels. Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid typically spreads to the lungs and bones and choriocarcinoma spreads early to the lungs, brain and vagina.

    Carcinomas of the prostate and thyroid, which lie near the vertebral column, may also embolise through the paravertebral venous plexus to vertebrae, and prostatic carcinoma spreads preferentially to bone. Bronchogenic carcinoma is another carcinoma that metastasises widely through the blood, to the brain, adrenals, liver and bone. Sarcomas, as a group, are the tumours that typically spread haematogenously.

    A4

    What is invasion?

    A4Q14

    Invasion is the progressive infiltration and destruction of the surrounding normal tissue by malignant cells, which do not respect anatomic boundaries
    it is a hallmark of malignancy and a prerequisite for distant spread.

    Invasion is an active process by which cancer cells breach the basement membrane, traverse the interstitial connective tissue and penetrate the walls of vessels. In contrast, nearly all benign tumours grow as cohesive, expansile masses that remain localised, compress their surroundings and usually develop a rim of compressed fibrous tissue (capsule), which makes them discrete, movable and easily removed.

    Malignant tumours are generally poorly demarcated and lack well-defined cleavage planes. A slowly expanding cancer may develop a pseudocapsule, but careful histologic examination almost always reveals tumour cells extending through it into the adjacent tissue. Next to metastasis, invasiveness is the most reliable discriminator between malignant and benign tumours. Its practical implication is that complete surgical removal of a cancer is difficult, and even if a tumour appears well circumscribed, a wide margin of apparently normal tissue must be removed.

    A4

    Steps of invasion.

    A4Q14

    Invasion of the extracellular matrix proceeds in four steps: loosening of tumour cell–tumour cell contacts, degradation of the extracellular matrix, attachment to novel (remodeled) matrix components, and migration of the tumour cells.

    1. Loosening of intercellular contacts. Normal epithelial cells are held together by adhesion molecules, notably E-cadherin. In several carcinomas E-cadherin function is lost by mutation, and in many others its expression is silenced through epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), which is controlled by the transcription factors SNAIL and TWIST, and in which epithelial markers fall and mesenchymal markers such as vimentin rise, favouring a migratory phenotype.
    2. Degradation of the basement membrane and interstitial matrix. Tumour cells, and stromal cells stimulated by them, secrete proteases, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMP2 and MMP9, which cleave type IV collagen), cathepsin D and urokinase plasminogen activator, while the concentration of metalloproteinase inhibitors is reduced. Proteolysis also releases growth factors stored in the matrix, such as VEGF, and generates fragments that are chemotactic, angiogenic and growth-promoting.
    3. Attachment to novel matrix components. Tumour cells change their expression of integrins. Free tumour cells resist anoikis, the apoptosis that normally follows loss of attachment to the matrix, and cleavage of collagen IV and laminin exposes new binding sites that stimulate migration.
    4. Migration. Locomotion propels the cells through the degraded matrix. It is driven by autocrine motility factors from the tumour, by cleavage products of matrix components, and by stromal factors such as hepatocyte growth factor/scatter factor acting on the MET receptor, and it depends on cycles of attachment at the leading edge, detachment at the trailing edge and actin-based contraction. The process culminates in penetration of the vascular basement membrane and entry into the vascular space.

    How does a malignant tumour spread through the hematogenous route?

    DU18NovDU17MDU14Ju

    Haematogenous spread is typical of sarcomas but is also common with carcinomas, and its mechanism is the metastatic cascade, in which the tumour cells go through a series of sequential steps, each of which they must complete successfully.

    1. Invasion of the extracellular matrix. The tumour cells loosen their intercellular attachments (loss of E-cadherin, EMT), degrade the basement membrane and interstitial matrix with matrix metalloproteinases and other proteases, attach to remodeled matrix through altered integrins, and migrate. Penetration of the thin-walled small veins at the primary site, and of capillaries and lymphatics, gives access to the circulation (intravasation). Veins are involved more often than arteries because of their thin walls.

    2. Survival in the circulation. Circulating tumour cells are vulnerable to shear stress, to anoikis and to attack by innate and adaptive immune cells. The cells that succeed travel preferentially as multicellular aggregates, whose formation is promoted by homotypic adhesion and by interactions with platelets. Platelets shield the cells, and tumour-derived anionic substances such as polyphosphate activate factor XII, causing fibrin deposition that stabilises the tumour emboli. Aggregates are more likely to contain cells with stem-like properties, which are needed to establish a metastasis.

    3. Arrest and extravasation. The cells commonly lodge in the first capillary bed they meet, which explains the frequency of hepatic and pulmonary metastases, and vertebral metastasis from thyroid and prostatic carcinomas through the paravertebral plexus. Extravasation involves transmigration between endothelial cells and passage through the basement membrane, using adhesion molecules (integrins, CD44), proteolytic enzymes and chemokines supplied by the tumour cells and by monocytes and neutrophils.

    4. Homing and colonisation. Where metastases finally form depends on the location and vascular drainage of the primary tumour, on tropisms of the tumour cells for particular tissues (adhesion molecules and chemokine receptors matched to ligands in the target organ, and the Paget "seed and soil" principle), and on escape from tumour dormancy. The metastatic cells must modify the new microenvironment: breast cancer cells in bone secrete parathyroid hormone–related protein, which acts through osteoblasts and RANKL to activate osteoclasts, and the growth factors released from the degraded bone support the tumour cells.

    The process is highly inefficient: many cells enter the bloodstream daily, but very few produce metastases. The clinical sites most frequently involved are the liver, lungs, bone and brain.

    Describe in short the mechanism of invasion and metastasis.

    DU08Ju

    Invasion and metastasis are the major causes of cancer-related morbidity and mortality. The metastatic cascade is considered in two phases.

    Phase 1: invasion of the extracellular matrix. To metastasise, a carcinoma cell must breach the underlying basement membrane, traverse the interstitial connective tissue and penetrate the vascular basement membrane. This takes place in four steps. First, tumour cells detach from one another because of reduced expression of adhesion molecules, especially E-cadherin, a process often achieved through epithelial–mesenchymal transition driven by SNAIL and TWIST.

    Second, proteolytic enzymes secreted by the tumour cells and by stromal cells (matrix metalloproteinases, cathepsins, urokinase plasminogen activator) degrade the basement membrane and interstitial matrix, and release matrix-bound growth factors and chemotactic fragments. Third, the cells attach to remodeled matrix components through altered integrins, and resist anoikis. Fourth, they migrate under the influence of autocrine motility factors, matrix breakdown products and stromal factors such as hepatocyte growth factor, and enter the vascular space.

    Phase 2: vascular dissemination, homing and colonisation. In the circulation, tumour cells, often as emboli aggregated with platelets, must survive shear forces and immune attack. They arrest in capillary beds, extravasate, and colonise the new site. The site of metastasis is determined by the anatomy of venous and lymphatic drainage, by tissue tropism related to adhesion molecules and chemokine receptors, and by the compatibility of the tissue as "soil" for the tumour "seed".

    Many metastatic cells then remain dormant before they grow, and successful colonisation requires them to alter the resident stromal cells so that the site becomes habitable.

    The process is inefficient and complex, and no single "metastasis gene" has been identified
    The metastatic phenotype probably requires the accumulation of multiple complementary genetic and epigenetic alterations.

    Carcinogenesis and Tumour Biology

    Carcinogenesis

    A4

    Fundamental cellular changes considered hallmarks of cancer.

    A4Q12

    All cancers display eight fundamental changes in cell physiology, the hallmarks of cancer: self-sufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals, altered cellular metabolism, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replicative potential, sustained angiogenesis, the ability to invade and metastasise, and the ability to evade the host immune response. Genomic instability and tumour-promoting inflammation are enabling characteristics that accelerate their acquisition.

    HallmarkBasis
    Self-sufficiency in growth signalsProliferation without external stimuli, usually through activation of oncogenes such as RAS, MYC, mutated growth factor receptors
    Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signalsInactivation of tumour suppressor genes such as RB, TP53, APC, CDKN2A
    Altered cellular metabolismSwitch to aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect), which supplies the carbon intermediates needed for rapid growth
    Evasion of apoptosisLoss of p53 function, overexpression of BCL2, amplification of MDM2
    Limitless replicative potentialEvasion of senescence and mitotic crisis through reactivation of telomerase, and a stem cell–like capacity for self-renewal
    Sustained angiogenesisHypoxia-induced HIF1α and VEGF
    Loss of angiogenesis inhibitors
    Invasion and metastasisLoss of E-cadherin, EMT, matrix proteases, integrin changes
    Evasion of the immune responseLoss of MHC class I, checkpoint ligands (PD-L1), immunosuppressive factors such as TGF-β, regulatory T cells

    Enabling characteristics: genomic instability (the mutator phenotype) and cancer-enabling (tumour-promoting) inflammation.

    A4

    Four principal classes of genes that cause cancer after mutation.

    A4Q11

    The principal targets of cancer-causing mutations are four classes of genes: growth-promoting proto-oncogenes, growth-inhibiting tumour suppressor genes, genes that regulate programmed cell death (apoptosis), and genes that are responsible for DNA repair.

    • Proto-oncogenes are converted to oncogenes by gain-of-function mutations. Because the mutant protein is constitutively active, one mutant allele suffices, and oncogenes are therefore dominant.
    • Tumour suppressor genes are disabled by loss-of-function mutations, and in most instances both alleles must be damaged, so that they behave in a recessive fashion (a state of haploinsufficiency is an exception, in which loss of one allele is enough).
    • Apoptosis-regulating genes acquire abnormalities that reduce cell death, either by gain of function in genes whose products suppress apoptosis (e.g., BCL2) or by loss of function in those that promote it (e.g., TP53, BAX).
    • DNA repair genes contribute indirectly. Their loss impairs the recognition and repair of nonlethal genetic damage in other genes, so that mutations accumulate at an accelerated rate (mutator phenotype), as in hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer, xeroderma pigmentosum, and BRCA1/BRCA2-related cancers.
    A4

    A4Q22

    Examples of oncogenes are RAS, MYC, ERBB2 (HER2), ABL and BRAF, and examples of tumour suppressor genes are RB, TP53, APC, NF1, PTEN, VHL and BRCA1/2.

    A4

    What is Li-Fraumeni syndrome?

    A4Q22

    Li-Fraumeni syndrome is an autosomal dominant cancer predisposition syndrome caused by inheritance of one mutated copy of the TP53 tumour suppressor gene.

    The affected individual carries the first hit in every cell, so that only one further somatic hit in the remaining normal allele is required to abrogate p53 function. Such persons have a 25-fold greater chance of developing a malignant tumour by the age of 50 than the general population. In contrast to the narrow spectrum seen with germline RB mutations, the spectrum of tumours is broad
    The most common are sarcomas, breast cancers, leukaemias, brain tumours and carcinomas of the adrenal cortex.

    The patients tend to develop cancer at younger ages and are more likely to have multiple primary tumours of different types. The syndrome illustrates the central position of p53, the "guardian of the genome", which is the most commonly mutated gene in human cancers, with loss-of-function mutations present in more than 50% of them, usually as somatic mutations of both alleles.

    A4

    What is angiogenesis?

    A4Q13

    Angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels, which in tumours takes the form of neoangiogenesis, the sprouting of new vessels from pre-existing capillaries. it is essential for tumour growth beyond 1 to 2 mm in diameter.

    A solid tumour, even if it carries all the genetic aberrations required for malignant transformation, cannot enlarge beyond 1 to 2 mm unless it can induce a blood supply, since this distance is the maximum across which oxygen, nutrients and waste products can diffuse from existing vessels. Early in their development most tumours do not induce angiogenesis and remain small or in situ, possibly for years, until an "angiogenic switch" terminates this stage of quiescence.

    Angiogenesis is controlled by a balance between angiogenesis promoters and inhibitors, and in tumours this balance is tilted in favour of the promoters. Angiogenesis is therefore an essential requirement for malignancy.

    Angiogenesis is also critical in healing at sites of injury and in the development of collateral circulation at sites of ischaemia.

    Steps. In tissue repair angiogenesis occurs mainly by sprouting:

    1. Vasodilation in response to nitric oxide and increased permeability induced by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
    2. Separation of pericytes from the abluminal surface and breakdown of the basement membrane by matrix metalloproteinases to allow formation of a vessel sprout.
    3. Migration of endothelial cells toward the area of tissue injury.
    4. Proliferation of endothelial cells just behind the leading "tip" cell.
    5. Remodelling into capillary tubes.
    6. Recruitment of periendothelial cells (pericytes for small capillaries, smooth muscle cells for larger vessels) to form the mature vessel.
    7. Suppression of endothelial proliferation and migration and deposition of the basement membrane.

    Mediators. VEGF-A (mainly) stimulates endothelial migration and proliferation, the "angiogenic switch", promotes vasodilation through NO and helps form the lumen. FGF-2 stimulates endothelial proliferation and the migration of macrophages and fibroblasts. Angiopoietins 1 and 2 contribute to the structural maturation of vessels. PDGF recruits smooth muscle cells, and TGF-β suppresses endothelial proliferation and enhances ECM production, thereby stabilising the vessel.

    The Notch pathway regulates sprouting and branching so that new vessels are properly spaced. Matrix metalloproteinases degrade ECM to permit extension of the vessel, and integrin-ECM interactions provide scaffold.

    Angiogenesis in tumours. Growing cancers stimulate neoangiogenesis, in which new vessels sprout from capillaries. A solid tumour cannot enlarge beyond 1 to 2 mm unless it induces angiogenesis, and early in their development most tumours do not do so until an "angiogenic switch" occurs. Hypoxia stabilises HIF1α, which activates the transcription of VEGF and bFGF. Tumour vessels are leaky, dilated and haphazardly connected, and angiogenesis also contributes to metastasis.

    A4

    Which factor induces angiogenesis?

    A4Q13

    Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is the principal factor that induces tumour angiogenesis, and its production is driven mainly by hypoxia through the transcription factor HIF1α. Basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF) also contributes.

    Hypoxia stabilises HIF1α, which activates transcription of VEGF and bFGF and creates an angiogenic gradient that stimulates endothelial proliferation and guides new vessels towards the tumour. Gain-of-function mutations of RAS and MYC upregulate VEGF, while loss of p53 removes thrombospondin-1, an inhibitor, and releases the suppression of VEGF. Loss of VHL function stabilises HIF1α even under normal oxygen tension. VEGF is also supplied by infiltrating macrophages and other stromal cells, and the antibody bevacizumab, which neutralises VEGF, is used in the treatment of several cancers.

    A4

    How does angiogenesis affect tumour growth?

    A4Q13

    Angiogenesis supplies the tumour with oxygen and nutrients and removes waste, allowing it to grow beyond 1 to 2 mm, and it also provides tumour cells with access to the circulation, thereby promoting metastasis.

    1. Growth. Neovascularisation permits growth beyond the diffusion limit. Without it, tumours stay small or in situ in a dormant state.
    2. Paracrine stimulation. Proliferating endothelial cells secrete growth factors, such as insulin-like growth factors and PDGF, which stimulate the growth of adjacent tumour cells.
    3. Metastasis. The tumour vessels are structurally abnormal (leaky, dilated and haphazardly connected), and they give tumour cells ready access to the circulation, which favours metastasis.
    4. Therapeutic target. Inhibitors of VEGF prolong the course of several advanced cancers, although they are not curative.
    A4

    Cells involved in the anti-tumour immune mechanism.

    A4Q15

    The principal effector cells of antitumour immunity are CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes, aided by dendritic cells, CD4⁺ helper T cells, natural killer cells and activated macrophages.

    • CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are the main mediators. They recognise tumour neoantigens (from mutated genes, viral proteins, or overexpressed and aberrantly expressed proteins) presented on MHC class I molecules, and kill tumour cells directly and serially.
    • Dendritic cells ingest tumour cells or antigens and present them in draining lymph nodes, with costimulation, to initiate the CTL response.
    • CD4⁺ T cells, especially Th1 cells, support the response, and their abundance in tumour infiltrates predicts a better prognosis in some cancers, such as colorectal carcinoma.
    • Natural killer (NK) cells, activated by IL-2 and IL-15, can lyse tumour cells without prior sensitisation, including those that have lost MHC class I expression, and may represent a first line of defence.
    • Macrophages, activated by interferon-γ from T and NK cells, can be cytotoxic to tumour cells.

    Antibodies against tumour cells have little demonstrated protective role. The suppressive cells that oppose these effectors are regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells and alternatively activated (M2) macrophages.

    A4

    What are the carcinogenic agents?

    A4Q16DU11Ja

    Also asked as: Carcinogenic agents.

    Carcinogenic agents fall into three principal groups: chemicals, radiant energy (ultraviolet and ionising radiation) and microbial agents (oncogenic viruses and certain bacteria and parasites). All of them cause cancer by producing genetic damage or by stimulating the proliferation of cells that have been damaged.

    1. Chemical carcinogens. Many hundreds of chemicals are carcinogenic in animals. All initiating chemical carcinogens are highly reactive electrophiles that damage DNA. Direct-acting agents need no metabolic conversion and include alkylating and acylating agents, such as the anticancer drugs cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil and the nitrosoureas, which may themselves cause second cancers, usually acute myeloid leukaemia.

    Indirect-acting agents (procarcinogens) require metabolic conversion to ultimate carcinogens, usually by cytochrome P-450 monooxygenases, and include polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzo[a]pyrene (in tobacco smoke, soot, and broiled or smoked meats), aromatic amines and azo dyes, the mould product aflatoxin B₁, and nitrosamines. Occupational carcinogens include asbestos, vinyl chloride, benzene, arsenic, nickel and chromium. Substances that stimulate proliferation of initiated cells (promoters), such as oestrogens, act in concert.

    2. Radiation. Ultraviolet B induces pyrimidine dimers in DNA and causes squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma and melanoma of the skin, and ionising radiation (x-rays, γ-rays, and particulate radiation) causes DNA breaks and cross-links and is associated with leukaemias, and with carcinomas of the thyroid, breast and lung.

    3. Microbial agents. These include HPV, EBV, HBV, HCV, HTLV-1, HHV8 and Merkel cell polyomavirus, the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, and parasites such as Schistosoma haematobium and Opisthorchis viverrini.

    Chronic inflammation, hormones and tissue injury with regenerative proliferation act as important promoting influences, so that several of these factors usually operate together.

    A4

    A4Q17

Tumour promoters form a third group, which stimulate proliferation of initiated cells but are not themselves carcinogenic.

    A4

    Steps of carcinogenesis.

    A4Q17

    Chemical carcinogenesis proceeds in stages: initiation, in which a cell sustains permanent DNA damage. Promotion, in which the initiated cell is driven to proliferate and expand clonally. and progression, in which further mutations accumulate in the proliferating cells until a fully malignant clone emerges.

    Initiation is rapid and irreversible and results from exposure to a sufficient dose of a carcinogen. Promotion by itself does not produce tumours, but induces tumours to arise from initiated cells, and it must follow initiation, not precede it. Driven to proliferate, subclones of the initiated cells acquire additional mutations, and eventually a cancerous clone possessing all the hallmarks emerges, which then continues to evolve under Darwinian selection (tumour progression).

    At the molecular level, carcinogenesis is a multistep process in which a series of complementary driver mutations in proto-oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes, apoptosis-regulating genes and DNA repair genes accumulate over time. The colon adenoma–carcinoma sequence shows this stepwise pattern, with early mutations in APC and late mutations in TP53.

    A4

    What do you mean by initiation?

    A4Q17

    Initiation is the first step of carcinogenesis, in which exposure of a cell to a sufficient dose of a carcinogenic agent causes permanent DNA damage (mutation), rendering the cell and its progeny susceptible to subsequent neoplastic transformation.

    Initiating agents are highly reactive electrophiles that react with nucleophilic atoms of DNA, and cause nonlethal damage that is repaired in an error-prone fashion, so that the mutation is fixed and transmitted to daughter cells. The process is irreversible and rapid. An initiated cell is not yet neoplastic and does not form a tumour by itself, since additional events are needed.

    Initiation does not target particular genes exclusively. Mutations occur throughout the genome, and cells that by chance sustain damage to the "usual suspects", such as RAS and TP53, gain a selective advantage. In the molecular scheme, the first driver mutation that starts a cell on the path to malignancy is the initiating mutation, which is maintained in all cells of the subsequent cancer.

    A4

    What do you mean by promotion?

    A4Q17

    Promotion is the second step of carcinogenesis, in which agents called promoters stimulate the proliferation and clonal expansion of initiated cells, so that tumours arise. Promoters are not tumourigenic by themselves.

    Promoters do not damage DNA directly, and do not affect cells that have not been initiated. By driving the initiated cells to divide, they cause clonal expansion of a preneoplastic population and increase the chance that these cells will sustain additional mutations, culminating in a cancerous clone with all the hallmark characteristics. Promotion in its early stage is reversible, in contrast to initiation.

    Many factors that contribute to human cancer act as promoters because they stimulate proliferation, for example unopposed oestrogenic stimulation of the endometrium and breast, and the chronic inflammation and regenerative proliferation associated with tissue repair and fibrosis, as in inflammatory bowel disease, chronic hepatitis and Barrett oesophagus. Environmental irritants such as airborne particulate matter probably promote cancer by fostering the outgrowth of cells bearing oncogenic mutations. The phorbol esters are the classic experimental promoters on mouse skin.

    A4

    Examples of chronic inflammation that cause risk of cancer.

    A4Q10

    Examples include chronic hepatitis B or C leading to hepatocellular carcinoma, Helicobacter pylori gastritis leading to gastric carcinoma and MALT lymphoma, inflammatory bowel disease leading to colorectal carcinoma, and Barrett oesophagus leading to oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

    Virchow proposed a link between chronic inflammation and cancer in 1863. The associations include:

    Oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes

    What do you mean by oncogene?

    DU08JaDU06MDU04S

    Oncogenes are mutated or overexpressed versions of normal cellular genes, called proto-oncogenes, that cause excessive cell growth even in the absence of growth factors and other growth-promoting external cues. Proto-oncogenes are the normal genes whose products promote cell proliferation, and they may encode growth factors, growth factor receptors, signal transducers, transcription factors or cell cycle components. The protein encoded by an oncogene is called an oncoprotein. It resembles the normal product in function, but it is constitutively active and resistant to control by external signals, so that the cell is freed from its normal dependence on growth factors and from normal checkpoints. Because the mutations produce a gain of function, oncogenes act dominantly: a single mutant allele is enough to transform the cell despite the presence of a normal copy.

    Oncogenes were first discovered in the genomes of transforming retroviruses (viral oncogenes), which had captured and altered host proto-oncogenes. Proto-oncogenes are converted into oncogenes by several mechanisms: point mutations (RAS, EGFR, BRAF), chromosomal translocations that either substitute a promoter or enhancer and cause overexpression (MYC in Burkitt lymphoma) or create a fusion gene encoding a chimeric oncoprotein (BCR::ABL in chronic myeloid leukaemia), gene amplification (ERBB2 in breast cancer, NMYC in neuroblastoma), and increased expression driven by upstream pathways.

    CategoryExampleTumour
    Growth factorsPDGFB, TGFA, FGF3Astrocytoma, sarcoma, breast, stomach
    Growth factor receptorsERBB1 (EGFR), ERBB2 (HER2), KIT, RET, ALKLung adenocarcinoma, breast carcinoma, GIST, MEN2, neuroblastoma
    Signal transducersRAS, BRAF, ABL, JAK2, PI3KPancreatic, colon cancer, melanoma, CML, polycythaemia vera
    Transcription factorsMYCBurkitt lymphoma
    Cell cycle regulatorsCyclin D1, CDK4Mantle cell lymphoma, glioblastoma

    Oncogenes are clinically important because tumour cells may become "addicted" to the oncoprotein, which therefore makes an effective drug target, as in imatinib for BCR::ABL, trastuzumab for HER2, and inhibitors of EGFR, ALK and BRAF.

    How does a cell become malignant?

    DU13Ju

    A cell becomes malignant through the stepwise accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations that confer upon it the hallmarks of cancer.

    Initial nonlethal genetic damage. The initial damage may be caused by environmental agents (chemicals, radiation, viruses, or reactive oxygen species), may be inherited in the germline, or may arise spontaneously from random errors. This damage is nonlethal and heritable, and is passed to daughter cells. A tumour therefore arises as a clonal expansion of a single precursor cell that has sustained genetic damage.

    Targets of the damage. Four classes of genes are affected. Gain-of-function mutations activate proto-oncogenes and so provide growth autonomy, loss-of-function mutations inactivate tumour suppressor genes and remove growth restraints, abnormalities of apoptosis-regulating genes reduce cell death, and loss-of-function mutations of DNA repair genes create a mutator phenotype with genomic instability that accelerates the acquisition of further mutations.

    Multistep acquisition. No single mutation is fully transforming. The first driver mutation (the initiating mutation) starts the cell on the path, and the "initiated" cell, which may have stem cell–like properties and persist for years, must acquire further complementary driver mutations. In addition, hundreds or thousands of "passenger" mutations of no functional consequence are acquired.

    The colon adenoma–carcinoma sequence is the classic example, with early APC and late TP53 mutations. Epigenetic changes (promoter hypermethylation silencing tumour suppressors, histone modifications) and altered microRNA expression contribute as well.

    Acquisition of hallmarks. The cell becomes self-sufficient in growth signals, insensitive to growth inhibition, metabolically reprogrammed (Warburg effect), resistant to apoptosis, immortal through evasion of senescence and reactivation of telomerase, capable of inducing angiogenesis, able to invade and metastasise, and able to evade immune destruction. Genomic instability and cancer-enabling inflammation accelerate the process.

    Progression. Under Darwinian selection, subclones with growth advantages dominate, so that tumours become more aggressive over time.

    Write about the role of genes in tumourigenesis.

    DU13Ju

    Cancer is fundamentally a genetic disease. Nonlethal damage to DNA lies at the heart of carcinogenesis, and four classes of normal regulatory genes are the principal targets.

    1. Proto-oncogenes (growth-promoting genes). These encode growth factors, growth factor receptors, signal transducing proteins (RAS, BRAF, PI3K, ABL), transcription factors (MYC) and cell cycle components (cyclin D, CDK4). Their gain-of-function mutations (point mutation, translocation, amplification) produce oncoproteins that drive proliferation constitutively. RAS is the most commonly mutated oncogene, being mutated in about 15% to 20% of all human tumours, and MYC acts as a master regulator of cell growth.

    2. Tumour suppressor genes (growth-inhibiting genes). These oppose the hallmarks of cancer and act as brakes on proliferation. RB governs the G1/S checkpoint, and TP53 is the "guardian of the genome", responding to DNA damage, hypoxia and oncogenic stress by inducing cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, senescence or apoptosis. APC restrains Wnt signalling, PTEN restrains PI3K, NF1 restrains RAS, and VHL regulates HIF1α. Loss-of-function of both alleles is generally needed (the two-hit hypothesis), and the germline inheritance of one defective allele underlies familial cancer syndromes.

    3. Genes regulating apoptosis. Overexpression of the anti-apoptotic BCL2 (follicular lymphoma, t(14;18)), MDM2 amplification, and loss of p53 or pro-apoptotic BAX and PUMA function allow damaged cells to survive.

    4. DNA repair genes. Defects in mismatch repair (MSH2, MLH1, as in hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer, with microsatellite instability), nucleotide excision repair (xeroderma pigmentosum), and homologous recombination repair (BRCA1/2, ataxia-telangiectasia, Bloom syndrome, Fanconi anaemia) lead to a mutator phenotype.

    Additional genetic mechanisms. Genes encoding epigenetic regulators (DNMT3A, KMT2D, ARID1A) and microRNAs (miR-15/16, miR-155) are also altered. Telomerase (TERT) reactivation confers immortality, and genes affecting the immune response, such as PD-L1, and the stroma contribute by non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. Oncogenic viruses introduce viral genes (HPV E6 and E7) that disable TP53 and RB.

    Mutations contributing to the hallmarks are called driver mutations, whereas passenger mutations are functionally neutral.

    Write a short note on tumour suppressor genes.

    DU08Ju

    Tumour suppressor genes encode proteins that act as negative regulators of cell proliferation, and loss of their function leads to excessive growth. More broadly, a tumour suppressor is any gene or protein that opposes one of the hallmarks of cancer, and the products may function as transcription factors, cell cycle inhibitors, signal transduction molecules, cell surface receptors, or regulators of cellular responses to DNA damage, metabolism and genomic stability. They control checkpoints that prevent uncontrolled growth, and induce senescence or apoptosis when damage is irreparable.

    The two-hit hypothesis. Retinoblastoma, the first tumour suppressor disease to be studied, was explained by Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. Both alleles of the RB gene must be inactivated to produce the tumour. In familial cases (about 40%), a child inherits one defective copy in the germline (first hit) and one normal copy, and a somatic mutation in a retinoblast (second hit) is virtually inevitable, so that tumours are often bilateral and the carriers have a 10,000-fold increased risk, as well as an increased risk of osteosarcoma.

    In sporadic cases (60%), both hits are somatic mutations in the same retinoblast, which is why they are unilateral and uncommon. The predisposition is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, but at the cellular level loss of function behaves as a recessive trait. A state of haploinsufficiency is an exception, in which loss of one allele is sufficient.

    Mechanisms of inactivation. Deletions, point mutations, promoter hypermethylation (epigenetic silencing, for example of CDKN2A), loss of heterozygosity, and binding and inactivation by viral oncoproteins (HPV E6 for p53 and E7 for RB), or increased degradation (MDM2 amplification).
