    Diseases of White Blood Cells, Lymph Nodes, Spleen, and Thymus

    16 questions · viva and written, in Robbins order.

    Reactive Leukocyte Disorders

    Granulopoiesis

    A8

    What is granulopoiesis?

    A8Q1

    Granulopoiesis is the orderly proliferation and maturation of marrow progenitor cells into mature granulocytes—neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils—under the control of colony-stimulating factors.

    All blood cells arise from pluripotent haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which have the twin properties of pluripotency and self-renewal. A stem cell gives rise to a multipotent progenitor, then to a myeloid-committed progenitor, and ultimately to a granulocyte–macrophage colony-forming unit (CFU-GM). This cell has lost the ability to self-renew and is committed to the granulocytic and monocytic pathways. From it arise the morphologically recognizable precursors, beginning with the myeloblast.

    Along this road the cells proliferate rapidly while differentiating, and the lineage-specific growth factors tune the output. KIT ligand and FLT3 ligand act on very early progenitors, whereas G-CSF and GM-CSF act on committed myeloid progenitors, G-CSF being the principal driver of neutrophil production, and IL-5 preferentially stimulates eosinophils.

    The marrow is functionally organised into compartments. A mitotic (proliferative) pool consists of myeloblasts, promyelocytes and myelocytes, which are capable of division. A maturation (post-mitotic) pool of metamyelocytes, band forms and segmented neutrophils then forms a large marrow storage pool, which is many times larger than the circulating pool. Transit from myeloblast to mature neutrophil takes about 10 to 14 days.

    In acute infection, TNF and IL-1 promote rapid egress of mature granulocytes from this storage pool. if the stimulus persists, these cytokines stimulate macrophages, stromal cells and T cells to produce more colony-stimulating factors, which expand granulocytic progenitors and sustain increased production over several days. Once in the blood, neutrophils are divided between a freely circulating pool and a marginal pool adherent to vessel walls, and they survive only hours in the circulation before migrating into the tissues.

    Disordered granulopoiesis underlies several important conditions: reduced or ineffective granulopoiesis causes neutropenia (aplastic anaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, megaloblastic anaemia, drug toxicity), accelerated or unregulated granulopoiesis causes neutrophilia and, when autonomous, myeloproliferative neoplasms such as chronic myeloid leukaemia, and arrested maturation at the blast stage characterises acute myeloid leukaemia.

    A8

    Stages of the granulocytic series.

    A8Q1

    The granulocytic series runs from myeloblast to promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band form and finally the segmented granulocyte. The cells up to the myelocyte can divide, and from the metamyelocyte onward they only mature.

    The morphological stages, in order of maturation, are summarised below.

    StageNucleusCytoplasm and granulesCapacity to divide
    MyeloblastLarge, round to oval, delicate fine chromatin, two to four distinct nucleoliScanty to moderate, basophilic, agranular or with a few fine azurophilic granules
    High nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio    		Yes
    PromyelocyteRound or oval, often eccentric
    Chromatin slightly coarser
    Nucleoli still visible
    The largest cell of the series    		Basophilic, with numerous coarse red-purple primary (azurophilic) granules that contain myeloperoxidase
    Prominent Golgi zone    		Yes
    MyelocyteRound to oval, chromatin condensed, nucleoli no longer visiblePrimary granules diminish and secondary (specific) granules appear, defining the neutrophil, eosinophil or basophil lineYes (the last dividing stage)
    Metamyelocyte (juvenile)Indented, kidney-shaped
    Chromatin clumped    		Abundant, pink-tan, full complement of specific granulesNo
    Band (stab) formElongated horseshoe- or band-shaped, uniform thickness, no segmentationAs in mature cellNo
    Segmented granulocyteTwo to five lobes joined by thin filamentsPale pink with fine specific granules (neutrophil)
    Bright red-orange granules and bilobed nucleus (eosinophil)
    Coarse blue-black granules obscuring the nucleus (basophil)    		No

    Normally only band and segmented forms are seen in the peripheral blood
    The appearance of metamyelocytes, myelocytes or blasts is a "left shift" and indicates either a reactive state (infection, inflammation), marrow infiltration, or a myeloid neoplasm.

    Leukocytosis and leukopenia

    Define neutrophilia.

    DU26M

    Neutrophilia (neutrophilic leukocytosis) is an increase in the absolute number of circulating neutrophils above the upper limit of the laboratory reference range for age. The adult range tabulated in Robbins is 1.4 to 6.5 × 10³/µL, and many laboratories regard an absolute neutrophil count above about 7.5 × 10³/µL as neutrophilia. It is the commonest form of leukocytosis and is usually a reaction to infection or inflammation, although it may also be physiologic, drug-induced or neoplastic.

    The peripheral neutrophil count reflects the balance among the size of the marrow precursor and storage pools, the rate of release from the marrow, the proportion of cells adherent to vessel walls (the marginal pool), and the rate of extravasation into tissues. Neutrophilia therefore arises by one or more of the following mechanisms:

    1. Increased release from marrow stores, as in acute infection and acute inflammation, mediated by TNF and IL-1 and appearing within hours.
    2. Increased marrow production, in which prolonged infection or inflammation stimulates macrophages, stromal cells and T cells to elaborate colony-stimulating factors, notably G-CSF, which expand committed granulocytic progenitors over several days. This growth factor–dependent pattern also occurs as a paraneoplastic phenomenon, for example in Hodgkin lymphoma. In myeloproliferative neoplasms such as chronic myeloid leukaemia, production is growth factor–independent.
    3. Demargination, in which cells shift from the marginal to the circulating pool under the influence of catecholamines, exercise or glucocorticoids, producing a rapid, transient rise without any increase in total body neutrophils.

    In sepsis and severe inflammatory states, reactive neutrophilia is often accompanied by a left shift and by toxic granulation (coarse, dark abnormal primary granules), Döhle bodies (sky-blue patches of dilated endoplasmic reticulum) and cytoplasmic vacuolation.

    Name four important causes of neutrophilic leukocytosis.

    DU26M

    Neutrophilic leukocytosis has several important causes, of which the most significant is infection. Four principal causes are as follows.

    1. Acute bacterial infections, especially those caused by pyogenic organisms such as staphylococci, streptococci and pneumococci. Cytokines such as TNF and IL-1 trigger the release of mature neutrophils from the marrow storage pool, and sustained infection drives increased production through colony-stimulating factors.
    2. Sterile inflammation and tissue necrosis, for example myocardial infarction, burns, trauma, surgery and gout, in which necrotic tissue evokes an acute inflammatory response and the same cytokine-mediated release of neutrophils.
    3. Physiologic and stress states and drugs, including strenuous exercise, emotional stress, pregnancy and labour, and the newborn period (through demargination and increased release), and drugs such as glucocorticoids, lithium and G-CSF, which mobilise neutrophils from the marginal pool and marrow and impair their egress into tissues.
    4. Neoplastic and paraneoplastic causes, namely myeloproliferative neoplasms, particularly chronic myeloid leukaemia, in which production is autonomous and growth factor–independent, and tumours such as Hodgkin lymphoma and some carcinomas that elaborate G-CSF.

    Other recognised causes include metabolic derangements (diabetic ketoacidosis, uraemia), acute haemorrhage or haemolysis, and splenectomy or hyposplenism.

    Write a short note on eosinophilia.

    DU10JaDU06Ja

    Definition. Eosinophilia is an increase in the absolute eosinophil count above the upper reference limit, which in adults is about 0.5 × 10³/µL (500/µL). It is graded as mild (0.5–1.5 × 10³/µL), moderate (1.5–5 × 10³/µL) and severe (more than 5 × 10³/µL). A persistent count above 1.5 × 10³/µL with tissue damage is called hypereosinophilic syndrome.

    Pathogenesis. Eosinophil production is driven principally by IL-5, produced by Th2 cells, with contributions from IL-3 and GM-CSF. Eosinophilia therefore characteristically accompanies Th2-type immune responses, as in allergy and helminthic infection. Mature eosinophils have bilobed nuclei and bright red-orange cytoplasmic granules containing major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein, eosinophil peroxidase and eosinophil-derived neurotoxin. These products kill helminths but also injure host tissue when eosinophils are present in excess or activated chronically.

    Causes

    CategoryExamples
    Allergic disordersBronchial asthma, hay fever, atopic dermatitis, urticaria, drug hypersensitivity
    Parasitic infestationsTissue-invading helminths—ascariasis, hookworm, strongyloidiasis, filariasis, schistosomiasis, trichinosis, toxocariasis, hydatid disease
    Drug reactionsPenicillins, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, allopurinol, many others
    Autoimmune and skin disordersPemphigus, dermatitis herpetiformis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides
    MalignancyHodgkin lymphoma and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, T-cell lymphomas, chronic myeloid leukaemia, some carcinomas
    Pulmonary and otherLöffler syndrome, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, eosinophilic pneumonias
    Adrenal insufficiency
    Transient eosinophilia in atheroembolic disease
    Primary (clonal)Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia and myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene rearrangements (e.g., FIP1L1::PDGFRA), which respond to imatinib

    Clinical significance. Mild eosinophilia is usually harmless, but sustained marked eosinophilia may cause endomyocardial fibrosis with restrictive cardiomyopathy and thrombosis, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy and skin lesions. The cause is determined by history (allergy, drugs, travel), stool examination for ova and parasites, and, where indicated, marrow examination and molecular testing for PDGFRA rearrangement.

    Leukocyte disorders and leukaemoid reaction

    A8

    What do you mean by leucocytosis?

    A8Q2

    Leucocytosis is an increase in the total number of circulating white blood cells above the upper limit of the reference range, which in adults is about 10,800 per µL.

    It is one of the commonest reactions to inflammatory states and is usually a physiologic response of the marrow to a need for more effector cells. Because the total count is made up of several cell types, leukocytosis is further designated by the cell type that is increased: neutrophilia, eosinophilia, basophilia, monocytosis and lymphocytosis. These tend to occur in different clinical settings because different growth factors and cytokines are produced in response to different stimuli. For example, IL-5 mainly stimulates eosinophil production, whereas G-CSF induces neutrophilia.

    Leukocytosis may be reactive or neoplastic. Reactive leukocytosis results from infection, inflammation, tissue necrosis, drugs, stress or physiologic states, and is accompanied by a polyclonal increase of mature or maturing cells. Neoplastic leukocytosis results from clonal proliferation, as in the leukaemias and myeloproliferative neoplasms, and is characterised by growth factor–independent production of abnormal cells.

    Two situations may cause diagnostic difficulty: acute viral infections in children, in which reactive lymphocytes resemble neoplastic cells, and severe infections in which immature granulocytes mimic myeloid leukaemia (leukaemoid reaction). Special laboratory studies help to distinguish them.

    A8

    Causes of neutrophilia.

    A8Q2

    The commonest cause of neutrophilia is acute bacterial infection, but it also occurs in sterile inflammation and tissue necrosis, with drugs and physiologic stress, in metabolic disorders, and in myeloproliferative neoplasms.

    Neutrophilia may be classified by mechanism and cause.

    MechanismCauses
    Increased release from marrow stores and demargination (rapid, transient)Acute infections
    Acute inflammation
    Strenuous exercise, anxiety, seizures, labour (catecholamine effect)
    Glucocorticoids, adrenaline
    Increased marrow production, growth factor–dependent (sustained)Chronic infection and inflammation (tuberculosis, chronic abscess, osteomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis)
    Paraneoplastic production of G-CSF (Hodgkin lymphoma, carcinomas)
    Increased marrow production, growth factor–independentMyeloproliferative neoplasms, especially chronic myeloid leukaemia, polycythaemia vera, primary myelofibrosis
    OtherAcute haemorrhage and haemolysis
    Tissue necrosis (myocardial infarction, burns, crush injury, surgery, pancreatitis)
    Metabolic (diabetic ketoacidosis, uraemia, gout, eclampsia)
    Drugs (corticosteroids, lithium, G-CSF/GM-CSF)
    post-splenectomy
    Down syndrome and leukocyte adhesion deficiency (impaired extravasation)

    Among infections, pyogenic bacteria (staphylococci, streptococci, pneumococci, gram-negative organisms) are the most important, while viral infections, typhoid, brucellosis, and many protozoal and rickettsial infections typically cause neutropenia or lymphocytosis rather than neutrophilia. In severe sepsis neutropenia may paradoxically occur because of overwhelming consumption.

    A8

    Causes of eosinophilia.

    A8Q3

    The commonest causes of eosinophilia are allergic disorders such as asthma and hay fever, and parasitic infestations. Other causes are drug reactions, certain malignancies like Hodgkin lymphoma, autoimmune disorders, and primary eosinophilic neoplasms.

    Eosinophilia reflects increased IL-5–driven production and is conveniently classified into reactive (secondary) and clonal (primary) forms.

    Reactive eosinophilia

    • Allergic disorders: bronchial asthma, hay fever, atopic dermatitis, urticaria, drug hypersensitivity (penicillins, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, allopurinol).
    • Parasitic infestations, especially those with a tissue-invasive phase: ascariasis, ancylostomiasis, strongyloidiasis, filariasis (including tropical pulmonary eosinophilia), schistosomiasis, trichinosis, toxocariasis, hydatid disease. Protozoal gut infections such as giardiasis do not typically produce eosinophilia.
    • Malignancy: Hodgkin lymphoma and some non-Hodgkin lymphomas, T-cell lymphomas, and some solid tumours (paraneoplastic).
    • Autoimmune and skin disorders: pemphigus, dermatitis herpetiformis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides.
    • Pulmonary and other conditions: Löffler syndrome, eosinophilic pneumonia, adrenal insufficiency, atheroembolic disease (transient), inflammatory bowel disease.

    Clonal (primary) eosinophilia: chronic myeloid leukaemia, chronic eosinophilic leukaemia and myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine kinase gene fusions (e.g., FIP1L1::PDGFRA).

    A8

    What is Loeffler syndrome?

    A8Q3

    Löffler syndrome is a transient, self-limited pulmonary eosinophilic infiltration—simple pulmonary eosinophilia—with peripheral blood eosinophilia, caused most commonly by the lung phase of larval migration of Ascaris lumbricoides.

    After ingestion of ascaris eggs, the larvae hatch in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa, travel through the portal and systemic circulation to the lungs, break into the alveoli, and ascend the bronchial tree to be swallowed and mature in the gut. During the pulmonary passage, 1 to 2 weeks after infection, the host mounts a hypersensitivity (Th2, IL-5–mediated) response, producing an eosinophil-rich alveolar infiltrate. Similar syndromes occur with hookworm (Ancylostoma, Necator) and Strongyloides larvae, and with some drugs (nitrofurantoin, sulfonamides, penicillins, methotrexate).

    The patient has dry cough, wheeze, breathlessness, low-grade fever and sometimes substernal discomfort and blood-tinged sputum. The chest radiograph shows transient, patchy, migratory, non-segmental infiltrates, and the blood count shows marked eosinophilia, often 10–30% of leukocytes or more. The syndrome resolves spontaneously within about 3 to 4 weeks, and treatment is supportive, with an anthelmintic for the parasite and corticosteroids if symptoms are severe.

    A8

    Define lymphocytosis.

    A8Q4DU07Ja

    Also asked as: What do you mean by lymphocytosis?

    Lymphocytosis is an increase in the absolute lymphocyte count above the upper limit of the reference range for age—in adults, more than about 4,000 per µL (4 × 10³/µL).

    The reference range for lymphocytes in the adult is 1.2 to 3.4 × 10³/µL, and a sustained count above about 4 × 10³/µL is regarded as lymphocytosis. Children normally have higher values, so the cut-off varies with age: lymphocytes are the predominant leukocyte in infancy and early childhood, and counts of up to 9–10 × 10³/µL may be normal in young infants. It is essential to evaluate the absolute rather than the relative count: a relative lymphocytosis (an increased percentage of lymphocytes) can occur simply because of neutropenia, whereas absolute lymphocytosis implies a true increase in lymphocyte numbers.

    Lymphocytosis may be reactive (polyclonal) or neoplastic (monoclonal). Reactive lymphocytosis is seen in many disorders associated with chronic immunologic stimulation and in some acute infections, particularly viral infections in children, in which large, atypical, activated lymphocytes (Downey cells, "reactive" or "atypical" lymphocytes) may mimic neoplastic cells. Neoplastic lymphocytosis occurs in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, in which the diagnostic requirement is an absolute lymphocyte count of more than 5,000 per µL of monoclonal B cells, and in other lymphoid leukaemias and leukaemic phases of lymphoma. Immunophenotyping and demonstration of clonality distinguish the two.

    A8

    What are the causes of lymphocytosis?

    A8Q4DU07Ja

    Also asked as: Causes of lymphocytosis.

    Lymphocytosis is caused by viral infections such as infectious mononucleosis, by certain bacterial infections like pertussis and tuberculosis, by chronic immunologic stimulation, and by lymphoid neoplasms, chiefly chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.

    Reactive (polyclonal) lymphocytosis

    • Acute viral infections: infectious mononucleosis (EBV), cytomegalovirus, viral hepatitis (especially hepatitis A), mumps, measles, rubella, varicella, adenovirus, and acute HIV seroconversion. In these the lymphocytes are atypical, activated T cells.
    • Bacterial and other infections: pertussis (Bordetella pertussis), in which pertussis toxin ("lymphocytosis-promoting factor") prevents lymphocytes from leaving the blood and may produce counts of 20–50 × 10³/µL with a mature-looking picture. Tuberculosis, brucellosis, secondary syphilis, typhoid fever, toxoplasmosis.
    • Chronic immunologic stimulation: tuberculosis, brucellosis and other chronic infections often cause lymphocytosis accompanied by monocytosis.
    • Endocrine and other: thyrotoxicosis, Addison disease, stress or post-splenectomy states. Persistent polyclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (young women who smoke). Drug hypersensitivity.

    Neoplastic (clonal) lymphocytosis

    • Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, the most common cause in older adults
      Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (precursor state).
    • Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
    • Leukaemic phase of non-Hodgkin lymphomas (mantle cell, follicular, marginal zone lymphomas), hairy cell leukaemia, prolymphocytic leukaemia, adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma, large granular lymphocytic leukaemia, Sézary syndrome.

    The distinction between reactive and neoplastic lymphocytosis rests on morphology (heterogeneous polymorphic cells versus a monotonous population), clinical context, and immunophenotyping and antigen receptor gene studies that demonstrate clonality.

    A8

    Write a short note on leukopenia.

    A8Q5DU07Ju

    Also asked as: What is leucopenia?

    Leukopenia is a reduction in the total circulating white cell count below the lower reference limit, in adults about 4,000 per µL. it is usually due to neutropenia, and lymphopenia is the next most common cause.

    Definition and types. Leukopenia is a decrease in the number of circulating white cells. A low count most commonly results from reduced numbers of neutrophils (neutropenia, granulocytopenia). Lymphopenia is less common, and monocytopenia, eosinopenia and basopenia are of little clinical consequence.

    Causes

    • Neutropenia: inadequate or ineffective granulopoiesis, or increased destruction or sequestration of neutrophils.
    • Lymphopenia: congenital immunodeficiency diseases
      Advanced HIV infection
      Therapy with glucocorticoids or cytotoxic drugs
      Autoimmune disorders such as lupus
      Malnutrition
      Radiation
      and certain acute viral infections. In the last setting the lymphopenia reflects redistribution rather than a true loss of cells: type I interferons activate T lymphocytes and alter their surface adhesion and homing molecules so that they are sequestered in lymph nodes and adhere to endothelium.
    • Pancytopenic states such as aplastic anaemia, marrow infiltration, megaloblastic anaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, hypersplenism and overwhelming sepsis.

    Clinical consequences. The clinical significance depends on the type of cell lost. Granulocytopenia is associated with diminished granulocyte function and susceptibility to bacterial and fungal infection, while lymphopenia produces defects of cell-mediated immunity and opportunistic infection. The patient presents with recurrent fever, malaise, oral ulceration and infections.

    Investigation. A full blood count with differential and smear, reticulocyte count, bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, a drug history, and where appropriate antinuclear and anti-neutrophil antibodies, vitamin B₁₂ and folate levels, and viral serology are required to find the cause.

    A8

    Write a short note on neutropenia.

    A8Q5DU09Ja

    Also asked as: What is neutropenia?

    Neutropenia is a reduction in the absolute neutrophil count in the blood below about 1,500 per µL. it carries a risk of serious bacterial and fungal infection, which rises steeply when the count falls below 500 per µL.

    Definition. Neutropenia is a reduction in the number of circulating neutrophils. It is graded as mild (1.0–1.5 × 10³/µL), moderate (0.5–1.0 × 10³/µL) and severe (below 0.5 × 10³/µL). Agranulocytosis denotes a marked reduction, usually to fewer than 100 per µL, and is a serious, often life-threatening condition.

    Pathogenesis. Neutropenia arises by two broad mechanisms.

    1. Inadequate or ineffective granulopoiesis, resulting from suppression of the HSC (aplastic anaemia, infiltrative marrow disorders such as tumours and granulomatous disease, in which anaemia and thrombocytopenia accompany the neutropenia). Suppression of committed granulocytic precursors by drugs. Disorders of ineffective haematopoiesis in which defective precursors die within the marrow (megaloblastic anaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms). and rare congenital conditions such as severe congenital neutropenia (Kostmann syndrome).
    2. Accelerated destruction or sequestration, due to immune-mediated injury (idiopathic, associated with a defined autoimmune disorder such as systemic lupus erythematosus, or drug-induced). Splenomegaly with sequestration and destruction by increased numbers of macrophages. and increased peripheral utilisation in overwhelming bacterial, fungal or rickettsial infection. Severe neutropenia is also seen with monoclonal proliferation of large granular lymphocytes (LGL leukaemia).

    Drug toxicity is the most common cause of agranulocytosis. Alkylating agents and antimetabolites cause predictable, dose-related marrow suppression that affects all lineages. Idiosyncratic agranulocytosis is seen with many drugs, including certain antibiotics, anticonvulsants, anti-inflammatory drugs, antipsychotic drugs and diuretics. Phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine exert a direct toxic effect on granulocytic precursors, whereas sulfonamides probably act by antibody-mediated destruction of neutrophils.

    Morphology. The marrow is usually hypercellular when the neutropenia results from excessive peripheral destruction or ineffective granulopoiesis, because of compensatory expansion of granulocytic precursors, but is hypocellular when agranulocytosis is caused by agents that suppress or destroy precursors. Infections produce characteristic necrotising, ulcerative lesions of the gingiva, floor of the mouth, buccal mucosa and pharynx, which are deep, undermined and covered by gray to green-black necrotic membranes harboring numerous organisms with little leukocytic response. Similar ulcers may occur in the skin, vagina, anus and gut, and severe invasive infections occur in the lungs, urinary tract and kidneys, with a particular risk of Candida and Aspergillus.

    Clinical features and treatment. The signs and symptoms stem from infection: malaise, chills and fever, followed by marked weakness and fatigability, and in agranulocytosis overwhelming infection may cause death within hours to days. Serious infections are most likely when the neutrophil count falls below 500/µL. Broad-spectrum antibiotics must be given expeditiously whenever signs or symptoms appear, offending drugs are withdrawn, and G-CSF is used in some patients, for example after myelosuppressive chemotherapy.

    A8

    What is agranulocytosis?

    A8Q5

    Agranulocytosis is a marked reduction in the number of circulating neutrophils, usually to fewer than 100 per µL (clinically, below 500 per µL), which makes the individual highly susceptible to overwhelming bacterial and fungal infection.

    Agranulocytosis is the extreme end of neutropenia. It results either from failure of production by the marrow or from accelerated destruction, and the most common cause is drug toxicity. Cytotoxic drugs (alkylating agents, antimetabolites) produce it in a predictable, dose-related manner, with concurrent suppression of red cell and platelet production, whereas idiosyncratic agranulocytosis may follow exposure to antithyroid drugs, sulfonamides, phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine, anticonvulsants, anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics and diuretics. Some drugs act by direct toxicity to marrow precursors and others by antibody-mediated destruction of neutrophils.

    The marrow is hypocellular when precursors are suppressed or destroyed, with few cells beyond the myeloblast and promyelocyte stage ("maturation arrest").

    The patient develops sudden fever, chills, severe sore throat and prostration. Necrotising, ulcerative lesions of the gingiva, floor of the mouth, buccal mucosa and pharynx (agranulocytic angina) are characteristic, with little pus because no neutrophils are available to mount an exudate. Deep invasive infections of the lungs, urinary tract and kidneys, and fungal infections with Candida and Aspergillus may follow.

    Infections are often fulminant and may kill within hours to days. Management consists of immediate withdrawal of the offending drug, urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics, antifungal cover when appropriate, and G-CSF.

    A8

    Define leukaemoid reaction / write a short note (incl. blood picture).

    13A8Q13DU25NDU25MDU23NDU22MDU16JuDU13JaDU12JaDU11JaDU09JuDU09JaDU08JaDU06Ja

    Also asked as: What is leukaemoid reaction?

    A leukaemoid reaction is a reactive, non-neoplastic leukocytosis—usually above 50,000 per µL—with a shift to the left and the appearance of immature cells in the peripheral blood, so that it mimics leukaemia, but it is caused by an underlying disorder such as severe infection and regresses when the cause is removed.

    Definition. The leukaemoid reaction is a marked, exaggerated reactive leukocytosis in which many immature white cells appear in the peripheral blood, mimicking a leukaemia, particularly myeloid leukaemia. It is a physiologic over-response of the marrow, driven by cytokines and colony-stimulating factors, to a severe stimulus. The white cell count commonly exceeds 50,000 per µL, although some authorities accept a lower threshold of about 30,000 per µL. By definition the cells are polyclonal and not neoplastic, and the leukocytosis subsides after the cause is treated.

    Causes. The reaction may involve any cell line. Neutrophilic (myeloid) leukaemoid reaction is the commonest and occurs in severe pyogenic infections (pneumonia, sepsis, abscess, meningitis, diphtheria), tuberculosis, severe haemorrhage and haemolysis, extensive burns, tissue necrosis, drug or chemical poisoning (mercury, ethylene glycol), and rarely carcinomas that secrete growth factors. Lymphocytic reactions occur in pertussis, infectious mononucleosis and tuberculosis, and eosinophilic reactions in Hodgkin lymphoma, parasitic infestations and drug reactions.

    Pathogenesis. In acute infection or severe inflammation, TNF and IL-1 promote a rapid egress of mature and immature granulocytes from the marrow storage pool. If the stimulus persists, these cytokines and others induce macrophages, stromal cells and T cells to produce haematopoietic growth factors, notably G-CSF and GM-CSF, which enhance proliferation and differentiation of committed granulocytic progenitors and sustain increased neutrophil production over days.

    Blood picture (neutrophilic leukaemoid reaction)

    • A marked leukocytosis, generally 50,000 to 100,000 per µL or more, with absolute neutrophilia.
    • A left shift that extends back to metamyelocytes and myelocytes, with occasional promyelocytes, but with an orderly gradation of maturation and blasts few or absent (usually below 5%)
      There is no leukaemic "hiatus".
    • Toxic changes in the neutrophils: toxic granulation (coarse dark primary granules), Döhle bodies, and cytoplasmic vacuolation.
    • Absolute basophilia and eosinophilia are not seen, in contrast to chronic myeloid leukaemia.
    • The red cells and platelets are normal or only modestly altered
      Marked anaemia and thrombocytopenia are not features, and any anaemia is of the underlying disorder.
    • The leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is high, reflecting activated, mature neutrophils.
    • The Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene are absent.

    Bone marrow. Granulocytic hyperplasia with a left shift and toxic granulation. The proportion of blasts and promyelocytes is not significantly increased, and there is no dysplasia or abnormal clone.

    Course. The reaction is transient and resolves when the underlying disease is controlled, and the prognosis depends on that disease. Clinical correlation, a careful search for an infective or inflammatory focus, and cytogenetic or molecular testing for BCR::ABL1 serve to distinguish it from leukaemia.

    A8

    What is subleukaemic leukaemia?

    A8Q13

    Subleukaemic leukaemia is a leukaemia in which the total white cell count is normal or only modestly raised, and few or no blasts are seen in the peripheral blood, although the bone marrow is heavily infiltrated by leukaemic cells.

    The terms leukaemic, subleukaemic and aleukaemic describe the peripheral blood findings in leukaemia. In the leukaemic form the white cell count is high and blasts are abundant in the blood. In subleukaemic leukaemia the leukocyte count is normal or only slightly increased and blasts are scanty. In aleukaemic leukaemia the count is low, with pancytopenia and no blasts in the blood.

    As Robbins notes, the number of leukaemic cells in the blood in acute myeloid leukaemia is highly variable. Blasts may exceed 100,000 per µL, but are below 10,000 per µL in about half of patients, and occasionally blasts are entirely absent from the blood (aleukaemic leukaemia). For this reason a bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukaemia in a pancytopenic patient.

    The significance of the subleukaemic and aleukaemic states is diagnostic. Because the peripheral smear may look unimpressive, with only anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, the condition is liable to be mistaken for aplastic anaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasm, megaloblastic anaemia, hypersplenism or infection. The diagnosis is established by a marrow aspirate and biopsy showing replacement by blasts (20% or more, or a defining genetic abnormality), with cytochemistry, immunophenotyping and cytogenetics.

    Subleukaemic leukaemia is usually acute, though it is also seen in some chronic leukaemias such as hairy cell leukaemia, which characteristically presents with pancytopenia and splenomegaly. The prognosis is determined by the type of leukaemia and not by the peripheral count.

    Write a short note on leukoerythroblastic blood picture.

    A8Q18DU19MDU12Ju

    Also asked as: What is a leukoerythroblastic blood picture?

    A leukoerythroblastic blood picture is the presence in the peripheral blood of immature granulocytic precursors together with nucleated red blood cells, usually with teardrop-shaped red cells, indicating that the marrow has been disturbed or infiltrated so that immature cells are released prematurely.

    Definition. Leukoerythroblastosis is a peripheral blood picture in which nucleated red cell precursors (normoblasts) and early granulocytic precursors (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and sometimes promyelocytes and a few blasts) appear together. In Robbins' account, processes that distort the marrow architecture, such as deposits of metastatic cancer or granulomatous disorders, cause the abnormal release of immature precursors into the peripheral blood.

    The marrow normally keeps these cells in the haematopoietic compartment, and it is thought that destruction of the sinusoidal and stromal organisation by infiltration or fibrosis allows premature egress. Extramedullary haematopoietic sites in the spleen and liver contribute immature cells as well.

    Blood picture. Anaemia, usually normocytic normochromic, with anisopoikilocytosis and teardrop cells (dacryocytes)
    Nucleated red cells
    a left shift with myelocytes and metamyelocytes
    The white cell count may be normal, low or raised. The platelet count may be normal, increased or reduced, with giant platelets. Teardrop cells are probably damaged during their passage from the fibrotic marrow.

    Causes. The most important are marrow infiltration by metastatic carcinoma and lymphoma or leukaemia, primary and secondary myelofibrosis, granulomatous disease (miliary tuberculosis), lipid storage disorders, and severe haemolysis and haemorrhage in which the marrow is stressed.

    Diagnostic importance. The finding demands a bone marrow trephine biopsy, because the marrow often cannot be aspirated ("dry tap") when fibrosis or infiltration is present, and because the biopsy shows the architectural change. The finding is characteristic of primary myelofibrosis, but it is not specific, being seen in other infiltrative disorders.

    Lymph Node Disorders

    A8

    What do you mean by lymphadenopathy?

    A8Q36

    Lymphadenopathy means enlargement of lymph nodes, whether localised to one region or generalised, produced by reactive hyperplasia, infection, infiltration by neoplastic cells, or accumulation of storage material.

    Lymph nodes are discrete encapsulated structures with separate B-cell zones (follicles) and T-cell zones (paracortex), richly invested with phagocytes and antigen-presenting cells. After antigenic stimulation the primary follicles enlarge and develop pale-staining germinal centres, and the paracortical T-cell zones may undergo hyperplasia. Consequently, adult lymph nodes are almost never truly "resting," and one must distinguish changes due to past exposure from those of present disease. A node is generally regarded as abnormally enlarged when it exceeds about 1 cm in diameter.

    The causes of nodal enlargement fall into four mechanistic groups: (1) reactive hyperplasia of lymphoid elements in response to antigen (follicular, paracortical or sinus patterns). (2) lymphadenitis, with infiltration by neutrophils or granulomatous inflammation in infections. (3) neoplastic infiltration, by primary lymphoid neoplasms (lymphomas, leukaemias) or by metastatic carcinoma and other cancers. and (4) storage diseases and histiocytic proliferations.

    Lymphadenopathy is localised when it involves a single region draining an area of infection or tumour, and generalised when it involves two or more noncontiguous regions, which suggests a systemic disorder. Features that favour malignancy are a hard, painless, non-tender, matted or fixed node, progressive enlargement, supraclavicular location, and size above 2 cm
    Tender, soft, mobile nodes with overlying warmth usually indicate acute inflammation.

    A8

    Common causes of lymphadenopathy.

    A8Q36

    Common causes of lymphadenopathy are infections, which are the most frequent, followed by reactive and immunologic disorders, lymphoid and other neoplasms, and drug reactions.

    Infections. Acute and chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis arising from local bacterial infection (in the neck from the teeth, tonsils and throat; in the axilla and groin from the extremities; in the mesentery from appendicitis and other gut inflammation). Viral infections (infectious mononucleosis, cytomegalovirus, HIV, rubella, measles, adenovirus), particularly in children; tuberculosis; syphilis; brucellosis; cat-scratch disease; toxoplasmosis; fungal infections.

    Immunologic and inflammatory disorders. Rheumatoid arthritis (follicular hyperplasia), systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, serum sickness and drug reactions (phenytoin, allopurinol).

    Neoplasms. Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas
    Acute and chronic lymphoid leukaemias
    Metastatic carcinoma and melanoma (nodes draining the primary cancer, e.g., axillary nodes in breast cancer, in which sinus histiocytosis may also be prominent). Histiocytic neoplasms.

    Others. Lipid storage disorders, amyloidosis, hyperthyroidism, Castleman disease and dermatopathic lymphadenopathy.

    The pattern of involvement is a useful clue: regional nodes enlarged by the infection or tumour in their drainage field. Generalised enlargement in systemic infection, lymphoma, leukaemia or autoimmune disease.

    A8

    Common causes of lymphadenitis.

    A8Q38

    Lymphadenitis is inflammation of lymph nodes and is classified as acute nonspecific, chronic nonspecific, and specific (granulomatous or distinctive) lymphadenitis according to the cause and the histologic pattern.

    Acute nonspecific lymphadenitis results from microbes or their products draining into the node. In the cervical region the source is most often infection of the teeth or tonsils
    in the axillary and inguinal regions, infections of the extremities. Mesenteric lymphadenitis occurs in acute appendicitis, in self-limiting viral infections, and with Yersinia and other enteric pathogens. Systemic viral infections (especially in children) and bacteraemia may produce generalised acute lymphadenopathy. Pyogenic organisms such as staphylococci and streptococci are the usual agents.

    Chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis results from a wide variety of chronic immunologic stimuli. It manifests as follicular hyperplasia (humoral immune responses: rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis, early HIV infection), paracortical hyperplasia (T-cell responses: viral infections such as infectious mononucleosis, vaccinations, drug reactions such as phenytoin), and sinus histiocytosis (reactive response in nodes draining cancers, e.g., carcinoma of the breast). It is particularly common in inguinal and axillary nodes.

    Specific lymphadenitis has a distinctive morphology:

    • Granulomatous: tuberculosis (caseating granulomas), sarcoidosis (non-caseating), leprosy, fungal infections (histoplasmosis), brucellosis, tularaemia.
    • Necrotising and suppurative with stellate abscesses: cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae), lymphogranuloma venereum.
    • Others: toxoplasmic lymphadenitis (epithelioid histiocytes in clusters near germinal centres with monocytoid B-cell hyperplasia), infectious mononucleosis, syphilis (plasma cell-rich with endarteritis), Kikuchi–Fujimoto necrotising lymphadenitis, filarial lymphadenitis, and kala-azar.
    A8

    Morphological features of chronic non-specific lymphadenitis / reactive hyperplasia.

    A8Q40

    Chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis shows one or more patterns within the same node—follicular hyperplasia, paracortical hyperplasia and sinus histiocytosis—and the nodes are enlarged but usually painless.

    A wide variety of chronic immunologic stimuli produce chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis, and several different patterns of change are seen, often in the same node.

    Follicular hyperplasia. It is caused by stimuli that activate humoral immune responses (rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis, early HIV infection). The node architecture is preserved and the cortex shows large, oblong secondary follicles with germinal centres, which are surrounded by a collar of small resting naive B cells, the mantle zone. Germinal centres are polarised into a dark zone of proliferating blast-like B cells (centroblasts) and a light zone of cells with cleaved nuclear contours (centrocytes).

    Scattered among them is an inconspicuous network of follicular dendritic cells and tingible-body macrophages containing nuclear debris of apoptotic B cells that failed to produce high-affinity antibody. Mitotic figures are frequent.

    Paracortical hyperplasia. It is caused by stimuli that trigger T-cell–mediated responses, such as acute viral infections (infectious mononucleosis). The T-cell zones are expanded and contain immunoblasts—activated T cells three to four times the size of resting lymphocytes with round nuclei, open chromatin, prominent nucleoli and pale cytoplasm. In exuberant reactions the expanded zones encroach on, or efface, the follicles, and special studies may be needed to exclude lymphoma. Hypertrophy of the sinusoidal and vascular endothelium, with infiltrating macrophages and eosinophils, is common.

    Sinus histiocytosis (reticular hyperplasia). There is an increase in the number and size of the endothelial cells lining the lymphatic sinuses and an increase in intrasinusoidal macrophages, which distend and distort the sinuses. it is particularly prominent in nodes draining cancers such as carcinoma of the breast.

    Features favouring a reactive over a neoplastic follicular proliferation: preservation of nodal architecture, including the interfollicular T-cell zones and the sinusoids. Marked variation in the size and shape of the follicles. and frequent mitoses, phagocytic macrophages and recognizable light and dark zones—all of which are usually absent from neoplastic follicles of follicular lymphoma.

    Clinical behaviour. Because enlargement occurs slowly and acute inflammatory tissue damage is absent, nodes in chronic reactions are typically non-tender. Chronic lymphadenitis is common in the inguinal and axillary nodes, which drain large areas that are frequently stimulated by trivial injuries and infections of the extremities.

    DU05M

    The cervical lymph nodes drain the scalp, face, oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, thyroid, and by way of the supraclavicular nodes the thorax and abdomen, so cervical lymphadenopathy is the commonest site of nodal enlargement. The causes may be classified as follows.

    • Chronic nonspecific lymphadenitis due to recurrent tonsillitis and dental infection, and reactive hyperplasia.

      Toxoplasmosis
      Syphilis
      actinomycosis.

    Leukaemias

    Leukaemia: definition and classification

    What is the etiology of leukaemia?

    DU24MDU22N

    Leukaemia, like all cancers, arises from acquired genetic alterations in haematopoietic progenitors that provide a growth or survival advantage and block normal differentiation. In most patients no single cause is identifiable, and leukaemia results from the interaction of inherited susceptibility, acquired driver mutations and environmental exposures.

    1. Acquired genetic alterations (the proximate cause). Nonrandom chromosomal abnormalities, most commonly translocations, are present in most leukaemias, and the genes involved usually play critical roles in the development, growth or survival of the normal counterpart cell. They act through four principal mechanisms: oncoproteins that block differentiation (e.g., RUNX1::RUNX1T1 from t(8;21), PML::RARA from t(15;17), ETV6::RUNX1 from t(12;21), NOTCH1 mutations in T-ALL), mutations that activate tyrosine kinases and progrowth signalling (BCR::ABL1, FLT3, JAK2, RAS), mutations in epigenetic regulators (IDH1/2, TET2, DNMT3A), and mutations that inhibit apoptosis or abrogate p53 function (BCL2, TP53). Leukaemias are usually the result of collaboration between a mutation that blocks differentiation and one that promotes growth.

    2. Inherited and constitutional factors. Genetic disorders that promote genomic instability—Bloom syndrome, Fanconi anaemia and ataxia telangiectasia—carry an increased risk of acute leukaemia. Down syndrome (trisomy 21), type I neurofibromatosis, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome and some immunodeficiency states are also associated with increased incidence, especially in childhood. The risk is higher in monozygotic twins of an affected child.

    3. Ionising radiation and chemicals. Atomic bomb survivors, radiologists exposed in the past, and patients treated with therapeutic radiation have increased rates of acute and chronic myeloid leukaemia. Benzene exposure and tobacco smoking (tobacco smoke contains benzene and other carcinogens; the incidence of AML is increased 1.3- to 2-fold in smokers) predispose to AML. Other implicated agents include pesticides and organic solvents.

    4. Iatrogenic factors. Radiation therapy and chemotherapy used to treat cancer increase the risk of later myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms. Alkylating agents produce therapy-related AML or myelodysplasia after 3 to 8 years, often with monosomy or deletions of chromosomes 5 and 7 and TP53 mutations, whereas topoisomerase II inhibitors cause AML after 1 to 3 years, characteristically with KMT2A (11q23) translocations. Chloramphenicol and phenylbutazone have been implicated rarely.

    5. Viruses. Human T-cell leukaemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1) causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma. EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, a portion of Hodgkin lymphoma and lymphomas in the immunodeficient, and human herpesvirus 8 with primary effusion lymphoma.

    6. Preexisting haematologic disorders and clonal haematopoiesis. Myelodysplastic neoplasms, myeloproliferative neoplasms, aplastic anaemia and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria predispose to AML, and clonal haematopoiesis (mutations in TET2, DNMT3A) carries approximately a 1% yearly risk of a haematologic neoplasm.

    7. Chronic inflammation and immune dysfunction. Helicobacter pylori infection and gastric lymphoma, gluten-sensitive enteropathy and intestinal T-cell lymphoma, and HIV infection and B-cell lymphoma exemplify how chronic antigenic stimulation and immunodeficiency predispose to lymphoid neoplasia.

    Acute leukaemias

    A8

    Define leukaemia.

    8A8Q6DU26MDU25MDU22NDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU18M

    Leukaemia is a malignant clonal neoplasm of haematopoietic progenitor cells that arises in the bone marrow, replaces normal marrow elements, and usually spills into the peripheral blood, with infiltration of the spleen, liver, lymph nodes and other organs.

    Neoplasms that present with widespread involvement of the bone marrow, and usually but not always the peripheral blood, are called leukaemias, whereas proliferations of white cells that typically present as discrete tissue masses are called lymphomas. The distinction is a matter of the usual tissue distribution at presentation, and is not absolute: many lymphomas have leukaemic presentations or evolve to leukaemia, and some leukaemias arise as soft tissue masses (e.g., myeloid sarcoma) without detectable marrow disease.

    Leukaemias arise from transformation of a pluripotent stem cell or a more committed progenitor, which acquires mutations that block differentiation or confer growth factor–independent proliferation and enhanced self-renewal. The consequences are accumulation of abnormal cells in the marrow, with suppression of normal haematopoiesis causing anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, and infiltration of extramedullary sites.

    Leukaemias are classified according to (1) the clinical course and degree of maturation, as acute (immature blasts accumulate, abrupt onset, rapid course) or chronic (relatively mature cells, insidious onset, slower course), and (2) the cell lineage, as lymphoid (lymphoblastic or lymphocytic) or myeloid. This yields four principal types: acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) and chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). Further types are defined by cytogenetic, molecular and immunophenotypic criteria in the current WHO classification.

    A8

    Classify (acute) leukaemia.

    4A8Q6DU24NDU21MDU17Nov

    Also asked as: Classify leukaemia.

    Acute leukaemia is classified by the lineage of the blast cell into acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and acute myeloid leukaemia, each further subdivided by morphology (FAB) or by genetic and immunophenotypic features (WHO).

    Leukaemias in general are first divided into acute and chronic types and then by lineage, as shown below.

    Acute leukaemias are classified as follows

    A. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (WHO)

    • B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (about 85% of ALL
      Childhood peak at about 3 years): with recurrent genetic abnormalities (hyperdiploidy, hypodiploidy, t(9;22) BCR::ABL1, t(12;21) ETV6::RUNX1, KMT2A rearrangement, t(1;19), others) or not otherwise specified.
    • T-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (adolescent males, thymic mass; NOTCH1 mutation).
    • FAB subtypes (historical): L1 (small uniform blasts, childhood), L2 (larger, heterogeneous blasts, adults), L3 (Burkitt-like, vacuolated basophilic cytoplasm).

    B. Acute myeloid leukaemia

    • WHO classification: AML with defining genetic abnormalities, AML with myelodysplasia-related changes, and AML defined by differentiation.
    • FAB classification: M0 (minimally differentiated) to M7 (megakaryoblastic).

    C. Acute leukaemias of ambiguous lineage: mixed phenotype acute leukaemia and acute undifferentiated leukaemia, in which blasts co-express myeloid and lymphoid markers or lack lineage-specific markers.

    D. Based on origin: de novo versus secondary AML (following myelodysplasia, myeloproliferative neoplasms, or genotoxic therapy).

    The distinction between ALL and AML is of practical importance because the therapy and prognosis differ, and it rests on cytochemistry, immunophenotyping and cytogenetics, since myeloblasts and lymphoblasts cannot always be separated by morphology.

    A8

    Clinical presentation of acute leukaemia.

    A8Q7

    Acute leukaemia has an abrupt, stormy onset, within days to a few weeks, with features of bone marrow failure—anaemia, infection and bleeding—together with signs of infiltration of bone, lymph nodes, spleen, liver, CNS and other tissues.

    1. Features of marrow failure (due to replacement of normal haematopoiesis by blasts and suppression by cytokines).

    • Anaemia: pallor, fatigue, weakness, dyspnoea, palpitations.
    • Neutropenia: fever and recurrent infections of the mouth, throat, skin, lungs and urinary tract, often with opportunists such as Pseudomonas and fungi.
    • Thrombocytopenia: spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeding—petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, haematuria and, occasionally, intracranial haemorrhage. In acute promyelocytic leukaemia, procoagulants released from the leukaemic cells cause DIC, with severe bleeding.

    2. Features of infiltration (mass effects). These are more common in ALL: bone and joint pain from marrow expansion and subperiosteal infiltration, sternal tenderness, generalised lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, testicular enlargement, and, in T-ALL, a mediastinal mass causing vascular and airway compression. In AML with monocytic differentiation, infiltration of the gums (gingival hypertrophy) and skin (leukaemia cutis) occurs, and rarely a localised soft tissue mass (myeloid sarcoma or chloroma).

    3. Central nervous system involvement. Headache, vomiting, nerve palsies and papilloedema due to meningeal infiltration, more frequent in ALL.

    4. Metabolic and hyperleukocytic features. Hyperuricaemia and tumour lysis, and leukostasis (visual disturbance, dyspnoea, confusion) when the blast count is very high, especially in AML.

    5. Constitutional symptoms. Fever, weight loss, anorexia and night sweats.

    A8

    How will you diagnose a case of acute leukaemia in the laboratory?

    8A8Q9DU24MDU22NDU17MDU11JuDU10JaDU09JaDU07Ju

    Also asked as: Laboratory diagnosis of acute leukaemia.

    I would diagnose acute leukaemia by a complete blood count and peripheral smear showing blasts and cytopenias, confirm it by bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing 20% or more blasts, and then determine the lineage with cytochemistry, flow cytometric immunophenotyping, and cytogenetic and molecular studies.

    1. Complete blood count and peripheral smear. There is normocytic normochromic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia in most. The total white cell count is variable: raised in about half, but normal or low in the subleukaemic and aleukaemic forms. The smear usually shows circulating blasts with a gap between the blasts and the mature cells (hiatus leukaemicus). Auer rods favour AML. Reticulocytes are reduced.

    2. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy (essential). The marrow is hypercellular, with replacement of normal elements by blasts, which constitute 20% or more of nucleated cells (WHO), although a lower count is accepted when a defining genetic abnormality is present. Erythroid and megakaryocytic precursors are reduced. The biopsy confirms cellularity and any fibrosis, and a bone marrow examination is mandatory in pancytopenia to exclude aleukaemic leukaemia.

    3. Cytochemistry. Myeloperoxidase (MPO) and Sudan black B are positive in myeloblasts (and negative in lymphoblasts). Nonspecific esterase (inhibited by fluoride) is positive in monocytic cells. Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) shows coarse block positivity in lymphoblasts, and acid phosphatase is positive focally in T-ALL.

    4. Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry (definitive for lineage). Lymphoblasts express terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) with CD19, CD22, CD79a and often CD10 (B-ALL) or cytoplasmic CD3, CD7, CD2 and CD5 (T-ALL). Myeloblasts express CD13, CD33, CD34, CD117 and MPO. Monocytic blasts CD14 and CD64
    Megakaryoblasts CD41 and CD61
    Erythroblasts glycophorin.

    5. Cytogenetics and molecular studies. Karyotype, fluorescence in situ hybridisation and PCR or sequencing for BCR::ABL1, t(12;21), KMT2A rearrangements, hyperdiploidy and NOTCH1 in ALL. t(8;21), inv(16), t(15;17), FLT3, NPM1, IDH1/2, TP53 in AML. These define the WHO subtype and prognosis and monitor minimal residual disease.

    6. Supportive investigations. Serum uric acid, LDH, creatinine, electrolytes and calcium (tumour lysis). Coagulation profile (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) especially in suspected acute promyelocytic leukaemia. Liver function tests
    Chest radiograph (mediastinal mass in T-ALL)
    Cerebrospinal fluid cytology in ALL
    Infection screening, HLA typing when transplantation is contemplated.

    A8

    Laboratory diagnosis of AML.

    A8Q10

    The diagnosis of AML rests on finding 20% or more myeloid blasts in the marrow—or fewer if a defining genetic abnormality is present—confirmed by myeloperoxidase positivity or myeloid antigens on flow cytometry, and classified by cytogenetic and molecular studies.

    Peripheral blood. There is normocytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and often neutropenia. The leukocyte count is variable, being above 100,000 per µL in some patients and below 10,000 per µL in about half. Occasionally blasts are absent from the blood altogether (aleukaemic leukaemia). The smear shows myeloblasts with delicate chromatin, two to four nucleoli and fine azurophilic granules, and many show Auer rods—distinctive needle-like azurophilic granules—which are particularly numerous in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

    Bone marrow. A hypercellular marrow with 20% or more myeloblasts (monoblasts and promonocytes are counted as blast equivalents in monocytic leukaemias), suppressed normal erythropoiesis and megakaryopoiesis, and dysplastic changes in the residual cells in some cases. When the marrow cannot be aspirated, a trephine biopsy is performed (e.g., in megakaryoblastic leukaemia with fibrosis).

    Cytochemistry. Myeloperoxidase and Sudan black B positivity indicates myeloid lineage. Nonspecific esterase positivity (fluoride-sensitive) indicates monocytic differentiation. Periodic acid–Schiff reaction in erythroid precursors.

    Immunophenotyping. Flow cytometry shows CD34, CD117, CD13, CD33, HLA-DR and MPO
    The subtype is shown by CD14 and CD64 (monocytic), CD41/CD61 (megakaryocytic) and glycophorin A (erythroid). Blasts in the example in Robbins express CD34 but not CD64, the latter being a marker of mature myeloid cells. APL is typically HLA-DR and CD34 negative.

    Cytogenetics and molecular genetics. These assign the WHO subtype and risk group. Chromosomal abnormalities are detected in 50% to 70% of cases by standard karyotyping, and in about 90% with high-resolution methods. Detection of t(15;17) by FISH or PCR for PML::RARA is an emergency test in a suspected APL. Sequencing for NPM1, FLT3, IDH1/2, TP53, CEBPA and others is routine.

    Other tests. Coagulation profile for DIC
    Uric acid, LDH, and electrolytes
    Renal and hepatic function
    Cerebrospinal fluid in selected cases
    HLA typing for transplant.

    A8

    Why is infection common in acute leukaemia?

    A8Q15

    Infection is common in acute leukaemia because replacement of the marrow by blasts causes profound neutropenia, the leukaemic cells and the therapy impair the function of the remaining immune cells, and the patient's mucosal and skin barriers are compromised.

    1. Neutropenia. The proliferating blasts replace and suppress normal granulocytic progenitors, so the absolute neutrophil count is low, and the risk of serious infection rises steeply as the neutrophil count falls below 500 per µL. The few neutrophils present may also be functionally defective.
    2. Functional immune defects. Monocyte and macrophage function is impaired. In lymphoid leukaemias there is also defective humoral and cell-mediated immunity, with hypogammaglobulinaemia.
    3. Breakdown of mucocutaneous barriers. Mucositis from chemotherapy, ulceration of the oral cavity and gut, skin breaks, and indwelling intravenous catheters provide portals of entry for commensal and environmental organisms.
    4. Treatment-related immunosuppression. Cytotoxic chemotherapy deepens the neutropenia, and corticosteroids and immunosuppressive drugs weaken the response further. broad-spectrum antibiotics promote overgrowth of resistant bacteria and fungi.
    5. Organisms. Infections are frequent in the oral cavity, skin, lungs, kidneys, urinary bladder and colon, and are often caused by opportunists such as fungi (Candida, Aspergillus), Pseudomonas, and commensal organisms, with viral reactivation (herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster) and Pneumocystis in lymphoid leukaemias. Infection may be fulminant with little inflammatory exudate because of the lack of neutrophils.

    Infection with fever in a neutropenic patient is a medical emergency and requires prompt empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics after cultures. Infection and haemorrhage are the principal causes of death.

    What are the common presentations of acute leukaemia/AML?

    DU10JaDU07Ja

    Acute leukaemia presents abruptly, usually within days to a few weeks (in AML within weeks to a few months) of the onset of symptoms, and the presentation reflects the suppression of normal haematopoiesis by the accumulating blasts, with tissue infiltration and metabolic derangements added to varying degrees.

    1. Anaemia. Pallor, fatigue, weakness, exertional dyspnoea and palpitations.

    2. Neutropenia and infection. Fever, sore throat, oral ulceration, and infections of the skin, lungs, urinary tract and colon, often caused by opportunists such as fungi and Pseudomonas and commensal organisms.

    3. Thrombocytopenia and bleeding. Thrombocytopenia causes abnormal bleeding, which is often prominent, with cutaneous petechiae and ecchymoses, serosal haemorrhages into the linings of body cavities and viscera, and mucosal bleeding from the gingivae, nose and urinary tract. Procoagulants and fibrinolytic factors released by leukaemic cells, particularly in AML with t(15;17) (acute promyelocytic leukaemia), exacerbate the tendency by causing DIC.

    4. Extramedullary infiltration. These signs are usually less striking in AML than in ALL. They include bone pain and tenderness, moderate splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Infiltration of the skin (leukaemia cutis) and gingivae (gum hypertrophy) in AML with monocytic differentiation. and a localised soft tissue mass of blasts (myeloid sarcoma, chloroma). CNS spread is less common in AML than in ALL.

    5. Hyperleukocytosis and metabolic features. When blast counts are very high there may be leukostasis with visual blurring, dyspnoea and neurologic symptoms, and tumour lysis with hyperuricaemia and renal failure.

    6. Constitutional symptoms. Fever, weight loss, malaise.

    Often the presentation is a combination of fatigue, fever and bleeding in an adult past middle age, and the diagnosis is first suspected from an abnormal blood count.

    A child has severe pallor, sore throat, bleeding, lymphadenopathy, blasts in PBF. What is the probable diagnosis?

    DU17MDU11JuDU10Ja

    The probable diagnosis is acute leukaemia, most likely acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL).

    Reasoning. The clinical picture is that of marrow failure and tissue infiltration. Severe pallor reflects anaemia from replacement of normal erythropoiesis by blasts. Sore throat and fever reflect neutropenia with infection of the oropharynx. Bleeding (petechiae, gum or nose bleeding) reflects thrombocytopenia. Lymphadenopathy, together with hepatosplenomegaly, represents infiltration, which is more common in ALL than in AML.

    The finding of blasts in the peripheral blood film is the hallmark of acute leukaemia. ALL is the most common cancer of childhood, with a peak around 3 years of age, so ALL is the most likely type, although AML must be excluded because it can produce an identical picture.

    Confirmation

    1. Complete blood count and peripheral smear: anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and variable leukocyte count, with blasts of high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio.
    2. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy: hypercellular marrow with 20% or more lymphoblasts
      Reduced erythroid, myeloid and megakaryocytic cells.
    3. Cytochemistry: lymphoblasts are myeloperoxidase and Sudan black negative and PAS positive.
    4. Flow cytometry: TdT and CD19, CD22, CD79a and CD10 for B-ALL
      Cytoplasmic CD3 and CD7 for T-ALL.
    5. Cytogenetics and molecular studies (t(12;21), hyperdiploidy, BCR::ABL1, KMT2A) for risk stratification, and CSF examination for CNS disease.

    Differential diagnosis. AML
    Aplastic anaemia (no blasts, hypocellular marrow, no lymphadenopathy). Infectious mononucleosis and other viral infections in which reactive lymphocytes mimic blasts. Pertussis
    and leukaemoid reaction.

    Give the blood picture and bone marrow findings of AML.

    4DU19NovDU17NovDU16JuDU14Ja

    Peripheral blood

    • Red cells: normocytic normochromic anaemia of variable severity, with a low reticulocyte count. Occasional nucleated red cells.
    • White cells: the leukocyte count is variable. Blast counts may exceed 100,000 per µL, but are below 10,000 per µL in about 50% of patients, and occasionally blasts are entirely absent from the blood (aleukaemic leukaemia). The smear shows myeloblasts with delicate nuclear chromatin, two to four nucleoli, and relatively abundant cytoplasm containing fine azurophilic, peroxidase-positive granules. Auer rods—needle-like azurophilic granules—are present in many cases and are particularly numerous in AML with t(15;17). Monoblasts have folded or lobulated nuclei, lack Auer rods and are nonspecific esterase positive. There is neutropenia with dysplastic neutrophils in some, and a hiatus leukaemicus (blasts and mature cells without intermediate forms).
    • Platelets: thrombocytopenia, often marked, sometimes with abnormal platelets.
    • Coagulation: in acute promyelocytic leukaemia there is a prolonged prothrombin time, hypofibrinogenaemia and high D-dimers (DIC).

    Bone marrow

    • A hypercellular marrow in most cases (hypocellular in a minority), with replacement of normal elements by myeloblasts. Blasts constitute 20% or more of the nucleated cells
      The WHO classification permits the diagnosis with fewer than 20% if a defining genetic aberration is present.
    • Auer rods in the blasts
      Types of blasts may be mixed or hybrid. Promyelocytes with bundles of Auer rods (faggot cells) in APL.
    • Reduced erythroid precursors and megakaryocytes, with dysplasia in the residual cells in some cases (especially secondary AML).
    • Megakaryocytic differentiation is often accompanied by marrow fibrosis from the release of fibrogenic cytokines, which may make the marrow difficult to aspirate (a "dry tap").
    • Cytochemistry: MPO and Sudan black positive
      NSE positive in monocytic types. Flow cytometry: CD34, CD117, CD13, CD33 and MPO. Cytogenetics: t(8;21), inv(16), t(15;17), KMT2A rearrangements, or complex karyotypes.

    Write down the clinical presentation of ALL.

    DU25N

    ALL is the most common cancer of childhood, with about 2,500 new cases a year in the United States, most under 15 years
    B-ALL peaks at about 3 years, and T-ALL typically presents in adolescent males. It is slightly more frequent in boys. Presentation is abrupt and stormy, with onset within days to a few weeks, and arises from three groups of processes.

    1. Depression of marrow function. Anaemia: pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea, weakness. Neutropenia: fever from infection, which may be severe. Thrombocytopenia: bleeding—petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeding.

    2. Mass effects from neoplastic infiltration, which are more frequent in ALL than in AML: bone pain and tenderness (sometimes a limp or refusal to walk in a child) resulting from marrow expansion and subperiosteal infiltration. Joint pain that may mimic arthritis
    Generalised lymphadenopathy
    Splenomegaly and hepatomegaly
    Testicular enlargement
    and, in T-ALL, an anterior mediastinal mass with compression of the great vessels and trachea (superior vena cava syndrome, respiratory distress, cough).

    3. Central nervous system involvement. Headache, vomiting, cranial nerve (especially facial) palsies and papilloedema from meningeal spread.

    Other features include fever of unknown origin, weight loss, skin infiltration, renal enlargement, and features of tumour lysis (hyperuricaemia). Prognosis is worse in infants under 2 years, in adolescents and adults, and when the leukocyte count exceeds 100,000 per µL. Favourable features include age between 2 and 10 years, a low leukocyte count, hyperdiploidy and t(12;21).

    Give the laboratory diagnosis/bone marrow findings of ALL.

    4DU25NDU25MDU15JaDU08Ju

    1. Peripheral blood. Normocytic normochromic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia are usual. The leukocyte count may be raised, normal or low, and in some cases is above 100,000 per µL. The smear shows circulating lymphoblasts, as described below.

    2. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy. The marrow is hypercellular and packed with lymphoblasts, which replace the normal marrow elements, with 20% or more blasts (usually 50–90%). The tumour cells have scant basophilic cytoplasm and nuclei that are somewhat larger than those of small lymphocytes. The chromatin is delicate and finely stippled, the nucleoli are small and sharply demarcated by a rim of condensed chromatin, and the nuclear membrane is often deeply subdivided, giving a convoluted appearance.

    The mitotic rate is high, and macrophages ingesting apoptotic tumour cells may give a "starry sky" appearance on the biopsy. Erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic precursors are markedly reduced. FAB L1 blasts are small and uniform, L2 larger and heterogeneous, and L3 have deeply basophilic vacuolated cytoplasm.

    3. Cytochemistry. Compared with myeloblasts, lymphoblasts have more condensed chromatin, less conspicuous nucleoli, and less cytoplasm, which usually lacks granules. They are myeloperoxidase negative and Sudan black negative, and often contain PAS-positive cytoplasmic material (coarse block pattern)
    T-lymphoblasts show focal acid phosphatase positivity.

    4. Immunophenotyping (definitive). Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positive in most lymphoblasts. B-ALL expresses CD19, CD22, CD79a, cytoplasmic IgM in some, and usually CD10
    T-ALL expresses CD3, CD7, CD2, CD5, CD1a, depending on the maturation stage.

    5. Cytogenetics and molecular studies. About 90% of cases have numerical or structural chromosomal changes: hyperdiploidy (more than 50 chromosomes; favourable), hypodiploidy (unfavourable), t(12;21) ETV6::RUNX1 (favourable), t(9;22) BCR::ABL1 (p190, unfavourable but responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors), KMT2A rearrangements (infants, poor), t(1;19), and NOTCH1 mutations in T-ALL. Molecular detection of minimal residual disease after therapy predicts outcome.

    6. Other investigations. Serum uric acid and LDH
    Renal and liver function
    Coagulation profile
    Chest radiograph for a mediastinal mass
    CSF examination for blasts
    Testicular ultrasound if indicated.

    Give the blood picture of ALL.

    DUno yr
    • Red cells: normocytic normochromic anaemia, which is often moderate to severe at presentation, with a low reticulocyte count and few nucleated red cells.
    • White cells: the total count may be high, normal or low, being greater than 100,000 per µL in a minority and a poor prognostic sign. The differential count shows a large proportion of lymphoblasts—cells slightly larger than a small lymphocyte, with a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, scanty basophilic agranular cytoplasm, finely stippled condensed chromatin, small indistinct nucleoli and often a convoluted or cleft nucleus. Blasts may be vacuolated in L3 disease. Auer rods are absent. Residual normal neutrophils are reduced (neutropenia), and there is often a hiatus between blasts and mature cells. Smudge cells may be seen.
    • Platelets: thrombocytopenia, commonly marked.
    • Special: lymphoblasts are myeloperoxidase negative and PAS positive on cytochemistry, and TdT positive on flow cytometry.

    In a minority the count is not raised and blasts are scanty or absent (aleukaemic or subleukaemic ALL), so marrow examination is essential.

    Write a short note on blast crisis.

    7DU24NDU22MDU17MDU17JaDU16JaDU15JaDU13Ju

    Definition. Blast crisis (blastic transformation, blast phase) is the terminal acute leukaemia–like phase of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and other myeloproliferative neoplasms, in which immature blasts accumulate in the marrow and blood, usually to 20% or more of the cells, and the disease behaves like an acute leukaemia that is resistant to therapy.

    Natural history of CML. CML begins in a chronic phase lasting a few years in which cells mature normally. After an average of about 3 years without treatment, roughly 50% of patients enter an accelerated phase marked by increasing anaemia and thrombocytopenia, sometimes with a rise in the number of basophils, and by new clonal cytogenetic abnormalities. Within 6 to 12 months this terminates in blast crisis. In the other 50% of patients blast crisis occurs abruptly, without an accelerated phase.

    Cells and pathogenesis. In about 70% of crises the blasts are of myeloid origin (myeloid blast crisis) and in most of the remainder pre-B lymphoblasts (lymphoid blast crisis). This is taken as evidence that CML arises in a pluripotent stem cell with myeloid and lymphoid potential. Additional genetic lesions accumulate on the background of the BCR::ABL1 fusion, such as trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q (with TP53 loss), duplication of the Philadelphia chromosome, and mutations of RUNX1, ASXL1 and other genes.

    In 85% of cases of lymphoid blast crisis there are mutations that interfere with the activity of Ikaros (IKZF1), a transcription factor regulating differentiation of haematopoietic progenitors. The same type of mutation is found in BCR-ABL–positive B-ALL. These changes block differentiation and enhance self-renewal.

    Features. Rapid enlargement of the spleen, fever, weight loss, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, increasing anaemia and thrombocytopenia (or paradoxical thrombocytosis), leukocytosis with 20% or more blasts in blood or marrow (or extramedullary blast proliferation, such as myeloid sarcoma), and increasing basophilia. The picture is that of acute leukaemia, and the blasts may be confirmed by cytochemistry and flow cytometry as myeloid (MPO-positive, CD13, CD33, CD34), lymphoid (TdT, CD10, CD19) or mixed.

    Treatment and prognosis. Blast crisis is refractory to therapy, and the median survival is only a few months (3 to 6 months for myeloid crisis). Tyrosine kinase inhibitors have reduced its incidence markedly by controlling the proliferative drive in the chronic phase, but the other major threat is resistance to first-generation BCR-ABL inhibitors, due in about half of cases to mutations in BCR::ABL1.

    Lymphoid blast crisis responds better to induction chemotherapy plus a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and allogeneic stem cell transplantation is offered when possible. Polycythaemia vera (about 2%) and primary myelofibrosis (5–20%) may likewise transform to AML, as may essential thrombocythaemia uncommonly, whereas transformation to ALL is rare.

    Chronic myeloid leukaemia

    A8

    How will you differentiate myeloblast from lymphoblast?

    5A8Q10DU25MDU16JuDU14JaDU12Ja

    Also asked as: Differences between myeloblast and lymphoblast.

    Myeloblasts are larger cells with delicate chromatin, two to four prominent nucleoli, more abundant cytoplasm with azurophilic granules and sometimes Auer rods, and are myeloperoxidase positive
    Lymphoblasts are smaller, with condensed chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli and scanty agranular cytoplasm, and are MPO negative, PAS positive and TdT positive.

    Morphologically, immature "blast" forms of different lineages look alike and can only be identified definitively with lineage-specific antibodies and histochemical stains. Compared with myeloblasts, lymphoblasts have more condensed chromatin, less conspicuous nucleoli, and smaller amounts of cytoplasm that usually lacks granules. These morphologic distinctions are not absolute.
