    Less common examples are chronic neutrophilic leukaemia (CSF3R), chronic eosinophilic leukaemia (FIP1L1::PDGFRA), and systemic mastocytosis (KIT). All of these disorders have increased proliferative drive in the marrow, variable extramedullary haematopoiesis, and variable transformation to a spent phase of marrow fibrosis or to acute leukaemia. Unlike CML, transformation to ALL is rarely seen in PV, as the cell of origin is a progenitor committed to myeloid differentiation.

    A8

    WHO diagnostic criteria for polycythaemia vera.

    A8Q23

    The WHO criteria for polycythaemia vera require either all three major criteria, or the first two major criteria plus the minor criterion. The major criteria are raised haemoglobin or haematocrit, a hypercellular marrow with trilineage growth, and the JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation, and the minor criterion is a subnormal serum erythropoietin.

    Major criteria

    1. Haemoglobin above 16.5 g/dL in men or above 16.0 g/dL in women, or haematocrit above 49% in men or above 48% in women (the earlier WHO scheme also allowed an increased red cell mass above 25% of the predicted mean).
    2. Bone marrow biopsy showing hypercellularity for age with trilineage growth (panmyelosis), including prominent erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic proliferation with pleomorphic, mature megakaryocytes (differing in size).
    3. Presence of JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutation.

    Minor criterion

    • Subnormal serum erythropoietin level.

    Rule. The diagnosis of PV requires all three major criteria, or the first two major criteria and the minor criterion. The bone marrow biopsy (major criterion 2) may not be required in patients with sustained absolute erythrocytosis (haemoglobin above 18.5 g/dL in men or above 16.5 g/dL in women, corresponding to haematocrits above 55.5% and 49.5%) when the JAK2 mutation and the low erythropoietin are present.

    A8

    Define myelofibrosis.

    A8Q24

    Myelofibrosis is a disorder in which the bone marrow is progressively replaced by fibrous tissue, leading to cytopenias, extramedullary haematopoiesis with splenomegaly, and a leukoerythroblastic blood picture.

    The hallmark of primary myelofibrosis is the development of obliterative marrow fibrosis. The replacement of the marrow by fibrous tissue reduces bone marrow haematopoiesis, leading to cytopenias and extensive extramedullary haematopoiesis, principally in the spleen, liver and lymph nodes. The fibroblasts are non-neoplastic. The fibrosis is caused by inappropriate release of fibrogenic factors, platelet-derived growth factor and TGF-β, from neoplastic megakaryocytes.

    TGF-β also promotes collagen deposition and angiogenesis. The disease may arise as a primary myeloproliferative neoplasm (about 90% have JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations), or the same histologic picture may represent the spent phase of polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia or CML, or result from other marrow-injuring processes (secondary myelofibrosis).

    A8

    Laboratory diagnosis of myelofibrosis.

    A8Q24

    Myelofibrosis is suspected from anaemia with a leukoerythroblastic blood picture and teardrop red cells in a patient with splenomegaly, and is confirmed by a bone marrow biopsy showing fibrosis with atypical megakaryocytes and by the finding of a JAK2, CALR or MPL mutation.

    Peripheral blood

    • Moderate to severe normochromic normocytic anaemia.
    • Leukoerythroblastosis: premature release of nucleated red cell precursors and early granulocyte precursors (myelocytes, metamyelocytes, occasional blasts), caused by marrow distortion and by immature cells entering the blood from sites of extramedullary haematopoiesis.
    • Teardrop-shaped red cells (dacryocytes), probably damaged during their passage from the fibrotic marrow.
    • The white cell count is usually normal or mildly reduced but may be markedly elevated (80,000 to 100,000/µL) early. The platelet count is usually normal or elevated at diagnosis, with large platelets (and basophilia), and thrombocytopenia may supervene with progression.
    • These findings are not specific
      Leukoerythroblastosis and teardrop cells are also seen in other infiltrative marrow disorders, including granulomatous diseases and metastatic tumours.

    Bone marrow

    • Aspiration: often a dry tap because of the fibrosis. The trephine biopsy is essential for diagnosis.
    • Early (prefibrotic) phase: hypercellular marrow with increased maturing cells of all lineages. Erythroid and granulocytic precursors appear normal, but megakaryocytes are large, with bulbous, hyperchromatic or "cloud-like" nuclei, and are abnormally clustered. Minimal fibrosis.
    • Fibrotic phase: the marrow becomes hypocellular and diffusely fibrotic (reticulin and then collagen). Atypical megakaryocytes in clusters
      Haematopoietic cells in dilated sinusoids
      Very late osteosclerosis (new bone formation).

    Molecular and other tests. JAK2 V617F in 50–60%, CALR in 25–35% and MPL in 5–10% (about 90% overall)
    Absence of BCR::ABL1 excludes CML. Serum uric acid, LDH and alkaline phosphatase are raised. The LAP score is variable. Imaging shows splenomegaly (up to 4,000 g), with extramedullary haematopoiesis and infarcts. Marrow cytogenetics may show del(13q), del(20q), trisomy 8 and 9.

    A8

    Types of myelofibrosis.

    A8Q25

    Myelofibrosis is of two types: primary (idiopathic) myelofibrosis, a myeloproliferative neoplasm, and secondary myelofibrosis, which follows other myeloproliferative neoplasms or other marrow-injuring diseases.

    1. Primary myelofibrosis (chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis, agnogenic myeloid metaplasia). A myeloproliferative neoplasm in which about 90% of cases have activating JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations. It occurs mostly after 60 years of age and passes through a prefibrotic (early) phase of marrow hypercellularity with atypical megakaryocytes and an overt fibrotic phase with marrow fibrosis, massive splenomegaly and cytopenias.

    2. Secondary myelofibrosis. Fibrosis resulting from another disease, in which the marrow fibroblasts are reactive.

    • Post-polycythaemia vera and post–essential thrombocythaemia myelofibrosis (the "spent phase" of myeloproliferative neoplasms, which is histologically identical to primary myelofibrosis. Spent phase of PV in 15–20% after about 10 years), and the fibrotic transformation of CML.
    • Myelofibrosis secondary to other disorders, such as metastatic carcinoma, lymphomas and other haematologic malignancies, granulomatous infections, toxins and radiation, and metabolic bone disease.

    3. Acute (malignant) myelofibrosis (acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis). A rare, rapidly progressive form with pancytopenia and fibrosis, often overlapping with megakaryoblastic leukaemia, without splenomegaly.

    It is not clear whether primary myelofibrosis is truly distinct from polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia or merely reflects unusually rapid progression to the spent phase.

    A8

    Conditions associated with secondary myelofibrosis.

    A8Q25

    Secondary myelofibrosis occurs in other myeloproliferative neoplasms, in marrow infiltration by tumour or granulomas, in other haematologic malignancies, and with toxic, infectious and autoimmune injury to the marrow.

    CategoryConditions
    Other myeloid neoplasmsPolycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia, chronic myeloid leukaemia (spent phase), myelodysplastic neoplasms, acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia (AML with megakaryocytic differentiation)
    Other haematologic malignanciesHairy cell leukaemia, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, multiple myeloma, systemic mastocytosis
    Metastatic and infiltrative diseaseMetastatic carcinoma (breast, prostate, lung, stomach), Gaucher disease
    Infections and granulomatous diseaseTuberculosis, sarcoidosis, fungal infection, HIV
    Toxins, drugs, radiationBenzene, thorium dioxide, ionising radiation
    Metabolic and bone diseaseHyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D deficiency (rickets), osteopetrosis, Paget disease
    Autoimmune and otherSystemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, pulmonary hypertension, gray platelet syndrome

    Marrow fibrosis in these settings arises from the inappropriate release of fibrogenic cytokines (PDGF, TGF-β) by abnormal megakaryocytes or inflammatory and malignant cells. Metastatic cancer and granulomatous disease induce local marrow fibrosis, in which the marrow usually cannot be aspirated, and the lesions are best seen in biopsy.

    A8

    Essential thrombocythaemia (in short).

    A8Q26

    Essential thrombocythaemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by a sustained, marked increase in platelet number, driven by JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations, with thrombosis and bleeding as the main complications, and without polycythaemia or marrow fibrosis.

    Definition and pathogenesis. Essential thrombocythaemia (ET) is associated with diverse mutations that increase JAK-STAT signalling and mimic constitutive growth factor receptor signalling. Over 90% of cases have activating mutations in JAK2 (approximately 50–60%), MPL (5–10%), the thrombopoietin receptor, or CALR (calreticulin, approximately 25–35%). The mutated CALR proteins are secreted and bind and activate the thrombopoietin receptor, an oncogenic autocrine loop. Constitutive signalling renders the progenitors thrombopoietin-independent.

    Morphology. The marrow is mildly hypercellular with markedly increased, large megakaryocytes. Delicate reticulin only, without the overt fibrosis of myelofibrosis. The blood smear shows large to giant platelets, up to the size of red cells, often with mild leukocytosis. Mild organomegaly in about 50%.

    Clinical features. Incidence 1 to 3 per 100,000 per year
    Usually over 60 years but also in young adults. Platelets are increased and functionally abnormal, leading to thrombosis (deep veins, portal and hepatic veins, myocardial infarction) and haemorrhage
    up to one-third have acquired von Willebrand disease. Erythromelalgia (burning pain in the hands and feet from occlusion of small arterioles by platelet aggregates) is characteristic.

    Diagnosis. Persistent platelet count of 450,000/µL or more, with JAK2, CALR or MPL mutation or exclusion of reactive thrombocytosis (iron deficiency, inflammation). Exclusion of PV, primary myelofibrosis and CML.

    Course. Indolent with long asymptomatic periods punctuated by thrombotic or haemorrhagic crises. Median survival 12–15 years
    Rare spent phase or transformation to AML. Treatment: low-dose aspirin and "gentle" cytoreduction (hydroxyurea).

    What do you mean by sub-leukaemic leukaemia (marrow picture)?

    DU11JuDU09JuDU08Ju

    Meaning. Subleukaemic leukaemia is a form of leukaemia, usually acute, in which the total leukocyte count in the peripheral blood is normal or only slightly increased (or low) and blasts are few or absent in the blood, whereas the bone marrow is heavily infiltrated by leukaemic cells. When the leukocyte count is low and no blasts are seen, the term aleukaemic leukaemia is used. In acute myeloid leukaemia the number of blasts in the blood is variable. Blasts are under 10,000/µL in about 50% of patients and occasionally absent altogether, which is why a marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukaemia in a pancytopenic patient.

    Peripheral blood. Pancytopenia or bicytopenia, with anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia. Very few or no blasts
    Normal or slightly raised total count
    The peripheral smear may be misleading.

    Marrow picture (diagnostic)

    • The marrow is hypercellular (occasionally normocellular), with replacement of the normal fat and haematopoietic elements by blasts that constitute 20% or more of nucleated cells (WHO), or fewer if a defining genetic abnormality is present.
    • Residual erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic cells are markedly reduced, and may show dysplasia.
    • The blasts are identified by cytochemistry (myeloperoxidase, Sudan black positive in myeloblasts; PAS positive in lymphoblasts) and immunophenotyping. Auer rods suggest AML.
    • The biopsy confirms hypercellularity with sheets of blasts and shows fibrosis if present (an aspiration "dry tap" may occur in AML with megakaryocytic differentiation and in hairy cell leukaemia).
    • Cytogenetics and molecular studies identify the type and prognosis.

    The importance of recognising the entity is that, without a marrow examination, the pancytopenia may be misdiagnosed as aplastic anaemia, myelodysplasia or megaloblastic anaemia.

    How will you differentiate sub-leukaemic leukaemia from aplastic anemia?

    DU13JuDU12Ju

    Both conditions present with pancytopenia (anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia) and may have a "normal" leukocyte count with no blasts in the blood, and therefore cannot be separated by the peripheral smear alone
    The distinction depends on the bone marrow examination, particularly the trephine biopsy.

    FeatureSubleukaemic leukaemiaAplastic anaemia
    NatureClonal neoplasm of haematopoietic progenitorsMarrow failure from stem cell injury (often immune-mediated; drugs, viruses, idiopathic)
    Clinical findingsPallor, fever, bleeding, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegalyPallor, fever, bleeding
    no organomegaly and no lymphadenopathy
    Peripheral bloodPancytopenia with few or occasional blasts
    Hiatus leukaemicus    		Pancytopenia without blasts or abnormal cells
    Bone marrow aspirateHypercellular with 20% or more blastsHypocellular, with fatty replacement, scanty haematopoietic cells, relative lymphocyte, plasma cell and stromal cell predominance
    no blasts
    Trephine biopsyPacked marrow, loss of fat spaces, infiltration by blastsMarkedly hypocellular, with the proportion of fat greatly increased
    Cytochemistry / flow cytometryMPO, SBB, TdT or myeloid/lymphoid markers positiveNo blast population
    CytogeneticsClonal abnormalities (t(8;21), t(15;17), etc.)Normal karyotype
    LDH and uric acidRaisedNormal
    SpleenEnlarged (often)Not enlarged
    Treatment and prognosisChemotherapy, transplantImmunosuppression, transplant
    Supportive care

    The aspirate in aplastic anaemia is typically dilute and haemodilute, and the trephine biopsy settles the question, since the proportion of fat is greatly increased in hypoplastic states, whereas fat cells are largely replaced when the marrow is infiltrated by haematopoietic tumours.

    Write a short note on polycythaemia rubra vera.

    DU06MDU04M

    Definition. Polycythaemia rubra vera (polycythaemia vera, PV) is a clonal myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes and platelets (panmyelosis), though it is the increase in red cells (polycythaemia) that is responsible for most of the clinical symptoms. It must be differentiated from relative polycythaemia due to haemoconcentration and from other causes of absolute polycythaemia.

    Pathogenesis. The transformed progenitor cells have markedly decreased requirements for erythropoietin and other growth factors because of activating mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2, which lies downstream of the erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and G-CSF receptors. More than 97% of cases have the JAK2 V617F mutation (valine to phenylalanine at residue 617). The rest have other JAK2 mutations such as those in exon 12.

    In 25% to 30% the tumour cells have two mutated copies of JAK2, associated with higher white counts, greater splenomegaly, pruritus and progression to the spent phase. Because the pathway is constitutively active, serum erythropoietin levels are low, in contrast to secondary polycythaemia. Elevated haematocrit causes hyperviscosity and sludging, and together with thrombocytosis and abnormal platelet function predisposes to both thrombosis and bleeding.

    Morphology. The marrow is hypercellular with residual fat
    Red cell, granulocyte and megakaryocyte precursors are increased. Reticulin fibres are moderately to markedly increased in about 10% of marrows at diagnosis. Mild organomegaly early, from congestion. The blood often contains increased basophils and abnormally large platelets. Late in the course, a spent phase with extensive marrow fibrosis, massive splenomegaly and extramedullary haematopoiesis occurs in 15–20% after an average of 10 years. Transformation to AML occurs in about 2%.

    Clinical features. Insidious onset in adults of late middle age (1–3 per 100,000 a year). Plethora and cyanosis, headache, dizziness, hypertension, gastrointestinal symptoms, intense pruritus and peptic ulceration (histamine from basophils), and hyperuricaemia with gout in 5–10%. About 25% present with thrombosis (deep vein thrombosis, myocardial infarction, stroke, Budd-Chiari syndrome, mesenteric thrombosis)
    Haemorrhage in 5–10% is life-threatening.

    Laboratory findings. Haemoglobin above 16 g/dL, often haematocrit above 55%
    White cell count 12,000–50,000/µL
    Platelets often above 500,000/µL with giant forms and defective aggregation. Low erythropoietin
    JAK2 mutation. Iron deficiency from chronic bleeding can lower the haematocrit into the normal range, masking the disease.

    Treatment and prognosis. Untreated, death from bleeding or thrombosis occurs within months. Maintaining the haematocrit at nearly normal levels by phlebotomy with low-dose aspirin extends median survival to about 10 years. Cytoreduction (hydroxyurea) in high-risk patients. JAK2 inhibitors (ruxolitinib) for the spent phase.

    Spleen and Hypersplenism

    A8

    Causes of hypersplenism.

    A8Q26

    Hypersplenism is enlargement of the spleen with cytopenias caused by increased sequestration and destruction of blood cells, and it complicates any cause of splenomegaly, the commonest being portal hypertension from cirrhosis, haematologic disorders such as haemolytic anaemias and myeloproliferative neoplasms, lymphomas and chronic infections.

    Hypersplenism is a syndrome characterised by anaemia, leukopenia and/or thrombocytopenia in the presence of splenomegaly. The probable cause of the cytopenias is increased sequestration of formed elements with enhanced phagocytosis by splenic macrophages. The normal spleen holds 30% to 40% of the platelet mass, and with splenomegaly up to 80% to 90% may be sequestered in the red pulp.

    In congestive splenomegaly, the increased portal pressure causes collagen deposition in the sinusoidal basement membranes and slows the flow of blood from the cords to the sinusoids, prolonging exposure of the blood cells to macrophages. An expanded plasma volume contributes by dilution.

    Causes (any condition causing significant splenomegaly may produce hypersplenism):

    CategoryExamples
    Congestive (portal hypertension)Cirrhosis (the main cause of massive congestive splenomegaly), schistosomiasis, portal vein or splenic vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure
    HaematologicHereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease (early)
    Myeloproliferative neoplasms (CML, primary myelofibrosis, polycythaemia vera)
    Extramedullary haematopoiesis
    LymphoproliferativeNon-Hodgkin lymphomas and lymphocytic leukaemias (CLL, hairy cell leukaemia), Hodgkin lymphoma
    InfectionsMalaria, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), tuberculosis, typhoid, brucellosis, infective endocarditis, infectious mononucleosis, HIV
    Infiltrative and storage disordersGaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis
    AutoimmuneFelty syndrome (rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly and neutropenia), systemic lupus erythematosus
    Primary (idiopathic)Rare
    Splenomegaly with cytopenias and no demonstrable cause
    A8

    Causes of splenomegaly.

    A8Q27

    Splenomegaly results from infections, congestion from portal hypertension, haematologic and lymphoid disorders, immunologic and inflammatory diseases, storage diseases and neoplasms. The spleen is involved secondarily in all systemic inflammations, generalised haematopoietic disorders and many metabolic disturbances.

    Splenomegaly is the major manifestation of splenic disorders, which are only rarely primary. When sufficiently enlarged, the spleen causes a dragging sensation in the left upper quadrant, discomfort after eating from pressure on the stomach, and may produce hypersplenism. Disorders associated with splenomegaly are as follows.

    MechanismExamples
    Infections (acute splenitis)Any blood-borne infection, particularly infective endocarditis
    Infectious mononucleosis
    Typhoid, tuberculosis, brucellosis, septicaemia
    Malaria
    kala-azar
    Schistosomiasis
    HIV
    CongestiveCirrhosis (the main cause of massive congestive splenomegaly), schistosomal "pipestem" fibrosis, portal or splenic vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure
    Lymphohaematogenous neoplasmsNon-Hodgkin lymphomas and lymphocytic leukaemias (CLL, hairy cell), Hodgkin lymphoma, multiple myeloma
    Myeloproliferative neoplasms (CML, polycythaemia vera, primary myelofibrosis) with extramedullary haematopoiesis
    Haemolytic anaemiasHereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, sickle cell disease (early), with red cell destruction and compensatory extramedullary haematopoiesis
    ImmunoinflammatoryRheumatoid arthritis (Felty syndrome), systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, serum sickness
    Storage and infiltrative diseasesGaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease, mucopolysaccharidoses, amyloidosis
    Primary splenic lesionsCysts, haemangioma, lymphangioma, other rare tumours
    Metastases rare

    Weights. The normal adult spleen weighs 150 g. Acute nonspecific splenitis gives 200–400 g. Systemic (right heart) congestion rarely exceeds 500 g
    long-standing portal congestion gives 1,000–5,000 g. Myeloproliferative neoplasms may reach 4,000 g or more.

    A8

    Diagnostic criteria of hypersplenism.

    A8Q27

    The classical diagnostic criteria of hypersplenism are splenomegaly, one or more cytopenias in the blood with a normocellular or hypercellular marrow, and correction of the cytopenias after splenectomy. Evidence of increased splenic sequestration supports the diagnosis.

    1. Splenomegaly. Clinically or by imaging.
    2. Cytopenia of one or more cell lines—anaemia, leukopenia (neutropenia), thrombocytopenia, or pancytopenia. Robbins describes hypersplenism as a syndrome characterised by anaemia, leukopenia and/or thrombocytopenia.
    3. Normal or hyperplastic (cellular) bone marrow with normal or increased precursors, reflecting a compensatory response to peripheral destruction, with no other cause of cytopenia (such as marrow failure, infiltration or drug effect).
    4. Evidence of increased destruction or pooling. Shortened survival of red cells or platelets, with increased splenic uptake demonstrated by radioisotope studies (⁵¹Cr-labelled red cells or ¹¹¹In-labelled platelets, with excess counting over the spleen), and increased plasma volume. Reticulocytosis if haemolysis is present.
    5. Response to splenectomy. Correction of cytopenias after removal of the spleen. This is retrospective but diagnostic. Splenectomy is reserved for severe cases as it increases the risk of overwhelming sepsis by encapsulated bacteria (pneumococci, meningococci, Haemophilus influenzae), so asplenic patients must be vaccinated.

    Clinical Scenarios

    A10

    Elderly man (55 or 65 years) with bone/back pain, punched-out skull lesions or osteolytic lesions, high ESR, vertebral fracture — Most probable diagnosis? How will you establish / confirm the diagnosis?

    A10Q7, Q19

    The most probable diagnosis is multiple myeloma, and I would confirm it with serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to show a monoclonal protein, a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showing clonal plasma cells, and tests for the CRAB features—calcium, creatinine, haemoglobin—and skeletal imaging.

    Diagnosis. The age (peak 65 to 70 years), bone and back pain, punched-out lytic lesions of the skull (1 to 4 cm, sharply demarcated), pathologic vertebral fracture and markedly raised ESR (from rouleaux formation due to the M protein) are characteristic of multiple myeloma. The lesions are destructive plasma cell tumours resulting from increased osteoclast activity (MIP-1α) and inhibition of osteoblasts (Wnt inhibitors), and involve the axial skeleton in decreasing order of frequency: vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis and femur.

    How to establish the diagnosis

    1. Blood: haemoglobin (normocytic normochromic anaemia), blood film with rouleaux, ESR, serum calcium (hypercalcaemia), urea and creatinine (renal impairment), uric acid, albumin, β₂-microglobulin, LDH
      Alkaline phosphatase is typically normal.
    2. Serum protein electrophoresis (a sharp M spike, usually IgG or IgA), immunofixation to type the immunoglobulin, quantitative immunoglobulins (reduced normal immunoglobulins), and serum free light chain assay with κ/λ ratio.
    3. Urine: 24-hour urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation for Bence Jones protein (the dipstick may be negative).
    4. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy: increased plasma cells (typically above 30%
      10% or more clonal plasma cells with a myeloma-defining event for diagnosis), atypical and multinucleate forms, flame cells, Mott cells, with CD138⁺, CD56⁺ and light-chain restriction.
    5. Imaging: skeletal survey, or MRI/low-dose CT/PET-CT
      MRI of the spine for cord compression if neurologic signs.
    6. Cytogenetics/FISH for prognosis: t(4;14), del(17p), t(11;14), del(13q).

    Diagnostic criteria. Clonal plasma cells in the marrow plus CRAB features (hypercalcaemia, renal dysfunction, anaemia, bone lesions) or other myeloma-defining events. Distinguish from MGUS (M protein below 3 g/dL, no end-organ damage), smoldering myeloma and solitary plasmacytoma, and from metastatic carcinoma (lytic bone lesions but no M protein).

    A10

    40-year-old man with massive splenomegaly and total WBC count 2,50,000/cu.mm — Diagnosis?

    A10Q11

    This is most probably chronic myeloid leukaemia in the chronic phase, and I would confirm it by peripheral smear, marrow examination and demonstration of the Philadelphia chromosome or BCR::ABL1 fusion gene.

    Reasoning. A middle-aged adult (peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decades) with a very high white cell count, well above 100,000/µL, and massive splenomegaly from extensive extramedullary haematopoiesis, is the typical presentation of CML. The onset is insidious, with fatigue, weight loss, anorexia and a dragging sensation in the left upper quadrant, and occasionally acute pain from splenic infarction.

    Confirmation

    1. Peripheral smear: neutrophils, bands, metamyelocytes and myelocytes (the full spectrum of granulocytic maturation), basophilia and eosinophilia, blasts below 10%
      Platelets often increased
      Mild anaemia.
    2. Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score: low or absent.
    3. Bone marrow: markedly hypercellular with granulocytic hyperplasia, increased megakaryocytes (small, hypolobated), sea-blue histiocytes.
    4. Cytogenetic and molecular tests: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11), or BCR::ABL1 by FISH or RT-PCR.
    5. Other: uric acid, LDH, vitamin B₁₂ raised
      Blasts and basophils to define phase.

    Differential diagnosis. Leukaemoid reaction (high LAP, toxic changes, no basophilia, no massive splenomegaly, Ph negative). Primary myelofibrosis (leukoerythroblastosis, teardrop cells, fibrotic marrow, lower WBC). Chronic neutrophilic leukaemia, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (lymphocytes), hairy cell leukaemia (pancytopenia), and the other BCR::ABL1-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms.

    Management note. With a count of 250,000/µL there is a risk of leukostasis and tumour lysis. Hydration, allopurinol and cytoreduction are needed, and BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors induce sustained haematologic remission in over 90% of patients and reduce the risk of progression to blast crisis.

    A10

    10-year-old boy with weakness, fever, joint pain and gum bleeding — Clinical diagnosis? Expected PBF findings?

    A10Q15

    This is most likely acute leukaemia—acute lymphoblastic leukaemia being the commonest in a child—and the peripheral blood film would show anaemia, thrombocytopenia and circulating blasts.

    Clinical diagnosis. The combination of weakness (anaemia), fever (neutropenia with infection, or the disease itself), joint and bone pain (marrow expansion and subperiosteal infiltration by leukaemic cells) and gum bleeding (thrombocytopenia) in a child suggests acute leukaemia: the stormy onset over days to weeks, the marrow failure triad and the bone pain are characteristic.

    ALL is the most common cancer of children and is more likely (peak at about 3 years, with a second adolescent peak for T-ALL), but AML can present identically
    Prominent gum hypertrophy and bleeding would suggest AML with monocytic differentiation. Other features sought are lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, testicular enlargement, mediastinal mass and CNS signs.

    Expected peripheral blood findings

    • Normocytic normochromic anaemia, with a low reticulocyte count.
    • Thrombocytopenia, often severe.
    • White cell count variable: raised in most, but normal or low in some. neutropenia.
    • Blasts in the smear: in ALL, lymphoblasts of high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, condensed finely stippled chromatin, small nucleoli and scant agranular cytoplasm. in AML, myeloblasts with delicate chromatin, prominent nucleoli, fine granules and Auer rods.
    • Hiatus leukaemicus (blasts and mature cells without intermediate stages)
      Smudge cells may be present.

    Confirmation. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showing 20% or more blasts
    Cytochemistry (MPO negative and PAS positive in ALL)
    Flow cytometry (TdT, CD19, CD10, CD3)
    Cytogenetics
    CSF examination.

    Differential diagnosis. Aplastic anaemia (no blasts, hypocellular marrow)
    Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (isolated thrombocytopenia). Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and rheumatic fever (joint pain, but normal blood counts and no marrow failure). Infectious mononucleosis (atypical lymphocytes)
    Scurvy (gum bleeding and bone pain).
