    Narrate the features of haemolysis found in PBF.

    DU12Ju

    The peripheral blood film in haemolytic anaemia shows two sets of changes: those reflecting compensatory erythropoietic activity of the marrow, which are common to all haemolytic anaemias, and those reflecting the specific mechanism of red cell injury.

    Features of increased erythropoiesis. Polychromasia: red cells with a bluish-pink cytoplasm due to RNA, corresponding to reticulocytes (confirmed with supravital stains and reported as a raised reticulocyte count, often 5% to 20%, or higher). These cells are larger than mature cells, contributing to macrocytosis and a raised MCV. Anisocytosis, nucleated red cells (normoblasts) and basophilic stippling are frequently present, with sometimes Howell-Jolly bodies. There is often a neutrophil leukocytosis and thrombocytosis.

    Features specific to the cause. Spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis, immune haemolysis), sickle cells and target cells (haemoglobinopathies), microcytes, target cells and teardrop cells (thalassaemia), schistocytes (microangiopathic haemolysis and mechanical valves), bite cells and blister cells (G6PD deficiency), red cell agglutinates (cold agglutinins), elliptocytes, and intracellular parasites (malaria).

    Write down the general evidence/laboratory features of haemolysis.

    DU12JuDU09Ja

    The laboratory evidence of haemolysis falls into three groups.

    1. Evidence of increased red cell destruction (increased haemoglobin breakdown)

    • Raised serum unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, with acholuric jaundice.
    • Reduced or absent serum haptoglobin
      Raised lactate dehydrogenase.
    • Increased urinary urobilinogen, and increased faecal stercobilinogen.
    • In intravascular haemolysis: haemoglobinaemia, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria and methaemalbuminaemia.
    • Reduced red cell survival on ⁵¹Cr-labelling, with excess splenic uptake.
    • Haemosiderosis and pigment gallstones in chronic haemolysis.

    2. Evidence of compensatory increased erythropoiesis

    • Reticulocytosis, polychromasia, nucleated red cells.
    • Bone marrow erythroid hyperplasia with a reversed myeloid:erythroid ratio.
    • Skeletal changes (in chronic severe haemolysis) and extramedullary haemopoiesis.

    3. Evidence of damaged red cells and identification of the cause

    • Blood film features: spherocytes, fragmented cells, sickle cells, bite cells, parasites.
    • Direct Coombs test (immune haemolysis)
      Osmotic fragility test (hereditary spherocytosis). G6PD assay
      Haemoglobin electrophoresis
      Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 (PNH).

    Normocytic normochromic anaemia (or macrocytic with raised MCV from reticulocytes) is the usual blood count finding, together with splenomegaly in extravascular haemolysis.

    Write down the evidence of intravascular haemolysis.

    DU21M

    Intravascular haemolysis is the lysis of red cells within the circulation. It is less common than extravascular haemolysis and results from mechanical injury (prosthetic valves, microangiopathy, march haemoglobinuria), complement fixation (ABO-incompatible transfusion, PNH, cold haemolysin), intracellular parasites (falciparum malaria) or toxic factors (clostridial sepsis). The evidence comprises:

    1. Haemoglobinaemia: free haemoglobin in the plasma, which makes the plasma pink or red.
    2. Haemoglobinuria: when the haptoglobin-binding capacity is saturated, free haemoglobin is filtered, and some passes in the urine, imparting a red-brown colour. Urine microscopy shows no red cells.
    3. Haemosiderinuria: renal proximal tubular cells reabsorb and break down haemoglobin. Iron accumulates as haemosiderin and is shed into the urine (positive Prussian blue stain of urine sediment), and may give rise to renal haemosiderosis. Chronic loss may produce iron deficiency.
    4. Low or absent serum haptoglobin, since the haptoglobin–haemoglobin complex is rapidly cleared by mononuclear phagocytes. Free haemoglobin oxidises to methaemoglobin, producing methaemalbuminaemia (a positive Schumm test).
    5. Raised LDH and unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (jaundice).
    6. Red cell fragments (schistocytes) in mechanical causes.
    7. Splenomegaly is absent, unlike in extravascular haemolysis.

    Write a short note on Coombs' test (direct).

    7DU23NDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU12JaDU08JaDU05Ja

    The Coombs (antiglobulin) test detects antibody or complement bound to the surface of red cells, and is the cardinal test for immunohaemolytic anaemia.

    Principle. Red cells coated with IgG or C3 do not agglutinate on their own in saline, since the sensitised cells are too far apart. Antihuman globulin (Coombs reagent), a polyspecific or monospecific antibody directed against human IgG and complement (C3d), bridges the gap between the coated cells and causes visible agglutination.

    Direct Coombs test (DAT). The patient's red cells, washed free of plasma, are mixed with Coombs reagent. If immunoglobulin or complement is present on the surface of the red cells (in vivo sensitisation), the cells agglutinate, seen as clumping. Specific anti-IgG and anti-C3 reagents identify the type of coating.

    Indirect Coombs test (IAT). The patient's serum is incubated with commercially available red cells bearing known antigens and then Coombs reagent is added, to detect free antibodies in the serum. it is used to characterise the target antigen and temperature dependence of the antibody, and in cross-matching and antenatal antibody screening.

    Clinical uses of the direct test. Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (warm: IgG ± C3; cold: C3), drug-induced haemolysis (penicillin, α-methyldopa), haemolytic disease of the newborn (positive in the infant's cells), delayed haemolytic transfusion reactions and acute haemolytic transfusion reactions.

    Interpretation and pitfalls. A negative test in a patient with spherocytic anaemia suggests hereditary spherocytosis, in which the combination of spherocytosis, reticulocytosis and negative Coombs test is highly suggestive. False positives occur in hypergammaglobulinaemia and some drug therapy. False negatives occur if too few IgG molecules are bound.

    What do you mean by haemolytic disease of newborn?

    DU18M

    Haemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN, erythroblastosis fetalis) is a haemolytic anaemia of the foetus and newborn caused by transplacental passage of maternal IgG antibodies directed against foetal red cell antigens inherited from the father that the mother lacks.

    The most important is Rh (D) incompatibility, in which an Rh-negative mother who has been sensitised to D antigen (usually at delivery of a previous Rh-positive infant, or by miscarriage, amniocentesis or transfusion) forms anti-D IgG, which crosses the placenta in a subsequent pregnancy and coats the red cells of an Rh-positive foetus, causing extravascular haemolysis in the spleen and liver. ABO incompatibility (mother group O, infant group A or B) is more common but milder, and may affect the first pregnancy because natural anti-A and anti-B IgG exist.

    The consequences are anaemia, compensatory erythroid hyperplasia and extramedullary haemopoiesis with hepatosplenomegaly, and nucleated red cells in the blood (hence erythroblastosis). Jaundice from unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in the first 24 hours, which may cause kernicterus. and, in the severe form, hydrops fetalis with generalised oedema, ascites, cardiac failure and foetal death.

    The direct Coombs test on the infant's cells is positive. Prevention is by giving anti-D immunoglobulin to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks and within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh-positive infant
    Treatment includes phototherapy, exchange transfusion and intrauterine transfusion.

    Haemoglobinopathies and Thalassaemia

    Haemoglobinopathies

    A7

    Normal types of haemoglobin.

    A7Q24

    The normal haemoglobins are HbA (α₂β₂), which constitutes about 95% to 98% of adult haemoglobin, HbA₂ (α₂δ₂) at about 2.5%, and foetal haemoglobin HbF (α₂γ₂), which predominates in the foetus and is below 1% in adults.

    Haemoglobin is a tetrameric protein composed of two pairs of globin chains, each with its own haem group. The α-globin genes lie on chromosome 16 (two genes per haploid genome, four per cell), and the β-like genes (β, δ, γ, ε) on chromosome 11.

    HaemoglobinChainsLevel
    HbAα₂β₂95–98% in adults
    HbA₂α₂δ₂2.5 ± 0.3%
    HbFα₂γ₂Main haemoglobin of the foetus, 70–80% at birth, falling to about 1% by one year
    Embryonic (Gower 1, Gower 2, Portland)ζ₂ε₂, α₂ε₂, ζ₂γ₂Present in the first trimester

    HbF, which has a higher oxygen affinity than HbA and inhibits the polymerisation of HbS, is the reason why infants with sickle cell disease become symptomatic only at 5 to 6 months of age.

    A7

    Name / classify congenital haemolytic anaemias due to defect in haemoglobin.

    A7Q21, Q22, Q24

    Congenital haemolytic anaemias due to a defect in haemoglobin are classified into the thalassaemia syndromes, in which globin chain synthesis is deficient (a quantitative defect), and the haemoglobinopathies, in which a structurally abnormal globin is produced (a qualitative defect).

    1. Quantitative defects of globin synthesis: α-thalassaemia and β-thalassaemia (and δβ-thalassaemia and hereditary persistence of foetal haemoglobin as related conditions).
    2. Qualitative defects (structural haemoglobin variants, haemoglobinopathies):
      • Sickle cell disease (HbS), HbC, HbD, HbE (which is also mildly thalassaemic).
      • Unstable haemoglobins (Heinz body haemolytic anaemias).
      • Haemoglobins with altered oxygen affinity (high affinity: polycythaemia
        Low affinity: cyanosis or anaemia).
      • M haemoglobins (methaemoglobinaemia).
    3. Combined disorders: HbS-β-thalassaemia, HbSC disease, HbE-β-thalassaemia.
    A7

    Define haemoglobinopathies.

    A7Q21, Q23

    Haemoglobinopathies are inherited disorders caused by mutations in the globin genes that produce structurally abnormal haemoglobin molecules, as opposed to thalassaemia, in which the globin chains are structurally normal but synthesised in reduced amounts.

    Several hundred haemoglobinopathies caused by mutations in globin genes are known, most of which are clinically silent. Only a few, namely sickle cell disease (HbS, in which a missense mutation replaces glutamic acid by valine at position 6 of the β-chain), and variants such as HbC (glutamic acid replaced by lysine) and HbE, are common enough to be of major clinical significance. The abnormal physicochemical properties of the variant haemoglobin cause polymerisation, instability, altered oxygen affinity or reduced solubility, leading to haemolysis and other consequences.

    A7

    Examples of haemoglobinopathies.

    A7Q21, Q23, Q27

    The commonest examples are sickle cell disease (HbS), haemoglobin C disease, haemoglobin E disease, haemoglobin D, unstable haemoglobins and M haemoglobins.

    • HbS (sickle cell disease and trait): β⁶ Glu→Val
      Polymerises on deoxygenation.
    • HbC: β⁶ Glu→Lys
      Mild haemolytic anaemia with target cells
      Compound HbSC heterozygotes have a symptomatic disorder, somewhat milder than sickle cell disease.
    • HbE: β²⁶ Glu→Lys
      Highly prevalent in Bangladesh, Thailand and Southeast Asia. Mild microcytosis, and with β-thalassaemia gives HbE-β-thalassaemia, a major cause of transfusion-dependent anaemia in the region.
    • HbD (Punjab), HbO-Arab and others, mild in the heterozygous state.
    • Unstable haemoglobins (Hb Köln, Hb Zürich): Heinz body haemolytic anaemia.
    • M haemoglobins: the haem iron is stabilised in the ferric state, causing cyanosis (methaemoglobinaemia).
    • High-oxygen-affinity variants: cause familial polycythaemia (Hb Chesapeake).

    Name the normal (and abnormal) haemoglobins.

    5DU22MDU20NDU20JuDU12JuDU11Ju

    Normal haemoglobins

    • Embryonic: Gower 1 (ζ₂ε₂), Gower 2 (α₂ε₂), Portland (ζ₂γ₂).
    • Foetal haemoglobin, HbF (α₂γ₂): the main foetal haemoglobin
      Less than 1% in adults.
    • Adult haemoglobin, HbA (α₂β₂): about 95% to 98% of adult haemoglobin.
    • HbA₂ (α₂δ₂): about 2.5% (± 0.3%).

    Abnormal haemoglobins

    • Structural variants (haemoglobinopathies): HbS (sickle haemoglobin), HbC, HbD, HbE, HbO-Arab, unstable haemoglobins (Hb Köln), M haemoglobins (HbM), and haemoglobins with altered oxygen affinity.
    • Tetramers of unpaired chains in thalassaemia: haemoglobin Barts (γ₄) in α-thalassaemia of the newborn and in hydrops fetalis. HbH (β₄) in HbH disease and older children and adults with α-thalassaemia. and excess free α chains in β-thalassaemia.
    • Elevated HbF in β-thalassaemia, hereditary persistence of foetal haemoglobin and sickle cell disease. Elevated HbA₂ in β-thalassaemia trait.
    • Derivative haemoglobins: methaemoglobin, sulphaemoglobin, carboxyhaemoglobin, glycated haemoglobin (HbA₁c).

    Write a short note on hemoglobinopathy.

    DU25MDU18NovDU17Ja

    Haemoglobinopathies are inherited disorders caused by mutations in globin genes that produce structurally abnormal haemoglobin, in contrast to thalassaemias, which result from reduced synthesis of structurally normal globin chains. Several hundred are known, but only those associated with sickle cell disease are prevalent enough in the United States to merit extensive discussion. in South Asia HbE is equally important.

    Genetic basis. Most variants result from a single amino acid substitution caused by a point mutation in the α- or β-globin gene. In sickle haemoglobin, a missense mutation in the β-globin gene replaces glutamic acid with valine at position 6. in HbC, glutamic acid is replaced by lysine.

    Classification by effect

    1. Polymerisation (HbS): sickle cell disease and trait.
    2. Reduced solubility and crystallisation (HbC and HbSC).
    3. Instability of haemoglobin (Heinz body anaemias).
    4. Altered oxygen affinity (polycythaemia or cyanosis).
    5. M haemoglobins (methaemoglobinaemia).
    6. Thalassaemic haemoglobinopathies (HbE, Hb Lepore).

    Clinical significance. The heterozygous state is usually asymptomatic (sickle cell trait, in about 8% to 10% of African Americans), and the homozygous or compound heterozygous state produces haemolytic anaemia and, in sickle cell disease, vaso-occlusive crises. The high prevalence in some populations results from the protective effect against falciparum malaria. Diagnosis is by haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, solubility and sickling tests, and DNA analysis. Prenatal diagnosis is possible, and newborn screening is routine in the United States.

    Thalassaemia

    A7

    Define thalassemia.

    9A7Q22, Q23, Q28, Q30DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU17JaDU07Ja

    Also asked as: Define thalassaemia.

    Thalassaemia is a genetically heterogeneous group of inherited disorders caused by germline mutations that decrease the synthesis of either α-globin or β-globin chains, leading to anaemia, tissue hypoxia and red cell haemolysis from the imbalance in globin chain synthesis.

    The two α chains of HbA are encoded by an identical pair of α-globin genes on chromosome 16, and the β chains by a single β-globin gene on chromosome 11. β-Thalassaemia is caused by deficient synthesis of β chains and α-thalassaemia by deficient synthesis of α chains. The haematological consequences of reduced synthesis of one chain stem not only from haemoglobin deficiency (hypochromic microcytic red cells with reduced oxygen carrying capacity) but also from the relative excess of the other chain, particularly in β-thalassaemia.

    Unpaired α chains precipitate in red cell precursors, causing membrane damage, apoptosis of precursors (ineffective erythropoiesis) and extravascular haemolysis of the released red cells. Thalassaemia is among the most common inherited disorders of humans, and its distribution (Mediterranean, Middle East, Africa, Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia) parallels that of malaria, from which heterozygous carriers are protected.

    A7

    How is thalassemia classified?

    5A7Q28, Q29DU20NDU20JuDU07Ja

    Also asked as: Classify thalassaemia.

    Thalassaemia is classified genetically into β-thalassaemia and α-thalassaemia according to the globin chain affected, and clinically into major, intermedia and minor (or trait) forms according to severity (Table 14.3).

    SyndromeGenotypeClinical featuresMolecular genetics
    β-ThalassaemiaMainly point mutations affecting transcription, splicing or translation of β-globin mRNA
    β-Thalassaemia majorβ⁰/β⁰, β⁺/β⁺, β⁰/β⁺Severe, transfusion-dependent anaemia
    β-Thalassaemia intermediaVariable (milder β⁺/β⁺ or β⁺/β⁰; unusual heterozygotes)Severe but not regularly transfusion-dependent
    β-Thalassaemia minor (trait)β⁰/β or β⁺/βAsymptomatic, mild or absent anaemia, microcytosis
    α-ThalassaemiaMainly gene deletions
    Silent carrier–α/αα (one gene deleted)Asymptomatic
    no abnormality or slight microcytosis
    α-Thalassaemia trait–/αα or –α/–α (two genes deleted)Asymptomatic, like β-thalassaemia minor
    HbH disease–/–α (three genes deleted)Moderately severe, resembling β-thalassaemia intermedia
    Hydrops fetalis (α-thalassaemia major)–/– (four genes deleted)Lethal in utero without transfusions

    β⁰ mutations result in absent β-globin synthesis, and β⁺ mutations in reduced but detectable synthesis.

    A7

    Clinical features of thalassaemia.

    A7Q22, Q28

    The clinical features of β-thalassaemia major are severe anaemia from 6 to 9 months of age, growth retardation, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal deformities with a mongoloid facies from marrow expansion, and iron overload, in contrast to the symptomless anaemia of the trait.

    β-Thalassaemia major. Anaemia appears 6 to 9 months after birth as haemoglobin synthesis switches from HbF to HbA. Untransfused haemoglobin is 3 to 6 g/dL. Features include pallor and mild jaundice, failure to thrive and growth retardation, marked hepatosplenomegaly caused by extramedullary haemopoiesis and phagocyte hyperplasia (spleen up to 1500 g), and the characteristic skeletal changes caused by expansion of the marrow: frontal and parietal bossing, prominent cheekbones and maxillary hypertrophy ("chipmunk" or mongoloid facies), and a "crew-cut" skull radiograph.

    Metabolically active erythroid progenitors cause cachexia. Excess iron, from increased gastrointestinal absorption (low hepcidin because of erythroferrone) and from transfusions, damages the heart (the main cause of death), liver, pancreas (diabetes) and other endocrine glands. Complications include gallstones, leg ulcers, and infections.

    β-Thalassaemia minor. Asymptomatic with mild microcytic anaemia.

    α-Thalassaemia. Silent carriers and trait are asymptomatic. HbH disease causes a moderately severe anaemia with splenomegaly. Hydrops fetalis causes severe pallor, oedema and hepatosplenomegaly, with intrauterine or neonatal death.

    A7

    Type of mutation in beta thalassaemia.

    A7Q29

    β-Thalassaemia is caused mostly by point mutations in the β-globin gene that disrupt splicing, transcription, or translation, and they are classified as β⁰ (absent synthesis) or β⁺ (reduced synthesis).

    More than 100 causative mutations have been described, falling into three major classes:

    1. Splicing mutations: the most common cause of β⁺-thalassaemia. Mutations that destroy normal splice junctions completely prevent the formation of normal β-globin mRNA (β⁰). Others create an ectopic splice site within an intron. Because the flanking normal splice site remains, both normal and abnormal splicing occur and some normal mRNA is made (β⁺).
    2. Promoter region mutations: reduce transcription by 75% to 80%, giving β⁺-thalassaemia.
    3. Chain terminator mutations: the most common cause of β⁰-thalassaemia
      Nonsense mutations that introduce a premature stop codon, or small insertions or deletions that shift the reading frame (frameshift), blocking translation.

    By contrast, α-thalassaemia is caused mainly by deletions of α-globin genes.

    A7

    Laboratory diagnosis of thalassaemia.

    A7Q29

    Thalassaemia is diagnosed by the finding of a hypochromic microcytic anaemia with target cells on the blood film, normal iron studies, and confirmation by haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC showing raised HbF and absent or reduced HbA in β-thalassaemia major, or raised HbA₂ in β-thalassaemia trait.

    Blood count. Haemoglobin 3 to 6 g/dL (untransfused β-thalassaemia major)
    Markedly reduced MCV and MCH
    Red cell count relatively high
    RDW normal in trait, raised in major. Reticulocytes are elevated, though lower than expected for the degree of anaemia because of ineffective erythropoiesis.

    Blood film. Marked anisopoikilocytosis, microcytosis and hypochromia, target cells, basophilic stippling, fragmented red cells and nucleated red cells (normoblasts). Inclusions of α chains are removed by the spleen and not seen.

    Iron studies. Normal or raised serum iron and ferritin (iron overload), which distinguishes it from iron deficiency.

    Haemoglobin analysis. Electrophoresis or HPLC: HbF markedly raised (30% to 90%) with absent (β⁰/β⁰) or reduced HbA in major
    HbA₂ raised to 4% to 8% in β-thalassaemia trait (normal 2.5%), HbF normal or slightly raised.

    Other. Bone marrow: erythroid hyperplasia (not needed)
    DNA analysis for the mutation and for prenatal diagnosis. Skull X-ray crew-cut appearance
    Family studies.

    A7

    PBF findings of thalassaemia major.

    A7Q30

    The film in β-thalassaemia major shows severe hypochromic microcytic anaemia with marked anisopoikilocytosis, numerous target cells, basophilic stippling, fragmented cells and many nucleated red cells.

    Blood smears show severe red cell abnormalities: marked variation in size (anisocytosis) and shape (poikilocytosis), microcytosis and hypochromia. Target cells (so called because haemoglobin collects in the centre of the cell), basophilic stippling and fragmented red cells are common. Variable numbers of poorly haemoglobinised nucleated red cell precursors (normoblasts) are seen in the peripheral blood, owing to "stress" erythropoiesis and abnormal release of precursors from sites of extramedullary haemopoiesis, the count increasing after splenectomy.

    The reticulocyte count is elevated but lower than expected for the severity of anaemia because of ineffective erythropoiesis. Inclusions of aggregated α chains are efficiently removed by the spleen and not easily seen. Tear-drop cells and Howell-Jolly bodies (after splenectomy) may be seen.

    A7

    Confirmatory test for thalassaemia.

    A7Q30

    The confirmatory test for thalassaemia is haemoglobin electrophoresis or high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), which shows raised HbF and absent or reduced HbA in β-thalassaemia major, and raised HbA₂ in β-thalassaemia trait.

    In β-thalassaemia major the major red cell haemoglobin is HbF, markedly elevated, and HbA is absent (β⁰/β⁰) or present in small amounts (β⁺ genotypes). In β-thalassaemia minor, HbA₂ (α₂δ₂) is increased to 4% to 8% of the total haemoglobin (normal 2.5% ± 0.3%), reflecting an elevated ratio of δ-chain to β-chain synthesis. HbF is normal or slightly increased. In HbH disease, HbH (β₄) and Hb Barts are demonstrable. α-Thalassaemia trait is diagnosed by exclusion (normal HbA₂, microcytosis) and by DNA analysis (gene deletion studies by multiplex PCR).

    Molecular analysis of DNA provides definitive diagnosis and permits prenatal diagnosis. Iron deficiency should be excluded, since it may reduce HbA₂ and mask the diagnosis of trait.

    Write the genetic basis of β-thalassemia major.

    DU19M

    The β-globin chains of HbA are encoded by a single β-globin gene on chromosome 11. β-thalassaemia major is an autosomal recessive disorder, in which an individual inherits two defective β-globin alleles (homozygous or compound heterozygous), one from each carrier parent. Parents with the β-thalassaemia trait carry a 25% risk in each pregnancy of having an affected child, 50% of having a carrier child and 25% of having a normal child.

    The causative mutations are mostly point mutations (more than 100 have been identified, not gene deletions), which are of two functional categories: β⁰ mutations, with absent β-globin synthesis, and β⁺ mutations, with reduced but detectable synthesis. They fall into three major classes:

    1. Splicing mutations: the most common cause of β⁺-thalassaemia
      Those that destroy normal splice junctions cause β⁰-thalassaemia, and those that create an ectopic splice site within an intron cause β⁺-thalassaemia, since some normal splicing persists.
    2. Promoter region mutations: reduce transcription by 75% to 80% (β⁺).
    3. Chain terminator mutations: the most common cause of β⁰-thalassaemia
      Nonsense mutations that produce premature stop codons, or frameshift insertions and deletions, that block translation.

    Genotypes β⁰/β⁰, β⁺/β⁺ and β⁰/β⁺ generally produce β-thalassaemia major. Impaired β-globin synthesis results in anaemia through hypochromia from HbA deficiency and, more importantly, through excess unpaired α chains that precipitate within red cell precursors, causing membrane damage and apoptosis of 70% to 85% of precursors (ineffective erythropoiesis) and shortened survival of released red cells. The coexistence of α-thalassaemia reduces the globin chain imbalance and ameliorates the disease, whereas extra α-gene copies worsen it.

    Give the laboratory diagnosis of thalassemia/β-thalassemia major.

    15DU25NDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19MDU17MDU17JaDU16JuDU14JuDU13JuDU12JaDU11JuDU10JuDU08JuDU06S

    The laboratory diagnosis of β-thalassaemia major rests on the blood count and film, haemoglobin analysis, iron studies and, where necessary, molecular tests.

    1. Complete blood count. Severe anaemia with haemoglobin typically 3 to 6 g/dL in untransfused patients
    MCV, MCH and MCHC markedly reduced
    Red cell count relatively preserved
    RDW raised
    Reticulocytes elevated but lower than expected for the anaemia (ineffective erythropoiesis). White cells and platelets raised or, with hypersplenism, reduced.

    2. Peripheral blood film. Severe hypochromia and microcytosis, with marked anisocytosis and poikilocytosis. Many target cells, basophilic stippling, teardrop and fragmented red cells. and numerous nucleated red cells (normoblasts), reflecting stress erythropoiesis and extramedullary haemopoiesis. After splenectomy, Howell-Jolly bodies and more nucleated cells appear.

    3. Haemoglobin analysis (confirmatory). Electrophoresis or HPLC shows markedly raised HbF (30% to 90%), HbA absent (β⁰/β⁰) or markedly reduced (β⁺), and HbA₂ normal or slightly raised. Parental studies show β-thalassaemia trait, with raised HbA₂ (4% to 8%).

    4. Iron studies. Serum iron, transferrin saturation and ferritin are raised (iron overload from increased absorption and transfusions), unlike in iron deficiency.

    5. Bone marrow. Marked erythroid hyperplasia (not necessary for diagnosis), and Prussian blue staining shows abundant iron.

    6. Other tests. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and raised LDH
    Radiographs showing the "crew-cut" skull and widened medullary cavities. DNA analysis for the causative mutations, which allows prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. Assessment of iron overload (ferritin, cardiac and hepatic T2* MRI) and endocrine function.

    A child has severe anemia, mongoloid face, hepatosplenomegaly, repeated transfusions, target cells. What is your probable diagnosis?

    9DU24NDU23NDU22NDU19NovDU18NovDU17NovDU11JaDU10JaDU08Ju

    The probable diagnosis is β-thalassaemia major (Cooley anaemia). The age of presentation (anaemia appearing from 6 to 9 months, as the HbF to HbA switch occurs), the severe transfusion-dependent anaemia, the mongoloid (chipmunk) facies due to expansion of the facial and skull marrow with frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth, hepatosplenomegaly resulting from extramedullary haemopoiesis, and target cells on the blood film are characteristic. Haemoglobinopathies such as HbE-β-thalassaemia present similarly, and are common in Bangladesh.

    The pathogenesis is a deficiency of β-globin chains with excess unpaired α chains, which precipitate in erythroid precursors and cause ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis. Iron overload from transfusions and increased intestinal absorption is the major long-term complication.

    Same child: how will you confirm the diagnosis?

    9DU24NDU23NDU22NDU19NovDU18NovDU17NovDU11JaDU10JaDU08Ju

    The diagnosis is confirmed by the following investigations.

    1. Complete blood count and peripheral blood film: severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia (Hb often 3 to 6 g/dL, MCV and MCH very low), anisopoikilocytosis, target cells, basophilic stippling, fragmented cells and nucleated red cells. Reticulocytosis lower than expected for the degree of anaemia.
    2. Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC (the confirmatory test): markedly raised HbF, with absent or markedly reduced HbA. HbA₂ normal or raised. In HbE-β-thalassaemia, HbE is prominent.
    3. Iron studies: raised serum iron and ferritin with high transferrin saturation, excluding iron deficiency.
    4. Family study: both parents show a microcytic picture with raised HbA₂ (4% to 8%) of β-thalassaemia trait.
    5. DNA analysis: molecular identification of the β-globin mutations (also used for prenatal diagnosis).
    6. Supportive: raised unconjugated bilirubin and LDH, skull radiograph showing the "crew-cut" appearance, and ultrasound for hepatosplenomegaly.

    Sickle cell anaemia

    A7

    Which type of abnormal haemoglobin is found in sickle cell anaemia?

    A7Q25

    The abnormal haemoglobin in sickle cell anaemia is haemoglobin S (HbS), which results from a point mutation in the β-globin gene that replaces glutamic acid with valine at position 6 of the β-chain.

    In the homozygous state, almost all the haemoglobin of the red cell is HbS (α₂βˢ₂), with a variable amount of HbF and no HbA. The substitution of a charged glutamate by a hydrophobic valine allows deoxygenated HbS molecules to polymerise into long needlelike fibres, which distort the red cell into a sickle or holly-leaf shape. In heterozygotes (sickle cell trait), about 40% of the haemoglobin is HbS and the rest HbA, which interferes with polymerisation, so the trait is largely asymptomatic. In compound heterozygotes for HbS and HbC (HbSC disease), 50% of the haemoglobin is HbS, giving a symptomatic but somewhat milder disease.

    A7

    Clinical features of sickle cell anaemia.

    A7Q25, Q26

    Sickle cell anaemia presents with chronic haemolytic anaemia and jaundice, punctuated by painful vaso-occlusive crises, and is complicated by splenic autoinfarction, increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms, and chronic organ damage.

    Infants are protected by HbF and become symptomatic at about 5 to 6 months of age.

    Chronic haemolytic anaemia. Moderate to severe anaemia, jaundice, pigment gallstones, reticulocytosis, and expanded marrow with skeletal changes ("crew-cut" skull).

    Crises.

    • Vaso-occlusive (pain) crises: episodes of hypoxic injury and infarction, in bones, lungs, liver, brain, spleen and penis. In children, hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) is frequent and may be confused with osteomyelitis.
    • Acute chest syndrome: fever, cough, chest pain and pulmonary infiltrates. Potentially fatal.
    • Priapism: in up to 45% of postpubertal males.
    • Stroke and retinopathy, which may lead to blindness.
    • Sequestration crisis: in children with intact spleens, massive splenic enlargement, hypovolaemia and shock.
    • Aplastic crisis: parvovirus B19 infection of red cell progenitors, causing a sudden worsening of anaemia.

    Spleen. Enlarged in early childhood by congestion, then progressive fibrosis and infarction leading to autosplenectomy by adolescence or early adulthood, with Howell-Jolly bodies.

    Infections. Impaired splenic function and defective alternative complement pathway lead to susceptibility to Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Salmonella osteomyelitis
    Reduced by vaccination and prophylactic penicillin.

    Other. Leg ulcers in adults, hyposthenuria and renal papillary necrosis, growth retardation, cor pulmonale, and chronic organ damage.

    A7

    How does leg ulcer occur in sickle cell anaemia?

    A7Q26

    Leg ulcers in sickle cell anaemia result from chronic vascular stasis and microvascular occlusion by sickled red cells in the subcutaneous tissues of the lower limb, leading to ischaemia and skin breakdown, usually after minor trauma.

    The skin over the ankles and lower legs has a sluggish circulation, with high venous pressure and slow transit times, which favours deoxygenation, polymerisation of HbS and sickling. Sticky sickled cells, with raised adhesion molecules, adhere to the endothelium and arrest in the microcirculation, which is further compromised by endothelial dysfunction from depletion of nitric oxide by free haemoglobin released in haemolysis (leading to vasoconstriction), inflammation and thrombosis.

    The resulting ischaemic damage and chronic hypoxia (aggravated by anaemia) impair healing, so minor trauma produces an ulcer. Vascular stagnation in subcutaneous tissues leads to leg ulcers in adult patients, but the complication is rare in children. The ulcers are typically painful, heal slowly and recur.

    A7

    Laboratory diagnosis of sickle cell anaemia.

    A7Q27

    Sickle cell anaemia is diagnosed by the finding of a normocytic haemolytic anaemia with irreversibly sickled cells on the film, demonstration of sickle haemoglobin by a sickling or solubility test, and confirmation by haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC.

    1. Blood count: haemoglobin 6 to 9 g/dL (low), normocytic normochromic
      Reticulocytosis
      Neutrophil leukocytosis and thrombocytosis.
    2. Blood film: variable numbers of irreversibly sickled cells, target cells (from dehydration), polychromasia, nucleated red cells and Howell-Jolly bodies (autosplenectomy).
    3. Sickling test: a drop of blood is mixed with a reducing agent, such as 2% sodium metabisulphite, under a sealed coverslip, and sickling is observed microscopically. Positive in both trait and disease.
    4. Solubility test: HbS is insoluble in a concentrated phosphate buffer with dithionite, producing turbidity.
    5. Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC (confirmatory): HbS above 80% with no HbA in the homozygote, HbF 2% to 20%, normal HbA₂
      HbAS (trait) has about 40% HbS with HbA predominating. Also detects HbSC and HbS-β-thalassaemia.
    6. Biochemical evidence of haemolysis: raised unconjugated bilirubin and LDH, low haptoglobin.
    7. Others: DNA analysis, prenatal diagnosis (amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling), and routine newborn screening using heel-stick samples.

    Aplastic Anaemia and Pancytopenia

    A6A7

    What is pancytopenia?

    13A6A7Q19DU25NDU24MDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU16JaDU14JaDU12JaDU10Ja

    Also asked as: Define pancytopenia.

    Pancytopenia is the simultaneous reduction of all three formed elements of blood, namely anaemia, leukopenia (particularly neutropenia) and thrombocytopenia, and it is a laboratory finding that reflects a number of different underlying disorders rather than a diagnosis in itself.

    Typical working criteria are haemoglobin below the reference range (often below 10 g/dL), a total leukocyte count below 4 × 10⁹/L and a platelet count below 150 × 10⁹/L (frequently below 100 × 10⁹/L). The reduction may result from decreased production in the marrow (aplastic anaemia, marrow infiltration, megaloblastic anaemia, myelodysplasia), from increased peripheral destruction or sequestration (hypersplenism), or from a combination of these mechanisms.

    The clinical consequences correspond to the deficiency of each cell line: anaemia produces weakness, pallor and dyspnoea. Neutropenia produces frequent and persistent infections, fever and prostration. and thrombocytopenia produces petechiae, ecchymoses and mucosal bleeding. Aplastic anaemia is the prototype of a disorder with pancytopenia and a hypocellular marrow, whereas in leukaemia, myelodysplasia, megaloblastic anaemia and marrow infiltration, the marrow is usually hypercellular or infiltrated.

    A6A7A10

    Write down the important causes of pancytopenia.

    14A6A7Q19, Q20A10Q9DU25NDU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU16JaDU14JaDU12JaDU10Ja

    Also asked as: Causes of pancytopenia.

    The important causes of pancytopenia are marrow failure as in aplastic anaemia, marrow infiltration by leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma or metastatic cancer, megaloblastic anaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, and hypersplenism.

    A. Decreased marrow production, with a hypocellular marrow

    • Aplastic anaemia: idiopathic (about 65% of cases), drugs (chemotherapeutic agents, chloramphenicol, gold salts, sulphonamides, NSAIDs, antithyroid drugs and carbamazepine), chemicals (benzene, insecticides), ionising radiation, viral infections (hepatitis, which accounts for about 5% of cases, EBV, CMV, parvovirus, HIV, herpes zoster), and inherited defects (Fanconi anaemia, telomerase defects, dyskeratosis congenita).
    • Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (with aplastic anaemia).

    B. Marrow infiltration, with a hypercellular or replaced marrow

    • Acute leukaemias (including aleukaemic forms), hairy cell leukaemia, lymphomas, multiple myeloma.
    • Myelofibrosis, metastatic carcinoma (breast, lung, prostate), granulomatous disease (tuberculosis, sarcoidosis), storage diseases (Gaucher disease), and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

    C. Ineffective haemopoiesis

    • Megaloblastic anaemia (vitamin B₁₂ and folate deficiency), myelodysplastic neoplasms.

    D. Peripheral destruction or sequestration

    • Hypersplenism (cirrhosis with portal hypertension, myelofibrosis, Gaucher disease, Felty syndrome, lymphomas).
    • Systemic lupus erythematosus and other autoimmune disorders (Evans syndrome), with overwhelming sepsis, kala-azar, malaria, miliary tuberculosis and HIV infection.
    A6A7

    How will you diagnose/investigate a case of pancytopenia?

    6A6A7Q19DU10JuDU07JuDU07JaDU05M

    Also asked as: How will you investigate a case of pancytopenia?

    I would confirm pancytopenia with a complete blood count and a peripheral blood film, then examine the bone marrow by aspiration and trephine biopsy, which is the decisive investigation, and look for the underlying cause with directed tests.

    1. History and examination. Exposure to drugs, chemicals, radiation, preceding viral illness, diet and alcohol, family history (Fanconi anaemia: short stature, thumb and radial anomalies, skin pigmentation). Symptoms of anaemia, infection and bleeding
      and enlargement of the spleen, liver or lymph nodes. Splenomegaly characteristically is absent in aplastic anaemia, and its presence should lead to question that diagnosis.
    2. Blood count and film. Degree of cytopenia and indices (normocytic or macrocytic red cells, low reticulocyte count). Search the film for blasts, dysplastic cells, nucleated red cells, hypersegmented neutrophils, teardrop cells, or parasites.
    3. Bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy. This distinguishes the principal causes: a markedly hypocellular marrow with fat, fibrous stroma and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells (aplastic anaemia, best shown on biopsy). a hypercellular marrow with blasts (leukaemia), megaloblasts (megaloblastic anaemia) or dysplasia (myelodysplastic neoplasm). Infiltration by lymphoma, myeloma or metastatic tumour, fibrosis (myelofibrosis) or granulomas. Cytogenetics and flow cytometry as necessary.
    4. Further tests. Serum B₁₂ and folate
      Liver function and viral serology (hepatitis, EBV, CMV, HIV, parvovirus). Antinuclear antibodies and anti-dsDNA
      Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 (PNH)
      Chromosomal breakage test (Fanconi anaemia)
      Telomere length
      Abdominal ultrasound to assess the spleen and liver. Chest radiography.
    A6A7

    Blood and bone marrow picture of aplastic anaemia.

    A6A7Q20

    Aplastic anaemia shows pancytopenia in the blood, with normocytic or slightly macrocytic normochromic red cells and a low reticulocyte count, and a markedly hypocellular marrow in which haemopoietic cells are largely replaced by fat.

    Blood. Anaemia, leukopenia (particularly granulocytopenia with relative lymphocytosis) and thrombocytopenia. The red cells are usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic. Reticulocytopenia is the rule. There are no abnormal or immature cells, and no nucleated red cells or teardrop cells. The ESR is raised.

    Bone marrow. The marrow is markedly hypocellular, largely devoid of haemopoietic cells. Often only fat cells, fibrous stroma and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells remain. Aspirates often yield little material (a "dry tap") or are diluted with blood, so aplasia is best appreciated in trephine biopsy, which shows less than 25% cellularity (in severe cases) with no fibrosis, no abnormal infiltrate and no blasts. Residual haemopoietic cells appear normal. Iron stores are increased, and in transfused patients systemic haemosiderosis can appear.

    A6

    Why does pancytopenia occur in acute leukaemia?

    A6

    Pancytopenia in acute leukaemia occurs because the proliferating leukaemic blasts replace and suppress the normal haemopoietic cells in the marrow, so that production of red cells, normal granulocytes and platelets all fail.

    The neoplastic cells accumulate in the marrow, crowd out and displace normal haemopoietic precursors and the supporting stroma, and produce inhibitory cytokines and factors that suppress normal stem cell proliferation and differentiation. The result is anaemia, neutropenia (despite a possibly high total white cell count made up of blasts) and thrombocytopenia. These are responsible for the presenting manifestations of acute leukaemia: fatigue and pallor, recurrent infections and fever, and bleeding (petechiae, epistaxis, gum bleeding), with additional platelet consumption in DIC in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

    In "aleukaemic" or subleukaemic leukaemia the peripheral count shows pancytopenia with few or no circulating blasts, which may mimic aplastic anaemia, and the distinction depends on the marrow. Treatment with chemotherapy further depresses the marrow.

    A6

    Why does pancytopenia occur in some cases of splenomegaly?

    A6

    Pancytopenia in splenomegaly is due to hypersplenism, in which the enlarged spleen sequesters and destroys blood cells and expands the plasma volume, so that all cell counts fall while the marrow is normal or hyperplastic.

    The red pulp of an enlarged spleen sequesters a large fraction of the circulating cells: the spleen normally holds 30% to 35% of the body's platelets, but this can rise to 80% to 90% when the spleen is enlarged. Red cells and granulocytes are similarly pooled, and these cells are exposed to prolonged contact with macrophages, which phagocytose and destroy them (the splenic environment is also hostile to metabolism: low glucose and low pH).

    In addition, splenic enlargement expands the plasma volume, causing a dilutional fall of the haemoglobin. The marrow is normocellular or hyperplastic as it responds to peripheral destruction, a point that distinguishes this from marrow failure. The criteria of hypersplenism are cytopenia, splenomegaly, a cellular marrow and correction after splenectomy. Examples are portal hypertension from cirrhosis, myelofibrosis, Gaucher disease, lymphomas, Felty syndrome, malaria and kala-azar.

    A8

    How will you differentiate aplastic anaemia from subleukaemic acute leukaemia in the laboratory?

    A8Q16

    The distinction rests on the bone marrow: aplastic anaemia has a hypocellular fatty marrow without blasts, whereas subleukaemic acute leukaemia has a hypercellular marrow packed with leukaemic blasts, even though both show pancytopenia with few or no blasts in the blood.

    FeatureAplastic anaemiaSubleukaemic (aleukaemic) acute leukaemia
    Peripheral bloodPancytopenia
    no blasts
    Lymphocytes relatively increased    		Pancytopenia
