    Write down the causes of marrow aplasia.

    DU11Ju

    Marrow aplasia (aplastic anaemia) is a syndrome of chronic primary haemopoietic failure with pancytopenia. The causes are as follows.

    1. Idiopathic: about 65% of cases, in which no initiating factor can be identified.
    2. Drugs and chemicals:
      • Dose-related, predictable and reversible: cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents, benzene and other organic solvents.
      • Idiosyncratic, unpredictable: chloramphenicol, gold salts, sulphonamides, phenylbutazone, carbamazepine, antithyroid drugs and others.
    3. Ionising radiation: whole-body irradiation destroys haemopoietic stem cells in a dose-dependent fashion (therapeutic radiation, nuclear accidents).
    4. Infections: viral hepatitis (seronegative hepatitis in about 5% of cases), Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes zoster, parvovirus B19, HIV, and rarely miliary tuberculosis.
    5. Inherited disorders: Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive DNA repair defect with congenital anomalies), telomerase defects (found in 5% to 10% of adult-onset aplastic anaemia) and dyskeratosis congenita.
    6. Immune-mediated: autoimmune suppression of stem cells by activated T cells (interferon-γ), eosinophilic fasciitis, thymoma, SLE.
    7. Other associations: pregnancy, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, and transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.

    What are the clinical presentations of pancytopenia?

    DU07Ju

    The clinical presentation of pancytopenia reflects the deficiency of each cell line and the underlying disease. The onset is usually insidious.

    • Anaemia: progressive weakness, fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea on exertion, palpitations, headache, dizziness, and angina in those with coronary disease.
    • Neutropenia: frequent and persistent infections (mucocutaneous bacterial infections, oral ulcers, sore throat, pneumonia), or the sudden onset of chills, fever and prostration. Fungal infections in prolonged neutropenia.
    • Thrombocytopenia: petechiae and ecchymoses, easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, haematuria, and, most feared, intracranial haemorrhage.
    • Signs of the underlying cause: splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain or sternal tenderness (leukaemia or infiltration), neurological signs and glossitis (megaloblastic anaemia), congenital anomalies and short stature (Fanconi anaemia), jaundice and cirrhosis (hypersplenism), and rash and arthritis (SLE). Splenomegaly is characteristically absent in aplastic anaemia.

    Give the laboratory diagnosis of aplastic anemia (PBF and bone marrow findings).

    8DU20NDU20JuDU19NovDU18MDU16JaDU14JaDU12JaDU11Ju

    Peripheral blood

    • Pancytopenia: anaemia (normocytic or slightly macrocytic, normochromic), granulocytopenia with relatively increased lymphocytes, and thrombocytopenia.
    • Reticulocytopenia (reticulocyte count usually below 1% and absolute count below 20 × 10⁹/L in severe disease).
    • Film: no immature cells, blasts, nucleated red cells or teardrop cells. Platelets are reduced and normal in size.
    • ESR is raised
      Serum iron raised with high transferrin saturation. Erythropoietin raised.

    Bone marrow

    • The aspirate often yields little material (a "dry tap") or is haemodiluted
      The aspirate shows fat, lymphocytes, plasma cells, mast cells and a few residual haemopoietic cells that appear normal.
    • Trephine biopsy is diagnostic: the marrow is markedly hypocellular and largely devoid of haemopoietic cells. Often only fat cells, fibrous stroma and scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells remain. No leukaemic infiltrate, fibrosis or granuloma. Cellularity below 25% defines severe disease.

    Criteria of severity (severe aplastic anaemia). Marrow cellularity below 25% (or 25% to 50% with fewer than 30% residual haemopoietic cells), with at least two of: neutrophils below 0.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets below 20 × 10⁹/L, reticulocytes below 20 × 10⁹/L
    Very severe if neutrophils are below 0.2 × 10⁹/L.

    Further tests. Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 (PNH clone), chromosomal breakage test for Fanconi anaemia, telomere length, cytogenetics (to exclude myelodysplasia), and viral serology.

    A boy of 11y has Hb 2 g, WBC 500/cmm, platelets 12000/cmm. What is the probable diagnosis?

    DU12Ja

    The probable diagnosis is severe aplastic anaemia. The picture is of profound pancytopenia: a haemoglobin of 2 g/dL, a total white cell count of 500 per cubic millimetre (neutrophils probably well below 200, therefore very severe disease) and a platelet count of 12,000 per cubic millimetre (below the 20,000 threshold for severe disease). This degree of marrow failure causes progressive weakness and pallor, persistent infections or fever, and petechial bleeding. In an 11-year-old, the possible causes are idiopathic (most likely), drug or viral-associated, and inherited, notably Fanconi anaemia.

    The principal differentials are aleukaemic acute leukaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasm and megaloblastic anaemia, which are distinguished by bone marrow examination. Confirmation requires a bone marrow trephine biopsy showing a markedly hypocellular marrow with fat replacement (cellularity below 25%), with no blasts, fibrosis or infiltrate, and a low reticulocyte count. Chromosomal breakage tests for Fanconi anaemia, PNH flow cytometry and viral serology complete the evaluation.

    Treatment is stem cell transplantation from an HLA-matched sibling if available (5-year survival above 75%), or immunosuppressive therapy with antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporine, with supportive care.

    Bleeding and Coagulation Disorders

    Bleeding disorders

    A9

    Define hemorrhagic disorders with example.

    A9Q21DU24N

    Also asked as: Define haemorrhagic disorder.

    Haemorrhagic disorders (haemorrhagic diatheses) are conditions characterised by abnormal or excessive bleeding, spontaneously or after minor trauma, due to defects in the blood vessel wall, in platelets, or in the coagulation system, alone or in combination.

    Haemostasis depends on the integrity of the vessel wall, adequate numbers and function of platelets, and the coagulation cascade with its regulating fibrinolytic system. Failure of any component produces bleeding, with a characteristic pattern. Examples are: vessel wall disorders (scurvy, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, Henoch-Schönlein purpura). Platelet disorders (immune thrombocytopenic purpura, aplastic anaemia, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, aspirin effect). and coagulation disorders (haemophilia A and B, von Willebrand disease, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease and disseminated intravascular coagulation).

    A9

    Classify haemorrhagic disorder.

    A9Q21

    Haemorrhagic disorders are classified according to the component of haemostasis that is defective into vascular, platelet and coagulation disorders.

    GroupSubtypes and examples
    Vascular (vessel wall) disordersInherited: hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Acquired: infections (meningococcaemia, septicaemia, infective endocarditis, rickettsial infections), drug reactions (hypersensitivity vasculitis), scurvy, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, Cushing syndrome and senile purpura, amyloidosis
    Platelet disordersQuantitative (thrombocytopenia): decreased production (aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, drugs, alcohol, HIV, megaloblastic anaemia)
    Decreased survival (ITP, drug-induced, DIC, TTP/HUS, HIV)
    Sequestration (hypersplenism)
    Dilution (massive transfusion). Qualitative (functional): Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, storage pool disorders, aspirin and NSAIDs, uraemia
    Coagulation disordersInherited: haemophilia A, haemophilia B, von Willebrand disease, other factor deficiencies. Acquired: vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC, anticoagulant therapy, inhibitors (autoantibodies to single factors)
    Combinedvon Willebrand disease (platelet adhesion and factor VIII), DIC (platelet and factor consumption), uraemia
    A9

    Approach to diagnosing a patient with a bleeding disorder.

    A9Q21

    I would approach the patient by taking a detailed bleeding history, noting the site and pattern of the bleeding, examining for petechiae or haematomas and signs of an underlying disease, and then performing screening tests (platelet count, PT and PTT) followed by specific tests.

    History. Age at onset, the pattern (spontaneous or after trauma, surgery, dental extraction), sites of bleeding, family history (X-linked inheritance in haemophilia, autosomal dominant in von Willebrand disease), drugs (aspirin, NSAIDs, warfarin, heparin, antibiotics), alcohol, liver or renal disease, and menstrual history.

    Clinical pattern. Bleeding from vessel wall and platelet disorders is mucocutaneous and immediate: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, and gastrointestinal bleeding, with small superficial bruises. Bleeding from coagulation factor deficiency is deep and delayed: large post-traumatic ecchymoses and haematomas, haemarthrosis, muscle bleeds and prolonged bleeding after surgery or tooth extraction, and petechiae are characteristically absent.

    Screening tests. Platelet count, with blood film, PT, PTT (and thrombin time and fibrinogen), and bleeding time (now largely replaced by platelet function tests). The pattern separates the groups: isolated low platelets with normal PT and PTT indicates thrombocytopenia. Normal platelets, normal PT and PTT suggests vascular or platelet function disorder. Prolonged PTT with normal PT suggests factor VIII, IX or XI deficiency or von Willebrand disease. Prolonged PT alone suggests factor VII deficiency, early warfarin or vitamin K deficiency. Both prolonged suggests liver disease, DIC or a common-pathway defect.

    Specific tests. Mixing studies, factor assays (VIII, IX), von Willebrand factor antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity, platelet aggregation studies, fibrin degradation products and D-dimers, and bone marrow examination for thrombocytopenia of uncertain cause.

    A9

    What are the causes of haemorrhagic disorders?

    A9Q19DU03M

    Also asked as: Causes of haemorrhagic disorders.

    The causes of haemorrhagic disorders are increased fragility of vessels, platelet deficiency or dysfunction, and derangement of coagulation, alone or in combination.

    1. Vessel wall abnormalities: infections (meningococcaemia, other septicaemias, infective endocarditis, rickettsioses) causing vasculitis or DIC
      Drug reactions (immune-complex hypersensitivity vasculitis). Scurvy and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (collagen defects)
      Acquired fragility in older adults and Cushing syndrome. Henoch-Schönlein purpura
      Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
      and perivascular amyloidosis. The platelet count and the PT and PTT are normal.
    2. Platelet disorders:
      • Thrombocytopenia: decreased production (aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, drugs, alcohol, HIV, megaloblastic anaemia), decreased survival (ITP, drugs including heparin, DIC, TTP and HUS), sequestration in hypersplenism, and dilution.
      • Qualitative defects: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GpIb/IX), Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa), storage pool disorders, aspirin and other NSAIDs, and uraemia.
    3. Coagulation disorders:
    • Inherited: haemophilia A (factor VIII), haemophilia B (factor IX), von Willebrand disease.
    • Acquired: vitamin K deficiency (factors II, VII, IX, X), liver disease (decreased synthesis), DIC (consumption), anticoagulant therapy and inhibitors.
    A9

    What do you mean by coagulation disorders?

    A9Q1DU08Ju

    Also asked as: What do you mean by coagulation disorder?

    Coagulation disorders are bleeding disorders caused by a quantitative or qualitative deficiency of one or more of the plasma clotting factors, or by the presence of inhibitors, resulting in defective fibrin clot formation.

    Bleeding due to coagulation factor deficiencies commonly manifests as large post-traumatic ecchymoses or haematomas, or prolonged bleeding from a laceration or after a surgical procedure. Bleeding often occurs in the gastrointestinal and urinary tracts and in weight-bearing joints (haemarthrosis). Petechiae are absent, unlike in thrombocytopenia. Typical stories include the patient who oozes blood for days after a tooth extraction or who develops haemarthrosis after minor stress on a knee joint.

    Hereditary deficiencies typically affect a single clotting factor (haemophilia A, factor VIII; haemophilia B, factor IX; von Willebrand disease). Acquired deficiencies usually involve multiple factors, from decreased synthesis (vitamin K deficiency, liver disease), consumption (DIC), or inhibitors, such as autoantibodies to factor VIII or heparin and warfarin therapy.

    A9

    Classify coagulation disorders.

    4A9Q1DU22NDU15JaDU11Ju

    Coagulation disorders are classified as inherited or acquired, depending on whether the factor deficiency is genetic or arises from another disease or from drugs.

    A. Inherited (hereditary) coagulation disorders

    • Factor VIII deficiency (haemophilia A, X-linked recessive), the most common.
    • Factor IX deficiency (haemophilia B, Christmas disease, X-linked recessive).
    • Von Willebrand disease (autosomal dominant, rarely recessive), the most common inherited bleeding disorder.
    • Factor XI deficiency (haemophilia C, autosomal), and rarer deficiencies of fibrinogen (afibrinogenaemia, dysfibrinogenaemia), prothrombin, and factors V, VII, X and XIII.

    B. Acquired coagulation disorders

    1. Decreased synthesis: vitamin K deficiency (obstructive jaundice, malabsorption, haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, warfarin), which affects factors II, VII, IX and X and protein C. Parenchymal liver disease.
    2. Increased consumption: disseminated intravascular coagulation.
    3. Inhibitors: circulating anticoagulants such as heparin, antibodies to factor VIII (in haemophilia A on treatment, or autoimmune acquired haemophilia), and the lupus anticoagulant (which prolongs PTT in vitro but causes thrombosis rather than bleeding).
    4. Increased fibrinolysis: primary hyperfibrinolysis (prostate surgery, thrombolytic therapy).
    A9

    What is bleeding time?

    A9Q22

    Bleeding time is the time taken for bleeding to stop from a standardised skin puncture or incision, and it measures the function of platelets and their interaction with the vessel wall, that is, the primary haemostatic plug.

    In the Duke method a small puncture is made in the earlobe or fingertip, and blood is blotted every 30 seconds until bleeding stops. in the Ivy method a sphygmomanometer cuff is inflated to 40 mmHg on the forearm and a puncture or standardised incision (template method) is made. The bleeding time is prolonged in thrombocytopenia, qualitative platelet defects (Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, aspirin), von Willebrand disease and some vascular disorders, and it is normal in coagulation factor deficiencies such as haemophilia.

    It is time-consuming, hard to standardise and an unreliable predictor of surgical bleeding, so the older bleeding time test has been discarded in many centres and replaced by platelet function analysis.

    A9

    What is clotting time?

    A9Q22

    Clotting time is the time taken for freshly drawn venous whole blood to clot in a glass tube under standard conditions, and it is a crude test of the overall intrinsic coagulation pathway.

    In the Lee-White method, 2 mL of venous blood is drawn into a clean glass tube at 37°C, and the tube is tilted every 30 seconds until the blood no longer flows. The elapsed time is the clotting time. It is prolonged when there is a marked deficiency of factors of the intrinsic and common pathways (factors VIII, IX, XI, XII, X, V, II) or fibrinogen, in the presence of heparin, and in DIC. it is insensitive and normal in mild deficiencies (factor levels must fall below about 1% to 5% for it to be prolonged), and for this reason it has been superseded by the PTT, which is more sensitive and standardised. It is normal in thrombocytopenia and vascular disorders.

    A9

    Normal limits of bleeding time and clotting time.

    A9Q22

    The normal bleeding time is about 2 to 7 minutes by the Duke and Ivy methods, and the normal whole blood clotting time is about 4 to 10 minutes by the Lee-White method.

    TestMethodNormal range
    Bleeding timeDuke (earlobe/fingertip)About 2–7 minutes (many laboratories accept up to 5 minutes)
    Ivy (forearm, cuff at 40 mmHg)About 2–7 minutes
    Clotting timeLee-White (venous blood, glass tubes at 37°C)About 4–10 minutes
    Capillary tube methodAbout 3–7 minutes

    Reference ranges vary with the method and the laboratory. Related tests have the normal ranges PT 11–15 seconds, PTT 25–40 seconds (compared with a control), and platelet count 150,000–350,000 per µL.

    A9

    Tests / screening tests / investigations for bleeding (haemorrhagic) disorders.

    A9Q15, Q22, Q23

    The screening tests for bleeding disorders are the platelet count, the prothrombin time (PT) and the partial thromboplastin time (PTT), supplemented by the bleeding time or platelet function tests, thrombin time and fibrinogen, and followed by specific tests according to the abnormality.

    1. Platelet count and peripheral blood film (150 to 350 × 10³/µL; confirm abnormal counts by film, since platelet clumping causes spurious thrombocytopenia).
    2. Prothrombin time (PT): tests the extrinsic and common pathways (factors V, VII, X, prothrombin and fibrinogen). Prolonged in vitamin K deficiency, warfarin therapy, liver disease and DIC.
    3. Partial thromboplastin time (PTT/aPTT): tests the intrinsic and common pathways (factors V, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, prothrombin and fibrinogen). Prolonged in haemophilia A and B, von Willebrand disease, heparin therapy, DIC, and with antiphospholipid antibodies.
    4. Thrombin time and fibrinogen assay: abnormalities of fibrinogen, heparin effect, and fibrin degradation products.
    5. Tests of platelet function: platelet aggregation studies (with ADP, collagen, epinephrine, ristocetin), von Willebrand factor antigen and activity (ristocetin cofactor), and the bleeding time (older, now largely discarded).
    6. Specific factor assays (factor VIII, IX and others), mixing studies to distinguish a factor deficiency (correction) from an inhibitor (no correction), and screening for circulating anticoagulants.
    7. Fibrin degradation products and D-dimers for DIC and fibrinolysis
      Clot retraction and clot solubility tests.
    8. Bone marrow examination for unexplained thrombocytopenia.
    A9

    Two causes of raised prothrombin time.

    A9Q23

    Two important causes of a raised prothrombin time are vitamin K deficiency (or oral warfarin therapy) and severe liver disease.

    The PT assesses the extrinsic and common pathways, and it is prolonged by deficiency or dysfunction of factors V, VII, X, prothrombin and fibrinogen. Warfarin inhibits the vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S), and the PT, which is sensitive to the short-lived factor VII, is the test used to monitor therapy (expressed as the INR).

    Vitamin K deficiency occurs in obstructive jaundice, malabsorption and with antibiotic therapy. In liver disease, there is reduced synthesis of nearly all coagulation factors. The prolongation of vitamin K deficiency is corrected by parenteral vitamin K, whereas that of hepatocellular failure is not. Other causes are DIC (consumption), factor VII deficiency, and a lack of fibrinogen.

    A9

    Normal findings in ITP, haemophilia and DIC in haemorrhagic screening tests.

    A9Q24

    In ITP only the platelet count (and bleeding time) is abnormal, in haemophilia only the PTT is prolonged, and in DIC the platelet count is low and the PT, PTT and thrombin time are all prolonged with low fibrinogen and raised D-dimers.

    TestITPHaemophilia A / BDIC
    Platelet countDecreasedNormalDecreased
    Bleeding timeProlongedNormalProlonged
    Prothrombin time (PT)NormalNormalProlonged
    Partial thromboplastin time (PTT)NormalProlongedProlonged
    Thrombin timeNormalNormalProlonged
    FibrinogenNormalNormalDecreased
    Fibrin degradation products / D-dimerNormalNormalIncreased
    Clotting timeNormalProlongedProlonged

    The normal findings in each disorder are the tests that remain normal, which are used to localise the defect.

    A9

    What is von Willebrand factor?

    A9Q2

    Von Willebrand factor (vWF) is a large multimeric plasma glycoprotein, synthesised by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes, that promotes the adhesion of platelets to the subendothelial matrix and stabilises coagulation factor VIII in the circulation.

    vWF is made by endothelial cells and by megakaryocytes, which are the source of the vWF in platelet α-granules. Secreted into the circulation, it exists as multimers containing up to 100 subunits, which can exceed 20 × 10⁶ daltons in mass. Some is deposited in the subendothelial matrix. The largest multimers are the most active. Factor VIII circulates bound to vWF, which increases its half-life from about 2.4 to 12 hours. vWF is cleaved and regulated by the metalloprotease ADAMTS13. Deficiency of the latter causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Its deficiency or dysfunction causes von Willebrand disease, the commonest inherited bleeding disorder.

    A9

    Functions of von Willebrand factor.

    A9Q2

    The two main functions of vWF are to mediate platelet adhesion to the subendothelial matrix at sites of vascular injury, and to carry and stabilise factor VIII in the plasma.

    1. Platelet adhesion: the most important haemostatic function. It forms a bridge between platelet glycoprotein Ib/IX and subendothelial components such as collagen, anchoring platelets to the injured vessel wall.
    2. Platelet aggregation: vWF can promote aggregation by binding to activated glycoprotein IIb/IIIa integrins, which is particularly important under high shear stress, as in small vessels.
    3. Carrier of factor VIII: binds and stabilises factor VIII, prolonging its half-life. Deficiency of vWF thus lowers factor VIII levels and prolongs the PTT.
    4. It also interacts with collagen, heparin and other proteins involved in haemostasis.

    Function is measured by the ristocetin cofactor (agglutination) assay: ristocetin makes vWF multimers bind to platelet GpIb/IX, so that the clumping of normal formalin-fixed platelets reflects the vWF activity.

    A9

    Why are both bleeding time and clotting time prolonged in von Willebrand disease?

    A9Q18

    Both are prolonged because vWF has a double function: it is required for platelet adhesion (so its deficiency prolongs the bleeding time) and it stabilises factor VIII (so its deficiency lowers factor VIII and impairs the intrinsic pathway, prolonging the clotting time and PTT).

    The platelet count in von Willebrand disease is normal, but platelet function is defective, because without vWF platelets cannot adhere normally to the exposed subendothelium
    The primary haemostatic plug forms slowly and the bleeding time is prolonged. The ristocetin cofactor activity is reduced. In the plasma, vWF binds factor VIII and protects it from degradation, so a deficiency of vWF decreases the stability of factor VIII, whose level falls (very markedly in type 3), which prolongs the PTT.

    The whole-blood clotting time, a crude test, is prolonged only when the factor VIII level is markedly reduced, as in severe type 3 disease. in most patients with mild type 1 disease it is normal, and the PTT may be only borderline. The PT is normal.

    A9

    What is haemophilia?

    A9Q25

    Haemophilia is a group of X-linked recessive inherited bleeding disorders caused by deficiency of coagulation factor VIII (haemophilia A) or factor IX (haemophilia B), characterised by haemarthroses and bleeding into soft tissues after minor trauma.

    Haemophilia A, the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding, results from mutations in the gene encoding factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the activation of factor X. It is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait and therefore affects males, and rarely females. Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) results from mutations of the gene encoding factor IX and is clinically indistinguishable.

    The severity correlates with the factor level: below 1% of normal is severe, 2% to 5% moderately severe and 6% to 50% mild. The clinical features are easy bruising, massive haemorrhage after trauma or surgery and "spontaneous" bleeds in joints (haemarthroses leading to disabling deformity) and muscles. Petechiae are absent. The PTT is prolonged and the PT is normal.

    A9

    Classify haemophilia.

    A9Q25

    Haemophilia is classified by the factor deficient into haemophilia A (factor VIII), haemophilia B (factor IX) and, less commonly, haemophilia C (factor XI), and by severity according to the residual factor activity.

    BasisClassification
    By the deficient factorHaemophilia A (classic): factor VIII deficiency, about 80% to 85% of cases, X-linked recessive. Haemophilia B (Christmas disease): factor IX deficiency, about 15%, X-linked recessive. Haemophilia C: factor XI deficiency, autosomal (recessive), mild, most frequent in Ashkenazi Jews
    By severity (factor activity)Severe: <1% of normal (spontaneous bleeding). Moderate: 1–5% (bleeding after minor trauma). Mild: 6–50% (bleeding after surgery or major trauma)
    By inheritanceX-linked recessive (A and B), autosomal (C)
    About 30% of patients with haemophilia A have no family history (new mutations)

    Von Willebrand disease, though it also lowers factor VIII, is classified separately.

    A9

    Give the laboratory diagnosis/findings of hemophilia.

    12A9Q2, Q25DU26MDU24MDU22MDU19NovDU17JaDU16JaDU14JaDU11JaDU09JaDU08Ja

    Also asked as: Laboratory diagnosis of haemophilia.

    The laboratory hallmark of haemophilia is a prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT) with a normal prothrombin time, platelet count and bleeding time, and the diagnosis is confirmed by a specific assay showing reduced factor VIII (haemophilia A) or factor IX (haemophilia B).

    1. Screening tests (haemostatic profile).
      • Platelet count: normal.
      • Bleeding time: normal (platelet function is intact).
      • Prothrombin time: normal (extrinsic pathway intact).
      • Partial thromboplastin time (aPTT): prolonged (the intrinsic pathway is defective)
        it corrects when the patient's plasma is mixed with normal plasma, excluding an inhibitor.
      • Whole-blood clotting time: prolonged in severe disease
        Thrombin time and fibrinogen normal.
    2. Specific assays. Factor VIII assay is reduced in haemophilia A (in severe disease below 1%), factor IX assay is reduced in haemophilia B
      The level determines the severity. Von Willebrand factor antigen and ristocetin cofactor are normal in haemophilia A, which distinguishes it from von Willebrand disease. In a minority of patients with haemophilia A the factor VIII protein is present by immunoassay but nonfunctional.
    3. Inhibitor screening. The Bethesda assay for antibodies to factor VIII (about 15% of patients with severe disease after treatment) or factor IX.
    4. Genetic studies. Detection of the factor VIII intron 22 inversion (the commonest cause of severe disease) or other mutations, carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling.
    5. Others. Blood count may show anaemia after bleeding
      Joints show haemarthrosis, with radiographic changes.
    A9

    What do you mean by DIC?

    A9Q3

    Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acute, subacute or chronic thrombohaemorrhagic disorder characterised by excessive activation of coagulation factors and the formation of thrombi in the microvasculature. Consumption of platelets and clotting factors and secondary fibrinolysis lead to both organ ischaemia and bleeding.

    DIC is not a primary disease but a secondary complication of a variety of disorders. It may be acute, subacute or chronic, and the coagulopathy is sometimes localised to a specific organ. Two major mechanisms trigger it: release of tissue factor or other procoagulants into the circulation, and widespread endothelial injury. The thrombotic diathesis consumes platelets, fibrin and coagulation factors and, secondarily, activates fibrinolysis.

    The commonest associations are obstetric complications, malignant neoplasms, sepsis and major trauma. The consequences are microvascular thrombosis with ischaemia and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, and a bleeding diathesis from the consumption of platelets and factors and the effects of fibrin degradation products.

    A9

    Give the laboratory diagnosis of DIC.

    A9Q3DU24N

    Also asked as: Laboratory diagnosis of DIC.

    The laboratory diagnosis of DIC rests on thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen and raised fibrin degradation products, particularly D-dimers, in a patient with a recognised predisposing condition.

    TestFinding in DICBasis
    Platelet countDecreased, and fallingConsumption in microthrombi
    Peripheral blood filmSchistocytes (fragmented red cells), helmet and triangular cells, burr cellsMicroangiopathic haemolytic anaemia
    Prothrombin timeProlongedConsumption of factors V, VII, X, II, fibrinogen
    Partial thromboplastin timeProlongedConsumption of factors V, VIII, IX, X, XI
    Thrombin timeProlongedHypofibrinogenaemia and FDPs
    FibrinogenDecreased (may be normal early, being an acute-phase reactant)Consumption
    Fibrin degradation products and D-dimerMarkedly increased (D-dimer particularly specific for plasmin-cleaved cross-linked fibrin)Fibrinolysis
    Factors V and VIIIReducedConsumption and plasmin digestion
    Antithrombin III, protein CReducedConsumption

    The diagnosis is based on clinical observation of the predisposing disorder together with these laboratory studies, including measurement of fibrinogen, platelets, PT and PTT, and fibrin degradation products, particularly D-dimers. Serial measurements are valuable, and scoring systems (ISTH DIC score) are used.

    A9

    Write a short note on ITP.

    4A9Q17DU13JaDU09JaDU08Ja

    Also asked as: What do you mean by ITP?

    Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is a bleeding disorder caused by autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets, in which the spleen is the major site of platelet removal, and which presents with isolated thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal PT and PTT.

    Types. Chronic ITP, mainly in adult women under 40 (female-to-male ratio 3:1), and acute ITP, mainly in children. It is primary (idiopathic) when no cause is found, or secondary to systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection, or B-cell neoplasms such as CLL. The diagnosis of primary ITP is made after secondary causes are excluded.

    Pathogenesis. IgG autoantibodies, most often directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX, coat the platelets, which are opsonised and removed by splenic macrophages through Fc receptors. Antibodies can also damage megakaryocytes, reducing platelet production.

    Clinical features. Insidious onset with petechiae (prominent in dependent areas), ecchymoses, easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, melaena or haematuria. Subarachnoid and intracerebral haemorrhage are rare but serious. Splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy are not features of primary disease.

    Laboratory findings. Low platelet count, normal PT and PTT, large platelets (megathrombocytes), and normal or increased megakaryocytes in the marrow. The spleen is of normal size. Tests for platelet autoantibodies are not clinically useful. Diagnosis is by exclusion.

    Treatment. Glucocorticoids (nearly all respond, but many relapse). Splenectomy for severe disease (normalises platelet count in about two-thirds). Intravenous immunoglobulin, rituximab and thrombopoietin-mimetics for refractory disease. Acute ITP follows a viral illness by 1 to 2 weeks, and is self-limited, resolving usually within 6 months.

    A9

    How are platelets destroyed in peripheral blood in ITP?

    A9Q16

    In ITP, IgG autoantibodies bind to platelet membrane glycoproteins and opsonise the platelets, which are then recognised through Fc receptors and phagocytosed by macrophages of the spleen, so that the platelet life span is shortened from 7 to 10 days to a few hours.

    Autoantibodies against platelet glycoproteins IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX can be demonstrated in the plasma and bound to the platelet surface in about 80% of patients. As in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, the antiplatelet antibodies, mostly IgG, act as opsonins recognised by IgG Fc receptors on phagocytes, leading to increased platelet destruction. The thrombocytopenia is usually markedly improved by splenectomy, which shows that the spleen is the principal site of removal of opsonised platelets, and may also remove a source of autoantibody (the splenic red pulp is rich in plasma cells).

    The antibodies may also bind and damage megakaryocytes, so that platelet production falls and exacerbates the thrombocytopenia. The marrow compensates with an increase in megakaryocytes, many of which are immature, and by releasing large platelets.

    A9

    How is ITP diagnosed in the laboratory?

    14A9Q17DU24MDU22MDU20NDU20JuDU18MDU17NovDU16JuDU15JaDU14JaDU12JaDU11JaDU09JuDU07Ju

    Also asked as: How will you diagnose a case of ITP in the laboratory?

    ITP is diagnosed in the laboratory by the finding of isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets on the blood film, normal PT and PTT, and a bone marrow with normal or increased megakaryocytes, after the exclusion of other causes of thrombocytopenia.

    1. Blood count and film. A low platelet count (below 150,000/µL; spontaneous bleeding when below 20,000/µL), with normal haemoglobin and white cell count (unless there has been blood loss), unless there is associated autoimmune haemolysis (Evans syndrome). The film shows reduced platelets with large platelets (megathrombocytes), which are a sign of accelerated thrombopoiesis. Platelet clumping and spurious thrombocytopenia must be excluded.
    2. Coagulation screening. Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are normal (as is the thrombin time and fibrinogen). The bleeding time is prolonged.
    3. Bone marrow examination. Normal or increased megakaryocytes, some of them immature, with large, nonlobulated single nuclei. This reflects accelerated thrombopoiesis and is found in most thrombocytopenias from increased destruction. Marrow examination is important to exclude marrow failure or other primary marrow disorders (leukaemia, aplastic anaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasm), especially in older adults.
    4. Platelet autoantibody tests. Antiplatelet antibodies (against GpIIb/IIIa or Ib/IX) can be detected, but the tests have low sensitivity and specificity and are not clinically useful.
    5. Exclusion of secondary causes. Antinuclear antibodies for SLE
      HIV, hepatitis C and H. pylori testing
      and drug history (heparin, quinine)
      The diagnosis is one of exclusion and can be made only after other causes (as in the list of causes of thrombocytopenia) have been ruled out. The spleen is of normal size on examination or ultrasound.
    A9

    What are the causes of thrombocytopenia?

    5A9Q19, Q20DU26MDU25MDU11Ja

    Also asked as: Causes of thrombocytopenia (incl. 3 important causes).

    The causes of thrombocytopenia fall into four categories: decreased platelet production, decreased platelet survival, sequestration, and dilution.

    1. Decreased production
      • Generalised marrow failure: aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, marrow replacement by metastatic cancer, granulomas or myelofibrosis, myelodysplastic neoplasm (which occasionally presents with isolated thrombocytopenia).
      • Selective megakaryocyte suppression: drugs (thiazides, cytotoxic drugs), alcohol, and infections such as measles and HIV (which can infect megakaryocytes), dengue.
      • Nutritional deficiency of B₁₂ and folate (megaloblastic anaemia).
    2. Decreased survival
      • Immunologic: autoimmune (chronic and acute ITP, systemic lupus erythematosus, B-cell neoplasms), alloimmune (post-transfusion and neonatal), drug-associated (quinine, quinidine, vancomycin, sulpha compounds, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia), and infections (HIV, infectious mononucleosis, dengue fever).
      • Nonimmunologic: disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP and HUS), giant haemangioma, and mechanical injury (prosthetic heart valves).
    3. Sequestration: hypersplenism
      The spleen normally sequesters 30% to 35% of platelets, rising to 80% to 90% in an enlarged spleen.
    4. Dilution: massive transfusion of stored blood and plasma replacement.

    A platelet count below 150,000 per µL is thrombocytopenia. Counts of 20,000 to 50,000 per µL aggravate post-traumatic bleeding, and counts below 20,000 per µL may produce spontaneous bleeding.

    Classify bleeding (haemorrhagic) disorders.

    6DU26MDU25NDU22MDU17NovDU16JaDU14Ja

    Excessive bleeding can result from increased fragility of vessels, platelet deficiency or dysfunction, and derangement of coagulation, alone or in combination. The bleeding disorders are therefore classified as follows.

    I. Disorders of the blood vessel wall (vascular purpura)

    • Hereditary: hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Rendu-Osler-Weber syndrome), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome.
    • Acquired: infections (meningococcaemia, septicaemia, infective endocarditis, rickettsioses), drug reactions (hypersensitivity vasculitis), scurvy, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, senile purpura, Cushing syndrome, perivascular amyloidosis.

    II. Platelet disorders

    • Thrombocytopenia: decreased production (aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, drugs, alcohol, HIV), decreased survival (immune: ITP, drug-induced, alloimmune
      Nonimmune: DIC, TTP, HUS), sequestration (hypersplenism), and dilution.
    • Qualitative defects of platelet function: inherited (Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann thrombasthenia, storage pool disorders) and acquired (aspirin and NSAIDs, uraemia, myeloproliferative neoplasms).

    III. Coagulation disorders

    • Inherited: haemophilia A, haemophilia B, von Willebrand disease, other single factor deficiencies.
    • Acquired: vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC, anticoagulant drugs, and inhibitors.

    IV. Combined and fibrinolytic disorders: von Willebrand disease, DIC, and hyperfibrinolysis.

    What screening tests are done for bleeding disorders (with interpretation)?

    10DU26MDU23NDU22NDU21MDU19NovDU18NovDU17MDU16JuDU13JuDU12Ja

    The normal haemostatic response involves the blood vessel wall, the platelets and the clotting cascade, and the following tests evaluate different aspects of haemostasis.

    1. Platelet count (reference 150 to 350 × 10³/µL): determined on anticoagulated blood with an electronic counter, and confirmed with a blood film because clumping can cause spurious thrombocytopenia. Counts of 20,000 to 50,000 per µL aggravate post-traumatic bleeding, and below 20,000 per µL may cause spontaneous bleeding. A high count may reflect a myeloproliferative neoplasm but more often reactive thrombocytosis.
    2. Prothrombin time (PT): the clotting of plasma after addition of tissue thromboplastin and calcium, measured in seconds (normal 11 to 15 seconds). It assesses the extrinsic and common pathways, and is prolonged by deficiency or dysfunction of factor V, VII, X, prothrombin or fibrinogen (vitamin K deficiency, warfarin, liver disease).
    3. Partial thromboplastin time (PTT, aPTT): the clotting of plasma after addition of kaolin, cephalin and calcium (normal 25 to 40 seconds). It assesses the intrinsic and common pathways, and is prolonged by deficiency or dysfunction of factors V, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, prothrombin or fibrinogen, by heparin, or by interfering antiphospholipid antibodies.
    4. Tests of platelet function: platelet aggregation studies with agonists, and quantitative and qualitative von Willebrand factor tests (including the ristocetin cofactor assay). The older bleeding time is time-consuming and difficult to standardise and has been discarded in many centres. it is prolonged in thrombocytopenia, platelet function defects and von Willebrand disease.
    5. Additional tests: thrombin time, fibrinogen, fibrin degradation products and D-dimers, factor assays and mixing studies.

    Interpretation

    LowNormalNormalThrombocytopenia (ITP, marrow failure)
    NormalNormalNormalVascular disorder or platelet function defect (check vWF, aggregation)
    NormalNormalProlongedHaemophilia A or B, factor XI deficiency, von Willebrand disease, heparin
    NormalProlongedNormalFactor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency
    NormalProlongedProlongedCommon pathway deficiency, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulants
    LowProlongedProlongedDIC (with low fibrinogen and raised D-dimer), severe liver disease

    DU18NovDU17M

    The screening tests used to distinguish these three disorders have the following normal values: platelet count 150 to 350 × 10³/µL, bleeding time 2 to 7 minutes, prothrombin time 11 to 15 seconds, partial thromboplastin time 25 to 40 seconds, thrombin time 15 to 20 seconds, fibrinogen 200 to 400 mg/dL, and D-dimer negative or below 0.5 µg/mL.

    What are the causes of gum bleeding?

    DU23N

    Gum (gingival) bleeding may be due to local oral disease or to a systemic bleeding disorder.

    Local causes: poor oral hygiene with gingivitis and periodontitis (the commonest), dental plaque and calculus, trauma from vigorous brushing or ill-fitting dentures, dental extraction, pregnancy gingivitis, and gingival tumours or epulis.

    Systemic causes

    1. Platelet disorders: thrombocytopenia (ITP, aplastic anaemia, acute leukaemia, drug-induced), and functional platelet defects (aspirin, NSAIDs, uraemia, Glanzmann thrombasthenia).
    2. Coagulation disorders: von Willebrand disease, haemophilia A and B, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC, anticoagulant therapy (warfarin, heparin).
    3. Vascular disorders: scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), with swollen spongy gums, and hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
    4. Leukaemia: gum hypertrophy and infiltration with bleeding, particularly in acute monocytic leukaemia.
    5. Drugs: phenytoin, nifedipine and cyclosporine cause gingival hyperplasia.

    In a child, gum bleeding should prompt consideration of ITP, acute leukaemia, scurvy and haemophilia.

    Platelet disorders and ITP

    Define thrombocytopenia.

    DU26MDU25M

    Thrombocytopenia is a reduction in the number of circulating platelets below the lower limit of the reference range, that is, a platelet count of less than 150,000 per µL (150 × 10⁹/L). It constitutes an important cause of generalised bleeding. Counts of 20,000 to 50,000 per µL can aggravate posttraumatic bleeding, and counts below 20,000 per µL may be associated with spontaneous (nontraumatic) bleeding, most often involving small vessels in the skin and the mucous membranes of the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts. The most feared complication is intracranial haemorrhage. When thrombocytopenia is isolated, the PT and PTT are normal. The causes fall into four categories: decreased production, decreased survival, sequestration (hypersplenism) and dilution.

    Discuss in short the pathogenesis of ITP.

    DU24M

    Chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets. It can occur in the setting of predisposing conditions (secondary, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection and B-cell neoplasms like chronic lymphocytic leukaemia) or without any known risk factors (primary, idiopathic).

    Autoantibodies, most often directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX, can be demonstrated in the plasma and bound to the platelet surface in about 80% of patients, and in most cases they are of the IgG class. As in autoimmune haemolytic anaemias, the antiplatelet antibodies act as opsonins that are recognised by IgG Fc receptors on phagocytes, leading to increased platelet destruction.

    The thrombocytopenia is usually markedly improved by splenectomy, indicating that the spleen is the major site of removal of opsonised platelets. The splenic red pulp is also rich in plasma cells, so part of the benefit of splenectomy may stem from the removal of a source of autoantibodies. In some instances, the autoantibodies also bind to and damage megakaryocytes, decreasing platelet production and further exacerbating the thrombocytopenia. The marrow responds with increased numbers of megakaryocytes and release of large platelets.

    In acute ITP, a self-limited viral illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier appears to trigger the development of autoantibodies through uncertain mechanisms.

    Give the blood and bone marrow picture of ITP.

    DU25MDU19MDU18Nov

    Blood

    • The platelet count is low (often below 30,000 per µL, and may be below 10,000), reflecting isolated thrombocytopenia.
    • The film shows reduced platelets, many of which are unusually large (megathrombocytes), a sign of accelerated thrombopoiesis. Red cell and white cell counts and morphology are normal unless there has been significant bleeding (in which case there may be a normocytic or iron deficiency anaemia).
    • The prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are normal. Bleeding time is prolonged.

    Bone marrow

    • The marrow shows a modestly increased number of megakaryocytes (normal or increased), with many apparently immature, with large, non-lobulated single nuclei and little granular cytoplasm. Platelet budding may be reduced.
    • Erythroid and granulocytic series are normal.
    • These findings are not specific, but merely reflect accelerated thrombopoiesis found in most forms of thrombocytopenia resulting from increased platelet destruction. The importance of bone marrow examination is to rule out thrombocytopenia due to marrow failure or other primary marrow disorders.

    Spleen. Normal in size, with congestion of sinusoids and enlarged follicles with reactive germinal centres, and scattered megakaryocytes in the sinuses.

    A child has purpuric rash/gum bleeding, thrombocytopenia, normocellular marrow with active megakaryopoiesis. What is the likely diagnosis?

    4DU20NDU20JuDU18MDU09Ju

    The likely diagnosis is acute immune thrombocytopenic purpura (acute ITP). It is mainly a disease of childhood, with equal frequency in both sexes, with abrupt onset of petechiae, purpuric rash and mucosal bleeding such as gum bleeding and epistaxis, often 1 to 2 weeks after a self-limited viral illness, which appears to trigger the development of autoantibodies. The isolated thrombocytopenia, with a marrow that is normocellular with active (normal or increased) megakaryopoiesis, shows that platelets are being destroyed peripherally by antibody-mediated opsonisation rather than being underproduced. The PT and PTT are normal.

    The condition is self-limited, usually resolving spontaneously within 6 months
    Glucocorticoids or intravenous immunoglobulin are given only if the thrombocytopenia is severe or there is significant bleeding. In about 20% of children, usually those without a viral prodrome, thrombocytopenia persists, and they follow the course of chronic ITP. Acute leukaemia and aplastic anaemia, which present with similar bleeding, are excluded by the normal blood count in the other cell lines and the marrow findings.

    Coagulation disorders and haemophilia

    Why is APTT prolonged in hemophilia?

    DU23N

    The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) assesses the intrinsic and common pathways of coagulation, in which the plasma is activated by kaolin (which activates the contact factor XII), with cephalin supplying platelet phospholipid, and calcium is added. In the intrinsic pathway, activated factor IX (IXa) with its cofactor VIIIa forms the tenase complex, which activates factor X on the phospholipid surface. This is the pivotal step in the generation of thrombin through the intrinsic route, reflecting the preeminent role of the factor VIIIa/IXa complex in the activation of factor X in vivo.

    In haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency), the tenase complex cannot form efficiently, so that the conversion of factor X is delayed, thrombin generation is slow, and the plasma takes longer to clot in the in vitro test. The prothrombin time, which relies on tissue factor and factor VII to activate factor X directly (the extrinsic pathway), is normal, and the platelet count and bleeding time are normal.

    A prolonged PTT with a normal PT in a bleeding patient thus points to an abnormality of the intrinsic pathway, and factor VIII–specific or factor IX assays are required for diagnosis.

    Write a short note on von Willebrand disease.

    DU10Ju

    Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder of humans, affecting about 1% of adults in the United States. It is caused by qualitative or quantitative defects of von Willebrand factor (vWF), a large multimeric glycoprotein made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes that promotes the adhesion of platelets to the subendothelial matrix (through glycoprotein Ib/IX and collagen), promotes aggregation under high shear stress, and binds and stabilises factor VIII (extending its half-life from about 2.4 to 12 hours).

    Inheritance and types. It is usually autosomal dominant, with rare recessive variants, and is clinically and molecularly heterogeneous.

    • Type 1 (about 70% of cases): autosomal dominant, with mild to moderate quantitative deficiency of vWF. Incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity
      Generally mild disease.
    • Type 2 (about 25%): qualitative defects, with normal amounts of vWF but missense mutations causing defective multimer assembly (type 2A, the most common subtype), so that large and intermediate multimers are missing. Mild to moderate bleeding.
    • Type 3: autosomal recessive, with deletions or frameshift mutations of both alleles, with almost no vWF and consequently very low factor VIII. Severe, haemophilia-like bleeding.

    Clinical features. The bleeding is usually mild, often unnoticed until surgery or a dental procedure reveals it, and resembles that of a platelet disorder: spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes (epistaxis), excessive bleeding from wounds and menorrhagia.

    Laboratory findings. Normal platelet count, defective platelet function with prolonged bleeding time, reduced ristocetin cofactor activity, reduced vWF antigen, and (because vWF stabilises factor VIII) prolonged PTT in types 1 and 3 with a normal PT.

    Treatment. Desmopressin (stimulates vWF release) or infusions of plasma concentrates containing factor VIII and vWF, or recombinant vWF for types 1 and 2. Type 3 requires prophylactic plasma concentrates and factor VIII.

    Write a short note on hemophilia (A) / its characteristic features.

    5DU24NDU22NDU12JuDU10JaDU07Ja

    Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency, classic haemophilia) is the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding. It is caused by mutations in the gene encoding factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the activation of factor X, and is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait, so that it affects mainly males and homozygous females. Rarely, heterozygous females bleed excessively because of unfavourable lyonisation. About 30% of patients have no family history, because the disease is caused by new mutations.

    Severity. The clinical severity correlates well with the level of factor VIII activity: below 1% of normal is severe, 2% to 5% moderately severe, and 6% to 50% mild. The most severe deficiencies are caused by an inversion involving the X chromosome that abolishes the synthesis of factor VIII. Point mutations impairing the function of the protein may give normal protein levels by immunoassay.

    Clinical features. A tendency toward easy bruising and massive haemorrhage after trauma or surgery, together with "spontaneous" haemorrhages in regions of the body susceptible to trauma, particularly the joints (haemarthroses, usually knees, elbows and ankles), muscles (haematomas) and central nervous system. Recurrent bleeding into the joints leads to progressive, disabling deformity. Bleeding after dental extraction, haematuria and gastrointestinal bleeding occur. Petechiae are characteristically absent.

    Laboratory findings. Prolonged PTT with a normal PT, normal platelet count and bleeding time
    Reduced factor VIII by specific assay, with normal vWF.

    Treatment. Infusions of recombinant factor VIII, or a bispecific antibody linking factor IXa and factor X (which bypasses the need for factor VIII and remains active in patients who develop inhibitors, which occur in about 15% of those with severe disease treated with recombinant factor VIII). The very high cost limits treatment in low-resource countries. Gene therapy is available for haemophilia B and being developed for A.

    Why is hemophilia called an X-linked recessive disorder?

    DU19Nov

    Haemophilia is called an X-linked recessive disorder because the genes encoding factor VIII (haemophilia A) and factor IX (haemophilia B) are located on the long arm of the X chromosome, and the disease is expressed fully only when there is no normal allele to compensate.

    A male has only one X chromosome (hemizygous), so a single mutant allele, inherited from his mother, is sufficient to produce the disease. There is no second X chromosome carrying a normal allele. A heterozygous female carrier has one normal and one mutant allele, and her normal factor VIII, produced from the normal X chromosome, is usually enough for haemostasis, so she is clinically normal (the trait is recessive).

    Hence the disease affects mainly males and is transmitted through carrier females. A carrier mother has a 50% chance of transmitting the gene to each child, so that half her sons are affected and half her daughters are carriers. an affected father transmits the gene to all his daughters (obligate carriers) and to none of his sons (no male-to-male transmission). A female is affected only when homozygous (affected father and carrier mother) or, rarely, in a heterozygote when most cells by chance inactivate the X chromosome carrying the normal allele (unfavourable lyonisation). About 30% of cases arise from new mutations with no family history.

    A boy has hemarthrosis after a small fall
    Maternal uncle bled after tooth extraction. What is your provisional diagnosis?

    5DU26MDU24MDU22MDU17JaDU14Ja

    The provisional diagnosis is haemophilia A (classic haemophilia, factor VIII deficiency)
    Haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is clinically indistinguishable and is the alternative. The occurrence of haemarthrosis after minor trauma in a boy is characteristic of a coagulation factor deficiency, in which bleeding is deep, into joints and muscles, rather than mucocutaneous. The history of excessive bleeding after tooth extraction in the maternal uncle indicates transmission through the mother's side of the family, as in X-linked recessive inheritance (the mother being an obligate carrier).

    The diagnosis is confirmed by a prolonged PTT with a normal PT, platelet count and bleeding time, followed by specific factor VIII and factor IX assays, with the normal von Willebrand factor level excluding von Willebrand disease.

    Same: what type of disease is it?

    DU26M

    It is an inherited (hereditary) coagulation factor deficiency disorder, transmitted as an X-linked recessive trait. Haemophilia A is a genetic bleeding disorder (haemorrhagic diathesis) caused by mutation of the factor VIII gene on the X chromosome, which leads to reduced or nonfunctional factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the activation of factor X. It principally affects males, with carrier females who are generally asymptomatic, and shows a wide range of clinical severity that correlates with the residual factor VIII level (severe disease with less than 1% activity).

    Disseminated intravascular coagulation

    Describe the pathogenesis of DIC.

    DU25NDU18MDU09Ju

    DIC is not a primary disease but an acquired coagulopathy that occurs in the course of a variety of clinical conditions. Normally, clotting is initiated by exposure of tissue factor, which activates factor VII. The tissue factor–factor VIIa complex activates factor IX and factor X, leading to the generation of thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin, activates factors V, VIII and IX, stimulates fibrin cross-linking, inhibits fibrinolysis and activates platelets. This process is sharply limited to the site of injury: thrombin swept into the circulation binds to thrombomodulin on uninjured endothelium and activates protein C, an inhibitor of factors V and VIII. Other activated factors are cleared by the liver, and plasmin removes the clot. DIC can result from pathological activation of coagulation or from impairment of the inhibitory mechanisms, the former being the usual cause. Two major mechanisms trigger it.

    1. Release of tissue factor or other procoagulants into the circulation. Sources include the placenta in obstetric complications (abruptio placentae, retained dead foetus, amniotic fluid embolism), tissues injured by trauma, burns or extensive surgery, mucin from certain adenocarcinomas (which directly activates factor X), and the granules of acute promyelocytic leukaemia cells.

    2. Widespread endothelial injury. Endothelial necrosis exposes the subendothelial matrix, activating platelets and the coagulation pathway. Even subtle injury can unleash procoagulant activity. TNF, implicated in sepsis-associated DIC, induces endothelial expression of tissue factor and decreases thrombomodulin expression, and increases adhesion molecule expression so that leukocytes adhere and damage endothelial cells by reactive oxygen species and proteases.

    Endotoxin of Gram-negative bacteria acts similarly (and activates factor XII). antigen-antibody complexes (SLE, infections) activate complement and platelets. Heat stroke, burns, hypoxia, acidosis, shock, and microorganisms (meningococci, rickettsiae) also damage endothelium.

    Consequences. Widespread deposition of fibrin in the microcirculation causes ischaemia of vulnerable organs and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. and consumption of platelets and clotting factors, together with activation of plasminogen to plasmin (which digests fibrin and factors V and VIII, and generates fibrin degradation products that inhibit platelet aggregation, fibrin polymerisation and thrombin), produces a haemorrhagic diathesis.

    Explain why bleeding occurs in DIC.

    DU09Ja

    Bleeding in DIC is a consequence of widespread intravascular coagulation, which causes both depletion of the elements required for haemostasis and the generation of anticoagulant substances, so that the patient bleeds even though the primary process is clotting (a "consumptive coagulopathy").

    1. Consumption of platelets and clotting factors: the thrombi forming throughout the microcirculation use up platelets, fibrinogen, prothrombin and factors V, VIII and X faster than they can be synthesised, so there are too few of them left to form haemostatic plugs and clots at sites of real injury or at venepuncture sites.
    2. Activation of the fibrinolytic system: deposition of fibrin activates plasminogen to plasmin. Plasmin dissolves fibrin clots, including haemostatic plugs, and also digests fibrinogen and factors V and VIII, reducing their concentration still further.
    3. Fibrin degradation products (FDPs and D-dimers): these inhibit platelet aggregation, interfere with fibrin polymerisation and inhibit thrombin, thereby acting as anticoagulants.
    4. Thrombocytopenia and acquired platelet dysfunction, and in some settings, vitamin K deficiency or liver disease, aggravate the defect.

    The result is spontaneous bleeding from multiple sites (skin petechiae and ecchymoses, mucosal and wound oozing, gastrointestinal, urinary, intracranial bleeding). In acute DIC with obstetric complications or major trauma the bleeding diathesis dominates, whereas chronic DIC such as occurs in cancer patients tends to present with thrombotic complications.

    Blood Groups, Transfusion and Anticoagulants

    A9

    Classify blood groups.

    A9Q4

    Blood groups are classified according to the antigenic systems on the red cell surface, of which the ABO and Rh systems are by far the most important in transfusion practice, and many minor systems also exist.

    A blood group system is a set of red cell membrane antigens controlled by alleles at a single genetic locus (or by closely linked loci). Over 30 systems are recognised.

    1. ABO system (Landsteiner, 1901): groups A, B, AB and O, defined by the presence of A and B antigens on red cells and the reciprocal naturally occurring antibodies (anti-A, anti-B) in the plasma. Antigens A and B are carbohydrates built on the H substance. Group O cells have only H.
    2. Rh system: defined by the D antigen (Rh-positive if D is present, Rh-negative if absent), with the associated C, c, E and e antigens. Anti-D is not naturally present and appears only after sensitisation.
    3. Other clinically important systems: Kell, Duffy (Fy), Kidd (Jk), MNSs, Lewis, P, Lutheran and Diego. Antibodies to Rh, Kell and Kidd antigens may cause severe delayed haemolytic transfusion reactions and haemolytic disease of the newborn.
    4. Rare phenotypes: for example the Bombay (hh) phenotype, lacking H substance, which makes red cells appear as group O but is incompatible with normal group O blood.
    A9

    Name the ABO and Rh blood groups with their agglutinins.

    A9Q4

    The ABO groups are A, B, AB and O
    Each person has the agglutinin (antibody) against the ABO antigen that he lacks, so group A has anti-B, group B has anti-A, group AB has neither and group O has both
    The Rh groups are Rh-positive and Rh-negative, and anti-D appears only after sensitisation.

    Blood groupAntigen on red cellsNaturally occurring agglutinins (antibodies) in plasma
    AAAnti-B
    BBAnti-A
    ABA and BNone (universal recipient for red cells)
    ONone (H only)Anti-A and anti-B (universal donor for red cells)
    Rh-positiveD (± C, E)No anti-D

    The natural anti-A and anti-B antibodies are chiefly IgM, preformed (probably induced by environmental polysaccharide antigens), able to fix complement and cause rapid intravascular haemolysis when ABO-incompatible blood is transfused. Anti-D is IgG, crosses the placenta, and causes Rh haemolytic disease of the newborn.

    A9

    What do you mean by cross matching?

    A9Q5

    Cross-matching is the laboratory test, performed before transfusion, in which the recipient's serum is mixed with the donor's red cells (and the reverse) to confirm that the donor blood is compatible with the recipient and will not be destroyed by the recipient's antibodies.

    It is the final safeguard in the compatibility testing, after the ABO and Rh grouping of donor and recipient and the screening of the recipient's serum for unexpected (irregular) antibodies. In the major cross-match, the recipient's serum is mixed with the donor's red cells. Agglutination or haemolysis indicates that the recipient has antibodies against the donor cells and the unit is incompatible. In the minor cross-match, the donor's plasma is mixed with the recipient's red cells (largely replaced by antibody screening of donors). A compatible cross-match shows no agglutination or haemolysis in any phase.

    A9

    How is cross matching performed?

    A9Q5

    Cross-matching is performed by mixing recipient serum with a suspension of donor red cells and testing for agglutination or haemolysis in successive phases, namely saline at room temperature, incubation at 37°C in albumin or low-ionic-strength solution, and finally the antiglobulin (Coombs) phase.

    1. Preliminary steps: ABO and Rh grouping of the recipient (forward grouping with anti-A and anti-B sera, and reverse grouping with known A and B cells) and of the donor unit. The recipient's serum is screened for irregular antibodies.
    2. Preparation: the recipient's serum is separated from a freshly drawn clotted sample. a 2% to 5% suspension of donor red cells in saline is made from a segment of the donor bag.
    3. Major cross-match: two drops of recipient serum and one drop of donor red cell suspension are mixed in a tube.
    4. Phases:
      • Immediate spin (saline phase, room temperature): centrifuge and examine for haemolysis or agglutination (detects ABO incompatibility and IgM antibodies).
      • Incubation phase at 37°C (with albumin or LISS to enhance antibody uptake) for 15 to 30 minutes, examined for agglutination or haemolysis (detects IgG antibodies such as Rh).
      • Antiglobulin (indirect Coombs) phase: the cells are washed, antihuman globulin is added, and the tube is spun and examined for agglutination (detects incomplete IgG antibodies such as Kell, Duffy and Kidd).
    5. Interpretation: no haemolysis or agglutination in any phase means compatible, and the unit may be issued. An electronic or computer cross-match may be used when the antibody screen is negative and two ABO determinations are on record.
    A9

    Why is cross matching essential for blood transfusion?

    A9Q7DU08Ja

    Cross-matching is essential to prevent a haemolytic transfusion reaction, because it detects incompatibility, including that caused by unexpected antibodies and clerical or labelling errors, which grouping alone may miss.

    ABO grouping and Rh typing of donor and recipient do not exclude all incompatibilities. The recipient may carry irregular alloantibodies, formed after previous transfusions or pregnancy, against minor red cell antigens (Kell, Duffy, Kidd, Rh variants), and such antibodies, usually IgG, can cause delayed or even severe haemolysis. Cross-matching also provides a final check against errors of patient identification or sample labelling, the commonest cause of ABO-incompatible transfusion.

    Acute haemolytic reactions occur when preformed, high-affinity "natural" IgM antibodies against A or B antigens bind to donor red cells and fix complement, producing complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis and haemoglobinuria, with fever, shaking chills and flank pain. in severe cases there is DIC, shock, acute renal failure and occasionally death. Cross-matching thus protects the patient from these life-threatening complications, and avoids wasting scarce blood by transfusing cells that will be rapidly destroyed.

    A9

    Mention 4 important hematological changes of stored blood.

    A9Q6DU08Ja

    Also asked as: Important haematological changes of stored blood.

    The important changes in stored blood, collectively called the storage lesion, are a fall in pH, a rise in plasma potassium, depletion of 2,3-DPG and ATP in the red cells, and loss of the viability of platelets, white cells and labile coagulation factors.

    1. Fall in pH (acidosis): continued glycolysis produces lactic and pyruvic acids, and the pH of stored blood falls from about 7.1 to 6.5 over 3 weeks.
    2. Rise in plasma potassium: potassium leaks from red cells because the Na⁺/K⁺ pump fails in the cold, causing high plasma potassium (up to 20 to 30 mmol/L at 3 weeks), which may be hazardous in massive transfusion, neonates or renal failure.
    3. Fall in 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) and ATP: the red cells have increased oxygen affinity (a left shift of the oxygen dissociation curve) and reduced ability to release oxygen to the tissues for the first 24 hours after transfusion
      Reduced ATP reduces red cell deformability and survival.
    4. Loss of viability of other cells and factors: platelets lose function within 24 to 48 hours in blood stored at 4°C, granulocytes are nonfunctional within 24 hours, and factors V and VIII are labile (reduced to about 50% or less by 1 to 2 weeks).
    5. Other changes: increased plasma haemoglobin from haemolysis, increased ammonia, falling glucose and rising lactate, microaggregates of platelets and leukocytes, and a reduction in the proportion of viable red cells (about 70% of cells survive 24 hours after 35 days of storage).
    A9

    What are the indications of blood transfusion?

    5A9Q7DU17JaDU15JaDU13JuDU08Ju

    Also asked as: Indications of blood transfusion.

    Blood transfusion is indicated to restore oxygen-carrying capacity or blood volume in acute haemorrhage and severe symptomatic anaemia, and to replace platelets or coagulation factors when these are deficient and bleeding is present or likely.

    Red cells (whole blood or packed red cells)

    • Acute blood loss with haemorrhagic shock (trauma, obstetric haemorrhage, gastrointestinal bleeding, surgery) when loss exceeds about 30% of the blood volume.
    • Symptomatic severe anaemia not correctable by haematinics (for example, haemoglobin below 7 g/dL, or higher in cardiovascular disease): chronic anaemias such as β-thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease (including exchange transfusion for stroke, acute chest syndrome and sequestration crisis), aplastic anaemia, myelodysplasia and marrow failure after chemotherapy.
    • Preoperative correction of severe anaemia, and in haemolytic anaemias with aplastic crisis.
    • Exchange transfusion in haemolytic disease of the newborn.

    Platelet concentrates

    • Thrombocytopenia with bleeding, or prophylactically when the platelet count is below 10,000 to 20,000 per µL, or before invasive procedures. Qualitative platelet dysfunction.

    Fresh frozen plasma

    • Multiple coagulation factor deficiencies: DIC, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency or warfarin reversal, massive transfusion, TTP (plasma exchange).

    Cryoprecipitate

    • Hypofibrinogenaemia, DIC, von Willebrand disease and haemophilia A (when factor concentrates are unavailable).

    Transfusion is not indicated for anaemia that can be corrected with haematinics (iron, B₁₂, folate) unless the patient is in cardiac failure or in imminent danger.

    A9

    Blood components used in transfusion.

    A9Q8

    Whole blood is separated into components so that each patient receives only what is needed: red cell concentrates, platelet concentrates, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate and others.

    ComponentContents and use
    Whole bloodRed cells with plasma
    Massive haemorrhage
    Packed red cells (red cell concentrate)Chronic anaemia and haemorrhage
    with additive solution (SAGM), shelf life 35 to 42 days at 2–6°C
